### BUGS — Fix These First

- 🟠 S — **get_financial_entity_naics reads from_id but every NAICS-bearing contract is agency->entity — the NAICS pass has written zero rows since inception** — **Filed, not fixed** — found while verifying [[FIX-910]], out of scope for the [[FIX-916]] curation PR because repointing it WRITES thousands of new industry tags on prod, which is a data change needing its own before/after. `get_financial_entity_naics()` (supabase/migrations/20260530020000_financial_size_tags_serverside_443.sql) aggregates `fr.from_id AS entity_id ... WHERE fr.from_type = 'financial_entity' AND fr.relationship_type IN ('contract','grant') AND fr.metadata->>'naics_code' IS NOT NULL`. But USASpending writes contracts in the **agency to recipient** direction: measured on prod 2026-07-28, `financial_relationships` holds 3,240,205 `agency -> financial_entity` contract rows of which **3,238,246 carry a `naics_code`**, plus 582,485 `agency -> financial_entity` grant rows with none, plus exactly 54 `financial_entity -> financial_entity` grant rows — also with none. So the contractor whose NAICS code we want is `to_id`, and the function's `from_type='financial_entity'` filter matches only those 54 naics-less grant rows. **`get_financial_entity_naics()` returns `[]` on BOTH envs**, and `SELECT count(*) FROM entity_tags WHERE entity_type='financial_entity' AND tag_category='industry' AND metadata ? 'naics_code'` is **0 on prod**. The entire NAICS half of `tagFinancialEntities()` is dead code that has never emitted a tag. Consequences: (1) the ~78 contractor rows the [[FIX-909]] NAICS2_INDUSTRY sector corrections were written to protect do not exist — those corrections are still right, they are just currently unreachable; (2) the function scans the contract/grant slice of a 3.8M-row table every nightly to produce an empty array; (3) US contractors get no industry label from their own federal contract industry code, only from name-keyword guessing. Fix is to aggregate `fr.to_id` where `to_type='financial_entity'` (keep the `from_id` arm too if the 54-row financial_entity-sourced grant path is ever populated). **Size the blast radius first** — count distinct `to_id` with a naics_code and diff the resulting tag set against today's keyword tags before shipping, because these rows land at confidence 0.85/primary and will collide with keyword tags on the `(entity_type, entity_id, tag, tag_category)` unique constraint. Cross-ref [[FIX-910]] [[FIX-909]] [[FIX-443]] [[FIX-916]]. <!--id:FIX-919-->

- 🟡 S — **TIGER district upsert never writes centroid — a refresh leaves every district's centroid at its old position** — upsert_district_jurisdiction() (supabase/migrations/20260428061525_district_boundaries.sql) sets boundary_geometry on both its INSERT and UPDATE paths and NEVER touches centroid. The 7211 district rows all have a centroid today only because the one-shot backfill migration 20260528180100 filled them WHERE centroid IS NULL, and pipelines/districts-tiger has not run since. Two consequences the next annual TIGER refresh delivers together: (1) any NEWLY published district inserts with centroid NULL, and the backfill that would have fixed it is a migration that has already run; (2) worse and quieter, every EXISTING district keeps the centroid computed from its OLD polygon while its boundary_geometry is rewritten, so map labels drift off their shapes wherever a boundary moved. Verified on prod 2026-09-10: 7211 tiger district rows, 0 null centroids, so nothing is broken yet — this is a loaded gun, not a wound. Fix is one line in each branch of the RPC, using the project convention ST_PointOnSurface(v_geom)::geometry(Point,4326) (see 20260528170000 and 20260528180100 — NOT ST_Centroid, which can land outside an irregular or multipart polygon). Surfaced by [[FIX-914]], whose derive_nh_floterials() does refresh centroid on its DO UPDATE — so after a tiger_year bump the 39 derived NH floterials would carry correct centroids while the 164 base districts they are unions of carried stale ones. Cross-ref [[FIX-914]].  APPEND 2026-09-19 (cc-135, CLOSED, prod): both paths now write ST_PointOnSurface(v_geom)::geometry(Point,4326) -- migration 20260919011000, pushed to Pro 01:39 UTC. The bullet's premise held exactly: prod read before the change was 7,250 district rows / 7,250 centroids / 0 NULL (7,211 tiger + the 39 FIX-914 derived), so nothing was wrong yet and nothing was re-run to fix it. districts-tiger is NOT fired here -- the next annual TIGER refresh is the receipt for the update path, which is the only path the live data can ever exercise. The prod body was read back with pg_get_functiondef first and was byte-identical to 20260428061525 on disk, so the migration is that definition plus two lines; SECURITY DEFINER, SET search_path and the FIX-834 grants restated, post-push ACL {postgres,service_role} unchanged. Covered by packages/data/src/data/district-upsert-centroid.test.ts, which fires the RPC twice at a fixture polygon inside a rolled-back transaction and asserts the centroid MOVES -- the assertion that fails on the old body -- plus a C-shaped polygon whose ST_Centroid falls outside it, pinning the ST_PointOnSurface convention rather than just the presence of a point. <!--id:FIX-1171-->

- 🟠 M — **A bulk landing must PRE-DRAIN the derived-layer debt it creates, in the same quiet window — not leave it for the next scheduled firing** — STANDING CONVENTION, proposed. The 2026-08-19 saturation is the cleanest instance yet of a repeating shape: a bulk write lands cheaply and hands an unbounded bill to whatever derives from it. The FEC same-person merge and re-split work bulk-rewrote financial_relationships; that rewrite bumped updated_at on ~70 percent of all donors; the EC incremental donations arm is watermark-driven, so its dirty set went from a normal few thousand to 3,357,701 rows over 1,961,194 from_ids; and the next scheduled firing spent six hours on it, wrote zero, and took the request path down with it. NONE of that cost appeared in the landing script. It appeared two days later, in a different job, at 08:00 UTC on a weekday, with no operator watching. THE RULE: a script that bulk-rewrites a table owns the derived-layer work its rewrite creates, and drains it in the same quiet window, before it exits. This is the exact sibling of the vacuum rule already standing in CLAUDE.md — any script that bulk-rewrites a table ends by vacuuming what it rewrote (FIX-943) — and it comes from the same failure: the cost is real, it is created by the landing, and leaving it to a background mechanism means it lands on a schedule nobody chose. Vacuum debt and derived-debt are the same category of unpaid bill; the vacuum half is already a written convention and the derived half is not. WHAT PRE-DRAINING MEANS CONCRETELY: after the bulk write and its vacuum, the script drives the derived arms its rewrite dirtied to convergence — for a financial_relationships rewrite that is the EC donations arm and the donor rollup — rather than assuming the weekly cron will absorb it. Post-[[FIX-1069]] this is cheap to do safely, because the donations arm is now 16 committed, budget-checked, resumable windows that can be driven to convergence and re-entered if interrupted. AMENDS THE PR 3b DISPATCH RECIPE: 3b lands per-cycle FEC replays, which is precisely a repeated bulk rewrite of financial_relationships. Its per-cycle dispatch recipe should gain a post-cycle derived-drain step so cycle N pays its own derived cost before cycle N+1 starts, instead of accumulating debt across cycles for a Monday firing to discover. The 3b sessions consume this bullet; it is NOT a request to rebuild the [[FIX-974]] bulk-regime pass here. OPEN QUESTION for whoever implements: whether the drain belongs in each landing script or in one shared post-bulk-landing helper that takes the set of tables rewritten and maps them to the derived arms that consume them. The second is better if more than two landing scripts need it, and the mapping table is small today: financial_relationships to EC donations plus donor rollup plus FE totals. Cross-ref [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-1018]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-974]], [[FIX-1002]]. APPEND 2026-09-09 (THE OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE HELPER EXISTS). This bullet asked 'whether the drain belongs in each landing script or in one shared post-bulk-landing helper... The second is better if more than two landing scripts need it.' The tree answers it rather than taste: THREE scripts already carried a byte-for-byte identical manifest-scoped tail -- remediate-role-ineligible-holders, remediate-cross-person-misattribution, merge-same-person-official-dupes -- and FIX-1106's residue sweep is a fourth. New module packages/data/src/lib/fr-rewrite-drain.ts holds it: entity_connections money-edge delete keyed on the deleted FR row ids (the 954:693 shape, scoped by evidence_source), donor_rollup_rebuild_recipients(affected), then financial_entity_donation_totals_rebuild and donor_party_rollup_rebuild_donors chunked at 5,000 donors. All four scripts now call it and none inlines those steps any more. TWO DESIGN POINTS WORTH THE INK. (1) The affected-officials table name AND its id column are parameters, because the three callers genuinely disagree -- _affected(official_id), _affected(id), _affected_officials(id) -- and an assumption there would have been a silent wrong-column bug. (2) THE HELPER'S SCOPE STOPS AT THE MANIFEST'S COST. It executes no platform-scoped step, with or without --defer-tails, and issues no VACUUM; those stay in the callers that already implement them correctly. That is FIX-1165's rule expressed as a boundary rather than a flag, and it also protects the FIX-965 hazard by construction: refresh_treemap_individuals_global() must never run under an armed statement_timeout, and folding it into a generic step loop in a shared helper is exactly how that would have come back. A source-reading unit test fails if any rebuild_/refresh_ function other than the three manifest-scoped ones appears in the helper, with a floor assertion so it cannot pass vacuously. THE BULK-LANDING HALF IS ALREADY THIS BULLET'S OWN and is NOT built here -- 'AMENDS THE PR 3b DISPATCH RECIPE... its per-cycle dispatch recipe should gain a post-cycle derived-drain step'. No new FIX was allocated for it; when 3b next lands a per-cycle replay, drainFrRewrite is the entry point, and the arm that needs adding there is the EC donations arm driven to convergence (cheap post-FIX-1069, 16 committed budget-checked windows). Bullet stays OPEN on that half. - 🟠 M — **Census the rows=200 planner-fallback signature beyond _conn — GROUP BY over UNION ALL / derived columns gets no statistics** — Census filing in the [[FIX-1112]] shape, not a build. When Postgres groups over an expression it has no statistics for — most commonly a GROUP BY sitting on top of a UNION ALL, or on a derived/computed column rather than a plain table column — it cannot estimate the group count and falls back to a HARDCODED default estimate of 200 rows. That estimate is almost never right, and being wrong by orders of magnitude in the CHEAP direction is what makes it dangerous: a 200-row estimate invites the planner to pick a nested loop, a hash aggregate sized for 200 groups, or a non-parallel path, and then the executor discovers millions of rows at runtime with the wrong plan already committed. The signature is visible in EXPLAIN as a node whose estimate is exactly rows=200 while actual rows is enormous. This was found and fixed in one place (_conn); the point of this item is that NOTHING established it was the only place. THE WORK: grep the whole SQL surface — supabase/migrations, packages/db, and any RPC body in pg_proc.prosrc — for the structural pattern (GROUP BY whose key is a UNION ALL output column or an expression), then EXPLAIN each candidate against PROD, not local, and keep the ones showing rows=200 against a large actual. Prod is the only valid measurement environment here for two reasons: local is cache-warm and small, and per [[reference_clone_understates_scan_bound_costs]] a clone can be ~6x cheap on scan-bound work, so a local EXPLAIN will happily hide the problem. Remedies once a site is confirmed, in increasing order of cost: CREATE STATISTICS on the expression, materialize the derived column so it carries real stats (the [[FIX-1034]] precedent for FR.from_id n_distinct and FE expression stats), or restructure the query so the GROUP BY lands on a plain indexed column. DELIVERABLE is the census table (site, estimate, actual, chosen remedy or explicit no-op), not a set of fixes — sizing the class comes first. Cross-ref [[FIX-1034]] [[FIX-1112]]. **cc-186 (2026-10-04), the census (docs/audits/2026-10-04-measure-first-census.md §1):** 117 prod definitions, 179 GROUP BY clauses, 69 candidates in 50 definitions (23 UNION-output, 42 expression, 24 derived; 7 inherit the fallback through primary_industry_tag(), an inlined UNION ALL), 45 EXPLAINed on prod (plain). 13 routines carry an exact rows=200 node. Only two exceed 100k on a called path — the EC-degree windows rebuild_entity_connection_stats_window and entity_search_conn_window, 200 against 303,160 actual groups per window on prod — and both are HARMLESS as planned (one-batch hash under their 64 MB proconfigs, 2.4-3.1x headroom; spill starts near 720k / 925k groups per window). The latent one is refresh_entity_connection_stats_mv: the exact pre-FIX-1123 whole-table shape (clone 3,225,903 groups, 540,737 kB hash, 5 batches, spills; no parallel-0 guard), with 0 cron, 0 in-DB and 0 pgss callers — only the local-dev rebuild script and the Franklin seed call it; retire or re-point it. The other eleven are over-estimates or small. CREATE STATISTICS fixes none of the 13 (no key is a base-table column or expression); expressions over base columns never produce 200 on PG 17.6. The FIX-1123 fix class was materialize + ANALYZE + windowing (the prompt credited FIX-1112, which is the ratchet census). Outside the signature: refresh_contract_flow_rollups statement 2 estimates 31 rows against 3,240,205 on the clone (a from_id selectivity of 1), driving a 3.24M-probe nested loop and ~718 MB of external sorts — the likelier cause of its 1,896.8 s mean CALL. Nothing filed. **cc-188 (2026-10-04), the pre-FIX-1123 stats function rewritten — nothing filed:** refresh_entity_connection_stats_mv() was the last whole-table GROUP BY over a UNION ALL of both entity_connections id columns. It has no SQL, cron or workflow caller but two TypeScript ones (rebuild-entity-connections.ts:509, the franklin seed's --refresh-all-mvs), so it was rewritten, not dropped. Clone, old body: one HashAggregate estimated at rows=200 against 3,225,903 groups, Batches 5, 139 MB memory, 319 MB spilled, 101.9 s. Migration 20261004100000 runs it as 16 calls of rebuild_entity_connection_stats_window() under work_mem 64MB and parallel 0. Each window still estimates rows=200 against ~203k (the signature survives, per window) but fits: Batches 1, 36.9 MB, no spill. Same end state on the clone (3,225,903 rows and an identical row hash, after 1,000 deletions, 1,000 corruptions and one orphan were injected) in 131.1 s, so this is bounded memory, not a speedup. FIX-1131 stays the census. **cc-190 (2026-10-04):** Closed as recognized 2026-10-04 (cc-190): the census was the deliverable; the one latent site was rewritten by cc-188. <!--id:FIX-1131-->
- 🟡 S — **Measured look: entity_connection_stats_mv.connection_count is definitionally _conn.c — reading the MV would delete the aggregation but couple correctness to a gated arm** — MEASURED LOOK, not a build — the deliverable is a numbers-backed recommendation, and NO-GO is an acceptable and possibly the correct outcome. Observation: entity_connection_stats_mv.connection_count is by definition the same quantity the request path recomputes as _conn.c, so a read path that selected the MV column instead would delete an aggregation from the hot path entirely rather than merely making it cheaper. That is the most attractive shape of optimization available here, which is exactly why it needs measuring before building. THE CATCH, and the reason this is filed as a look: correctness would become coupled to the completion state of a GATED pipeline arm. entity_connection_stats_windows is the 16-window stats arm behind the FIX-1117 source-fingerprint gate, and it is precisely the arm most likely to be skipped, deferred, budget-cancelled, or left mid-cycle — measured on prod 2026-09-01, one window ran 1810 s and inserted ZERO rows, and the cron-budget watchdog cancelled ec-crawl twice that day at 1915 s and 2087 s. So the MV can legitimately be STALE at read time, and today the live aggregation hides that from users. Selecting the MV would surface pipeline lateness as WRONG COUNTS on the page, which is a materially different failure mode from slow counts. WHAT TO MEASURE, on prod: (1) the actual request-path cost of the _conn.c aggregation today, from pg_stat_statements filtered to pgrst_source per [[reference_pgss_rpc_cost_audit_gotchas]], since if it is not actually expensive there is nothing to buy; (2) the observed staleness distribution of entity_connection_stats_mv — how far behind does connection_count actually run, across a normal week and across a bad day; (3) whether the two values agree today, which is the cheap falsification step and should be done FIRST because if they already disagree the premise is dead. Decide only after (1) through (3). If it proceeds, the read path needs the live-compute fallback convention from packages/db/CLAUDE.md rather than a bare MV read, and the freshness bound has to be stated as a product decision, not an implementation detail. Cross-ref [[FIX-1117]] [[FIX-1118]] [[FIX-775]] and the connection-counts MV swap precedent. **cc-186 (2026-10-04) — GO, reframed (docs/audits/2026-10-04-measure-first-census.md §4):** the premise is wrong: get_official_page carries no _conn (prod body; anon 1,432 calls, mean 189 ms since 09-22). That owner is fr-vacuum-analyze, schedule 0 1 * * 1 — WEEKLY, Monday 01:00. Post-apply FR sat at 204,091 dead tuples and 82.7 percent all-visible (631,265 relpages, 522,325 relallvisible), down from 100.0 percent. Autovacuum cannot collect it: the per-table autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor is 0.02, so the trigger is 50 + 0.02 x 14,469,877 = 289,448 dead tuples and the table is below it. So a bulk FR rewrite on any day but Sunday leaves the table degraded for up to six days with nothing able to collect it — the exact FIX-884 shape where all-visible loss turns index-only scans into per-row heap fetches, and precisely what the FIX-943 standing rule exists to prevent. - 🟠 S — **A cancelled get_official_page renders as a real official with an empty record — the data swallow hides 57014 from the visitor and the crawler** — Measured by cc-137 (2026-09-19): 80 of 446 get_official_page calls over 3.50 days were cancelled — 17.9 percent (11.2 percent excluding the 09-16/09-17 event window) — making it the single most-cancelled statement on prod. Every visitor is anon (the page calls the RPC through createPublicClient, so there is no authenticated cohort with a longer bound), and withDbTimeout(..., 5000) is a CLIENT-SIDE Promise.race that issues no SQL, so it always loses to the server's 3s anon bound and cannot even report the cancel as a timeout. The page then destructures { data }, shims data ?? {}, and every section renders its empty state — so a cancelled page is indistinguishable from the FIX-683 recordless-shell skip: a real official, right name, right party, right photo, with no votes, no spending, no career, no promises. No error, no 500, nothing but a 57014 in the logs. Two harms: a visitor is told this official has no record, and a crawler is told the same and may cache it. The fix is to classify the three outcomes (skipped / ok / failed) before the shim, render a visible degraded state on failed, noindex that render, and mark it no-store so a transient cancel is never cached as an empty official. Cross-ref [[FIX-1180]], [[FIX-683]], [[FIX-646]]. FILED AND CLOSED 2026-09-20 (cc-138). classifyOfficialPage() separates skipped / ok / failed BEFORE the data ?? {} shim, and a failed render now gets: a banner saying the record could not be LOADED (not that it is empty), robots noindex so a crawler cannot cache the claim, noStore() so the 300 s ISR window does not hand a transient cancel to the next five minutes of visitors, and one greppable log line carrying the official id and the SQLSTATE. Deliberately keyed on error and NEVER on data == null — a content-bearing official whose RPC answered with nothing to show must not get a red banner saying the read broke, because it did not; the test pins both directions, three failure shapes (57014, client timeout, PGRST202) against three quiet-but-fine shapes, since a classifier returning failed for everything would satisfy the failure cases alone. WHAT IT COSTS, stated rather than buried: robots can only be set from generateMetadata, which runs before the page body, so the RPC moved into a React.cache'd fetcher both can reach and therefore resolves BEFORE the page's Promise.all rather than inside it — sequential with the donor-rollup read on a cold render. [[FIX-1180]] having just cut this RPC 39.7 percent of its buffers is what makes that trade payable now. The FIX-683 skip path is untouched. <!--id:FIX-1202-->

- 🟠 S — **The generic EC arm loop livelocks on a cancelled arm — it retries the same arm into the same wall every 2 h and the cycle never closes** — Census §2.6 item 6 (docs/audits/2026-10-04-measure-first-census.md). run_entity_connections_rebuild's generic arm loop (20260911000200_fix950_guards_rebuild_family.sql:782-786) catches query_canceled, banks nothing, and records the unit as canceled (:838-845); crawl_record_unit then trips the 2 h backoff on seconds >= backoff_abs_seconds 1500, and the next firing after the backoff retries the SAME arm into the same wall. A generic arm that outgrows the 1,800 s unit bound is therefore cancelled every 2 h forever, the cycle never closes, and the stats fingerprint never advances, so entity_connection_stats_mv freezes behind it. No per-arm consecutive-failure state exists (only the 50-entry recent_units ring). One real instance: _contracts 2026-08-31, 1,878 s, 0 rows. Fix: after a canceled outcome, if the same arm's last two ring entries are canceled, park it in pipeline_state.ec_arm_parked, stamp the run partial with the reason, and let the cycle carry on to the next arm; a parked arm is skipped with a (parked) unit mark until its source fingerprint changes or an operator deletes the key. Built by cc-188. <!--id:FIX-1270--> <!--lane:ops-->

- 🟡 S — **The postgres role's work_mem default is the AD-HOC floor — lower it to 64MB (rollback by SET, never RESET)** — Found by cc-210 (docs/audits/2026-10-09-work-mem-allowance-census.md §1, §2, §6). The role row `postgres@postgres {statement_timeout=3h, work_mem=256MB}` was set once, by [[FIX-697]] (`20260630000000:37`), and it is the floor only for sessions that do not SET their own: every ad-hoc `db-query --prod` read, every migration, platform-counts-daily, abuse-events-retention, the probes, and every direct-pg writer under packages/data except two (R6: only rebuild-entity-connections.ts:262 at 256MB and donor-rollup-sweep.ts:227 at 128MB set their own — the nightly, FEC / USASpending bulk via direct-pg-upsert, IRS 990, receipts, canary, the paced runners and the gate all inherit). The 10-07 02:03Z cif_ledger SUM (cc-198) is in pgss: 1 call, 509.7 s, **temp written 0**, 494,675 blocks read — every hash held in RAM — and it brackets the 02:02-02:12Z swap storm exactly (swap-in 1,494-3,485/s, MemAvailable 491 -> 249 MB). The fix: `ALTER ROLE postgres IN DATABASE postgres SET work_mem = '64MB'`, with a read-back asserting both statement_timeout=3h and work_mem=64MB. ### GENERAL / CROSS-CUTTING

- 🟡 M — **Alphabetical DISTINCT ON tie-break silently redistributes multi-tag donor dollars across eight surfaces** — **Filed, not fixed** — surfaced by the [[FIX-916]] curation work and deliberately left alone there, because changing it moves numbers on eight surfaces whose conservation proofs would all have to be re-derived, which is not something a curation PR should do quietly. When a donor carries more than one industry tag, every consuming surface picks ONE via `DISTINCT ON (...) ... ORDER BY ... tag` — i.e. **alphabetically**. That is not a neutral tie-break, it is a systematic gradient: measured 2026-07-27, `agriculture` sorts first so it exports exactly $0.00 and keeps 100% of its dollars, while `transportation` sorts last so it imports exactly $0.00 and loses 44.4% of its dollars to earlier-sorting co-tags. A donor tagged both `agriculture` and `transportation` is counted entirely as agriculture on every surface, for no reason other than the letter it starts with. **Affected surfaces:** `sector_affinity_rebuild_officials()`, `official_sector_dollars_mv`, `chord_industry_flows_mv`, `chord_industry_flows_for_official()`, `chord_top_pacs_for_official()`, `get_official_donors()`, `refresh_group_donor_rollup()`, `fetchIndustryTagsByEntityId()`, plus the [[FIX-873]] contract-flow bodies. **[[FIX-916]] removes most of what this was mishandling** — it collapses 96.4% of the multi-tag donation dollar mass ($328.4M of $340.8M across 478 multi-tag donating donors) down to exactly one tag at the source — so the residual is the unaudited multi-tag tail, and the honest fix here is a deliberate ranking (by tag confidence, then by the donor's own dollar concentration) rather than by spelling. Note the same alphabet already bit [[FIX-908]]: renaming `pharma` to `health` moved the key's position in the ORDER BY so `health` now beats `labor`/`legal`/`lobby` where `pharma` lost to all three, moving ~$41.6M between buckets on the next incremental refresh with no data change whatsoever. Cross-ref [[FIX-916]] [[FIX-873]] [[FIX-875]] [[FIX-908]] [[FIX-872]]. <!--id:FIX-918-->
- 🟡 S — **financial_entity_industry_overrides cannot address a donor with a NULL fec_committee_id** — Surfaced by the [[FIX-921]] oil_gas sweep. public.financial_entity_industry_overrides is keyed on fec_committee_id (PRIMARY KEY), so any financial_entity carrying a NULL fec_committee_id is **structurally unreachable** by the curation mechanism — it can be neither re-assigned nor de-tagged, no matter what an audit finds. Two oil_gas escapees are in exactly that position and were dropped from the FIX-921 list for this reason alone: **Cumberland Energy Action Fund ($135k)** and **Ridge Coal Legacy Trust ($15k)**, both of which the audit judged mis-tagged. **Measured 2026-07-29 — the blind spot is SMALL:** 4 industry-tagged donating donors carry a NULL fec_committee_id ($416,500 total outflow), of which 2 are oil_gas. Small enough to leave the key as-is rather than revisit the table's PK, which is why this is filed rather than fixed — but it is a real hole and it will grow with any ingestion path that mints financial_entities without a committee id (IE-only spenders, USASpending recipients, IRS 990 orgs). **Suggested shape when it becomes worth doing:** add a nullable financial_entity_id column to the override table and make the resolver prefer fec_committee_id, falling back to the UUID, so the common case keeps its portable-across-re-seed key ([[FIX-916]]'s reason for choosing fec_committee_id) while the tail is still addressable. Do NOT swap the PK to the UUID — that is the portability the current key exists to protect. **REFRAMED 2026-08-01: this is an entity-DEDUP problem, not an override-key-coverage problem.** At least two of the four NULL-key donors are duplicates of FEC-keyed entities that already exist (verified on local 2026-08-01): National Rifle Association of America Political Victory Fund exists BOTH as C00053553 (`pac`) and as a NULL-keyed `other`-type row, and Pharmaceutical Care Management Association exists BOTH as C00388819 (`pac`) and as a NULL-keyed `other`-type row. The override mechanism already reaches the FEC-keyed twin; what is broken is that the NULL-keyed duplicate splits the donor's money and tags across two rows — the [[FIX-544]] merge class. The nullable-financial_entity_id column suggested above would ADDRESS the duplicate rather than merge it. Dedup first; only then see whether any genuinely FEC-less donor (the Cumberland/Ridge pair may be the same shape) leaves a residual blind spot worth a schema change. Cross-ref [[FIX-921]] [[FIX-916]] [[FIX-544]]. <!--id:FIX-922-->
- 🟡 S — **ai_summary_cache is never invalidated when the summary prompt changes — stale framing survives a prompt fix** — **File only.** Surfaced while shipping [[FIX-931]]. `ai_summary_cache` is keyed on `(entity_type, entity_id, summary_type)` and nothing in the key or the write path encodes **which prompt produced the text**, so editing a prompt has no effect on any already-cached summary — the old wording is served indefinitely. Concretely: cached summaries written before [[FIX-931]] still carry the pre-fix "Total raised" framing for official money, which [[FIX-931]] corrected precisely because it overstates what the FEC-itemized figure actually measures (it excludes unitemized small-dollar giving, joint-fundraising transfers, loans and other receipts). So the label on the page is now right and the AI prose next to it is still wrong, which is worse than either alone. Fix: add a **prompt-version component to the cache key** (a hash of the prompt template, or an explicit `prompt_version` column bumped when the template changes) so a prompt edit naturally misses the cache and regenerates, rather than requiring anyone to remember a manual purge. A targeted purge on prompt edit is the cheap interim, but it is the same class of "a comment/convention does not enforce" problem [[FIX-901]] documented — the durable fix is making the key carry the dependency. Check the same question for the tagger and narrative caches while in there. Note the regeneration cost is real (every affected entity re-summarised), so pair the key change with a count of what would invalidate before shipping it. Cross-ref [[FIX-931]], [[FIX-901]]. <!--id:FIX-938-->
- 🟡 M — **Decide the fate of the 6,888 pre-versioning summaries, and whether superseded text is retained** — Two questions FIX-938 deliberately deferred rather than answered. (1) Its migration backfilled all 6,888 ai_summary_cache rows (all proposal/plain_language; official/profile is EMPTY on both envs, so the pre-FIX-931 framing the bullet cited had no rows to invalidate) to the CURRENT version rather than 'legacy', because FIX-938 changed no prompt text and stamping them stale would force ~6,888 regenerations, roughly 11 USD at Haiku 4.5 rates against a 4 USD/month platform cap — blowing the cap and leaving the on-demand routes refusing on miss. The unproven part is that those rows actually match today's wording: they were written over months by three different producers. Deciding to re-stamp them 'legacy' is a cost decision, not a code change, and wants a budget window. (2) FIX-938 keeps ONE row per entity and overwrites on regeneration, so superseded text is not retained. If audit retention is wanted, the shape is a separate ai_summary_cache_history table, NOT a fourth column on the UNIQUE — the migration header records that 13 read sites exist, four of which cannot express the current key, and that versioning the key would blank the home page, the proposals index, proposal detail and entity search until regeneration. Related: packages/ai#generateSummary is dead code (no callers, only comment references from the two routes that reimplement it) and carries a summary_type vocabulary matching nothing in the table; delete it or make the routes use it. See FIX-938 and FIX-931. cc-187 (2026-10-04): CLOSED AS RECOGNIZED on Craig's decision of 2026-10-03: no re-stamp of the 6,888 pre-versioning summaries, and no history table for superseded text. FIX-938's backfill to the current version stands, because no prompt text changed. Superseded text is not retained. <!--id:FIX-1206-->

### GRAPH

- 🟢 S — **group_donor_rollup full refresh is ~6min on prod — top-N storage could cut it** — FIX-500's refresh_group_donor_rollup() full re-aggregate measured ~6min on prod under IOWait load (519,886 donor rows across 573 cohorts; the long pole is the INSERT + PK/read-index maintenance, seen as IPC/BtreePage waits). It runs off-path at the tail of the twice-weekly rebuild-entity-connections workflow (4h GHA budget, donations chunk alone ~90min), so 6min is ~1% of budget and NOT currently painful — but it is close enough to the 1800s hook timeout under heavier load to note. Cheap durable cut if it ever bites: store only top-N (e.g. 200) donors per cohort via ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY gb_id,party_key ORDER BY total_cents DESC) <= 200 — the route reads <=100, and group_donor_rollup_summary already carries the TRUE donor_count + full total_cents independent of stored rows, so top-N rows lose nothing the request path uses. Shrinks the table ~519k -> ~tens-of-thousands and makes the INSERT seconds. Gated follow-up from [[FIX-500]] decision-2 (full per-donor rows shipped as-is per 'don't pre-optimize; file a follow-up if painful'). <!--id:FIX-501-->
- 🟢 M — **Saved views can't persist a hand-picked ids group (BrowseState is a predicate)** — [[FIX-886]] added `GroupFilter.officialIds` so BUNDLE AS GROUP means what it says, but an ids-group is **in-session only**: `BrowseState` is a predicate (scope + facets + q), and cannot express a hand-picked id list, so `compileBrowseToGroupFilter` never emits `officialIds` and the v2 saved-view payload has nowhere to put it. Consequences today: saving a view while an ids-group is in focus silently drops the group's membership, and a shared/reloaded session resolves nothing. Deciding this needs a call on semantics that [[FIX-886]] deliberately deferred — a saved id list is a SNAPSHOT (members who leave office, get merged by [[FIX-544]], or are promoted by `promote_candidate_to_elected()` would silently drift or 404), so the options are (a) persist ids with a resolution-time reconciliation pass that reports drops, (b) persist nothing and make the UI say ids-groups are session-scoped, or (c) materialize the selection into a real `user_custom_groups` row with an explicit membership table. The coverage manifest and a compiler test currently pin option (b) as the status quo — changing it must update both. <!--id:FIX-888-->
- 🟢 M — **Floterial overlay layer for the SLD choropleth (NH, 39 districts)** — FIX-914 seeded the 39 New Hampshire floterial House districts as real jurisdictions rows and taught query_districts() to keep them OUT of the bbox/state fill so a state choropleth stays a partition (design D7). They are therefore invisible on every map today, and the 58 representatives now linked to them are dropped from /api/graph/voting-divergence because their district_jurisdiction_id is not in the fill id set. Build the overlay: a second layer drawn on top of the base fill (outline or hatch, toggleable), fed by query_districts with the floterials INCLUDED. Two concrete traps for whoever picks this up. (1) voting-divergence pages query_districts per state at p_limit 200; NH lower is 164 base rows and 203 with the overlay folded in, so that cap MUST be raised in the same change or three districts vanish silently. (2) query_districts already returns overlay rows on the exact-p_id and point-containment paths; the fill exclusion is a single predicate in 20260910130000_fix914_query_districts_floterial.sql and the clean extension is a p_include_floterial boolean DEFAULT false, which changes the signature and so needs a DROP before CREATE or PostgREST sees two overloads. Overlay rows are identifiable by metadata floterial = true. NH is the only state with floterials in the residual, so this is one state problem today. Cross-ref [[FIX-914]], [[FIX-913]].  APPEND 2026-09-19 (cc-135, CLOSED, prod): shipped as migration 20260919011500 (p_include_floterial boolean DEFAULT false appended last, DROP before CREATE as the bullet predicted, plus a floterial boolean output column so the client needs no second lookup) and the UI half in packages/graph/src/ChoroplethGraph.tsx. THE CHOROPLETH IS NOT IN GraphPage.tsx and it is NOT per-state -- it is packages/graph/src/ChoroplethGraph.tsx drawing a single nationwide geoAlbersUsa map, and voting-divergence loops all 51 states server-side to build it; the overlay is a second d3 layer (dashed outline, fill none, pointer-events on the stroke) over the base fill, with a role=switch toggle keyed on the response carrying overlay rows rather than on a hard-coded NH. FIX-914's D7 partition is preserved rather than relaxed: the default is still 164 for an NH lower fill on prod, and the reader test that pins it is unchanged. - 🟡 M — **Ratchet ESLint warnings to zero and enforce --max-warnings 0** — Follow-up to [[FIX-459]], which wired the ESLint presets across all packages + apps and promoted the tests.yml lint step to blocking by downgrading several high-volume rules from error to warn (so the gate could go green without ballooning that PR). The lint gate is now blocking but warnings are still allowed. Backlog at FIX-459 landing time: ~76 warnings — no-console x23, @typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars x21, @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any x21, no-inner-declarations x5, react/no-unescaped-entities x2, @next/next/no-img-element x2, react/no-children-prop x1, react-hooks/exhaustive-deps x1. The ratchet: (1) drive the backlog to zero — remove/underscore unused vars, replace explicit any with real types, gate console behind a logger or allow-list, fix the genuine react/no-children-prop + exhaustive-deps sites; (2) re-promote the downgraded rules in packages/config/eslint/{base,next}.js from warn back to error as each category reaches zero; (3) add --max-warnings 0 to every package lint script (or 'next lint --max-warnings 0' for apps) so new warnings fail CI. Do it rule-by-rule to keep diffs reviewable. See packages/config/eslint/base.js + next.js for the current warn-level overrides flagged with FIX-459 comments. <!--id:FIX-460-->
- 🟢 S — **Moderation-harness pollution check doesn't watch auth.users/public.users** — The SF-P3 moderation harness's zero-pollution self-check (POLLUTION_TABLES in packages/data/src/pipelines/moderation-harness/index.ts) counts only 8 public tables before/after each run and does NOT watch auth.users or public.users. Its fixtures create ephemeral auth.users + public.users rows inside a rolled-back txn; if a rollback ever fails to take, leaked rows go undetected while the run still reports 'zero pollution'. That is exactly how ~30 bare-id auth.users rows leaked and poisoned admin.listUsers ([[FIX-660]]). FIX-660 hardened the three inserts (createUser / createAgedUser / createSyntheticUser) to be GoTrue-complete so a leak is now harmless, but leak DETECTION is still missing. Fix: add auth.users + public.users (schema-qualified counts) to the harness pollution watch so a future rollback failure surfaces loudly. Low priority — the harmless-leak hardening already shipped. <!--id:FIX-825-->
- 🟠 M — **Seven pg_cron jobs blow the 6h statement_timeout; each blowout starves every other job that fires in its window (rule-taggers-weekly fails 4 of 5 runs)** — **Found while diagnosing [[FIX-968]]; the envelope data is filed at `docs/audits/2026-08-06-fix968-cron-window-envelopes.md`.** Measured across the full retained `cron.job_run_details` window (2026-06-29 → 08-06, 177 runs), **seven distinct jobs have been cancelled by the 6h `statement_timeout` that the `postgres` role carries via pg_db_role_setting**: jobid 22 rebuild-ec-incremental-mon (2 of 3 runs), 26 treemap-individuals-global-refresh, 17 donor-party-rollup-refresh, 24 donor-rollup-refresh (4 consecutive, 07-27..07-30), 13 financial-entity-totals-incremental (2 of 5), the retired jobid 1, and worst — **jobid 12 rule-taggers-weekly, which has failed 4 of its 5 retained runs at exactly 21601-21613s with nothing watching it at all**, i.e. the weekly industry tagger has essentially not completed since late June. **Two compounding harms.** (1) Each of these is silent: `cron.job_run_details` is the only place the failure is recorded, nothing reads it except the [[FIX-968]] `check_cron_job_health()` shipped today, and that detector deliberately treats blowouts as REPORT-ONLY (escalating on them would fail the canary most Tuesdays and train the alert to be ignored — the FIX-943 cause-vs-consequence rule). So they stay greppable but unalerted by design, pending this fix. (2) **A blowout does not fail fast — it runs flat out for six hours and then dies**, and on a 2-vCPU Pro Small that sustained load is the single largest cause of the `job startup timeout` class: pg_cron runs with `cron.use_background_workers=off`, so it opens a fresh libpq connection per firing with a ~10s window, and under a 6h squatter that window is blown. Measured directly — on 08-03 jobid 24 was starved by jobid 22 mid-blowout; on 08-04 jobids 13, 24 AND 12 were all starved by jobids 26+17 both mid-blowout. So the blowouts are self-amplifying: a job that cannot finish takes out the jobs scheduled after it. **Fix shape — ⚠ CORRECTED 2026-08-09:** the original shape below is necessary but NOT sufficient, and it names the wrong severity. **jobid 24 was ALREADY chunked ([[FIX-944]]) and still took the site down on 08-08** — so the harm that matters is **request-path saturation**, not job-vs-job starvation, and a fix that merely reschedules cron jobs so they stop colliding does nothing for it. Each arm needs a per-run cost/time budget that keeps a firing off the request path at all, not just a cursor that lets it resume. Original shape, still correct as far as it goes: chunk the remaining arms the way [[FIX-944]] and [[FIX-965]] chunked theirs (per-chunk COMMIT + a resume cursor in `pipeline_state`, so a 6h cancel keeps its progress instead of discarding it), starting with jobid 12 since it is the one that essentially never succeeds — but pair every chunking with a budget. **Scope note 2026-08-09:** jobid 24 has since been addressed by [[FIX-1002]]/[[FIX-1003]]; FIX-969 remains OPEN for jobids 12, 13, 17, 22 and 26. Note `SET statement_timeout` inside a procedure body does NOT re-arm the running timer (measured 2026-07-31, documented in donor-rollup-sweep.ts) — chunking is the only lever, not a timeout bump. Prerequisite input for the rollup-capacity work; the per-job p50/p95/max envelope table is already filed in the audit above so it need not be re-derived. **DATED OCCURRENCE — 2026-08-24, the THIRD PGRST002 outage (appended cc-prompt-76; append-only).** Prod ran degraded 08:00–13:16 UTC: 327 cron firings with 199 dead on `job startup timeout` (60.9 percent), PostgREST answering 503 on every sampled path, and `canceling authentication due to timeout` at 12:15:44. **The offender is named: jobid 22 `rebuild-ec-incremental-mon`**, whose donations window 5 ran as a single 3h49m statement ([[FIX-1101]]); the ~200 MB WAL burst at 11:21–11:28 and the 50.2 s checkpoint fsyncs belong to it. **The 57014s were NOT the site's own queries.** Craig expanded the 12:16:29 UTC log row: user `authenticator`, statement = PostgREST's schema-cache catalog load. `pg_roles` confirms `authenticator` carries `statement_timeout=8s` (with `lock_timeout=8s`; `anon` is 3s, `authenticated` 8s), so under I/O starvation the recursive catalog walk cannot complete, PostgREST fails its cache load, and every request becomes PGRST002 → 503. That is the [[FIX-1063]] mechanism for the third time — 08-18 treemap, 08-19 unwindowed EC, 08-24 windowed-but-skewed EC. **THE PATTERN ACROSS THE THREE, which is what this bullet's regime must inherit: each closure bounded ONE offender while the cliff itself stayed.** FIX-1002/1003 bounded jobid 24; [[FIX-1069]] bounded jobid 22's statement count; [[FIX-1071]] gave it an external budget — and the box still went unavailable, because nothing yet bounds the AGGREGATE concurrent write pressure, and nothing protects the `authenticator` schema-cache load from it. A per-job budget is necessary and demonstrably not sufficient. **Corollary measured the same morning: a starved job's budget is not a control at all** — both `donor-rollup-refresh` firings (09:00 and 12:00) died with `job startup timeout` and never ran, so FIX-1002's per-run budget never engaged, and `rule-taggers-daily` (06:30) died the same way. Cross-ref [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-951]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-950]], [[FIX-1002]], [[FIX-1003]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1072]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1102]]. **PARTIAL STRUCTURAL ANSWER FILED 2026-08-27 — [[FIX-1111]].** This bullet's corrected shape ("each arm needs a per-run cost/time budget that keeps a firing off the request path at all, not just a cursor that lets it resume") is now implemented for jobids 2/22 by replacing them with a paced crawl: one bankable unit per firing, a duration-based throttle sensor that backs off 2 h when the box slows, and blackout windows. Does NOT close this bullet — jobids 12, 13, 17 and 26 still have the shape described above, and the [[FIX-1112]] census establishes that three of them cannot even converge after a cancel because they write their watermark only at end-of-run. Fix order and the proposed schedule moves: docs/audits/2026-08-27-io-budget-burst-ledger.md sections 5 and 7. **RE-MEASURED 2026-09-20 (cc-139) — cc-139 EXPECTED to close this as superseded and THE MEASUREMENT REFUSED IT; the bullet stays OPEN.** Prod, read-only, full retained `cron.job_run_details` window 2026-06-29 08:00 → 2026-09-20 19:22 UTC (56,931 runs / 48 jobs — note retention is the entire history, not the ~30 days usually quoted). **WHAT IS GONE:** the 6 h ceiling this bullet is named for no longer exists — `pg_db_role_setting` has `postgres` at `statement_timeout=3h` (with `work_mem=256MB`) since [[FIX-1185]], and across ALL 41 scheduled jobs there were **ZERO** `canceling statement due to statement timeout` failures in the last 30 days. Its own shape has resolved (no statement-timeout blowout in 45 days, last two runs 5x inside budget) but the window is not clean. (2) **jobid 17 has ZERO successes in its last four firings** and is in a worse state than when this bullet was written: 08-25 `job startup timeout`, 09-01 watchdog cancel at 1,814.6 s, and BOTH 09-08 and 09-15 dead on `server restarted` with a NULL `end_time`. [[FIX-993]] owns the staleness but not the `server restarted` cause. **TO CLOSE:** a clean 30-day window on 26, and an explanation for 17's `server restarted` legs. jobid 17 donor-party-rollup-refresh vs the September restarts — REFUTED (cc-141 read 11; Craig's call 2026-09-21: leave the job ACTIVE and record the negative result). The Logs API for 2026-09-15 15:00-15:20 UTC, read before its 7-day window closed, shows job 17 starting at 15:00:00.011, a healthy box through 15:08:01.829 (time checkpoint writing 14 buffers / 0.0 percent; both 2-minute watchdogs completing in under 2 s), then 106 s of total log silence and a new postmaster at 15:09:48.281 reporting 'database system was interrupted; last known up at 2026-09-15 15:06:05 UTC'. Crash recovery yes — but NO 'out of memory', NO 'terminated by signal', NO 'server process was terminated', and no shutdown request: the postmaster vanished without logging anything, which is a container or host-level event, not a Postgres-side memory kill. The coincidence then dissolves on the census: prod restarted SEVEN times in the retained window — 08-18 (rule-taggers-weekly), 08-24 and 08-26 (entity-connection-stats-rebuild), 08-29 at 06:00 and 07:30 (ec-crawl, refresh-derived-mvs-daily), 09-08 and 09-15 (jobid 17) — spread across Tue/Mon/Wed/Sat, and jobid 17 was in flight for only TWO of them. Only LONG jobs are ever caught, which is exactly what random restart timing produces, because catch probability scales with time in flight. The one CONFIRMED resource failure, 09-01's 1,814.6 s watchdog kill on array_agg(DISTINCT fr.from_id), was already removed by [[FIX-950]] and is verifiably absent from the live procedure. SEPARATELY, and still open: jobid 17 has ZERO successes since 2026-07-28 (08-04 hit the 6h ceiling at 21,628.6 s; 08-11, 08-18 and 08-25 startup timeouts; 09-01 watchdog cancel; 09-08 and 09-15 server restarted) — that is its own bug, not a restart cause. jobid 26 treemap-individuals-global-refresh (Tue 14:00) is 2 of 4 over 30 days and SUCCEEDED on both restart days (09-15 994.1 s, 09-08 1084.2 s), finishing about 53 min before the 15:09:48 restart, so it is not implicated either. - 🟡 S — **financial_entities carries 310 MB of never-scanned indexes that every non-HOT update still maintains** — Found in the [[FIX-1008]] write-surface census. A non-HOT UPDATE inserts a new entry into EVERY index on the table, whether or not that index's columns changed — so an index nothing reads is still paid for on every write. `pg_stat_user_indexes` on prod 2026-08-09 (counters cumulative, `stats_reset` NULL, so this is the full post-cutover window) shows five `financial_entities` indexes with **idx_scan = 0**: `financial_entities_donated_positive` 145 MB, `financial_entities_recipient_count_idx` 70 MB, `financial_entities_individual_state_idx` 61 MB, `financial_entities_canonical_name_type` 19 MB, `financial_entities_canonical` 15 MB — **310 MB across 5 of 19 indexes**, never once scanned. The donor stage does 840,338 upserts per cycle and ~73% of its updates are non-HOT, so this is real write amplification on the pipeline's most expensive stage, and it competes for a 256 MB `shared_buffers` that the working set already dwarfs. `financial_entities_individual_state_idx` deserves particular attention: it is an EXPRESSION index over `(metadata->>'state')`, and `metadata` is rewritten by the donor upsert on every conflict, so it re-evaluates the expression on every non-HOT write and it is a HOT blocker in its own right. Do NOT batch-drop these on the strength of idx_scan alone — verify each against the read paths first, because a zero-scan index can still be (a) a uniqueness constraint, (b) an ON CONFLICT arbiter, or (c) serving a route that has simply not run since the counters started. None of these five is unique or an arbiter, which is what makes them candidates. Note the contrast on the other table: `financial_relationships_usaspending_unique` is also idx_scan = 0 at 485 MB but MUST stay — it is the usaspending pipeline's conflict arbiter, and that pipeline is manual-dispatch-only since [[FIX-740]]. - 🟠 M — **FIXES.md is both hand-edited and machine-edited — derive status from done.log instead of flipping checkboxes in place** — Filed 2026-08-09 out of the cc-prompt-55 trunk-guard work; this is the real fix, of which the guard is only the detector. **The class.** docs/FIXES.md carries two kinds of content under one writer contract: bullet prose, which only Craig edits by hand, and the leading checkbox, which fixes:sync flips in place. An in-place machine edit of a hand-edited file is the entire concurrent-write class — syncFixesMd reads the whole file, maps every line, and writes the whole file back, so any hand edit that lands inside that window is silently reverted with no conflict, no error, and a diff that looks intentional. docs/done.log does NOT have the problem, and the reason is structural rather than lucky: it is append-only, and appends from two sessions merge where in-place edits do not. **Proposal.** Make done.log the single source of truth for status: FIXES.md holds prose and the id marker only, and fixes:check COMPUTES the checked set from the log rather than reading it back out of the markdown. Then FIXES.md is only ever hand-edited, done.log is only ever appended, and the class disappears rather than being detected. **Two known bugs die with it.** (1) fixes:sync silently no-ops its checkbox flips on a CRLF working copy — it normalizes CRLF on read but the bullet regex still has to match, and a mismatch is indistinguishable from nothing-to-do. (2) The state-in-two-places reconciliation that produced checkboxesFlipped: 2 against four closures on 2026-08-09; with status derived there is nothing to reconcile. **Cost, honestly.** A one-time migration of the current checkbox state into the log for any bullet whose [x] has no completion row, plus updating every reader of [x] — fixes-clean.mjs (which selects source bullets by checkbox), fixes-archive.mjs, fixes-housekeep.mjs and session-check.mjs. Do NOT change done.log format as part of this; the append-only contract is what makes the whole thing work. **Relationship to the guard.** scripts/lib/trunk-guard.mjs now aborts any of these scripts when origin/main or HEAD moves between their read and their write, which converts the silent revert into a loud refusal — necessary, and strictly weaker than removing the in-place write. Keep the guard afterwards regardless: fix:add still appends to FIXES.md and fixes-archive still rewrites it. Cross-ref [[FIX-461]], [[FIX-462]], [[FIX-361]], [[FIX-314]], [[FIX-369]], [[FIX-1015]]. <!--id:FIX-1016-->

Provisioned baseline is **1,000 IOPS / 22 MB/s**; the disk cap is **3,000**. So the box holds roughly **30–75 minutes per day of above-baseline I/O**, and once spent it runs at **~150 IOPS / 60–75 percent IOwait for hours** while the balance refills. Every bulk writer must fit that envelope or it does not merely fail — it spends the whole day's credit and starves every job behind it. **The contrast that proves this is a budget and not a load problem:** on 08-26 donor-rollup-refresh ran 09:00–10:59 AND 12:00–13:59 (7,171.9s and 7,186.6s, both `partial — budget exhausted`) — four hours of sustained work — and jobids 40/44 recorded **5/60 failures across the entire day**. Sustained load inside the budget is harmless; a burst that exhausts it is not. Cross-ref [[FIX-1031]] (the writer, now paused), [[FIX-969]] (the regime it needs), [[FIX-1101]] (the 08-26 EC run that stayed inside the envelope). **STRUCTURAL ANSWER FILED 2026-08-27 — [[FIX-1111]].** This bullet's operational fact (the I/O budget, not CPU, is the scarce resource, and it is small) is now the premise of a shipped design: the EC rebuild runs as a background CRAWL, one bounded unit per firing at */15, paced so aggregate spend stays under the refill rate rather than bursting through the daily pool in 75 minutes. The per-firing ceiling is 96 x 346 s = 60 percent of the day's refill and cannot be exceeded by any cycle shape. - 🟠 M — **89 public functions carry a decorative statement_timeout proconfig that cannot bound them** — Surfaced by the FIX-1123 class census. A FUNCTION-level SET statement_timeout proconfig NEVER bounds that function's own execution: the timer is armed once when the top-level statement begins and changing the GUC mid-statement does not re-arm it. The value IS applied (current_setting inside the body reads it) which is exactly why the pattern looks like it works. Verified on this PG 17 local: CREATE FUNCTION _t() RETURNS int LANGUAGE plpgsql SET statement_timeout = '1s' AS 'BEGIN PERFORM pg_sleep(3); RETURN 1; END'; SET statement_timeout='60s'; SELECT _t(); returns 1 and does NOT error, while current_setting('statement_timeout') inside the body reads 1s. This is the same PG 17 behaviour [[FIX-703]] recorded for procedures, never generalised to functions. THIS IS NOT THEORETICAL: rebuild_entity_search_index carries statement_timeout=1200s and ran 21,638 s on 2026-08-31, ended only by the postgres role's statement_timeout=6h, taking prod's REST API down from 06:11 to the manual reset at 23:01 ([[FIX-1123]]). 89 public functions carry the pattern. Triage by gap between believed and real bound: the heavy writers are the dangerous ones because the real ceiling is the role's 6h -- rebuild_entity_connections (believed 60min), rebuild_entity_connections_contracts (30min), rebuild_financial_entity_donation_totals / _full / _received_totals (30min each), rebuild_entity_connections_appointments / _external / _votes / _votes_full (15min), rebuild_entity_search_index (1200s), refresh_jurisdiction_page_cache and refresh_official_content_ids (600s). The request-path ones (get_official_page 5s, get_agency_page 3s, the 2s trigger helpers) are mostly benign because the authenticator role's statement_timeout=8s is a REAL bound that arms at statement start and is tighter than most of them -- but any request-path function whose proconfig claims MORE than 8s (get_financial_entity_naics 120s, get_group_donor_totals 30s, get_official_donor_rollup_full 300s, chord_contract_flows_full 300s, get_top_connected_officials 60s, get_quality_counts 60s, get_proposal_counts_by_agency 60s) is claiming a bound it does not have and is silently getting 8s instead, which is a DIFFERENT bug in the opposite direction. Fixes to evaluate: (a) for pg_cron-driven writers, an EXTERNAL watchdog is the only thing that works -- FIX-1030's per-unit watchdog shape -- but see [[FIX-1125]], it must be able to fork; (b) for callers that CAN re-arm, issue SET LOCAL statement_timeout as its own statement BEFORE the call so the next statement arms from it; (c) at minimum relabel every inert proconfig so nobody reads it as a guard again. Cross-ref [[FIX-703]] [[FIX-1123]] [[FIX-1125]] [[FIX-1030]]. HALF 1 LANDED 2026-09-13 (cc-124), no Fixes: trailer — stripping alone makes no bound real. CENSUS: 91 not 89, clone and prod byte-identical, all prokind=f — A 24 (request path), B 21 (service_role RPC), C1 15 (called from a COMMITting procedure), C2 5 (single-transaction procedure), D 10 (direct-pg script), E 16 (trigger/helper/inner); docs/audits/2026-09-13-fix1128-proconfig-census.tsv. ALSO MEASURED: a proconfig cannot LOOSEN either (2s session, 30s proconfig, cancelled at 2.001s, identical to no proconfig), so the strip is behaviour-neutral in both directions. STRIP: supabase/migrations/20260913000000_fix1128_reset_inert_statement_timeout.sql, applied local and prod, 91 to 0 on both, remaining-proconfig md5 identical 91/91 0 changed. GUARD: pnpm check:proconfig (scripts/check-proconfig-timeouts.mjs, 18 fixture assertions, seventh blocking check in tests.yml), baselined at that migration because history carries the pattern 183 times. HALF 2 (cc-125) SCOPE IS NOT WHAT THE DESIGN ASSUMED: the per-unit C1 re-arm is dead (experiment 3), so the only mechanism that bounds a pg_cron procedure is the job's command string (SET statement_timeout='...'; CALL ...), which bounds the WHOLE CALL, not a unit; a per-unit budget needs the procedure to time itself against a budget and stop, the cron_job_budget shape ([[FIX-1063]] [[FIX-1125]]); and whatever it does must handle experiment 5 — one caught cancel unbounds every unit after it. (ii) Worse, the replacement is false too: SET statement_timeout = 'N'; CALL public.proc() in a pg_cron command string does not bound the six census procedures, it stops them running — a multi-statement pg_cron command executes in an IMPLICIT TRANSACTION BLOCK and a procedure cannot COMMIT inside one, so the run dies at its first COMMIT about 10 ms in with 'invalid transaction termination' and zero units executed. - 🟡 M — **official_homepage_stats_mv full-scans financial_relationships, and a covering index alone will not change that** — MEASURED under [[FIX-1133]], not built — see docs/audits/fr-index-census-2026-09.md. official_homepage_stats_mv's defining query reads every to_type='official' row of financial_relationships with no to_id predicate: SELECT to_id, count(*) FILTER (rt='donation'), count(*), sum(amount_cents) FILTER (...) FROM financial_relationships WHERE to_type='official' GROUP BY to_id. The prod plan is a Parallel Seq Scan of the whole 4,932 MB heap, filtering out 59.6% of rows. Note it does NOT ride financial_relationships_derivation, which is what the FIX-1133 premise assumed. THE MEASUREMENT, on the prod-scale clone (10.4M rows): the planner's Parallel Seq Scan costs 442,306 buffers (431,714 read) and 1,543.7 ms. A candidate covering partial index (to_id) INCLUDE (relationship_type, amount_cents) WHERE to_type='official' — 200 MB over 4.2M rows, about 250 MB on prod — gives a Parallel Index Only Scan at 182,716 buffers (36,828 read) and 628.8 ms. That is 2.42x on total buffers, 11.72x on physical reads, 2.45x on time. THE CATCH, and the reason this is a FIX rather than a one-line index build: THE PLANNER WILL NOT TAKE IT. With the candidate index present it still chose the seq scan. With enable_seqscan=off it chose a Bitmap Heap Scan on financial_relationships_to — 315,773 reads and 4,456 ms, WORSE than the seq scan it replaced. Only enable_seqscan=off AND enable_bitmapscan=off produced the index-only plan. So building the index on its own would add about 250 MB to an 18-index table (see [[FIX-1133]] — index bytes times index count is the vacuum budget), add one more sweep to every vacuum pass, and change nothing at runtime. THE WORK is therefore twofold: add the index AND make the daily refresh actually take it. Options, cheapest first: (1) set a session-scoped cost GUC in the refresh path only, which is narrow but fragile; (2) reshape the aggregate so the index-only path wins on cost honestly; (3) reconsider whether the MV needs the all-relationship-types count(*) at all, since the donation-only half could ride an existing sibling. - 🟠 S — **nightly.yml starts 4.5-11.5h after its 02:00 UTC cron, and the FEC drop probe rides only in the fec-phase that the drift can kill** — nightly.yml is scheduled cron: 0 2 * * * but has actually STARTED between 06:43 and 13:51 UTC on every run since 2026-08-27 — 4.5 to 11.5 hours late. GitHub Actions queues scheduled workflows hardest at the top of the hour, and the FIX-903 header in packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/drop-check.ts already documents ~3.5h of that queueing as a known constant; the drift has since roughly tripled. TWO CONSEQUENCES, and the second is the one that costs data. (1) The start time is now unpredictable enough that the nightly can land inside windows it was placed to avoid — the 05:45-09:00 blackout the heavy-op rule protects, and the 06:00 UTC refresh-derived-mvs daily, which is the co-tenancy question FIX-1152 had to rule out by hand on 2026-09-06 (nightly 06:54:07 vs the daily 06:00:00-06:05:30, a 48-minute gap that happened to be clean and might not be next time). (2) The FIX-903 FEC drop probe (indivDropPending) runs ONLY inside the fec-phase job. A fec-phase that is killed at its timeout-minutes cap, or that never starts because the run queued past its own window, loses the day's collection AND the probe that would have noticed — the probe is downstream of exactly the failure it exists to detect. FIX SHAPE, two independent halves: (a) move the cron off the top of the hour to a :17-style minute, which is the standard mitigation for GHA scheduled-queue contention and costs nothing; (b) run the drop probe in the enrichment-light or tail job as WELL as in fec-phase, so a late or killed fec-phase still records whether a new indiv drop is pending. The probe is a best-effort HEAD that fails closed, so a second call site is cheap and cannot itself launch an ingest. BUILD THIS TOGETHER WITH [[FIX-1060]] — both are single edits to nightly.yml and landing them separately means two workflow-file churns for one file. Measured from gh run list on 2026-09-06 for the last ten scheduled nightly runs. Cross-ref [[FIX-903]], [[FIX-1060]], [[FIX-1156]], [[FIX-1011]], [[FIX-1152]], [[FIX-998]]. APPEND 2026-09-08 (SHIPPED, receipt pending). TWO CHANGES. (1) CRON: nightly.yml '0 2 * * *' -> '17 2 * * *'. Drift baseline, the ten scheduled starts to 2026-09-07 via gh run list --workflow nightly.yml --event schedule: 08:40, 07:57, 08:10, 07:21, 06:51, 06:55, 06:59, 06:43, 06:54, 07:03 UTC — 4h44 to 6h41 late, EVERY day, never once near the slot. Off-the-top-of-the-hour is the standard GHA scheduled-queue mitigation; the hour stays 02 so an on-time fec-phase lands ahead of the hour-04 vacuums and the 06:00 derived-MV daily instead of inside the 05:45-09:00 prod-read blackout the current drift puts it in. (2) THE PROBE IS NOW RECORDED FROM enrichment-light. Gate chain confirmed in the tree exactly as suspected: shouldProbeDrop = shouldLoadResumeState && !resumeStatePresent, and shouldLoadResumeState = runFec && !isWeekly && !held (fec-hold.ts:38, :47-52), so on the split-phase path the probe was skipped BY CONSTRUCTION in every phase but fec, and inside fec it is skipped on Sundays and whenever the hold is on. And the result was persisted NOWHERE: pipeline_state held only fec_bulk_cycle_watermarks and fec_indiv_watermark, and no data_sync_log metadata key mentioned the probe — the sole trace was a console line in a GHA log. - 🟡 S — **ec-vacuum-analyze is a fixed daily cost on quiet days — gate it on pg_class rather than running it unconditionally** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-09-09. ec-vacuum-analyze (jobid 6, daily 04:30 UTC, added by FIX-1152) ran 124 s on Tue 09-08 and 133 s on Wed 09-09. Both are QUIET days: no Sunday FEC ingest, no remediation apply, no bulk rewrite. The read that matters is what it found — entity_connections at the 06:00 daily's vm_before probe was 98.7 pct all-visible with 14,352 dead tuples on 09-08 and 100.0 pct with 0 dead on 09-09, i.e. the table was already in the state the vacuum exists to restore, and the run still cost two minutes of prod IO inside the 04:30 slot. FIX-1152 sized these slots off the FAILURE case (the 09-04/09-05 dailies at 1,015 s and 1,012 s with EC at 79 pct all-visible) and the fix worked -- Wed's rebuild_entity_search_index unit came in at 241.1 s. The cost being questioned here is the floor, not the ceiling. DIRECTION: gate the daily EC vacuum on a pg_class-keyed predicate rather than the clock -- skip when relallvisible/relpages is above a threshold (95 pct is the obvious first cut, given the observed failure mode begins below 90) AND n_dead_tup is under the tuned autovacuum trigger. The state is already read every morning by check_rebuild_autovacuum_status() and recorded by the 06:00 daily's vm_before, so the predicate needs no new instrumentation. Keep the unconditional run on the day after any bulk rewrite -- that is the case the standing FIX-943 rule covers and it must not be gated away. NOT URGENT: two minutes a day inside a quiet 04:30 window is a small bill and the current job is CORRECT, merely unconditional. File-only from cc-117; no change made. Cross-ref [[FIX-1152]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1133]], [[FIX-884]]. APPEND 2026-09-12 (THE SERIES NOW COLLECTS ITSELF): [[FIX-1176]]'s receipts file carries ec-vacuum-analyze and fe-vacuum-analyze durations in its section 4 every night, and docs/receipts/bands.json holds the <= 140 s quiet-day ceiling as a checked band rather than a remembered number. First prod reading through it, 2026-09-12: ec 9.0 s at 04:30 and fe 10.8 s at 04:50, both far under the 124-133 s the series opened with -- so the fixed-cost argument this bullet rests on needs re-reading against the newer numbers before the pg_class gate is built. APPEND 2026-09-14 (cc-119, SERIES THROUGH 09-13 PLUS A STAMP-SITE CORRECTION). Six days from the receipts files' section 4 -- ec 123.6 / 132.6 / 88.0 / 8.9 / 9.0 / 97.3 s and fe 107.9 / 10.9 / 15.6 / 10.9 / 10.8 / 16.2 s for 09-08..09-13; the 09-14 04:30 point is after this session. The cost is NOT fixed: ec swings 8.9 s to 132.6 s, a 15x range, and the two quiet days (09-11, 09-12) sit at ~9 s while 09-13 rebounded to 97.3 s. That is write-volume-keyed, which is the opposite of the premise this bullet was filed on, and it is also why a pg_class gate would save ~9 s on the days it fires and nothing on the days that cost real time. THE STAMP-SITE CORRECTION, and it undercuts the bullet's own evidence: vm_before is computed at refresh_derived_mvs RUN START, which for the daily is 06:00 UTC -- ninety minutes AFTER ec-vacuum-analyze at 04:30. So 'the table was already 100 percent all-visible before the vacuum' was read from a POST-vacuum probe and is not evidence about the pre-vacuum state at all (rule 107). Nothing in the tree measures entity_connections' visibility map immediately BEFORE the 04:30 vacuum, so the question this bullet asks is currently unanswerable from the instruments that exist. No gate built; the next move is an instrument, not a gate.  APPEND 2026-09-19 (cc-136, context only, no change): a second table now asks this bullet's instrument question, and answers it in the opposite direction. entity_tags (see [[FIX-1178]]) is exactly the table a pg_class gate would correctly decline to vacuum -- 98.1 percent all-visible, 71,198 dead against a 268,044 trigger, autovacuum already firing 17 minutes after each bulk rewrite -- and yet it is the table whose daily job has crept +32 percent per row. So the gate this bullet proposes would be right AND the job would still be slow, because the cost is 1.72x heap bloat, which no vacuum decision reaches. Two consequences for the gate's design: the pg_class predicate should be stated in terms the reader can act on (dead-tuple headroom against the trigger, which is what a vacuum fixes), and the thing worth ALSO recording per run is a bloat ratio (relpages against reltuples x avg_width), which is what a vacuum does not fix and which no job currently stamps anywhere. APPEND 2026-09-19 (cc-132, A SECOND EC SLOT WAS OFFERED AND REFUSED; the two numbers that refused it): cc-132 carried an option to add ec-vacuum-analyze-pm at 0 13 * * *, conditional on BOTH (i) the 04:30 job's 30-day median wall <= 140 s and (ii) EC accumulating >= 10k dead tuples/h between vacuums measured INSIDE the landing window. (i) PASSES: 17 firings in 30 days, median 123.6 s, avg 322.4 s, max 3,147.9 s (the 09-17 set-1 outlier), zero failures. (ii) FAILS: two readings 59 minutes apart inside the window, 2026-09-19 17:46:04 and 18:45:18 UTC, both read entity_connections at 0 dead tuples and 100.00 percent all-visible, 13.3 hours after its 04:31:39 vacuum — a rate of 0/h. No second slot was scheduled. BUT THE REFUSAL RESTS ON A SATURDAY, and that is a gate-design problem this bullet should own rather than a settled answer. The same instrument on the two preceding days reads ~20,500 dead/h (457,118 dead at 2026-09-18 02:49, cc-131) and ~12,300 dead/h (228,963 dead at 2026-09-18 23:07, from the receipts file's 'Visibility map now' block, which is stamped at generation time — 23:07 the evening BEFORE its nominal day — not at 06:00). Either would have passed (ii) comfortably. So the gate as written decides a seven-day schedule from whichever day the landing window happens to fall on, which is the same error class as cc-131's 03:00-trough reading one level up: the fix is not to loosen the threshold but to state which POPULATION the rate must be measured over (a weekday, or a trailing-7-day maximum), per rule 127. Two further notes for whoever builds the pg_class gate. First, this bullet's 2026-09-14 append is confirmed rather than superseded: EC's cost is write-volume-keyed, and the 0/h Saturday against 20,500/h Thursday is the sharpest instance of that yet measured. Second, and this is the instrument gap that matters more than the gate: cc-132's drain check found that a sub-second ec-crawl firing is AMBIGUOUS — ec_crawl_gate() returned run false / reason cycle_cooldown / 'last cycle closed 256 min ago, minimum interval is 360 min' at 19:33:21, and by FIX-1111's deliberate logging asymmetry (only backoff writes a data_sync_log row) that firing wrote no row at all, so entity_connections_rebuild shows a GAP at 19:30 where financial_entity_totals_refresh shows complete. A reader checking 'is EC caught up' from wall time or from data_sync_log cannot distinguish caught-up from cooling-down; the satisfiable form is ec_crawl_gate()'s own reason plus the entity_connections_donations watermark. - 🟡 S — **A supervised prod session longer than ~48 minutes reports financial_entity_totals_refresh stale, because a skipped firing correctly does not advance the freshness clock** — Found while building [[FIX-950]] (2026-09-11); not a defect in it, an unpaid interaction between two correct behaviours. check_rollup_freshness() and list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() both count ONLY status='complete' ([[FIX-1140]]), so a firing that stands down for a supervised prod session writes 'skipped' and the freshness clock keeps running — which is the honest reading, nothing happened. But the thresholds are derived from each pipeline's own cadence at 1.5x (report) and 2.5x (escalate), and the fastest crawl arms have very short cadences. Measured on prod 2026-09-11 from list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines(): financial_entity_totals_refresh cadence 0.50h, reports at 0.8h, escalates at 1.3h; entity_connections_rebuild 7.75h/11.6h/19.4h; donor_rollup_refresh 12h/18h/30h; everything else 24h or slower. So a hold under ~45 min is invisible, a hold past 48 min produces a 'stale rollup: financial_entity_totals_refresh' report, and past 78 min an escalation — for a session that is doing exactly what it is supposed to. The FIX-950 receipt was sized at 35 min specifically to stay under it. The mechanism to fix it already exists and is already read by the census: rollup_watch_overrides.held_since / hold_reason, which list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() consults to NULL out report_after_hours and escalate_after_hours. Fix shape: claimProdSession() sets held_since + hold_reason on the fast-cadence pipelines (or on all guarded pipelines) and clears them on release, in the same best-effort way it writes the pipeline_state label — never able to fail the claim. Open question worth deciding first: whether suppression should be scoped to the pipelines a hold can actually affect (the guarded set) or to all of them, since a hold does not stop a GHA-driven pipeline from being genuinely late for its own reasons. Documented meanwhile in docs/ops/prod-holds.md. Cross-ref [[FIX-950]], [[FIX-1140]], [[FIX-1011]], [[FIX-1135]]. MECHANISM BUILT by cc-133 (cd81917c, local); STAYS OPEN for the receipt. claimProdSession() upserts held_since/hold_reason for the GUARDED set only, derived at claim time from [[FIX-1190]]'s mapping - the open question in this bullet was decided that way (D1(a)): a hold cannot make a GHA- or Vercel-driven pipeline late for its own reasons, so suppressing a threshold a session cannot affect would make the hold a blindfold rather than a mute. No migration: list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() already NULLs both thresholds on held and canary-check gates on !w.held. Measured on the clone: 16 rows, not 17 - entity_connection_stats_rebuild is retired and the upsert's retired_at guard correctly skipped it - all 16 reading back as held:true with both thresholds NULL, and zero session rows after release. CLOSES ON: a hold longer than 48 minutes on prod with no stale rollup: financial_entity_totals_refresh report and no escalation from the nightly canary. No qualifying hold yet (cc-141): no supervised prod session ran and none exceeded 48 minutes, so financial_entity_totals_refresh produced nothing to read. Far below the ~48 min point at which financial_entity_totals_refresh would report stale, so check_rollup_freshness was not read and this run adds nothing to the case. Still waiting on a long supervised session.  APPEND 2026-09-22 (cc-144, second reading — still no evidence): same three windows as [[FIX-1177]]'s append (38 s / 46 s / 60 s). financial_entity_totals_refresh was never at risk of reporting stale and was not read. cc-187 (2026-10-04): the post-release half is closed. check_rollup_freshness() measures hours_since_complete (and so stale, and the canary's escalation) from GREATEST(last complete, newest status='skipped' row since it whose metadata->>'skip_reason' starts 'prod session held: '). A deliberate stand-down restarts the clock from the look. hours_since_data keeps the un-restarted age, and last_held_skip_at names the skip. A skip older than the last complete changes nothing. With no complete at all a skip invents nothing (status missing). A skip is still never a closure: last_complete_at and the registry's cadence read only 'complete'. Thresholds are unchanged (prod 02:13 UTC: FE 0.50 h, report 0.8, escalate 1.3). Note that skip_reason lives in data_sync_log.metadata, not in a column.
