- 🟠 S — **The 'cron' kill switch is dead — nothing reads pipeline_state.kill_switches.cron, and FLAGS.CRON_ENABLED has no consumer, but the admin UI offers both** — Found by enumerating the three hold mechanisms for [[FIX-950]]'s precedence doc (2026-09-11), which required answering 'what reads kill_switches.cron' by reading every caller rather than assuming. The answer is nothing. isKillSwitchEnabled(db, 'cron') is never called anywhere in apps/ or packages/ — the only live callers of that function pass 'mapbox_geocode', 'ai_summaries' and 'cf_auto_mitigation'. FLAGS.CRON_ENABLED in packages/data/src/feature-flags.ts is defined and has zero consumers. The env half, CRON_DISABLED=true, IS live, but only in two Vercel cron routes: apps/civitics/app/api/cron/nightly-sync/route.ts and apps/civitics/app/api/cron/notify-followers/route.ts. It does not affect the GitHub-Actions nightly and it does not affect a single one of the 38 pg_cron jobs. WHY THIS MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING TIDY-UP: 'cron' is listed in KillSwitchName and is therefore rendered and flippable from /api/admin/kill-switches alongside switches that DO work. An operator who flips it off expecting the platform's scheduled work to stop would be wrong, would get no feedback saying so, and would then be surprised by a rollup rebuild landing mid-incident. A dead switch that looks live is worse than no switch. Three candidate shapes, pick one: (a) delete 'cron' from KillSwitchName and the admin route, leaving CRON_DISABLED as the honest env-only control for the two Vercel routes it actually covers; (b) make it real by having the pg_cron guard family and the nightly consult it the way they now consult prod_session_state() — note [[FIX-950]] deliberately did NOT do this, because merging the three hold mechanisms was out of scope; (c) keep it and rename it to what it actually gates (vercel_cron_routes). (a) is the cheapest and the most honest; (b) is the most useful and is a real design decision about whether an indefinite operator-level platform-wide stop should exist at all. Documented meanwhile in docs/ops/prod-holds.md section 3. Cross-ref [[FIX-950]], [[FIX-311]]. CLOSED by cc-133 (1f4159a6, local) via option (a). Removed 'cron' from KillSwitchName, ENV_RULES and the admin route's ALLOWED_NAMES, and deleted FLAGS.CRON_ENABLED; CRON_DISABLED stays as the honest env-only control for the two Vercel routes. (b) and (c) stay unbuilt, and (b) deliberately so - whether an indefinite operator-level platform-wide stop should exist at all is a different question from removing a switch that never worked, and what exists today for stopping scheduled work is the supervised session, which is bounded by a live process rather than by somebody remembering to undo it. THE PART THAT WAS NOT DELETION: prod's pipeline_state.kill_switches row still carries a cron key and kill_switch_events still carries its history, neither migrated - rewriting a JSONB blob to satisfy a TypeScript union is a schema change in service of a type. That left two casts over old data, loadMap's and auto-trip-evaluator's Object.entries key cast, so both now go through a new filterKillSwitchesMap() parse boundary. OPERATIONS.md's CRON_DISABLED row said 'Stops nightly cron from running', which is the exact wrong belief this bullet is about, and was corrected. <!--id:FIX-1173-->
- 🟡 M — **Twenty-odd operator-run prod-writing scripts still do not claim the supervised prod session — FIX-950 wrapped only the five FR-rewrite landings** — Filed by [[FIX-950]] at its own boundary (2026-09-11). D3b says the safe path is the default path (rule 47) and withProdSession() implements it, but FIX-950 wired it into exactly the five scripts that call drainFrRewrite — remediate-role-ineligible-holders, remediate-cross-person-misattribution, remediate-fec-emit-residue, remediate-bound-cross-person, merge-same-person-official-dupes — because those are the family cc-119's Monday apply belongs to and the family whose contention FIX-1165 actually measured. Everything else in packages/data/package.json that ends ':prod' and writes is still on the honour system. The ones that write, from the 2026-09-11 census: data:merge-dc-jurisdiction:prod, data:merge-territory-jurisdictions:prod, data:merge-unicameral-legislatures:prod, data:merge-fe-collisions:prod, data:backfill-gb-seat-counts:prod, data:backfill-gb-attribution:prod, data:donor-rollup:sweep:prod, data:donor-rollup:bulk:prod, data:treemap:sweep:prod, data:backfill-donor-totals:prod, data:backfill-small-dollar:prod, data:backfill-vote-stats:prod, data:backfill-contract-flow-rollups:prod, data:backfill-sector-affinity:prod, data:backfill-agency-staffing:prod, data:backfill-treemap-individuals:prod, data:move-stub-senate-votes:prod, data:recategorize-complexity-tags:prod, data:backfill:sld-links:prod. The three donor-rollup/treemap sweeps are the most valuable of these to wrap, because they drive the very procedures the guards now cover and can therefore contend with a session that is itself driving them. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE: --allow-prod is NOT the right hook and must not be used as one. It is a low-level guard inside createAdminClient() and the SCHEDULED pipelines carry it too — data:nightly:ci, data:fec-bulk:ci, data:irs990:ci, data:usaspending-bulk:ci, data:audit:ci. Auto-claiming on --allow-prod would make the nightly claim the session and then read its own lock as held, skipping every writer phase it just claimed the box to run. The correct hook is the entry point of an OPERATOR-RUN script, which is what runUnderProdSession() takes. Fix shape: one line per script tail, the same edit FIX-950 made five times, plus a per-script expectedMinutes. Worth doing in one pass with a test that greps package.json for ':prod' scripts and asserts each named entry point calls runUnderProdSession, so the next one added cannot silently be outside the interlock. Cross-ref [[FIX-950]], [[FIX-1165]], [[FIX-1074]]. CLOSED by cc-134 (d9a1c030, local). The census from package.json rather than from this bullet: 41 :prod entries, 11 wrapped before (six files - the five FR-rewrite landings plus restore-fec-ids), 30 not. Twenty-one script files gained the FIX-950 entry-point wrapper in the existing shape, taking it to 35 of 41 entries; six entries are audited reads. expectedMinutes is from each script's own measured history where one exists (the clone's data_sync_log, restored from prod): donor-rollup 240 from donor_rollup_refresh's 188-minute max over 27 runs, treemap 90 from 46.3, vote-stats / agency-staffing / contract-flow 10 from 1.2 / 1.0 / 0.0; 30 where there is none, 5 for set-vercel-plan-pro, which is one upsert. THREE THINGS THE BULLET DID NOT ANTICIPATE. (a) Three dual-mode sweeps (donor-rollup-sweep, donor-rollup-bulk, treemap-global-sweep) share one file between a writer and a --status read, so the wrapper carries a deliberate --status bypass: a read that claimed the interlock would hold all seventeen guarded pipelines and REFUSE under another session, making the cheapest check the one you cannot run when you need it. (b) audit-cross-person-misattribution.ts said READ-ONLY in its header and is not - it runs a genuine UPDATE over the whole non-colliding population inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK, which commits no data but writes a heap tuple per row, takes the row locks, and leaves them all dead; wrapped, header corrected. (c) grep over the .ts misses a writer whose SQL lives in a sibling .sql file - recategorize-proposal-complexity-tags.ts reads sql/recategorize-proposal-complexity-tags.sql and shows zero write verbs in its own source. prod-scripts-interlock.test.ts is the standing guard: every :prod key either names a file containing runUnderProdSession( or sits in an explicit READ_ONLY map with a one-line reason, the map is audited against package.json so a renamed writer cannot return under a stale exemption, and the hook is deliberately NOT --allow-prod because the scheduled :ci pipelines carry it and would self-lock. <!--id:FIX-1174-->
- 🟡 M — **CC prompts and reports live in the repo, and a report's claims are checkable** — Craig is the transport in both directions of the CC loop: he copies a Cowork prompt into Claude Code, and pastes CC's report back. Neither leg needs a human. Build: (a) .claude/cc.config.json names a promptsDir and reportsDir, both resolved against the MAIN checkout via git rev-parse --git-common-dir so they work identically from a session:worktree; (b) a /cc N slash command reads the newest cc-prompt-N-*.md from promptsDir, runs it, and writes its after-commit report to docs/cc/reports/cc-N.md; (c) the report opens with YAML front matter (cc, prompt, started_at, finished_at, head_before, head_after, commits, fixes_closed, fixes_filed, fixes_reopened, migrations_pushed, prod_writes, ci, stopped_items) which pnpm cc:verify N checks against git and done.log — every commit sha exists and is an ancestor of origin/main, head_after is on trunk, every claimed close derives CLOSED with a row naming one of this run's shas, every filed id has a marker, every reopened id derives OPEN on a reopen row, and ci green is cross-checked with gh when available; (d) docs/cc/PROMPT_TEMPLATE.md holds the invariant prompt sections and the rules checklist so a rule change is one edit instead of remembered each time; (e) a Stop hook runs fixes:check and cc:verify so a report whose claims the tree contradicts never reaches the chat. Status derivation comes from FIX-1016, whose fixes:status --json is what the verifier consumes. Cross-ref [[FIX-1016]]. <!--id:FIX-1175-->
- 🟡 M — **Daily receipts file: a read-only receipts:daily script and a nightly tail job commit docs/receipts/YYYY-MM-DD.md + .json** — The same dozen reads are banked by hand in every Cowork prompt — the nightly's createdAt vs its slot, per-phase status/duration/peak_rss_mb, the hour-04 vacuum durations, the 06:00 daily's unit_seconds and vm_before, a dozen pg_cron jobs against their bands, the FEC drop probe, the FIX-950 interlock's footprint, the canary's conditions, the SLD linkage residual. None of it needs a model. A read-only pnpm receipts:daily writes docs/receipts/YYYY-MM-DD.md (human) + .json (machine) with every number next to the query that produced it, verdicts computed against a hand-edited docs/receipts/bands.json (no band = no-band, never in-band), and a receipts job chained after enrichment-tail-phase in nightly.yml (if: always(), contents: write, docs-only push to main) commits it. Turns receipt = the next scheduled run into receipt = tomorrow's file and shrinks the no-prod-contact-while-a-receipt-is-taken window to the job's own duration. Nominal day = the slot's NIGHTLY_SLOT_OFFSET_HOURS rule from weekly-gate.ts, so the file is named for the day the run itself gated on. Pattern B: the first scheduled firing is the receipt. Cross-ref FIX-1163, FIX-1169, FIX-1152, FIX-950, FIX-1175. - 🟡 S — **A FIX-950 interlock skip is invisible to every freshness reader — check_rollup_freshness and the FIX-1011 registry both count only status='complete'** — Read for [[FIX-1176]] Phase 0 (2026-09-12), answering the question cc-121 left open. Both readers filter on complete and nothing else. check_rollup_freshness (20260903060000_fix973b) derives last_complete_at / hours_since_complete / stale from a single last_good CTE, WHERE pipeline = p_pipeline AND status = 'complete'. list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines (20260903000000_fix1135_1059_1011) measures cadence over a closures CTE, WHERE a.status = 'complete', and closures_any likewise. So a firing that the FIX-950 prod-session guard turned into a status='skipped' row with skip_reason 'prod session held: …' is, to both, indistinguishable from a firing that never happened: the freshness clock keeps climbing and the cadence median is computed over the gap as if the job had missed it. THE TWO CONSEQUENCES ARE DIFFERENT SIZES. (a) Cosmetic and already handled: any census column built on the freshness verdict renders a deliberate skip as 'missing' — FIX-1176's receipts file sidesteps this by reading data_sync_log directly for status + skip_reason and emitting verdict skipped(reason) as its own value, never in-band and never missing. (b) The real one: a hold long enough to span escalate_after_hours (cadence x 2.5 — 60h for a daily rollup, ~420h for a weekly) makes the canary escalate ON A DELIBERATE OPERATOR ACTION, and the operator gets a red X for using the interlock correctly. No current hold is close (FIX-950's are minutes), so this is latent, not live. NOT FIXED HERE by decision — cc-123's Out of scope says file only. The honest fix is a third state rather than counting skipped as a closure: a skip is not evidence the rollup is fresh, so folding it into last_complete_at would be worse than the bug. Candidate shape: carry last_skipped_at + last_skip_reason alongside last_complete_at and suppress escalation (not the report) while the most recent row is a prod_session skip. Cross-ref FIX-950, FIX-1011, FIX-1148, FIX-1135, FIX-973, FIX-944, FIX-1176. MECHANISM BUILT by cc-133 (cd81917c, local); STAYS OPEN for the receipt. Resolved the other way than the candidate shape in this bullet: rather than a third state in check_rollup_freshness, the session now HOLDS the guarded pipelines for its duration and the existing held suppression does the work - so neither check_rollup_freshness nor the FIX-1011 registry changed, and a skip still never counts as a closure. The release clears only holds whose hold_reason carries the prefix 'prod session held: ' (the same prefix the guard procedures write into skip_reason), so a human-declared hold is never cleared by a session and a human hold is never taken over. Because a hold SUPPRESSES instruments, a leftover one is itself a finding: new canary condition prod_session_hold_stale (report tier) fires when session-prefixed holds exist and the lock does not, proved on the clone by SIGKILLing a held claim. CLOSES ON: the same receipt as [[FIX-1172]]. cc-134 (d80a7a28): the instrument for gate (f) of the drain-and-wait block is now a command - pnpm --filter @civitics/data data:census:cancellations:prod reads 57014/min from postgres_logs and front-door 5xx from edge_logs through the Logs API, prints both against their gates, and exits non-zero when either fails. It opens no Postgres connection, which is what makes it readable during the wedge it exists to report. Smoke run 2026-09-18T22:29:15Z to 23:29:15Z: 2 cancellations, 0.0333/min, ratio 1.01x of the 0.033/min baseline, last closed front-door bucket 0 of 1208 = 0.00 percent, both PASS, exit 0 - which independently reproduces cc-129's baseline to two decimal places. The receipt that CLOSES this FIX is unchanged and still Monday's: a supervised hold longer than 48 minutes on prod with no stale-rollup report for financial_entity_totals_refresh and no escalation from the nightly canary. So the receipt did not fire and cannot be claimed. Three of the four fr-rewrite landing scripts do it: DrainOptions.printTable's own comment says 'The three remediation scripts already print it at their dry-run planning stage -- before the go-ahead, which is the point of it (FIX-1165 c) -- so they pass false to avoid a second copy at execution time.' remediate-fec-emit-residue.ts is the fourth and does neither. - 🟠 S — **fec_emit_runs leaks a never-completed row per nightly per incomplete cycle-source, and Guard 1 keys on the newest row** — complete_at is stamped only at the FIX-754 run_state clear (index.ts:2518), i.e. at CYCLE completion. A nightly that opens an emit run for a cycle-source it does not finish leaves the row open forever, and the next nightly opens another. Prod 2026-09-14 shows three such rows already, from two nights: 96260b92 (2024/fec_bulk_pac, started 2026-09-12T22:47:37Z), 5697a031 (2026/fec_bulk_pac, 2026-09-12T22:48:48Z) and b09496d6 (2024/fec_bulk_pac, 2026-09-13T22:53:52Z), all keys=0, all complete_at NULL. WHY IT IS NOT COSMETIC: audit-fec-emit-residue.ts Guard 1 takes the newest run for the slice by started_at -- deliberately NOT the newest COMPLETE one, because anti-joining an older set would delete rows this week's run legitimately re-emitted -- and refuses when that row is incomplete, with no --force. So one orphan row makes the audit permanently unrunnable for its slice. (2024, fec_bulk_pac) is in that state now and cannot be audited at all. (2026, fec_bulk_pac) was in it on 09-13 and only escaped because the 09-14 run happened to complete; the same night's 2024 arm did not. The guard is right and the leak is what is wrong. FIX SHAPE, and the choice matters: either close the run row on the same exit paths that abandon the cycle -- a terminal status distinct from complete, so Guard 1 can tell 'abandoned' from 'still running' and refuse only on the latter -- or stop opening a run row until the cycle actually starts emitting. The first is better because an abandoned run's partial key set is still evidence about what got emitted before the abandonment. Either way Guard 1's predicate should become 'newest row that is complete OR terminally abandoned', never 'newest row'. Cross-ref [[FIX-1106]], [[FIX-754]], [[FIX-995]], [[FIX-957]]. **SHIPPED 2026-09-14 (cc-126) IN A DIFFERENT SHAPE — the premise above is wrong in the direction that matters, and the read is what changed it.** This bullet assumes the orphan rows are PARTIAL and proposes a terminal 'abandoned' status so the guard can tell abandoned from running. **They are not partial: each of the three holds a FULL key set — 135,192 / 111,729 / 135,192 — and the two cycle-2024 rows from consecutive nightlies hold byte-identical counts.** The keys column reads 0 only because it is written at the stamp. Reading the branch rather than inferring: the pas2 arm reaches openEmitSink for every cycle in CYCLES on every fec phase — it sits AHEAD of the FIX-193 indiv watermark short-circuit and has no gate of its own — while stampEmitRunsComplete stamps cycleSinks, filtered to the ONE cycle whose indiv work completed. The indiv arms cannot produce this leak on the FIX-754 skip path, because 'complete in prior run — skipping' takes a branch in which openEmitSink is never evaluated, so no row is opened at all. SO THE FIX IS TWO PARTS, NOT A STATUS COLUMN. **(B1)** the pas2 arm stamps ITSELF, per cycle, at the end of its own stage — admissible where the indiv arms' single stamp is not, because it is one un-cursored batch with no resume and FIX-686's loud-abort contract THROWS rather than returning short, so there is no prefix it could stamp; cycleSinks now excludes fec_bulk_pac. **(B2)** superseded_at / superseded_by (migration 20260914000100, pushed to prod 2026-09-14): at the next begin() for a slice, an older incomplete row is superseded, its TRUE key count written into keys from the pre-delete snapshot, and its keys deleted — one statement, and the run_id inequality leaves a resumed run alone. Guard 1 now walks newest-first: complete -> use it; superseded with keys=0 -> skip; superseded with keys>0 -> REFUSE naming it (a prefix WAS written, which is the whole reason the guard is 'newest' and not 'newest complete'); neither -> REFUSE as before. Closure is Pattern B — the receipt is the next scheduled nightly showing every pre-existing orphan superseded with zero live keys and the night's pac rows stamped per cycle. cc-141 could NOT confirm the supersession on prod, and the bullet stays open. Both fec_emit_runs and fec_emit_keys are UNLOGGED (pg_class.relpersistence = u), so PostgreSQL TRUNCATED them during the 2026-09-15 15:09:48 UTC crash recovery (see [[FIX-969]]). The three 09-12/13 open pac rows named above (96260b92, 5697a031, b09496d6) and the 09-14 complete indiv run 84470d3b were destroyed then, NOT superseded: fec_emit_runs holds 6 rows, every one started 09-19 or later, with superseded_at set on NONE and open rows = 0. The drop night therefore had nothing older to supersede, and the FIX-1184 path in emit-set.ts:119-140 has still never been exercised against prod. A zero open-row count is the right state but is not evidence for the mechanism.  APPEND 2026-09-22 (cc-144, READ ONLY — the leak shape did NOT recur): read the ledger after Monday's weekday nightly (fec phase 23:44:54-23:50:01 UTC on 09-21) and fec_emit_runs holds exactly the six rows cc-141 saw, every one with complete_at set and superseded_at NULL. Monday opened NO row at all — not an incomplete one. The reason is that begin() in emit-set.ts is what INSERTs the row, and a weekday nightly whose fec phase finds no new bulk inputs never reaches it, so there is nothing to leak. So the leak needs a nightly that STARTS a slice and does not finish it, which a no-input weekday run cannot do. Also worth recording: the (2024, fec_bulk_pac) orphan this bullet names as 'what it is today' is GONE — both the 09-19 and 09-20 2024 pac rows are complete — so the supersession logic already on trunk is doing its job. Guard 1 consequently refused nothing across all three cc-144 audits. <!--id:FIX-1184-->
- 🟠 M — **No in-backend per-job bound exists for a COMMITting pg_cron procedure — pick the replacement for the command-string route** — cc-125 measured FIX-1128 Half 2's plan and it is unbuildable. SET statement_timeout = 'N'; CALL public.proc() in a pg_cron command string does NOT bound any of the six census procedures — it stops them running: a pg_cron command with more than one statement executes in an IMPLICIT TRANSACTION BLOCK, and a procedure cannot COMMIT inside one, so the run dies at its first COMMIT about 10 ms in with 'invalid transaction termination' and ZERO units executed. It is not the SET: SELECT 1; CALL proc fails identically, while the same CALL alone succeeds. Four cases on the clone's live scheduler plus two transaction-boundary escapes that also fail, in docs/audits/2026-09-14-fix1128-half2-census.md section 4. Same rule as cc-124's experiment 2 (atomic context implies no COMMIT) on a different surface; cc-124 experiment 6 measured a SELECT of a non-COMMITting SQL function and the generalisation to PROCEDUREs was never re-measured. SO THE FIX-1063 cron_job_budget WATCHDOG IS THE ONLY PER-JOB BOUND THERE IS, and [[FIX-1125]] is the standing objection to relying on it alone: it must fork to act, and it is starved by exactly the condition it exists to end. Measured on prod, all 11 rows of cron_job_budget_action: the watchdog fires late by 4.8 s to 973.9 s past budget on a */2 (120 s) cadence, and SIX of the eleven were more than one full cadence late (286.9 / 315.9 / 973.9 / 846.9 / 176.4 / 125.1 s) — so the effective bound is budget plus an unbounded tail, not budget. Unwind after the cancel signal adds a median 12 s and once 249.4 s. THREE OPTIONS TO EVALUATE, none built: (a) dblink per firing — a single-statement command calling a function that opens one connection and issues SET then CALL as SEPARATE statements, which works because the two are separate round trips; costs one extra backend per firing, which is the FIX-1125 starvation class but ONE backend per job rather than one per unit, and dblink is available-but-not-installed on both databases so it is a security-surface decision; (b) a per-job role carrying the bound as a role-level GUC — REFUSED TODAY, cron.alter_job(username) needs superuser and postgres is not superuser on Supabase (pg_user.usesuper = f, local and prod), so it needs Supabase support or is dead; (c) lower the global ceiling, ALTER ROLE postgres IN DATABASE postgres SET statement_timeout, today 6 h — the ONE in-backend mechanism proven to bound a whole CALL across COMMITs (it is what ended FIX-1123's 21,638 s run), and the census separates cleanly because every healthy run fits under 7,125.6 s while every incident starts at 12,546.6 s, so a 3 h ceiling would cut every incident and no healthy run; the cost is that it applies to every postgres-role statement including migrations and interactive sessions. Supersedes the general command-string sweep Half 2 planned to file. Cross-ref [[FIX-1128]] [[FIX-1125]] [[FIX-1063]] [[FIX-1123]] [[FIX-1030]]. cc-127 RAN THE PHASE 0 CENSUS AND THE D3 GATE FIRED — no migration was written and nothing was pushed to prod (docs/audits/2026-09-14-fix1185-ceiling.md). - 🟡 S — **Receipts cron-jobs table lets a job with no data_sync_log writer INHERIT its neighbour's verdict — vacuum jobs reported 'skipped' on someone else's skip_reason** — receipts-daily.ts builds its cron-jobs table with a LATERAL that matches ANY data_sync_log row whose pipeline is LIKE 'pg_cron%' within plus-or-minus 90 seconds of the firing. A job that writes no data_sync_log row of its own therefore picks up whichever neighbouring job's row happens to land in that window, and reports that row's status and skip_reason as its own. Seen in docs/receipts/2026-09-15.md: ec-vacuum-analyze (132.9 s, squarely inside its own 0-140 s band) and officials-vacuum-analyze (3.8 s) both reported 'skipped' carrying financial_entity_totals_refresh's skip_reason. The verdict is not merely cosmetic — it feeds the receipt's health columns, so a genuinely healthy vacuum can read as skipped and a genuinely skipped one can read as fine. A job with no data_sync_log writer must resolve to its cron.job_run_details status alone, and the LATERAL should key on the job, not on a time window. Filed by cc-128 from the FIX-1187 design section 7. CLOSED by cc-133 (0b37ebca, local). Q_CRON_JOBS now keys the data_sync_log LATERAL on the job's DERIVED pipeline - cron.job.command -> the procedure it CALLs -> the pipeline literal in its prosrc, shared with claimProdSession()'s hold set as packages/data/src/lib/cron-job-pipelines.ts - with the +/-90 s window kept only as the disambiguator for the four shared pipelines. A NULL pipeline correlates to nothing by construction, so verdictFor() falls through to the cron status and needed no change; a test feeds it the old inherited shape to record that it was never the bug. WIDER THAN FILED: measured old-vs-new in one prod read session, 12 of 38 jobs had an inherited correlation, not 2, and in every one the borrowed row came from a different pipeline (financial_entity_totals_refresh ten times - fe-crawl runs */30 so its rows blanket the timeline - and entity_connections_rebuild twice). Four of the twelve DO have a pipeline and were borrowing FE's because their own writer had not logged inside the window. Only three verdicts move, all three pipeline-less vacuum jobs that were inheriting; zero non-inherited verdicts change. The table gains a pipeline column. <!--id:FIX-1190-->
- 🔴 M — **A deferred tail relocates its cost into a window the FIX-950 interlock cannot guard — set 1's deferred EC vacuum collided with set 2 and put the front door at 51.7 percent errors** — Measured on the FIX-1187 prod apply (cc-129, 2026-09-17). Two distinct failures of the back-to-back-sets assumption, both caused by what set 1 DEFERRED. First: set 1 deferred 87,206 dead entity_connections tuples to ec-vacuum-analyze (daily 04:30). Set 2 started 04:05:54 and was still in its FR move when that vacuum fired. VACUUM jobs carry NO prod_session_state guard — only the 20 procedures whose prosrc references it are deferred — so the interlock could not coordinate them. Two IO-bound writers on a 2-vCPU box with 256MB shared_buffers: set 2's UPDATE reached 66 minutes for ~26k rows where set 1 had moved 40,649 rows in 265.8s, ec-vacuum-analyze took 3,147.9s against a normal few seconds, fe-vacuum-analyze FAILED at 04:50 with job startup timeout (pg_cron could not fork — a mode recorded at ~0 percent in the 18:00-05:00 UTC band), and edge_logs showed 14x500 + 1x401 of 29 requests = 51.7 percent errors with cancellations at 2.800/min against a 0.033/min baseline. Set 2 was cancelled by operator decision and rolled back atomically; errors fell to 5.1 percent within ten minutes. Second: set 1 deferred 14 entity_connections_rebuild and 7 financial_entity_totals_refresh firings, which resumed the instant the session released at 03:53 — so set 2's first attempt at 04:01 was REFUSED by the preflight with 2 live writers. That refusal is correct and --force was not used, but it means a second set can never follow a first immediately. The FIX-1183 cost table should price a deferred step's collision risk against the NEXT set, and a multi-set landing needs a drain-and-wait step between sets. Evidence in docs/audits/2026-09-17-fix1187-prod-apply.md section 3. cc-130 is the first run to actually take the drain-and-wait readings this bullet asks for, and two of them are unsatisfiable AS WRITTEN. (a) 'no partial EC units, max wall <= 131 s' describes a state prod does not visit: partial is the DESIGNED terminal status of the bounded-crawl arm (unit cap reached, resumable), and over 30 hours prod logged exactly one complete EC unit against dozens of partial and skipped. (c) 'EC n_dead_tup <= 5,000' cannot coexist with 'start >= 90 min clear of 04:25-05:00': EC's only vacuum owner is 04:30 daily, it accumulates ~25,000 dead tuples an hour (0 dead at 05:19:41 to 457,118 at 23:23), so <= 5,000 means starting within ~12 minutes of the vacuum the same rule forbids being near — and the 05:45-09:00 blackout pushes the earliest legal start to 09:00. A usable version needs a ratio, or a vacuum that runs near the window. Readings that DID hold: watchdogs 30/30, 57014 at exactly the 0.033/min baseline, front-door 5xx 0.069 percent. cc-131 (2026-09-18) is this bullet's FIRST SATISFIABLE INSTANCE: eleven of thirteen gates PASS, and both failures are the clock rather than the data (a daily vacuum 31 minutes out at reading time, and the window being Saturday). The two gates cc-130 proved unsatisfiable are replaced and both now read cleanly. 'No partial unit' becomes 'nothing running at start and no unit wall over its own interval' - partial is the crawl arm's DESIGNED terminal status, so the old form failed on correct behaviour; it reads ec-crawl 4/4 at 0.1-0.3 s against a 15-minute interval. 'At most 5,000 dead tuples on EC' becomes a headroom-and-rate gate, (trigger - n_dead_tup) / rate > 2x expected wall, which asks the question that actually matters - can autovacuum trip DURING the set - and reads 65,371 dead tuples of headroom where the old form read 457,118 against 5,000. Readings, all 2026-09-18: unguarded-owner census derived from cron.job joined to pg_proc gives 16 unguarded of 34 active (12 vacuums, both */2 watchdogs, abuse-events-retention, platform-counts-daily); watchdogs 60/60 succeeded in 60 min with zero non-succeeded firings of any job and no startup timeout; prod_session_state clear with 0 live writers; 57014 at 1 per 60 min = 0.0167/min against a 0.033/min baseline; front door 0 of 501 requests 5xx over 15 min. The rate gate carries a caveat it has earned: 0 dead tuples/hour measured across 70 minutes at 03:00-04:00 UTC, the quietest hour, is the weakest possible input to a rate gate even though the collector is provably live, and cc-132 must re-read it INSIDE the Saturday window rather than reuse it. An owner name with no cron.job row renders NOT SCHEDULED, which is the FIX-1165 orphan signal by another route; an unread owners map renders ? rather than NOT SCHEDULED, so a missing connection cannot manufacture a dozen orphans. - 🔴 M — **A large FR/EC landing starves pg_cron of workers while its derived EC work drains — both 2-minute watchdogs fail with job startup timeout, so budget enforcement is offline exactly when it is needed** — Measured after the FIX-1187 set-1 prod apply (cc-129, 2026-09-17). Set 1 deleted 87,206 entity_connections money edges and moved 40,649 financial_relationships rows. The incremental EC arm then has to re-derive all of that, one bounded unit per ec-crawl firing. Units that normally run 0-131s grew to 956s and beyond: the 05:30 run was still executing at 16 minutes, longer than the job's own 15-minute interval, so pg_cron queues behind its own overrun and the arm runs effectively continuously. The box saturation that produces is enough that pg_cron CANNOT FORK a worker: cron-job-budget-watchdog and derived-mvs-unit-watchdog both failed with job startup timeout at 05:36, 05:38, 05:42 and 05:44, each after 10-32 seconds, and fe-vacuum-analyze failed the same way at 04:50. Front door measured 19.5 percent errors in the 05:29-05:44 window (19x500 + 12x504 of 164 requests) — worse than the 5.1 percent ten minutes earlier, and this is at the lowest-traffic hour of the day. Two things follow. First, the budget watchdog is the only in-backend bound for a COMMITting pg_cron procedure (see [[FIX-1185]] / [[FIX-1128]]), so a landing that starves the forker disables the one mechanism that would cancel a runaway — the failure mode CLAUDE.md already names as the case the watchdog cannot cover. Second, this is the FIX-1074 convention unpaid: a landing owns the DERIVED work its rewrite creates, not just the watermark correctness of it, and neither the FIX-1183 cost table nor --defer-tails prices the post-landing EC drain at all. Candidate handling: drain the EC arm under the landing's own session before releasing it, or widen p_max_units for a bounded catch-up window, or hold the interlock until the derived backlog is measured clear. Evidence in docs/audits/2026-09-17-fix1187-prod-apply.md sections 3 and 4, and cross-refs [[FIX-1191]] [[FIX-1193]]. cc-130 WIDENS this: the starvation is not specific to a landing's derived EC work. Of 158 job startup timeout failures on 2026-09-17, 117 fell in 04:00-09:00 (set 1's drain, the known mode) but 41 fell in 14:00-15:00 — during contract-flow-rollups-refresh, an ORDINARY SCHEDULED JOB with no landing anywhere near it. In the 15:00 hour alone cron-job-budget-watchdog failed to fork 14 times. So any sufficiently long job starves the forker, and the bullet's ownership question is broader than a landing's post-hoc EC drain. For scale on the drain itself: set 1's donations_incr_windows arm crawled windows 2/16 to 13/16 from 05:30 to 11:30 at 410-956 s per unit and 27k-32k rows each, then the entity_connection_stats_windows arm restarted at window 1/16 at 14:45 (1,887.1 s, 0 rows) and reached 15/16 by 23:15. cc-131 (2026-09-18) adds the follow-through on the fe-vacuum-analyze casualty this bullet already names. It failed 2026-09-17 04:50 with job startup timeout and is the ONLY non-succeeded firing of any vacuum job in nine days; FE's last_vacuum is consequently still 2026-09-16 04:50 with vacuum_count 1. FE happens to be fine at 99.9 percent all-visible so the miss cost little this time, but the shape is the point - the landing's starvation removes the maintenance job that exists to clean up after the landing, which is the FIX-1074 ownership question in its sharpest form. Alongside it, ec-vacuum-analyze ran 3,147.9 s (52m 28s) that same morning against 9-133 s on each of the eight preceding days, a 24-350x blow-up with set 1's churn the only candidate, and the 09-17 receipts show that job SKIPPED under the FIX-950 interlock the day set 1 landed. For scale on the other side: by 2026-09-18 02:49 the drain has fully caught up - ec-crawl units run 0.1-0.3 s and fe-crawl 0.1-0.2 s, with zero dead-tuple accumulation measured over 70 minutes, so the post-landing backlog clears in well under two days. NO CHANGE from cc-133's hold work, checked rather than assumed: the two every-two-minutes watchdogs (enforce_cron_job_budgets, enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget) are UNGUARDED - they do not consult prod_session_state() and they INSERT no data_sync_log row of their own, so they resolve no pipeline in [[FIX-1190]]'s mapping and are not in the [[FIX-1172]] hold set. A supervised session therefore neither defers them nor suppresses anything about them, which is the right answer: the watchdog is the one instrument that must keep running while a human holds the box. Measured on prod 2026-09-21 — both functions are SECURITY INVOKER (`prosecdef=f`) and owned by `postgres`; `service_role` DOES hold EXECUTE on both (Supabase's default grant, which survived because every REVOKE in the family names PUBLIC/anon/authenticated and never service_role) but has `has_schema_privilege('service_role','cron','USAGE')=false` and `pg_has_role('service_role','pg_signal_backend','MEMBER')=false`, so as INVOKER the read dies at the cron schema gate (the table SELECT grant is present and unreachable without schema USAGE) and the cancel would be refused anyway. `postgres` is NOT superuser (`rolsuper=f`) but IS a member of `pg_signal_backend`, which is the actual mechanism FIX-1030's comment describes. - 🟠 S — **refresh-disposable-emails monthly workflow has failed at push since 2026-09-03 — the repo pre-push hook aborts create-pull-request** — Run 33769138373 (2026-09-03, schedule) failed with '[pre-push] fixes:check:trunk failed — push aborted' then 'failed to push some refs'. The root prepare script wires core.hooksPath=.githooks on pnpm install, so peter-evans/create-pull-request's git push runs the repo's own pre-push hook inside CI, where fixes:check:trunk cannot pass (shallow checkout, no trunk ref). The 08-03 run predates that wiring and succeeded. Consequence: the branch chore/refresh-disposable-emails was frozen at its 08-03 content for six weeks and the blocklist went unrefreshed; cc-135 landed that content by hand as e738116a and closed PR #3, but 2026-10-03 fails the same way unless the workflow either skips hooks for its own push or does not run the install that wires hooksPath. Note the hook is doing its job — the fix is to scope it, not to disable it. Cross-refs FIX-462, FIX-794.  APPEND 2026-09-19 (cc-136, CLOSED, local): shipped as ad623386. THE BULLET'S DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG IN ITS MECHANISM, and the real one is worse. Run 33769138373 did not fail because no trunk ref resolved. actions/checkout@v4 fetched +808fc5a2:refs/remotes/origin/main at --depth=1, so origin/main resolves fine -- it just reaches exactly one commit. The failure text names FIX-960 (54d9206d, aa278b7a) and FIX-962 (09ab3ab9) as recorded-as-done-but-never-shipped; all three are ancestors of origin/main today and were on 2026-09-03. A false positive. The mechanism: create-pull-request fetches its long-lived branch at --depth=11, that branch was cut from main on 2026-08-03, so its ancestry IS early-August main and those objects become present while origin/main stays depth 1 -- and merge-base --is-ancestor then answers false for genuine ancestors. Reproduced on a real depth-1 clone 2026-09-19: fetch chore/refresh-disposable-emails at depth 11, 09ab3ab9 present, origin/main still 1 commit, is-ancestor exits 1. Filed as [[FIX-1200]]. The receipts bot passes the same hook only by luck -- its object store is depth 1 so every done.log SHA classifies unknown and the gate is inert (nightly run 35403626528, trailersScanned 0). So in CI the gate was never meaningful in either direction. The fix scopes the TRUNK gate only: under GITHUB_ACTIONS, when the repo is shallow or no trunk ref resolves, it prints a reason and steps aside. The typecheck gate is untouched and still runs. Not --no-verify (drops typecheck too, and for humans), not --ignore-scripts (unwires the hook for every other consumer of pnpm install). scripts/test-pre-push-hook.mjs, 15 assertions, pins the scope in both directions. RECEIPT: dispatch run 35415836771 (2026-09-19 02:30 UTC, workflow_dispatch on main) SUCCEEDED in 49 s; its log carries 'fixes:check:trunk SKIPPED under GITHUB_ACTIONS: shallow checkout' immediately after 'typecheck clean', the push to chore/refresh-disposable-emails went through, and PR #4 opened (+698/-1 across the two allowed paths) -- six weeks of upstream drift, awaiting Craig's review per the workflow's own design. The SCHEDULED receipt is still the 2026-10-03 11:00 UTC run; a dispatch tests the push path, not the schedule. APPEND 2026-09-20 (cc-138): the guard now self-detects, and this bullet's early exit is belt-and-braces rather than the mechanism. [[FIX-1200]] moved the shallow-clone test inside classifySha(), where it is computed once per run and yields unknown instead of not-ancestor — so the CI false-positive class is fixed in the tool and the gate would be correct under GITHUB_ACTIONS even without the hook stepping aside. The early exit is KEPT: it does not depend on the guard being right, and it saves the typecheck minute on every CI push that could not have learned anything from the check. What changed is its meaning, and the hook's comment now says so. <!--id:FIX-1199-->
- 🟡 S — **fixes-sync trunk guard cannot tell 'not an ancestor' from 'trunk is shallow so I cannot tell' — classifySha keys its escape hatch on object presence, not on trunk reachability** — Surfaced by [[FIX-1199]]. scripts/fixes-sync.mjs classifySha() returns 'unknown' (and is skipped) only when git cat-file -e fails, i.e. when the OBJECT is absent. It never asks whether TRUNK is reachable. In a shallow checkout git rev-list origin/main yields one commit and git merge-base --is-ancestor answers 1 for genuine ancestors, so any done.log SHA that happens to be present is reported as an off-trunk violation. Reproduced 2026-09-19 on a real depth-1 clone: after a depth-11 fetch of a sibling branch (what peter-evans/create-pull-request does), 09ab3ab9 is present, origin/main still resolves 1 commit, and merge-base --is-ancestor 09ab3ab9 origin/main exits 1 although the full clone answers ancestor. That is exactly run 33769138373, which named FIX-960 and FIX-962 as recorded-but-never-shipped. FIX-1199 scoped the pre-push hook so CI no longer reaches this path, and fixes-integrity.yml checks out fetch-depth 0, so there is no live consumer today — but the guard is still wrong for any shallow clone and the failure mode is a confident false accusation rather than an error. Fix: have classifySha (or resolveTrunkRef) consult git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository and downgrade every not-ancestor verdict to unknown when trunk is shallow, with a warn line naming the degradation, so the guard fails open loudly instead of closed wrongly. Test alongside scripts/test-trunk-guard.mjs. Cross-refs [[FIX-461]], [[FIX-1199]]. CLOSED 2026-09-20 (cc-138). classifySha() now computes trunk reachability ONCE per run and classifies every SHA unknown — never not-ancestor — when the repository is shallow or no trunk ref resolves, printing one reason line. The old escape was per-SHA and keyed on git cat-file -e, i.e. on whether the OBJECT was present, which is precisely what the failing shape defeats: a depth-1 clone that then fetches a SIBLING branch more deeply has the objects AND a resolving origin/main while rev-list origin/main yields ONE commit, so merge-base --is-ancestor answered 1 for genuine ancestors (run 33769138373 accused FIX-960 and FIX-962, all of whose SHAs were on main). PREDICATE CHOSEN: git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository, NOT rev-list --count >= the oldest done.log SHA's distance — the count test needs the history it is trying to prove it has, and in the failing case that count is 1, so any distance derived from it is meaningless rather than merely small; the truncated-before-that-SHA case is already covered by the per-SHA cat-file escape, which stays for the non-shallow path. Drift detection is untouched: unknown already means no evidence either way downstream, evaluateTrunkViolations skips an ID whose SHAs are all unknown, and the FIX-461 filter only drops on an explicit not-ancestor. The test builds cc-136's exact fixture and asserts BOTH halves of it — the clone really is shallow and origin/main really is one commit, AND an on-trunk SHA's object really is present — because without those the case would pass against the old code; paired with the inverse, a full clone with a real off-trunk SHA, which must and does still accuse. Two harness bugs surfaced building it, both of which had made the fixture lie: git clone --depth is SILENTLY IGNORED for a local-path source (it needs file://, with three slashes on Windows), and a --depth deeper than the whole history un-shallows the repo outright; and runScript threw stderr away on a SUCCESSFUL run, so a warning printed by a script that exits 0 was invisible to every assertion. The pre-push hook keeps its CI early exit — it is an optimisation now rather than a workaround, and the comment says so. Cross-ref [[FIX-1199]], [[FIX-461]]. <!--id:FIX-1200-->

But it did not reach TAIL_OWNERS in packages/data/src/scripts/fec-orphan-classify.ts around line 1021, a separate exported constant whose vacuum entry is the literal string 'fr-vacuum-analyze  financial_relationships  Mon 01:00'. printDeferredTail() prints it, and four remediation scripts call that: merge-same-person-official-dupes, remediate-cross-person-misattribution, remediate-role-ineligible-holders and remediate-fec-emit-residue. FIX-1191 moved fr-vacuum-analyze to 0 3 * * * on prod on 2026-09-19, so that string is now WRONG, and it was printed wrong by the FIX-1187 set-2 apply itself at 18:5x UTC the same evening, about 40 minutes before the migration landed. Two more copies of the same stale fact sit in remediate-fec-emit-residue.ts, in the module header around line 30 and in the over-threshold console warning around line 211, both reading 'fr-vacuum-analyze (Mon 01:00)'. The operator-facing banner is exactly where a stale owner schedule does damage: it is the line an operator reads to decide whether deferring the vacuum is safe, and it now understates the collection by six days in the wrong direction. Fix is the FIX-1193 one applied a second time, since readOwnerSchedules() already exists and the tail table already proves the pattern: have printDeferredTail() take the live Map and render schedule and guarded per owner rather than carrying prose. Cross-ref [[FIX-1193]] [[FIX-1191]] [[FIX-1165]]. CLOSED 2026-09-20 (cc-138). TAIL_OWNERS no longer carries schedule text at all: each entry is a job NAME plus what that job collects, and printDeferredTail(kind, owners?) renders the schedule and guarded columns through ownerColumns() — the SAME function FIX-1193's tail cost table uses, imported rather than re-derived, so the banner and the table cannot disagree about what ? / NOT SCHEDULED / [INACTIVE] mean. The owners map comes from readOwnerSchedulesOnce(client), a per-client memoised readOwnerSchedules: the banner is printed from runVacuum / runMvsAndVacuum / runRollups, which are reached on several paths and NOT always after main() has read the owners, so threading the map through ~20 call sites would have passed it through unchanged at most of them; memoising keeps the one-query-per-run property and leaves printDeferredTail a pure function of its arguments, which is what makes it testable with stubbed rows. cc-132 section 9g said two more copies sit in remediate-fec-emit-residue.ts and THAT IS NOT WHAT THE TREE HELD: that script already calls printTailTable(..., owners) and its only stale copy was one doc comment; the real second copy was a STALE UNTIL THEIR OWN SCHEDULE string literal carrying Sun + Wed 08:00 UTC, present in BOTH merge-same-person-official-dupes.ts and remediate-cross-person-misattribution.ts, and the source-scan test found the second one on its first run. Those two name the workflow (rebuild-entity-connections.yml) instead of a clock, because their owner is a GitHub Actions schedule and there is no cron.job row to read live. The guard is a source scan asserting no (Mon|Tue|...) The call graph does the work and nothing about the instrument has to be believed. THE STAMP SITS IN ITS OWN EXCEPTION HANDLER, which is the one decision here worth arguing about: this function's existing discipline is that each inner watchdog runs inside its own handler so one failing never blinds the other, and an instrument must obey that rule more strictly than the things it measures -- an unhandled error in the stamp would take down the CANCEL path P2-A exists to keep alive, and a watchdog that dies because its odometer jammed is worse than no odometer. A failed stamp surfaces as stamp_error in the payload and the watchdogs' results return regardless. The route's verdict line gains at=<iso> so the Vercel log itself carries the DB clock and the two instruments can be compared without a query; a payload without at prints at=? rather than at=undefined or dropping the segment, because a missing clock is exactly the reading that matters when the stamp is also missing. - 🔴 M — **The FIX-1074 drain's entity_connections stale-money-edge delete has never worked — two schema errors, hidden by a test that regexes the SQL string** — fr-rewrite-drain.ts step 1 (delete stale money edges) is wrong in two independent ways and has never executed successfully. (1) e.connection_type = ANY($2::text[]) compares an ENUM column to text and raises 42883 operator does not exist: connection_type = text. (2) e.evidence_id does not exist — the column is evidence_ids, uuid[]. Error (1) aborts the parse before (2) is reached, so only the first is visible. It survived because the single test asserted on the SQL TEXT with a regex (assert.match(del, /evidence_id = d.fr_id/)) and never executed it; a PREPARE against local Docker reproduces the failure instantly and always would have. Surfaced on prod in cc-144 at 2026-09-22 09:02 UTC, where it threw AFTER the landing's DELETE of 675 financial_relationships rows had already COMMITTED, leaving 675 stale entity_connections donation edges for one official (Everton Blair, overstating by 604,079 dollars). Those edges are unreclaimable by any scheduled work: the EC donations arm is incremental on financial_relationships.updated_at and a DELETED row has no updated_at, so nothing short of a full rebuild_entity_connections() will ever remove them. This is the [[FIX-1074]] hazard realised through a code defect rather than an omission — the landing owned its derived debt, tried to pay it, and the payment instruction was invalid. evidence_ids being an array also changes the semantics: an edge may only be deleted when EVERY id it rests on was deleted (<@), since one that lost only part of its evidence would take live evidence with it; such an edge is now counted and reported instead. Fixed here with the cast, the array containment predicate, a partial-staleness warning, and a test that PREPAREs the statement against the real schema. Cross-refs [[FIX-1106]], [[FIX-544]], [[FIX-693]]. <!--id:FIX-1210-->

- 🔴 S — **The FIX-950 interlock defers the claimant's own CALL — session:claim-prod then CALL of any guarded procedure logs skipped, so no guarded procedure can be run supervised** — Surfaced by cc-146 (2026-09-23) preparing the [[FIX-1212]] supervised bootstrap. prod_session_state() returns defer = held, where held is whether ANY backend holds the prod_supervised_session advisory lock; it never asks which backend. Every guarded pg_cron procedure checks defer before its first write and logs skipped. So the FIX-950 recipe for a supervised run (session:claim-prod, then CALL the procedure) defers the claimant's own CALL. MEASURED on local 2026-09-23: pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('prod_supervised_session')) then CALL public.refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental() from the SAME backend logged status skipped, skip_reason 'prod session held: (no label)'. The claim script is its own process, so a separate backend is no different. Consequence: no guarded procedure can be run supervised under the interlock that exists to protect supervised runs. The only way today is an unclaimed CALL, which lets every other guarded job (ec-crawl */15 avg 61 s max 721 s, fe-crawl */30, donor-rollup-refresh 09:00/12:00) fire beside it. Prod: the cc-147 runner claimed at 09:02:46Z, SET the GUC on its CALL connection, read held=true defer=false claimant_bypass=true, and its CALL ran (data_sync_log 0e7c8e74, partial, windows 1-2). - 🟠 M — **Next 14 caches supabase-js fetches in GET Route Handlers even with force-dynamic — 36 admin-client routes send no no-store signal** — Surfaced by cc-146 closing [[FIX-1208]]. Read from next@14.2.35's own source (server/future/route-modules/app-route/module.js and server/lib/patch-fetch.js), not the docs. In a GET Route Handler, export const dynamic = force-dynamic sets only staticGenerationStore.forceDynamic, and revalidate defaults to false (userland.revalidate ?? false). patch-fetch's auto-no-cache for an Authorization-header or POST fetch fires only when the store's revalidate === 0. So every supabase-js fetch is auto cache with revalidate false, a one-year Data Cache entry keyed on URL+body+headers, UNTIL something earlier in the same request lowers revalidate to 0: a fetch with cache no-store, cookies(), headers(), or noStore(). That is why the cron-watchdog route (its RPC was its only fetch) answered from one cached payload for 17 h while platform-snapshot's RPCs do reach the gateway: supabase-prometheus.ts:629 makes a no-store fetch before its get_supabase_cpu_max RPC at :720. The docs' claim that force-dynamic equals fetchCache force-no-store does not hold for a Route Handler in this version. CENSUS (grep, file level, 2026-09-23): 36 route.ts under apps/civitics/app export GET only, call createAdminClient(), and contain no cookies()/headers()/noStore/no-store; 33 of them export no revalidate. Three are crons: nightly-sync, notify-followers, platform-snapshot (its platform_alert_state reads may run before the no-store fetch). File level is not request order, so each needs its first-fetch order read. Probably also the real mechanism of the FIX-878 stale chord RPC in project memory. REMEDY candidates: per route, createAdminClient({ fetch: noStoreFetch }) (the FIX-1208 shape, shipped 07d193a5) or export const fetchCache = force-no-store; or make no-store the admin client's default inside Next (a behaviour change for ~90 app callers, so enumerate first). Verify each against edge_logs, never against the route's own response. Cross-refs [[FIX-1208]] [[FIX-1194]]. <!--id:FIX-1214-->

- 🟠 M — **GHA scheduled runs start 1.6-2.7 h after their slot and skip wholesale; a Vercel-cron dispatcher fires workflow_dispatch at the slot, the nightly is idempotent by nominal day, and schedule: stays as the free fallback** — Craig asked 2026-09-23 16:07 PDT whether Repository Dispatch would give more consistent GHA timings. Yes, with a dispatcher -- and it is workflow_dispatch through the REST API, not repository_dispatch: repository_dispatch is a webhook event for EXTERNAL systems that needs a new on: trigger and carries a free-form client_payload, while POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{file}/dispatches is the same mechanism with no on: change and per-workflow typed inputs, which is what the nominal-day rule needs. THE MEASURED PROBLEM (cc-150 read 2, gh run list, 2026-09-24 01:40 UTC): nightly.yml on 0 21 * * * since 09-10 -- 14 scheduled starts 09-10..09-23, createdAt minus 21:00 = 1.86 1.90 1.73 1.73 2.63 2.33 2.44 2.29 1.93 1.59 1.82 2.74 2.39 2.37 h (min 1.59 / median 2.11 / max 2.74), no missing day since 09-10 (09-08 was skipped outright under the old slot, FIX-1163 append 2026-09-09). platform-snapshot.yml (the FIX-1026 request-path pager, */10): 13 runs in 48 h against 288 advertised, gaps 132-315 min, mean 233 min -- worse than the ~hourly its own header states. sync-canary-check.yml (0 5): starts 3.67-5.25 h late every day for a month. GitHub applies an OFFSET specific to the cron hour and stable over days (rule 79) and does not pre-queue (rule 83); no cron edit can remove it. THE DESIGN (cc-150, ratified by Craig 09-23 16:43 PDT): D1 dispatch at the slot itself, 21:00 UTC, and prod_op_gate() check (a) nightly start constant moves 22:35 -> 21:00; D2 /api/cron/gha-dispatch?workflow=<file> on three Vercel crons (nightly.yml 0 21, sync-canary-check.yml 0 5, platform-snapshot.yml */10), a literal allowlist, a no-store fetch with a fine-grained PAT (GITHUB_DISPATCH_TOKEN, this repo only, Actions: Read and write) and a per-call liveness stamp pipeline_state.gha_dispatch_<stem> written on EVERY call via record_gha_dispatch() (rule 167 -- a 401/403 expired token or a 422 is stamped refused, never silent); D3 the nightly becomes idempotent by nominal day -- workflow_dispatch inputs slot_offset_hours/dispatched_by, nominal_day + dispatched_by stamped into the nightly_cron start and terminal rows, and a data:nightly:preflight step in fec-phase that exits already_ran when an automated trigger finds a running/complete/partial nightly_cron row for its nominal day, so the late scheduled run becomes a one-runner-minute no-op fallback that fully covers a dead dispatcher; D4 receipts section 1 reads ALL events (not --event schedule, which would have rendered every dispatched night missing), prints event/dispatched_by/offset per run and the dispatcher stamp as a liveness line, and the canary gains report-only gha_dispatch_refused / gha_dispatch_stale; D5 platform-snapshot keeps NO concurrency by design (FIX-1026). RECEIPT (rule 71 as rewritten: the next run AT ITS SLOT, dispatched or scheduled) is the first dispatched nightly -- event=workflow_dispatch, dispatched_by=vercel-cron, createdAt minus 21:00 under 5 min -- plus the same nominal day scheduled fallback concluding already_ran. Cross-ref [[FIX-1163]] [[FIX-1215]] [[FIX-1176]] [[FIX-1026]] [[FIX-1011]] [[FIX-1208]] [[FIX-1127]]. - 🟡 S — **Startup-timeout streaks count RUNS, so the */1 box-health-probe escalates a 6-minute fork stall that a */2 job needs 12 minutes to reach** — Rule 178 (a new */1 job recalibrates every alert that counts failures per run), surfaced by cc-149 section 5.1 and measured by cc-153. check_cron_job_health() escalates cron_startup_streak:<jobid> at 6 CONSECUTIVE startup-timeout runs (v_streak_n), sized when every sub-hourly job was */2 or slower: 6 runs = 12 min of a starved forker. box-health-probe (prod jobid 53, * * * * *) reaches 6 in 6 min. Measured on prod 2026-09-24 23:48 UTC over all retained history (from 07-26): the probe has had 0 startup timeouts since it went live at 09-24 02:02, so today it adds 0 escalations. The streak read as minutes ALONE (last - first + the job interval >= 12 min, runs ignored) would ADD 84 escalations (11 in the last 7 days), every one a short run on a slow job: a weekly or twice-daily job with a single lost firing spans days, which contradicts FIX-1073 (a lone startup timeout is weather). BUILT: escalate at runs >= 6 AND runs x the job interval >= 12 min. That reproduces the current decision on 87 of 87 historical streaks (2 of 2 in 7 days, 85 of 85 older, 0 demoted) and holds the probe to 12 runs = 12 min. The interval is the median gap between the job consecutive firings over the 52 h history (watchdogs 2.0, ec-crawl 15.0, fe-crawl 30.0 on prod), not start-time arithmetic: under stress pg_cron fires late and bunched (09-22 16:01:04, 16:02:07, 16:03:25, 16:04:06), and a span can undercount a */2 streak. The burst half is NOT built: [[FIX-1222]]. Cross-ref [[FIX-1073]] [[FIX-1194]]. <!--id:FIX-1220-->
- 🟡 S — **cron.job_run_details has no retention, and a 30-day purge is blocked: list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() reads it over 90 days and takes its FIX-1135 era boundary from ALL history** — Surfaced by cc-149 section 5.2; cc-153 read 4 STOPPED the build (its D2). pg_cron ships no retention. Prod 2026-09-24 23:52 UTC: 64,862 rows since 2026-06-29 08:00, heap 10.1 MB (12 MB total), one index (the runid pkey), no start_time index. Owner supabase_admin: postgres holds DELETE (with grant option) but cannot own an index, so none can be added. 16,270 rows are older than 30 days. Rows/day 1,486-1,613 before the */1 probe, 2,917 on 09-24 (partial day), about 3,050 steady. Every seq-scan reader grows with it (the probe 22 ms at 62k rows; prod_op_gate (d) 112-133 ms before cc-153). THE BLOCKER: the canary calls list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() with no argument, so p_lookback_days = 90: it reads job_run_details over 90 days (job_counts, and by_time: pipeline-to-job correlation within 90 s) and takes min(start_time) over ALL history (driver_start.first_firing, the FIX-1135 era boundary). A 30-day purge would move every era boundary to 30 days ago and leave a weekly rollup about 4 closures (3 gaps), under v_min_support = 4, so no weekly observed cadence could page. Every other live reader is 14 days or less: check_cron_job_escalations 336 h, receipts CRON_LOOKBACK_DAYS 14, get_ec_crawl_health 7 d, check_cron_job_health 52 h, prod_op_gate 14 d, record_box_health 1 d, enforce_cron_job_budgets running rows only (0 older than 30 d). A longer retention does not help: at 3,050/day, 100 days is about 305k rows, which puts the probe scan near 100 ms. So the order is to move list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines era boundary to cron_job_first_seen and its correlation window to 30 days, then purge at 30 days. Even that CAPS the table near 91k rows (1.4x today) rather than shrinking it. Build as a single-statement pg_cron DELETE (the first purge is 16,270 rows, under the 200k batching line) with a cron_job_budget row, at a slot such as 01:50 UTC. Its neighbours are officials-vacuum-analyze (Mon 01:30, 3 s) and dpr-vacuum-analyze (Sun/Wed 02:00, 4 s); the slot is outside the 05:45-09:00 blackout and the 21:00 nightly. Cross-ref [[FIX-1194]] [[FIX-1135]] [[FIX-1011]]. **cc-156 (2026-09-25):** built in 173a301f (migration 20260920160000, on Pro 03:47 UTC). N = 42 days: the smallest window in which every weekly pipeline on an observed cadence keeps v_min_support = 4 gaps (irs990, 190 h, binds: 4 closures at 35 d, 5 at 42 d); upper bound the probe's one scan, 20.2 ms at 65,290 rows now, ~40 ms at the ~128k rows 42 d holds (gate (d) ~46 ms). The era boundary is now the earlier of cron_job_first_seen.first_seen_at and the oldest retained firing (13 of 15 unchanged on prod, 2 earlier onto their ledger rows, output byte-identical), and correlation reads both sides over the same 42 d. Job cron-job-run-details-retention = prod jobid 54 at 51 1 * * * (01:51, not 01:50: the FIX-1141/1129/1146 guard refuses an even minute), one DELETE, cron_job_budget 300 s; first purge 986 rows. Closes on its first firing, 2026-09-26 01:51 UTC: rows older than 42 d before/after and its job_run_details wall. **cc-157 (2026-09-25):** not fired yet at 22:58 UTC: jobid 54 active, 0 job_run_details rows. Rows older than 42 d = 1,596 of 67,799 at 2026-09-25 22:58:22 UTC (986 at 03:15), oldest 2026-06-29 08:00. The receipt is the first firing, 2026-09-26 01:51 UTC, for the next docs-only session: that count before and after, and the job's own job_run_details row (status succeeded, wall; return_message carries DELETE n). <!--id:FIX-1221-->
- 🟡 S — **The startup-timeout burst counts RUNS across jobs, so the */1 probe doubles its sampling; the distinct-minutes rule cc-153 was given silences 2 of 13 historical paging days** — Rule 178, the burst half of [[FIX-1220]]; cc-153 stopped it on read 2. check_cron_job_health() escalates cron_startup_burst when one hourly bucket holds >= 10 startup-timeout runs across ALL jobs (v_burst_m). The threshold was sized while both */2 watchdogs fired on the same even minutes, so one stalled minute counted TWICE. Replayed on prod 2026-09-24 23:48 UTC over all retained history (from 07-26): runs >= 10 = 64 buckets on 13 days (6 in the last 7 days, all Tue 09-22 15:00-21:00). The rule cc-153 was given, DISTINCT minutes >= 10, gives 50 buckets on 11 days. It silences two paging days outright (08-26: max 11 runs = 6 minutes; 09-14: max 16 runs = 8 minutes) and demotes 09-22 16:00 (19 runs) and 20:00 (16). Its claim that a */1 job cannot fill a bucket alone fails by construction, because each probe firing is its own minute. It matches the old calibration only in a FULL stall where the probe also fails on odd minutes, and it halves the burst the day the probe is paused. Measured alternative: weight each failure by min(1, job interval / 2 min), i.e. count every job at the */2 cadence the threshold was sized on (the same interval [[FIX-1220]] already computes). It is exact on all 64 buckets, because every pre-probe job weighs 1. The probe counts as one more */2-rate sensor, so a full stall reaches 10 in about 6.7 min instead of 10. Counting (job, 2-minute slot) is also exact on the 64 threshold decisions, but it drops bunched firings under stress (09-22 16:00: 19 runs count 17). The probe had 0 startup timeouts in its first 22 h, so leaving the burst unchanged costs nothing measurable until a rule is chosen. Cross-ref [[FIX-1073]] [[FIX-1194]]. <!--id:FIX-1222-->
- 🟠 S — **The canary's derived rollup registry has timed out on every run since 2026-09-08: list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() takes 35.7 s against the 8 s role timeout, so the canary watched a 1-entry fallback literal for 17 days** — Found by cc-156 read 2 while re-reading list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() for [[FIX-1221]]. The canary calls it through PostgREST (authenticator statement_timeout 8 s) and has logged 'rollup registry query failed (non-fatal, falling back to the 1-entry literal): canceling statement due to statement timeout' on every run from 2026-09-08 09:11 UTC (09-07 09:47 still read 51 pipelines), so for 17 days the FIX-977/1135 derived registry watched nothing and the canary checked freshness for 1 pipeline. Nothing paged because the failure is a console.warn. Measured on prod 2026-09-25 03:11 UTC: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() = 35,709 ms, 3.27M shared-buffer hits, all of it by_time: a range predicate (run started_at BETWEEN firing start - 90 s AND end + 90 s) that can only nested-loop, 2,353 pg_cron runs x 64k job_run_details rows = 151M comparisons. It grows with the table, and the */1 box-health-probe doubled the table's daily rate on 09-24. The correlation window alone does not help (the 42-day window measured 89.6 s): the crawl arms' runs are all recent. Fix: join through the minute a run and a firing window share (the firing lists each minute its window touches, MATERIALIZED; the exact BETWEEN still decides), and SET enable_nestloop TO off on the function because the planner estimates the jsonb-LIKE runs CTE at 1 row and would otherwise choose the nested loop on a close call. Same output byte-for-byte on prod (52 pipelines, drivers, orphans), 422-431 ms. With the registry restored, the 09-25 03:1x state escalates 0 pipelines and reports 6. Receipt: the canary's next run logs 'rollup registry: 52 pipeline(s)'. Cross-ref [[FIX-977]] [[FIX-1135]] [[FIX-1221]]. <!--id:FIX-1223-->
- 🟡 S — **The canary's prod-session and session-hold detectors have read unknown on every GHA run since they shipped: sync-canary-check.yml gives buildDbUrl() no DSN** — Found by cc-156 §5.10; confirmed by cc-157 Phase 0. canary-check.ts fetchProdSessionStatus() (FIX-950, de8a9525, 2026-09-11) and fetchHoldStale() (FIX-1177/1172, cd81917c, 2026-09-17) both read through withClient(buildDbUrl(), ...), and buildDbUrl() (packages/data/src/lib/heavy-rebuild.ts) needs SUPABASE_DB_URL, a local NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, or NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL + SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD. sync-canary-check.yml's env carries NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY, ADMIN_EMAIL and RESEND_* and no DB password, so every run logs 'prod session read failed (non-fatal): buildDbUrl: need ...' then 'prod session: unknown (read failed)', and the same pair for session holds (runs 36120891482 09-25 09:53, 36096724716 09-25 05:00, 35982177366 09-24 09:36 UTC). Prod data_sync_log read 2026-09-25 22:58 UTC: of the canary_check meta rows since 09-11, 17 carry a prod_session key and 0 hold a read; 11 carry session_holds and 0 hold a read. So prod_session_overrun, prod_session_label_stale and prod_session_hold_stale have never been able to fire on prod, and the meta row's FIX-950 trail has been null since it shipped. Same shape as [[FIX-1223]]: a console.warn where an instrument should be. Fix: pass SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD in the workflow env exactly as nightly.yml's phase jobs do (the secret exists), and make a failed read loud: a null from either direct-pg detector raises the report-only canary key prod_session_read_failed (the posture of front_door_corroborator_unavailable), so the next env regression shows on the tile instead of in a log line. Closes on its receipt: the next 05:00 UTC canary run dispatched by /api/cron/gha-dispatch/sync-canary-check logging both session reads (prod session: a state; session holds: a state) and its meta row carrying both. **cc-157 (2026-09-25):** env + key landed in a6986bc9, pushed ~23:06 UTC; receipt = the 2026-09-26 05:00 UTC dispatched run. - 🟡 S — **fix:add can allocate an id another session already landed — fixes:check should fail a duplicate id marker and a trailer whose bullet does not match its commit** — Three collisions so far (cc-184 §4.9): FIX-1238 twice (cc-166 / cc-167) and FIX-1265 (cc-184 / cc-185). fix:add allocates max(FIXES.md, done.log, fixes-archive.md) + 1 from the LOCAL tree, so a session that has not pulled can allocate an id another session has already pushed, and nothing fails until a human notices two bullets, or a done.log row closing the wrong one. The workaround every prompt now restates (cc-187 used it): git pull --rebase main immediately before each fix:add, then git fetch and git grep the printed marker on origin/main, and re-allocate on a hit. Build the guard into the tooling: (a) fixes:check (and so the pre-push hook) FAILs when one <!--id:FIX-n--> marker appears on two live bullets, and (b) it FAILs when a Fixes:/Closes: trailer names an id whose bullet title does not match the FIX tag in that commit's subject. A reused id then cannot reach trunk silently. Cross-ref [[FIX-1016]], [[FIX-1243]]. **cc-190 (2026-10-04), the rule as built:** (a) duplicateIdMarkers reads docs/FIXES.md only; the archive keeps its historical FIX-194 duplicate, which fixes:status already resolves live-wins. (b) compares each Fixes:/Closes:/Reopens: id with the FIX tags in the commit OWN subject, since subjects never carry the bullet title. Shorthand siblings count (FIX-1044/1045, FIX-1014, 936, FIX-826..829, through), and a subject with no FIX tag is exempt. Its scope is rows done.log has not logged: on-trunk new entries plus the commits HEAD carries ahead of origin/main, because newEntries alone is trunk-filtered and never holds the commit a pre-push is pushing. 37 historical commits would fail it if widened, 1 of them since 09-20. cc-184 c2c968af is caught by (a) on rebase, not by (b): its subject and trailer agreed on FIX-1265. <!--id:FIX-1271--> <!--lane:hygiene-->

Clone read 2026-10-04 02:1x UTC: max(FR.updated_at) is 2026-09-03 01:34, and pipeline_state.donor_party_crawl carries full_rebuild_lag_days 30, so the lag is 29 d, under 30, and crawl is the right answer. Changing the assertion to crawl would make case (i) wrong-but-green, because every later assertion in it is full-mode: 16 windows, the cursor gone, watermark = cycle_target. Fix: derive the watermark from the procedure's own target (max(FR.updated_at) minus full_rebuild_lag_days minus a margin, read from donor_party_crawl), then re-run the heavy serial suite (CIVITICS_DB_HEAVY_TESTS=1, about 4 min a mode) to 0 fail. Cross-ref [[FIX-1212]], [[FIX-1216]]. <!--id:FIX-1272--> <!--lane:hygiene-->

It was cancelled at 21:15:16Z after 15m02s with zero steps and an empty runner_name. Three things compound. (1) The three enrichment jobs gate on if: !cancelled() && needs.fec-phase.outputs.already_ran != 'true'. A job-level cancel is not a run-level cancel, and an empty output reads as not-already-ran, so heavy, light and tail all ran. They wrote complete nightly_cron rows for nominal_day 2026-10-06 (21:25:47Z, 21:29:55Z and 21:30:51Z). (2) The late schedule: run is the designed fallback for a missed night. So the fallback stands down on the enrichment rows, and the night's FEC phase is lost with no retry. That phase holds congress_officials, congress_votes and the recent bills, promote-candidates, the FIX-1189 O1 bind, fec_bulk, edgar_daily and openstates_bulk_people. Past roughly **200 uuids** the URL exceeds Kong's header limit and the gateway returns 414 `URI too long` **before PostgREST ever sees the query**. `withDbTimeout` converts that into `{data: null}`, and the near-universal `?? []` / `data?.x` fallback at the call site turns a hard failure into an empty result on an HTTP 200. Nothing logs, nothing 500s, the page renders — just missing. **The bound is URL LENGTH at ~200 ids. It is NOT the 1,000-row PostgREST `max_rows` cap** — do not reason about this class in terms of row counts, and do not assume a list under 1,000 is safe. **Four independent prior instances**, each found by accident rather than by monitoring: [[FIX-509]] (treemap, 414 verified at ~356 uuids / ~13 KB), [[FIX-514]], [[FIX-774]] (established the 200 bound), [[FIX-899]] (officials directory rendered ZERO tag pills for every official for months; ~1,000 ids / ~40 KB; surfaced only because [[FIX-897]] added pills to that surface and they did not appear). **Census at HEAD e5056d8b** — 248 total `.in(` call sites across `apps/` + `packages/` (excluding node_modules and tests); of those, on the order of **96–108 pass an id-list VARIABLE and are not obviously chunked** (96 under the strict single-line regex below; ~108 under a looser hand-classification that also catches multi-line and spread forms). Recipes: total = `grep -rn '.in(' --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx apps packages | grep -v node_modules | grep -v '.test.ts' | wc -l`; candidates = the same grep narrowed to `.in("col", identifier)` with chunk/batch/slice/page-named variables filtered out. **Most are probably bounded in practice — classifying them is the whole job.** Per site, the question is a BOUND ASSESSMENT: what feeds this id list, and can it exceed ~200? Note `.in("status", [...])` over a small literal enum list is fine and common — those are not in scope. Sites where the list is a fixed-arity literal, a `.slice(0, N<=200)`, or provably capped upstream should be marked bounded and left alone (ideally with a one-line note recording the bound, so the next auditor does not re-derive it). Sites where an unbounded or growth-prone collection feeds the filter are real latent bugs: migrate onto `fetchChunkedByIds` from `apps/civitics/src/lib/paginate.ts` ([[FIX-901]]), which chunks at 200 and **surfaces failed chunks in its result object instead of swallowing them**. Prioritise request-path renders and API routes that feed user-visible surfaces — those are where a silent empty result reads as 'this entity has no data' rather than as an error. **Deliberately NOT bundled into [[FIX-901]]:** that was a small mechanical PR migrating three sites whose correct behaviour was already verified; this is open-ended investigation over ~100 sites and would have swallowed it. **Explicitly out of scope here:** a lint rule or codemod banning raw `.in()`. Tempting, but it would have to distinguish id lists from small enum lists, and that discrimination is a design question of its own. <!--id:FIX-902-->

- [x] 🔴 S — **An out-of-vocabulary `other` tag reaching an official's top-3 kills the ENTIRE nightly rule tagger — live on local, latent on prod** — **Filed, not fixed** — found while running the [[FIX-916]] verification, and it is a strictly sharper consequence of [[FIX-911]] than that bullet's 'display wart' framing. `tagOfficials()` reads official_sector_affinity_rollup, excludes ONLY `'Untagged'`, and then calls `assertIndustryVocabulary()`, which THROWS on any value outside VALID_INDUSTRIES. `other` is written into entity_tags by ai-classifier.ts ([[FIX-911]]), flows into the rollup like any other tag, and is NOT in VALID_INDUSTRIES — so the moment an `other`-tagged donor lands in an ACTIVE official's top-3 by dollars, the assert fires and takes down the **entire nightly rule tagger**: proposals, officials AND financial entities, all three phases, because runRuleBasedTagger() catches the throw at the top level and calls failSync. **This is not hypothetical — it is LIVE on local today.** Measured 2026-07-28: 6 active officials carried `other` at rank<=3 on the local prod-clone before [[FIX-916]] and 7 after, so `pnpm data:tag-rules` cannot complete on local at all, and the [[FIX-916]] run-twice proof had to invoke tagFinancialEntities() in isolation to get around it. **Prod is currently safe but only by margin, not by design**: all 8 prod `other` rollup rows sit at rank 11-13 of 13 carrying $1,000-$5,500 against rank-3 values of $83k-$745k. A read-only simulation of the post-[[FIX-916]] state confirmed prod stays safe (rank 10-17, tightest margin Dave Min at $2,000 vs a rank-3 of $31,000, ~15x) — but the local 6->7 shift proves the promotion mechanism is real, and ANY change that reduces an official's classified mass (a de-tagging, a donor merge, a cycle rolling off) can push `other` up. **The asymmetry is the bug:** `'Untagged'` is excluded at the read as 'not an industry', and `other` is exactly the same kind of thing — an abstention — yet it is allowed through to an assert that kills the pipeline. Two candidate fixes, not exclusive: (1) stop writing `other` at all ([[FIX-911]]'s suggested shape) and delete the existing rows, which removes the input; (2) exclude non-vocabulary values at the rollup read the same way `'Untagged'` is excluded, so an out-of-vocabulary tag degrades to 'no pill' instead of 'no nightly'. (2) is the durable one — it makes the pipeline robust to the NEXT out-of-vocabulary writer rather than just this one — but it must not silently swallow real drift, so pair it with a logged count. Note the assert itself is correct and worth keeping; what is wrong is that a display-layer vocabulary violation is fatal to an unrelated data pipeline. Cross-ref [[FIX-911]] [[FIX-897]] [[FIX-916]] [[FIX-908]] [[FIX-890]]. <!--id:FIX-920-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **matchRow's state-narrowing falls back to the UNFILTERED NATIONAL surname pool** — **File only.** `matchRow` in `packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/index.ts` (~line 474) narrows the weball name-fallback candidate pool by state, then does `statePool.length > 0 ? statePool : candidates` — so when state narrowing yields NOTHING, the pool silently widens back to **every official in the country with that surname**. That is the inverse of the intended safety property: the case where narrowing failed is precisely the case where a name match is least trustworthy, and the code responds by making the pool maximally permissive. [[FIX-929]]'s first-name gate mitigates it but does NOT remove it — a coincidental national single-match whose first names happen to agree still binds, and the [[FIX-930]] audit showed first names agreeing by coincidence is common at national scale. This fallback is also the write path that produced [[FIX-937]]'s population: an official whose jurisdiction `short_name` is not a two-letter state code can NEVER satisfy state narrowing, so for them the fallback is not an edge case, it is the only path. Fix is to tighten to **"no state match ⇒ no name match"**, or to require a stronger corroborator (committee linkage via `ccl`, district agreement, or an existing `external_source_refs` binding) before a national-pool single-match is allowed to bind. Prefer the strict form: the cost of refusing to bind is a row in [[FIX-935]]'s UNIQUE HOLDER branch (recoverable, non-destructive), while the cost of a wrong bind is another person's donors rendered under an official's name ([[FIX-934]]).
