- [x] 🔴 S — **Senate vote writer binds by lastname:state with last-write-wins — 1,755 votes across 49 senators landed on invisible candidate stubs** — **File only — found while implementing [[FIX-933]], and it is live on the clone today.** `buildOfficialMaps` in `packages/data/src/pipelines/congress/votes.ts` (~line 300) builds `senatorByNameState` by iterating every official in the Senate governing body `.order("id")` and doing `senatorByNameState.set(lastName.toLowerCase() + ":" + stateAbbr, s.id)` — **no tier filter, no is_active filter, and last-write-wins**. The query's own comment already says "candidate pollution included", so the pool is known to contain the `cn{yy}`-minted candidate-tier rows; nothing then stops one from taking the map slot. Because uuids are random, roughly **half** of contested `(surname, state)` slots resolve to the candidate row rather than the sitting Senator, and the Senate branch (unlike the House branch, which correctly keys on bioguide from `@_name-id`) has no stable identifier to fall back on. **Measured on the local prod-clone 2026-07-30: 1,755 `votes` rows sit on 49 candidate-tier officials, and 48 of those 49 have an elected same-surname twin that also holds votes.** The split is cleanly dated — Jon Ossoff's elected row holds 1,801 votes spanning 2021-01-20 → **2026-05-20** while his candidate row holds 57 spanning **2026-06-01** → 2026-07-23 — so this began the moment the candidate rows joined the Senate governing body and **every sitting Senator on the losing side of the map has had roughly two months of votes missing from their public page ever since**, with no error anywhere: the insert succeeds, it just points at a row nobody can see. Fix is small and should mirror the House branch's determinism: filter the senator pool to `tier = 'elected'` (and/or `is_active`) before building the map, and make the collision explicit — refuse to overwrite an existing slot and log it, rather than silently taking the last row. Prefer resolving Senators by bioguide (`source_ids->>'congress_gov'`) where the Senate XML permits it, so the name key is a fallback rather than the primary. **Do NOT simply move the existing 1,755 votes to the elected rows without fixing the map** — the next nightly would re-insert them onto the candidate row and re-split, since `votes` is unique on `(roll_call_id, official_id)`. [[FIX-933]] deliberately left these votes in place for exactly that reason. Same last-write-wins map-collision class as [[FIX-941]]. Note `official_vote_stats` is materialized off `votes`, so bipartisan/attendance figures for the affected Senators are understated too. - [x] 🟠 S — **officials.total_received_cents has NO scheduled maintainer — two graph surfaces render unbounded-stale money** — **Found while shipping [[FIX-933]].** `officials.total_received_cents` is a denormalized money column with **no owner**: 21 pg_cron jobs and not one of them touches it, `rebuild_official_donation_totals()` appears nowhere outside a comment and [[FIX-933]]'s own script, and `data:rebuild:received-totals` (FIX-675) rebuilds **financial_entities**, not officials. So the column drifts from the moment any relationship write lands and never converges. The asymmetry is the tell: [[FIX-702]]/[[FIX-726]] deliberately moved the heavy `rebuild_financial_entity_donation_totals` / `_received_totals` full rebuilds out of the FEC phase and onto incremental dirty-scoped pg_cron jobs (`financial-entity-totals-incremental`, Tue) because they saturated Pro Small — but the **officials** equivalent was left with no replacement at all. The comment block at `packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/index.ts` ~1897 names only the financial-entity pair as moved, and `rebuild_official_donation_totals` is mentioned there purely as "pattern mirrors". Measured pre-[[FIX-933]] on the local prod-clone: Jon Ossoff's column read **$11,555,275** against a live rollup of **$14,585,287**, and his candidate row read **$0** against **$14,627,225** — i.e. the column was already ~21% low on a sitting Senator before any merge. **Read sites that render it directly:** `/api/graph/treemap` (route.ts ~400-513 — selects it per official and builds `totalByOfficial`, which sizes the treemap's cells) and `/api/graph/small-dollar` (route.ts ~87-120 — `totalReceivedCents` is the DENOMINATOR of the small-dollar share, so a low column inflates the reported small-dollar percentage). Also `/api/search/entity`, `/api/browse/typeahead`, `/donors/[id]`, and `rebuild_entity_search_index` (which copies it into `entity_search_index`, so search sort/facets inherit the drift). **[[FIX-933]] incidentally repaired this platform-wide on local** — it calls `rebuild_official_donation_totals()` in-transaction, and the local clone now shows **0 disagreements across all 4,321 officials with donation rows** (abs gap $0). That is a side effect of one PR, not a fix: the next relationship write re-opens the gap, and prod stays stale until [[FIX-933]]'s prod run does the same one-shot repair. Durable fix: give the column a scheduled owner, shaped like the [[FIX-702]]/[[FIX-726]] incremental jobs rather than a full-table UPDATE — note `rebuild_official_donation_totals()` is a bare full-table `UPDATE … FROM (SELECT … GROUP BY to_id)`, so it is both expensive on Pro Small AND unable to zero an official whose last donation row was deleted (no aggregate row → no UPDATE → stale non-zero forever; [[FIX-933]] has to zero its duplicates explicitly for exactly this reason). Either fold it into the existing `donor-rollup-refresh` daily job (which already recomputes `official_donor_totals` per dirty recipient and is the natural place), or drop the column and read `official_donor_totals.total_cents` at the call sites — the rollup is already materialized, per-official, and correctly maintained. Prefer the latter: a denormalized copy of a materialized aggregate is a second source of truth with no benefit. - [x] 🟠 M — **Eight incremental rollups key their watermark off updated_at columns stamped by NOW() in a BEFORE trigger — rows written by a transaction that starts before and commits after a watermark read are excluded permanently** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 5 — lying timestamps (population 153 routines).** Unlike the rest of class 5 this is a **correctness** defect, not an observability one: it silently drops rows from incremental rollups. **The mechanism.** `financial_relationships.updated_at` and `votes.updated_at` are stamped by a `BEFORE` trigger (`financial_relationships_updated_at` → `public.set_updated_at()`) using `NOW()`, which is `transaction_timestamp()` — **the moment the writing transaction BEGAN**, not the moment it committed. An incremental rollup then reads `WHERE updated_at > last_watermark` and advances the watermark to the read time. Any transaction that **began before** the watermark read but **committed after** it stamps its rows with a timestamp *below* the new watermark while being invisible at read time — so those rows are never picked up by that run, and never by any later run either, because the watermark has already moved past them. **The loss is permanent and silent.** **Eight watermark read sites, enumerated from live bodies:** `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk:101,127`; `rebuild_entity_connections_donations:26,28`; `rebuild_entity_connections_votes:23,27`; `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental:54,64`; `refresh_donor_party_rollup_mv:16,25`; plus `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental`. **Exposure window = the duration of the longest concurrent writing transaction on that table.** That is not small here: the FEC bulk pipeline's `INSERT INTO financial_relationships` measured `calls=1549, mean_exec_time=29,436 ms` on prod `pg_stat_statements` — a **~29-second mean per statement**, inside longer transactions — and the [[FIX-933]] money move ran ~12 minutes atomic. So a rollup firing during an FEC load can miss any row whose transaction spans the read. **Why it has not obviously bitten yet:** most of these rollups are also re-derived by periodic full passes, which paper over the gap — which is exactly the [[FIX-968]] shape where a frozen rollup makes deltas look clean while the absolute is wrong (playbook **E1**). **Fix shape:** the standard remedies, cheapest first — (a) subtract a safety lag from the watermark (`watermark - interval '1 hour'`), trading a little re-work for correctness, which is the smallest change and fits every one of the 8 sites; (b) stamp `updated_at` with `clock_timestamp()` so the value at least reflects statement time rather than transaction start — necessary but **not sufficient**, since the commit still lands later; (c) the rigorous fix is to advance the watermark to `min(backend_xmin)`-safe territory rather than to wall-clock, i.e. key the incremental read off a transaction-id horizon rather than a timestamp. **Verify before choosing:** confirm against a known-count run whether rows are actually being dropped today (playbook E2 — validate the sizing metric against a run whose true count is independently known), because the safety-lag fix costs re-work on every run and should be justified by a measurement rather than by the argument alone. Cross-ref [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-974]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-702]], [[FIX-726]]. <!--id:FIX-983-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Nine unscoped DELETEs rebuild from relationship types that have zero rows — the lobbying arm deletes all 10,431 live edges and reinserts nothing, and a search predicate matches a value the CHECK domain forbids** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 7 — equal-by-coincidence predicates; SURVIVED adversarial verification with every number re-derived.** Enumerated by mechanism: all **88** live `refresh_|rebuild_|backfill_|reconcile_|promote_|merge_` bodies, **274 predicate sites**, each compared against its column's actual value domain. **(1) Delete-then-rebuild-from-nothing.** `rebuild_entity_connections_lobbying` DELETEs by `connection_type` alone — **10,431 live lobbying edges, 100% of them `evidence_source='external_relationships'`** — then reinserts `WHERE relationship_type = 'lobbying_spend'`. An **exact count** (not an EXISTS probe) over `financial_relationships` returns **0 rows** for `lobbying_spend`, and likewise 0 for `gift`, `honorarium`, `owns_stock`, `owns_bond`, `property` — **6 of 13 enum labels are empty**, so `_lobbying`, `_gifts` and `_holds` all delete real edges and insert exactly nothing. The edges exist today only because a *later* arm in the same array happens to restore them from `external_relationships` (603,745 rows, behind that arm's own 15-min `statement_timeout`). **This is not theoretical — the precedent is realized:** `cron.job_run_details` jobid 22 runid 156 **died at 6h00m** on an FR `WITH agg` cancel on 2026-08-03, and the last successful EC rebuild was **2026-07-29**. If a run dies between the DELETE and the restoring arm, the lobbying edges are simply gone until the next successful full rebuild — which has not happened in over a week. The graph renders `entity_connections`. **(2) A predicate matching a value the CHECK forbids — the [[FIX-073]] `'not_voting'` trap exactly.** `rebuild_entity_search_index`'s contract/grant money branch is gated on `f.entity_type IN ('corporation','organization')`, but `financial_entities_entity_type_check` permits exactly `individual, pac, super_pac, corporation, union, party_committee, small_donor_aggregate, tribal, 527, nonprofit, other` — **`'organization'` is absent from the domain, and a `GROUP BY` over all 3.64M `financial_entities` returns zero rows carrying it.** The literal appears in **both** occurrences in the live body (the `amount_cents` branch and the `amount_label` branch). Real, permanent, silent, and small. (The 5 `super_pac` rows that do carry spend take the `ie>0` precedence branch and are unaffected.) **Fix shape:** (a) an arm must not DELETE what it cannot rebuild — either assert its source is non-empty before deleting, or scope the DELETE to the rows it actually owns (this is the [[FIX-808]]/[[FIX-692]] co-ownership rule applied to the EC arms); (b) fix the `'organization'` literal to `'other'`/`'nonprofit'` or drop the second arm, and add a **write-boundary vocab guard** the way [[FIX-889]]/[[FIX-891]] did for tag categories, so a predicate can never again name a value outside its own CHECK constraint — that guard is the mechanism-level fix and would have caught both this and FIX-073; (c) consider whether the six empty enum labels should be removed from the type or backfilled, since every predicate referencing them is dead code today. Cross-ref [[FIX-073]], [[FIX-889]], [[FIX-891]], [[FIX-808]], [[FIX-692]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-974]]. <!--id:FIX-985-->

THE MECHANISM: FIX-965 characterises this proc as unable to complete inside a 2400s budget, but that measurement was a MANUAL CALL with statement_timeout set in the session. On the pg_cron path there is no such session setting, and per the FIX-1056 finding a SET statement_timeout inside a CALLed procedure is DECORATIVE — statement_timeout is armed at CALL start and a nested function cannot re-arm it. So the scheduled firing is effectively UNBOUNDED: instead of failing at 40 minutes it runs until something else breaks. FIX-965 has been reasoning about a budget the scheduled job does not have. RESOLUTION APPLIED: pg_cancel_backend on the treemap pid (ran 1h47m54s) restored the catalog query from a 60s timeout to 28ms immediately; refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental was also cancelled at 1h31m58s; PostgREST did not self-recover so the project was restarted via the Management API and REST returned 200 in 0.12-0.25s. FIX SHAPE: set a hard statement_timeout on the pg_cron job COMMAND itself (the only layer that can arm it), e.g. schedule the job as SET statement_timeout=1800000; CALL ... — or wrap in a SECURITY DEFINER function whose ALTER FUNCTION SET statement_timeout applies at the outermost call. Audit every other CALL-based pg_cron job for the same gap; jobs 17/24/25/26/28 are all CALL-shaped. Cross-ref FIX-965, FIX-1056, FIX-943, FIX-1030, FIX-961. <!--id:FIX-1063-->

PR 3b moves the floor to EMIT time: every itemized row enters the aggregation, an aggregate at or above 200 dollars becomes an FR row with the CORRECT (full) amount, and a sub-floor aggregate emits NO FR row and NO financial_entities row but is counted into per-recipient size brackets (small_dollar_bracket_rollup, FIX-1068 migration) so the residual is measured rather than silently discarded. - [x] 🟠 S — **Hot-path tables accumulate dead tuples below their autovacuum trigger — six untuned tables at 42.7–85.4% all-visible** — **Found while preparing the [[FIX-933]] prod run.** **⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-01 — the original bullet's central number was wrong; see below.** Originally filed as "`financial_relationships` carries 411,555 dead tuples against a **1,663,805** threshold, so autovacuum mathematically never fires". **That arithmetic used the CLUSTER default scale factor (0.2), but `financial_relationships` already carries a per-table override of 0.05** (verified on prod AND local, 2026-08-01 — alongside `entity_connections`, `entity_tags`, `enrichment_queue`, presumably from the FIX-331/[[FIX-884]] work). Its real trigger is `50 + 0.05 × 8,208,155` = **410,458**, so the 411,555 dead tuples measured on 07-30 were ~1,100 PAST the line, not 1.25M short of it — and prod confirms autovacuum did fire (`last_autovacuum` 2026-07-30 05:28, `autovacuum_count` 7). The table was never in a "never fires" state. **The real defect is the one the wrong number pointed at anyway, and it is a CLASS, not this table:** the trigger is a *floor of tolerated bloat*, and a heap page loses its all-visible mark if ANY tuple on it is dead — these tables carry 4.6–60 tuples per page, so a few-percent dead ratio un-marks most of the heap and every index-only scan degrades to a per-row heap fetch. Sorting every large prod table by visibility map settles it: **`donor_party_rollup_mv` 42.7%, `votes` 61.1%, `external_source_refs` 63.8%, `external_relationships_review_queue` 65.0%, `financial_entities` 77.3%, `proposals` 85.4%, `external_relationships` 97.3% — every one untuned — against `financial_relationships`, `entity_connections`, `entity_tags` and `enrichment_queue` all at 100.0%, every one tuned.** The correlation is total: the tuning works and was simply never extended past the tables [[FIX-884]] happened to touch. Two tables are textbook near-misses sitting *just* under their line (`donor_party_rollup_mv` 261,534 dead vs 262,622; `proposals` 16,145 vs 17,323) and two have **never been autovacuumed in their lives** (`votes` and `external_source_refs`, `autovacuum_count` = 0 — autoANALYZE runs because its trigger is 0.1, half the vacuum trigger, so they cross the analyze line forever and the vacuum line never). The one that matters most is **`financial_entities`**: 13.12% dead, 77.3% all-visible, no custom setting at all, 2.9M rows across 19 indexes — and it is the large table in the donor-rollup join path that dominates that job's runtime today (`financial_entities_pkey`, 11,780 ms of arm 1b). **This is NOT [[FIX-884]]**, which was `entity_connections` stranded at `autovacuum_enabled=false` by the rebuild (an explicitly-disabled flag, since fixed); here autovacuum is enabled and simply never fires. Same *consequence* as FIX-884 though — a stale visibility map kills index-only scans, which is how FIX-884's 0.9% all-visible turned a clean plan into 34,534 heap fetches. Measured impact on the local prod-clone: the [[FIX-930]] audit's suspect query went from completing in ~8 min to **blowing its 600s `statement_timeout`** purely from ~260k additional dead tuples left by the [[FIX-933]] merge, and completed again after a VACUUM. So this already degrades a read path today at 411k, before any migration adds to it. Fix (shipped, `20260801000000_fix943_autovacuum_hot_path_tables.sql`): extend the per-table scale factors to the hot-path class, **sized per table from its measured write pattern and index footprint rather than a blanket value** — `financial_relationships` 0.05→0.02 (410,458→**164,213**), `financial_entities` →0.05 (582,987→**145,784**), `votes` →0.05 (193,681→**48,458**), `donor_party_rollup_mv` →0.02 (262,622→**26,307**), `external_source_refs` →0.05 (114,191→**28,585**), `proposals` →0.05 (17,323→**4,368**). Note the original bullet's `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 50000` suggestion is a **no-op for this purpose** — the formula is `threshold + scale_factor × reltuples`, i.e. additive, so the threshold only raises the trigger and only matters on small tables; lowering the *scale factor* is the only lever on a large one. `entity_connections` is deliberately **left at 0.05** (not 1.07M — it too is already tuned, real trigger 259,648): 2,919 MB heap / 3,544 MB across 10 indexes means every extra pass is real standing I/O on an already-I/O-bound Small instance, and it has both the monthly `ec-vacuum-analyze` backstop and the [[FIX-885]] startup reconcile. Five self-maintaining rollups (`entity_connection_stats_mv`, `entity_search_index`, `group_donor_rollup`, `official_donor_rollup_mv`, `treemap_individuals_rollup`) are untuned yet all at 100.0% all-visible — their rebuilds delete millions of rows and clear even the 0.2 trigger every run — so they are left alone, as is pipeline-only `external_relationships_review_queue`. Note Pro Small has limited I/O and a VACUUM on this table took **>17 min on local Docker**, so tune the thresholds rather than scheduling blanket full-table VACUUMs, and prefer off-peak (cf. the no-heavy-prod-ops-during-active-hours rule). [[FIX-933]]'s script ends with an explicit `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` on `financial_relationships`/`entity_connections`/`officials` — filed here as "a workaround local to one script, not the fix", and that framing was **too modest**: autovacuum tuning narrows the window but cannot close it (a bulk rewrite lands its whole dead-tuple load inside the remaining floor at once), and that vacuum running on 07-31 02:35 is the *only* reason [[FIX-944]]'s four-day backlog cleared. So it is now a **standing convention, not a workaround** — "any script that bulk-rewrites a table ends by vacuuming what it rewrote", landed in root `CLAUDE.md` (Data-state changes) with the reference table and sizing rules in `packages/db/CLAUDE.md`. **[[FIX-934]] is the next bulk `financial_relationships` rewrite and must carry a vacuum tail regardless of these settings.** Also shipped: `check_rebuild_autovacuum_status()` ([[FIX-650]]/[[FIX-885]]) now watches the whole tuned class instead of only `entity_connections` — which is how `donor_party_rollup_mv` sat at 42.7%, *below the canary's own 50% escalation floor*, completely unseen — and gains `bloat`/`bloat_degraded` keys reporting dead tuples against each table's computed trigger. `bloat_degraded` is **report-only by design**: a table can sit under its trigger harmlessly, so `vm_degraded` remains the escalating signal and this exists to make the cause greppable before the consequence arrives. Cross-ref [[FIX-884]], [[FIX-650]], [[FIX-885]], [[FIX-590]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-934]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-702]], [[FIX-726]]. <!--id:FIX-943-->

An official whose `financial_relationships` rows were all deleted (exactly what [[FIX-933]]'s merge does to the neutralised duplicate) keeps its last non-zero value forever; only `rebuild_official_donation_totals_full()`, which zeroes first, can clear it, and nothing on the schedule calls `_full()`. **Measured on the local prod-clone 2026-07-31 (post-FIX-933): ZERO drift** — all 4,321 officials in `official_donor_totals` match the column exactly (Ossoff $15,633,810 both sides), and ZERO officials carry a non-zero column value with no surviving donation rows. That design question is the durable part and is worth answering either way: now that `official_donor_totals` exists, is refreshed daily and is authoritative, the column is a second source of truth for the same quantity with a refresh function that structurally cannot converge. At a 6 h blowout the cursor's lie grows to one chunk of a six-hour run, which is exactly the magnitude that made FIX-972 expensive. **Related, from the same pass and same mechanism** (filed here rather than separately because the fix is one sweep): three more rollup freshness columns are stamped at chunk-transaction START inside the very loop FIX-972 audited but were left untouched by it — `public.small_dollar_rebuild_officials:15`, `public.sector_affinity_rebuild_officials:47`, and `official_donor_totals.updated_at`'s `DEFAULT now()`, all executed inside `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental`'s per-chunk transaction, where the measured `slowest_chunk_seconds` has reached **6,546 s**. **Fix shape:** `clock_timestamp()` at every one of these sites (playbook E7 — `NOW()` for transactional consistency, `clock_timestamp()` for anything read as progress), and then **grep the mechanism rather than the site**: `SELECT proname FROM pg_proc WHERE prosrc ~* '\\mNOW\\s*\\(\\s*\\)' AND prosrc ~* '\\mCOMMIT\\M'` is the enumeration that would have caught all of them in one pass, and should be the standing check when any new chunked writer lands. Cross-ref [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-964]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-974]]. <!--id:FIX-981-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **All 68 bulk-read sites paginate by OFFSET via seven independently-written helpers — measured 175x row-visit amplification on the largest walk, and the page quanta are tuned to table sizes that have since grown** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), classes 1 and 3 converging; SURVIVED adversarial verification with its scale claims corrected downward — read the corrections, they matter.** Playbook **A2** (*chunk by key RANGE aligned to the read index, never by ordinal position*) and **D5** (*guard constants are tuned to a table size and go stale when the table steps*). **Enumerated by mechanism:** `grep -rnE "\.range\((from|offset|f|sFrom|page \*|\(page)" apps packages` returns **68 bulk-read sites**, driven by **seven independently-written paging helpers** (`selectAllOrThrow`, two separate `fetchAllPaged` definitions, `fetchAll`, `fetchAllPages`, two separate `fetchAllRows`). **Every one is OFFSET paging.** Counter-check: keyset IS a known pattern in this repo — `littlesis/matcher.ts:137` does it correctly — but it appears in **zero of the 68**. **Why OFFSET is quadratic:** page *k* generates and discards the first *k × pageSize* rows, so a full walk is O(n²/pageSize) against O(n) for keyset. **(1) The stale quantum, verified 🟠 — this is the half with a live consequence.** `packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/rules.ts:675` is `const PAGE_SIZE = 500` and `packages/db/src/read-helpers.ts:69` defaults to 1000, both tuned when the tables were smaller; `rules.ts`'s own comment still says *"proposals is ~73k rows"* against an actual **87,403**. Planner cost for the exact query it issues, measured on prod (plan only, no ANALYZE): page 0 = **129.07**, page 57 = **7,462.20 (57.8×)**, last page = **22,476.08 (174.1×)**. There are **three recorded production statement-timeout failures on deep pages**. **(2) The largest walk, verified but downgraded to 🟡 on frequency.** `packages/data/src/pipelines/littlesis/writer.ts:51` (`preloadKnownLittleSisIds`) reads **348,508** `external_source_refs` rows through **349 OFFSET pages** — `pgss: calls=1045, mean 374.63 ms, total 391.5 s, 289,313 buffers/call`. Row-visit amplification is **175×** (`349 × 350 / 2 × 1000` = **61.08M** filtered row-visits against **348,508** for a keyset walk), and the keyset form already exists one file over. **But the original finding's framing was wrong and is corrected here:** this is **WEEKLY, not nightly** — `pg_stat_statements_info.stats_reset = 2026-07-17`, so 1045 calls / 349 pages = **exactly 3 runs in 21 days**, confirmed against `data_sync_log` (littlesis rows 07-19, 07-26, 08-02). The nightly enrichment job *does* fire, but `runLittleSisPipeline` short-circuits at the SHA256 freshness gate (`littlesis/index.ts:94-98`, `skipSync('dumps_unchanged')`) **before** the preload runs. Real cost: **130.7 s per run, ~18.6 s/day amortised, ~6% of the ~35-min LittleSis stage.** **And it carries no PR 3 growth term** — `external_source_refs` is keyed to imported source records, not to the donor population. **What this finding is and is not.** It is not "the pipelines are burning hours on OFFSET" — that claim was tested and died. It is: a repo-wide pattern with **one measured live failure mode** (deep-page timeouts on `proposals`, already observed three times) and a **175× structural inefficiency** on the largest walk, sitting behind **seven duplicated helpers** so any future large table inherits it by default. The cost of fixing is small and the cost of not fixing grows with whichever table crosses the threshold next. **Fix shape:** (a) convert the seven helpers to keyset (`WHERE id > $last ORDER BY id LIMIT n`) — one change at the helper layer covers most of the 68 sites, which is the mechanism-level fix rather than site-by-site; behaviour-preserving only where the `ORDER BY` column is unique and non-null (`id` is — audit any caller ordering by something else); (b) re-derive the two page quanta and record the table size they were tuned against, per D5; (c) `littlesis/writer.ts:51` is the cheapest single win and its keyset twin already exists in the sibling module. **Explicitly refuted and NOT part of this bullet:** `tags/ai-classifier.ts:241-251` — its paged subset is far smaller than claimed and does not justify a finding. Cross-ref [[FIX-974]] (A2, the 33.0 → 0.118 ms/row unlock), [[FIX-976]], [[FIX-443]], [[FIX-444]], [[FIX-902]]. <!--id:FIX-984-->

CONCURRENTLY` requires a unique index**, so the missing index is the *cause* and the `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock is the *consequence* — for the whole duration of the refresh, on a materialized view the **homepage reads**. **Why this is not hypothetical.** This exact object is the receipt behind playbook **C4** (*"runtime measurements are floors — design to survive the miss"*): `refresh_homepage_stats_mv()` takes **0.7 s on local** and ran **22 minutes** against an otherwise-idle prod on 2026-07-31, pushing the homepage to **18.5 s**. The containing job is not small either: jobid 9 has 34 retained runs with a slowest of **3h29m06.623s** (2026-08-05, whole 13-unit job) against a typical 5–20 minutes. **The fix is unusually cheap for the risk it removes.** `homepage_stats_mv` is a **single row, 8,192 bytes** — a unique index on it costs nothing, and adding one lets the refresh become `CONCURRENTLY` like its seven siblings. That is a one-line migration plus a one-word change in the procedure body. **Sequence:** add the unique index first (it must exist before `CONCURRENTLY` will run), then flip the refresh; verify the homepage stays served during a refresh rather than blocking. Note `CONCURRENTLY` trades the lock for a longer refresh and needs the MV to be populated, so confirm the first post-change run on local before prod. The autovacuum trigger is `threshold + scale_factor x reltuples`. On a large table the default threshold (50) is rounding error and only the scale factor is a lever — but on a relation of a few dozen rows the scale-factor term is ~1-5 and the THRESHOLD is effectively the entire trigger, so a small, frequently-rewritten relation can sit indefinitely just under it. Measured on prod 2026-08-09, every public relation with no autovacuum override, ranked by dead ratio: `proposal_popularity_24h` 100% (0 live / 6 dead), `supabase_prometheus_state` 75.0%, `platform_alert_state` 70.3%, `pipeline_runtime_stats_mv` 47.2%, `platform_usage` 29.6%, `platform_limits` 22.6% — several at 0.0% all-visible. [[FIX-1003]] fixed five instances of this class (four `chord_*_flows_mv` and `pipeline_state`) by setting `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 20` alongside the scale factor, and prod confirmed the lever within seconds: all five went from 24.9-62.0% dead / 0.0% all-visible to 0 dead / 100% all-visible at 2026-08-09 14:36:42, on the first autovacuum evaluation after the override landed. The rest of the class is untreated. Honest scoping: the direct cost of bloat on a 1-5 page relation is near zero, so this is a hygiene/consistency item, not a performance one — the value is that these are the relations where the [[FIX-884]] all-visible mechanism is invisible in monitoring precisely because the absolute numbers look harmless. Fix shape: a threshold-led override on the enumerated set, no new framework and no per-table cron jobs (autovacuum genuinely suffices once the trigger is reachable). Deliberately NOT a vacuum registry or dashboard — see [[FIX-1003]]'s scope note. Cross-ref [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-884]]. <!--id:FIX-1006-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **The burn-rate RPC scanned every snapshot payload — 427ms and ~12k buffer blocks per tick** — Self-inflicted by [[FIX-1044]] and caught within hours because Craig noticed a Supabase spike and asked. **MEASURED ON PROD from pg_stat_statements 2026-08-16:** get_platform_daily_cost_deltas — calls 9, mean 427.4 ms, max 966.7 ms, 109,087 buffer blocks total, i.e. **~12,000 blocks (~95 MB of buffer traffic) PER CALL** — against 115 calls of everything else touching that table at 18.1 ms mean. It runs on EVERY snapshot tick, forever. **THE CAUSE:** the function read every platform_usage_snapshot row in a 14-day window (measured: 276 rows, 4.6 MB of payload, 17 kB average, so nearly all TOASTed) and ran jsonb_array_elements over the metrics array of each one, purely to take max() per MTD day at the end. On an instance with 256 MB shared_buffers and a ~54 pct cache hit rate ([[project_prod_buffer_churn_baseline]]) that is exactly the churn packages/db/CLAUDE.md warns about under "Cost note: profile the COMPUTE, not just the read" — the read path was considered and the cron-side compute was not. **THE FIX:** Vercel counters are cumulative and step ONCE PER DAY, and consecutive snapshots inside a day are byte-identical to 16 decimal places (established by the 2026-08-15 audit). So ~19 of every 20 rows carry information already present in another, and the whole series is recoverable from a couple of rows per Vercel billing day. Bucket by Pacific day using ONLY fetched_at — no payload is detoasted to make the selection — take the first and last row of each bucket via DISTINCT ON, and only THEN do the jsonb extraction, on ~28 rows instead of ~276. Same output; if anything more correct than max(), since the last snapshot of a day is the settled end-of-day value whereas max() would have preferred a larger mid-day reading had one occurred. **WHY BOTH ENDS AND NOT JUST THE LAST:** insurance against boundary jitter, not a fix for an observed skip. The audit dates the step at "~06:00-07:00 UTC" and the bucket boundary is Pacific midnight = 07:00 UTC. Measured on the clone the step lands cleanly (last row with an old window_days is 03:45-06:29 UTC, first with the new one is 07:07-09:32), but a step at 06:00 — the early end of the audit own range — would put a row bearing the NEW window_days into the OLD bucket where, being last, it would become that bucket sole representative and silently drop a whole MTD day. Bracketing costs one extra detoast per day and removes the failure mode. **METHOD NOTE worth keeping:** during this fix MTD day 1 appeared to vanish from the local series and was briefly misdiagnosed as bucket masking. The real cause was the rolling 14-day window moving past it in the two hours between runs. Verified by widening p_days to 16, which returned days 28-31 and 2-9 all consecutive — no skip. Check the window before blaming the query. Cross-ref [[FIX-1044]], [[FIX-281]]. <!--id:FIX-1049-->

- [x] 🔴 M — **rebuild_entity_search_index work_mem sized for a 2.4M-row entity_connections that is now 10.4M — the named memory holder in the 08-29 seizure** — rebuild_entity_search_index is the named holder of the memory that took prod down on 2026-08-29 06:00 UTC. Evidence chain, all from durable sources: the reaped refresh_derived_mvs data_sync_log row records current_unit rebuild_entity_search_index, current_unit_index 9 of 13, current_unit_started_at 2026-08-29T06:08:34, backend_pid 328403; the derived-mvs-unit-watchdog and cron-job-budget-watchdog firings began failing with job startup timeout at 06:12:00, three and a half minutes later, which is the postmaster losing the ability to fork a backend; the box crash-restarted at 07:21:57, dated by pg_stat_statements_info.stats_reset, which discards on an unclean restart and persists across clean ones and therefore also proves the 07:40:57 pg_postmaster_start_time was a separate later manual bounce. The mechanism is a stale size assumption. The function sets work_mem to 256MB via SET LOCAL and its header comment describes scanning entity_connections at about 2.4M rows; prod entity_connections is now 10,435,594 reltuples and 7470 MB, a 4.3x growth since FIX-748 shipped 2026-07-06. Its first act builds an ON COMMIT DROP temp table from a UNION ALL of from_id and to_id over that table, about 20.9M input rows into a GROUP BY hash aggregate. On this box hash_mem_multiplier is 2, so that node is permitted 512MB, and max_parallel_workers_per_gather is 1, so leader plus one worker is up to 1GB for that single node, against a commit limit of roughly 2.18GB with shared_buffers already at 256MB and max_connections 60. Note the prod GLOBAL work_mem is also 262144kB (256MB), and refresh_derived_mvs sets 128MB for its own session but rebuild_entity_search_index overrides it back up to 256MB. Candidate fixes to measure before choosing: lower the SET LOCAL work_mem to a value sized against the current table, replace the UNION ALL degree count with a precomputed source (entity_connection_stats_mv already holds per-entity connection counts), or SET LOCAL max_parallel_workers_per_gather 0 for this statement so the worker copy is not doubled. pg_stat_statements cannot be consulted for the incident window because it reset at the crash; absence of pgss data is not absence of cost. - [x] 🟠 M — **An ad-hoc VACUUM of financial_relationships is a front-door incident, and its scheduled-job history is the wrong way to size it** — MEASURED THE HARD WAY on prod 2026-09-01, in a supervised window, by causing it. A VACUUM (ANALYZE) of financial_relationships was run ad-hoc at 23:09 UTC as a prerequisite for [[FIX-1118]] (an index-only scan needs a fresh visibility map). It was sized at about 4 minutes from jobid 38 fr-vacuum-analyze's last three firings — 227.2 s, 20.3 s, 97.8 s. It was cancelled at 675.5 s, still inside its FIRST pass over the indexes, after putting 8 statement timeouts (SQLSTATE 57014) through the front door between 23:03 and 23:19 UTC, peaking at 4 per minute, which Craig observed live. Errors stopped at 23:20 the moment it was cancelled. TWO SEPARATE LESSONS, both worth encoding. FIRST, the sizing error: a scheduled vacuum's history measures the STEADY STATE, not a catch-up. jobid 38 is cheap precisely because it is weekly and runs 01:00 UTC, so it never has much to do; the ad-hoc run had two days and 187,000 updates behind it. Never size an ad-hoc vacuum from the cron job's runtimes. Size it from n_dead_tup and the index footprint. SECOND, and the more useful finding: the heap was never the cost. The heap phase finished 631,265 blocks in about 115 seconds. The remaining 560 s was the INDEX phase, because financial_relationships carries EIGHTEEN indexes totalling 6,926 MB, all of which a vacuum must sweep in full to remove 187,854 dead item IDs, on a box with 256 MB of shared_buffers (see [[project_prod_buffer_churn_baseline]]). So FR's vacuum cost is dominated by its index count, which also means every FR write pays 18-index maintenance. An index census on this table — which of the 18 are actually used, per pg_stat_user_indexes idx_scan — is probably the highest-leverage thing available here, and would cut vacuum cost, write amplification and disk together. THIRD, a corollary that bit us the same evening: a cancelled VACUUM banks NOTHING. vacuum_count stayed 1, last_vacuum stayed 2026-08-31 01:03, n_dead_tup stayed 187,854, so the 675 s bought zero progress and the next attempt restarts from the top. That is the same cancel-discards-the-work property documented for the ec-crawl stats windows in docs/audits/front-door-degradation-2026-09-01.md. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE STANDING RULE: the FIX-943 convention (any script that bulk-rewrites a table ends by vacuuming what it rewrote) is still right, but on this table the tail is a front-door risk, not a formality. Bulk-rewrite scripts touching FR must be scheduled off-peak and budgeted in the tens of minutes, per the no-heavy-prod-ops-during-active-hours rule. Cross-ref [[FIX-943]] [[FIX-884]] [[FIX-1118]] [[FIX-1107]] [[FIX-1034]]. <!--id:FIX-1133-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **official_homepage_stats_mv scans financial_relationships THREE times per refresh — collapse to one pass with FILTER** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-09-02, surfaced by the jobid-9 unit_seconds regression. official_homepage_stats_mv is the second-largest unit in refresh-derived-mvs-daily and it went 253.9 s (08-31 06:00) to 252.8 s (08-31 23:36) to 800.5 s (09-01 06:00). THE STRUCTURE: its defining query has four CTEs, and THREE of them scan public.financial_relationships independently — donor_counts (to_type=official AND relationship_type=donation), fin_counts (to_type=official), donation_sums (to_type=official AND relationship_type=donation AND amount_cents IS NOT NULL) — each GROUP BY to_id. FR is 4,932 MB of heap and 14.5M rows, so one refresh reads it three times, roughly 15 GB of I/O against a box with shared_buffers 256 MB. All three share the SAME to_type=official predicate and the SAME grouping key, so they collapse to a single scan with conditional aggregates: count(*) FILTER (WHERE relationship_type=donation), count(*), sum(amount_cents) FILTER (WHERE relationship_type=donation AND amount_cents IS NOT NULL), all GROUP BY to_id. Expected saving is about two thirds of the FR work in this unit. VERDICT STRUCTURAL, NOT TRANSIENT, and the instrument matters: EXPLAIN on prod shows the three FR nodes are Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan, Parallel Seq Scan, Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan — ZERO Index Only Scans over FR — and neither a bitmap heap scan nor a seq scan consults the visibility map, so visibility-map decay CANNOT be the mechanism here no matter what the surrounding tables look like. That rules out the tempting VM-decay story and it is why this needs a query change rather than a vacuum. The 3.2x excursion on 09-01 06:00 is a separate same-morning contention event (homepage_stats_mv also went 11.8 to 64.5 s and rebuild_entity_search_index went 383.9 to 490.7 s on that same run, three unrelated units regressing together); the 253 s baseline is the structural part and it grows linearly with FR. WHY IT ESCAPED FIX-1123: that census filtered on functions setting work_mem >= 128MB, and a REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY sets no work_mem at all, so an unbounded refresh over a growing source was invisible to it. Note this unit lives in jobid 9, the job that has now twice taken prod down. Cross-ref [[FIX-1123]] [[FIX-1125]] [[FIX-1129]] [[FIX-775]]. <!--id:FIX-1134-->

- [x] 🟡 S — **entity_tags.tag needs a statistics target, not a planner hint** — entity_tags carries about 55 distinct tags but the default statistics target (100) samples only enough of a 2.9 M row, 2,714 MB table to store 21 of them in the MCV list. Any tag outside those 21 falls to the ndistinct fallback, so tag='health' estimates 124 rows against an actual 8,480 - a 68x underestimate that made the FIX-902 fetchEntityIdsByIndustryTag plan pick a Sort it did not need. It does NOT defer or scope the two remaining global steps in runRollups: rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals() and refresh_group_donor_rollup(). Both rebuild the whole platform for a manifest-sized change. OWNERSHIP IS SPLIT AND WAS NEVER CHECKED: rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals IS owned — the fec_bulk pipeline calls it at packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/index.ts:2418 and it ran on prod 2026-09-06 06:58 and 2026-09-07 07:12, both complete — so running it from a remediation script is pure duplication. refresh_group_donor_rollup has NO scheduled owner at all: no cron.job command names it, no SQL function or procedure calls it (checked via pg_proc.prosrc on prod), and its only non-script caller is scripts/rebuild-entity-connections.ts, whose workflow became workflow_dispatch-only when FIX-688 moved the EC rebuild schedule to pg_cron. So the group rollup silently lost its cadence and is currently re-derived ONLY as a side effect of a remediation script's tail. FIX SHAPE: (a) rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals — defer it under --defer-tails and name fec_bulk as the owner, or scope it to the affected financial_entities; (b) refresh_group_donor_rollup — either give it a real scheduled owner (its own pg_cron job, off-peak) and defer it here, or scope it to the affected groups; (c) the dry run must PRINT each tail step's cost class — manifest-scoped, platform-scoped-with-owner, or platform-scoped-orphan — so the trade is visible before the go-ahead rather than discovered at minute 28. THE STANDING RULE THIS EARNS, and it generalises past these scripts: a manifest-scoped remediation must not carry a platform-scoped tail. Every tail step either SCALES WITH THE MANIFEST or HAS A SCHEDULED OWNER; anything that is neither is a bug in the script, not a cost of the change. Corollary: a step's presence in a tail is not evidence it has an owner — check cron.job by name, pg_proc.prosrc, and the GHA workflows, because FIX-688-style schedule migrations orphan callers silently. Cross-ref [[FIX-1153]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-964]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-688]], [[FIX-1129]], [[FIX-1144]]. THREE PLATFORM-SCOPED READS FOUND, not one: besides rebuild_financial_entity_ie_totals() and refresh_group_donor_rollup(), the CONSERVATION check (PLATFORM_SQL, a full aggregate over every official donation row) and the CLOSING NUMBER were both platform-scoped -- PLATFORM_SQL is the conservation phase that cost the other 132 cancellations. - [x] 🟡 S — **Missing set_updated_at trigger on public.financial_entities (lost in shadow→public promotion)** — `public.financial_entities` has **no `updated_at` trigger** on prod. Migration 0004 created `CREATE TRIGGER financial_entities_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON financial_entities ... EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at()`, but the shadow→public promotion (migration 20260422000000) promoted/recreated `public.financial_entities` WITHOUT re-creating the trigger. Confirmed on prod 2026-06-30: `pg_trigger` shows zero non-internal triggers on `public.financial_entities`. `set_updated_at()` is unconditional (`NEW.updated_at = NOW()`), so with the trigger gone, `updated_at` is set only on INSERT (column DEFAULT NOW()) and is **never bumped on UPDATE** — it has been stale on every updated row since the 2026-04-22 cutover. The `financial_entities_updated_at` index consequently points at insert-time, not last-modified, so any freshness/recency consumer of `financial_entities.updated_at` is wrong. **Scope (verified prod 2026-06-30):** only `financial_entities` lost the trigger — `financial_relationships`, `votes`, `proposals`, `officials`, `agencies`, `career_history` all RETAIN their `set_updated_at` trigger, so the incremental `entity_connections` rebuild (keys on `financial_relationships.updated_at` / `votes.updated_at` dirty sets) is NOT affected (the worst case checked for). `entity_connections` also lacks the trigger but is TRUNCATE-rebuilt wholesale, so `updated_at` is cosmetic there. **How found:** FIX-677 backfill monitoring — the donor-entity upsert was mostly UPDATEs yet `count(updated_at >= run_start)` tracked only `n_tup_ins` (~37k) while `n_tup_upd` was ~1.5M. **Fix:** migration recreating `CREATE TRIGGER financial_entities_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ON public.financial_entities FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION public.set_updated_at();` (optionally also on `public.entity_connections`); apply local + prod; audit promotion migration 20260422000000 for any other dropped triggers. Optional one-time `updated_at` backfill is low priority. Cross-ref [[FIX-677]]. <!--id:FIX-699-->

Root cause is NOT dirty keywords: ai-classifier.ts forced a **12-way choice made from the donor name alone**, and the vocabulary had no bucket at all for electric utilities, industrial manufacturing, chemicals, autos, steel, mining or media. A model asked to place *Duke Energy PAC* into those twelve answers oil_gas and is not wrong to — it is the nearest available label. That single gap is the largest error mass in eight of the twelve tags. **Adds four keys** (utilities, manufacturing, mining, media; VALID_INDUSTRIES 12 to 16) and **renames pharma to health** — a blanket key rename, correct for the unaudited tail too, because the entire keyword list feeding the tag is health-sector and the tag measured **20.4% pharmaceutical but 91.2% health-sector** (hospital/physician assocs 32.0%, health trade assocs 20.7%, health insurers 11.6%). manufacturing already existed as a 1-donor out-of-vocabulary tag (NAM-PAC) and is PROMOTED, not deleted. **oil_gas keeps its key AND stays narrow** — widening it to Energy and Utilities would take it 40.7% to 91.8% honest but would destroy the money_vote_influence HR 26 measure, which needs fossil-fuel money specifically; the fossil core is coherent (upstream 18.0% + refining 9.1% + pipeline 6.0% + trade assoc 3.7% + fuel marketing 2.8% + oilfield svcs 1.0%) and the honest fix is moving the utilities OUT. Labels widen where contents justify (tech to Technology and Communications, legal to Legal and Professional Services, retail to Consumer Goods and Services, real_estate to Real Estate and Construction, defense to Defense and Aerospace, agriculture to Agriculture and Food, lobby to Advocacy and Lobbying, finance to Finance and Insurance). **Consolidation:** INDUSTRY_LABELS was duplicated in four places (tags/rules.ts, tags/ai-classifier.ts — which additionally carried an 'other' key never in VALID_INDUSTRIES — enrichment/queue.ts INDUSTRY_DISPLAY, and app-side CANONICAL_INDUSTRY_TOKENS); all now resolve to ONE exported constant beside VALID_INDUSTRIES in tags/topics.ts, which is already the FIX-890 drain write-boundary source. UI keeps its own key-to-lucide registry (different type, no dep edge from apps/civitics to @civitics/data) mirrored by packages/graph/src/industries.ts, pinned by a test that reads that file off disk. **No donor is re-assigned by this change** — the curated override list that actually moves donors into the new buckets is a separate follow-up. Cross-ref [[FIX-890]] [[FIX-889]] [[FIX-897]] [[FIX-896]]. Explicitly NOT bundled: [[FIX-873]]/[[FIX-875]] industry-tag dedup, and the DISTINCT ON alphabet-gradient tie-break. <!--id:FIX-908-->

- [x] 🟡 S — **ai-classifier writes 'other' as a real industry tag — out-of-vocabulary rows that bypass the write-boundary guard** — Documented at the call site by [[FIX-908]], filed here rather than fixed there because changing it changes what gets written. buildPrompt() in packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/ai-classifier.ts offers 'other' as an answer for 'if unclear', and classifyPac() ALSO coerces any unrecognised or unparseable model answer to 'other'. That value is then upserted into entity_tags as a real industry tag with display_label 'Other' — but 'other' is NOT a member of VALID_INDUSTRIES. Three consequences. (1) **It bypasses the guard**: the [[FIX-890]] write-boundary check lives in drain/vocabulary.ts and only covers the drain path; ai-classifier upserts straight over PostgREST, so the one vocabulary enforcement point in the codebase never sees it. (2) **An abstention is indistinguishable from a parse failure** — both collapse to the same string, so 'the model declined to classify this PAC' and 'the model returned malformed JSON' are the same row, and neither is visible in the skipped count. (3) **It renders a meaningless pill**: a donor labelled 'Other' is worse than an unlabelled donor, because it looks like a classification. Measured 2026-07-27: **8 rows on prod, 0 on local** — small, but it is the same out-of-vocabulary class as the energy/pharmaceutical singletons [[FIX-909]] deleted, still being actively written. The [[FIX-909]] migration's vocabulary assertion explicitly TOLERATES 'other' for exactly this reason (asserting it away would fail the migration on prod today, and would fail again on the next classifier run even after a cleanup) — that tolerance should be removed as part of this fix. **Suggested shape:** stop writing the row at all when the model abstains, record the abstention in the sync-log counters as its own category distinct from parse failures, and clean up the 8 existing prod rows in the same change. Consider also routing this upsert through checkTagVocabulary so the guard covers every writer, not just the drain. Cross-ref [[FIX-908]] [[FIX-909]] [[FIX-890]]. <!--id:FIX-911-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Curated industry overrides — 742 hand-audited donors re-assigned or de-tagged** — Follow-up to [[FIX-908]]/[[FIX-909]], which added the four missing vocabulary keys but deliberately moved no donor into them. The 2026-07-27 dollar-weighted audit hand-classified 1,438 donors covering 90-100% of each industry tag's donation dollars and produced a **742-donor override list** committed at `docs/audits/2026-07-27-industry-tag-overrides.tsv`: **380 donors carrying the wrong industry** and **362 that are not industries at all** (leadership PACs, party committees, abstract vanity PACs — WinRed, NRSC, Save America, Huck PAC, AmeriPAC were all tagged `lobby`). Decision was explicitly hand-curation, NOT an AI re-run. **New table `public.financial_entity_industry_overrides`** keyed on `fec_committee_id` (text PK), not `financial_entities.id` — UUIDs are not portable across a re-seed and FEC committee IDs are the stable external key (`financial_entities.fec_committee_id` is already UNIQUE); all 742 audited donors have one and all 742 are distinct. `industry IS NULL` is a POSITIVE ASSERTION — 'this donor carries no industry, ever' — not 'unknown', and it SUPPRESSES tagging rather than merely omitting it. **The override is applied INSIDE `tagFinancialEntities()`** in packages/data/src/pipelines/tags/rules.ts, as the last word after the keyword and NAICS passes. It cannot live anywhere else: that function calls `clear_financial_entity_rule_tags(['industry'])`, which DELETEs every `entity_type='financial_entity' AND generated_by='rule' AND tag_category='industry'` row and re-inserts from the keyword list, so an override written by any other job would be shadowed by a freshly re-inserted keyword tag on the very next nightly — the same authoritative-rebuild trap [[FIX-897]] hit with the official industry pills and the co-owned-rows class of [[FIX-808]]. Override rows are written `generated_by='curated'`, confidence 1.0, visibility 'primary', with `metadata` carrying `source`, `audited_sector` and `fec_committee_id` so the number behind the label stays auditable. Because the nightly clear is scoped to `generated_by='rule'`, curated rows SURVIVE it — so the producer owns them with its own authoritative delete-then-insert over the same direct-pg connection as the upsert, making a re-run a no-op rather than an accumulation. **Exactly one industry per overridden donor**, which has a second payoff: it collapses 96.4% of the multi-tag donation dollar mass ($328.4M of $340.8M across 478 multi-tag donating donors) to a single tag at the source, leaving the alphabetical `DISTINCT ON` tie-break ([[FIX-918]]) almost nothing to arbitrate. The migration also does a **one-time delete of the surviving `generated_by='ai'` industry rows for overridden donors only** — the nightly clear never touched them, so the AI-derived tags carrying most of the dollars (93.7% of `lobby`, 71.5% of `oil_gas`, 66.4% of `defense`) would otherwise persist forever and shadow the curation. AI rows for NON-overridden donors are left alone. **KNOWN, ACCEPTED LIMITATION:** 742 rows is the audited set at 90-100% dollar coverage per tag; the unaudited tail keeps its current tag. In particular `oil_gas` retains a tail of small utility PACs (~8% of its dollars) the audit did not reach. - [x] 🟠 S — **Rule-tagger phase order lagged official industry pills a full night — reorder around the affinity refresh + content-keyed staleness alarm** — Companion to [[FIX-958]], split out because the order fix is independently verifiable and would otherwise hide inside the trigger diff. runRuleBasedTagger() ran tagProposals → tagOfficials → tagFinancialEntities, so tagOfficials — which reads official_sector_affinity_rollup to write the FIX-897 industry pills — executed BEFORE that night's donor tag changes existed, and any rollup rebuild came later still. **Even with a perfect trigger, pills would lag a full night.** Fix half 1 (order): the phases now run proposals → financialEntities → refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes() → officials, so the targeted rebuild completes before tagOfficials reads the rollup; proven by the single-run test (flip one donor's industry via the override table, run the tagger ONCE, the receiving official's pill reflects it — not on the second run). - [x] 🟠 S — **Officials 'Total raised' and 'Donors on record' both describe numbers the page does not have** — Three surfaces render the same two mislabelled figures: apps/civitics/app/officials/[id]/page.tsx StatCells 'Total raised' + 'Donors on record', apps/civitics/app/officials/components/OfficialCard.tsx, and the prompt string in apps/civitics/app/api/officials/[id]/summary/route.ts. **'Total raised' is not total raised.** It is the ALL-CYCLE sum (2020+2022+2024+2026) of ITEMIZED donation financial_relationships only — it excludes unitemized individual contributions entirely (51% of Ossoff's receipts, and FEC never discloses them at any grain so that is not a closeable coverage gap), joint-fundraising transfers, independent expenditures, loans and other receipts. For Jon Ossoff it renders $14.6M against $77.3M of FEC receipts for the 2025–26 cycle ALONE. **'Donors on record' is not a donor count.** It sums official_donor_rollup_mv.tx_count, which counts financial_relationships ROWS — i.e. donor×cycle pairs, since the table is unique on (relationship_type, from_id, to_id, cycle_year). Measured for Ossoff: 16,646 rows vs 15,761 distinct donors vs 26,520 underlying FEC transactions — so the label overstates donors by 5.6% and is not a transaction count either. official_homepage_stats_mv.donor_count (which OfficialCard and the summary route read) is the same COUNT(*) over the same rows. Neither MV can produce a distinct-donor count without a grain change, so this is a RELABEL, not a recompute: 'Itemized donations' and 'Donor records', with the coverage caveat given a placement that survives the note slot already being contended by the IE support/oppose totals. Cycle-scoping the money figure is a schema change tracked separately as [[FIX-932]]. Cross-ref [[FIX-518]], [[FIX-836]]. <!--id:FIX-931-->
- [x] 🟢 S — **$0 candidate stubs left behind by the FIX-933 merge — cosmetic duplicates, but 16 of them hold real Senate votes** — **File only.** [[FIX-933]] deliberately does NOT delete any `officials` row — "neutralise the duplicate" means it ends up holding zero `financial_relationships` rows, which keeps the merge fully reversible, keeps every FK intact, and keeps that PR out of the officials-dedup design question. The residue is 47 candidate-tier rows carrying $0, a retired `merged_fec_candidate_id` for provenance, and their original `metadata.cand_status/cand_ici/fec_election_yr`. They are same-person duplicates of a sitting member (`T Ossoff` alongside `Jon Ossoff`) and will surface in search, browse facets and any same-name cluster audit. **Not purely cosmetic though:** 16 of the 83 candidate rows [[FIX-933]]'s CAND_ID reconciliation touched hold **real Senate votes** — that is [[FIX-940]], a separate live bug, and those rows must NOT be deleted until it is fixed or the votes would go with them. So the ordering is [[FIX-940]] first, then this. Options when it is picked up: (a) leave them and filter candidate-tier $0 rows out of the surfaces where they are noise; (b) fold them properly, which means deciding the general officials-dedup question — note [[FIX-325]]/[[FIX-375]] closed the *casing*-dupe merge and explicitly scoped elected+candidate clusters OUT (they collide via the [[FIX-248]] promotion path), so this is genuinely undecided territory rather than a re-run of prior work; (c) mark them with an explicit `merged_into` pointer so they are self-describing and cheap to filter. (c) is the cheapest thing that makes the state legible. Cross-ref [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-940]], [[FIX-375]], [[FIX-325]], [[FIX-248]]. <!--id:FIX-939-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Two SAME-PERSON duplicates hide inside the CROSS-PERSON branch — Shontel Brown and Al Green hold their own money twice** — Surfaced by the [[FIX-934]] phase-1 manifest, which classifies each (suspect, owner) pair SAME-vs-CROSS instead of classifying the suspect once against its single best-overlap twin. **[[FIX-933]] could not see these because cross-person contamination dominated the overlap ranking.** Two sitting House members in the [[FIX-934]] cross-person population hold money that is duplicated onto **their own** `tier='candidate'` row: **Shontel M. Brown** (`f29bbd4e-944f-4840-adbd-16a4706a3c02`, Representative OH-11) has **$2,984,275 / 881 rows** duplicated onto `M Brown` [`H2OH11169`] — *Candidate for Representative, OH, district 11*, i.e. her own seat, holding $2,261,183; her elected row's overlap ranking is dominated by **Sherrod** Brown's $47.3M, which is why [[FIX-933]] never surfaced it. **Al Green** (`e9015ab5-913e-4f2c-a917-190ebd0dde22`, Representative TX-9) has **$941,978 / 596 rows** duplicated onto `Alexander Green` [`H4TX09095`] — *Candidate for Representative, TX, district 09*, his own seat (FEC files his legal name, so the first names disagree on the surface and only the seat signal decides it), holding $1,195,809; his best twin is **Mark** Green [`H8TN07076`], a different person. Total $3,926,253. **These are [[FIX-933]] merges, not [[FIX-934]] deletes — the direction is opposite.** The elected row survives and the candidate row is neutralised; deleting the suspect's side (which [[FIX-934]]'s originally-specified 'high collision rate → DUPLICATED → delete from the suspect' rule would have done, at 97.1% and 45.0% collision respectively) would have deleted a sitting member's own donors from their own page. Both pairs fail [[FIX-933]]'s own manifest gates as written (its survivor must be an attribution orphan whose twin is the sole `fec_candidate_id` holder, and it requires `stateOk` on the classifier's single best twin), so re-running that script unchanged will NOT pick them up — the merge needs the per-owner relation from `ownerRelation()` in `packages/data/src/scripts/fec-orphan-classify.ts`. Note both officials ALSO hold cross-person money that [[FIX-934]] phase 2 removes, and 2020/2022 residue blocked by [[FIX-952]]; sequence this AFTER [[FIX-934]] phase 2 so the merge operates on a cleaned row. Cross-ref [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-934]], [[FIX-930]], [[FIX-952]], [[FIX-929]]. <!--id:FIX-953-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **merged_fec_candidate_id is single-valued, so a House→Senate member's stub can only retire ONE id (4 pairs, $3.0M re-split)** — Surfaced by the [[FIX-955]] repair pass. [[FIX-933]] records a retired claim in `officials.source_ids->>'merged_fec_candidate_id'`, a single scalar. That is sufficient for a member who only ever held one seat, but **4 sitting Senators who previously served in the House have a candidate stub carrying TWO of their CAND_IDs**: the stub retired the Senate id and has since re-claimed the House one. Measured on the local clone: **Jim Banks** (elected `S4IN00196`; stub live `H6IN03229`, retired `S4IN00196`, 414 rows / $1,516,488), **Ted Budd** (`S2NC00505` / live `H6NC13129`, 269 rows / $1,368,057), **Jon Ossoff** (`S8GA00180` / live `H8GA06195`, 1 row / $91,883), **Tom Cotton** (`S4AR00103` / live `H2AR04083`, 7 rows / $27,198). Total $3,003,625 across 691 rows, all of it the member's own House-era money now double-held with their elected row. The [[FIX-955]] repair **deliberately excludes these four** and its post-merge assertion refuses them by design: merging while a LIVE second claim remains on the stub means the next FEC run re-binds the House id and re-splits the same money, so the merge would undo itself exactly as [[FIX-955]] describes. Note [[FIX-955]]'s pipeline guard is keyed on the single retired value too, so it does not cover the second id either. Options: (a) make the marker an ARRAY (`merged_fec_candidate_ids`) and have `hasRetiredClaim()` test membership — cleanest, but touches the [[FIX-933]] write path, the [[FIX-955]] guard and `persistNewFecIds`; (b) retire only the id whose seat the SURVIVOR does not currently hold, keeping one scalar — works for this population (a Senator's House id is always the stale one) but breaks the moment someone holds three; (c) leave them and accept a bounded $3.0M double-count. (a) is the durable answer and is small. Ordering: this is only reachable once [[FIX-955]] has landed, and it should be applied to prod in the same pass. Cross-ref [[FIX-955]], [[FIX-933]], [[FIX-941]], [[FIX-939]]. <!--id:FIX-956-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **/api/officials/[id]/summary fails open — a DB error returns 200 with summary:null, indistinguishable from an official with no record** — Noticed while choosing a probe target for the FIX-1021 supervised firing (cc-prompt-60); the route was rejected as a liveness probe BECAUSE of this, and the probe now routes around it via `/responsiveness`. The route never returns a non-200 for an infrastructure failure. Four separate paths all emit the same `200 {"summary": null}` body: (1) the `officials` read at route.ts:79-86 — supabase-js returns `{data: null, error}` rather than throwing, so a DB outage lands on `if (!official) return NextResponse.json({ summary: null })` and is reported as 'this official does not exist'; (2) the genuine no-data case at route.ts:109-111 (`voteCount === 0 && donorCount === 0`); (3) an empty model response at route.ts:163; (4) the catch-all at route.ts:197-200, which console.errors the exception and then returns the same null body. `getMonthlySpendCents` compounds it at route.ts:38-40 by swallowing its own error and returning 0, so a failed spend-cap read silently reads as '$0 spent this month' and the cap is not enforced for that request. **Why this is wrong on its own terms, independent of the probe use:** a caller cannot distinguish 'we have nothing to say about this official' from 'the database is down', so the surface is structurally incapable of reporting an outage — the same class of signal-laundering as [[FIX-1027]], where an outage was reported as health. The CDN discipline is already correct and should be preserved: FIX-796 deliberately stamps cache headers ONLY on the two summary-bearing 200s (route.ts:64, 196), leaving every null variant unstamped so a transient null is never pinned at the edge — so this fix must not start caching an error. **Fix shape:** distinguish the cases. Return 503 (uncached) when the `officials` read or the spend-cap read errors, keep 200 `{summary: null}` for the genuine no-data and kill-switch cases, and let `getMonthlySpendCents` propagate rather than defaulting to 0 so the cap fails CLOSED. Cross-ref [[FIX-1027]], [[FIX-796]], [[FIX-311]], [[FIX-893]]. <!--id:FIX-1029-->

### PROPOSALS

- [x] ⬜ S — **Wire CRS summary backfill into a schedule for ongoing capture** — Follow-on to [[FIX-435]] Phase 2. The CRS backfill (`data:backfill-crs-summaries`, `src/scripts/backfill-crs-summaries.ts`) is resumable: it only selects congress proposals with `summary_plain IS NULL`, so re-running it captures summaries for newly-ingested bills with zero hot-path cost. It was deliberately NOT wired into the batched congress ingest path (`votes.ts → resolveBillsBatch → upsertBillProposalsBatch`) because a per-bill `/summaries` call would add ~thousands of API calls to every nightly run and break that path's round-trip-minimizing design. Wire a low-frequency (weekly) invocation — e.g. a Sunday-block step in the nightly orchestrator or a small standalone GHA workflow with `--allow-prod`, throttled to the ~5,000/hr Congress.gov ceiling. Until then, new congress bills stay `title_only` until someone re-runs the backfill manually. <!--id:FIX-447-->

(3) SharedConnectionsBar was permanently empty (`focusIds.has(e.fromId)` compared raw uuid set vs `official:{uuid}` endpoints). Fix: record {addedNodeIds,addedEdgeKeys} per focus id at fetch time (mirror FIX-827 expansions machinery); on removal drop edges owned solely by the removed focus, then prune nodes with no surviving edge and no surviving owner; SharedConnectionsBar matches via the helper. Post-G5 wave 2. <!--id:FIX-850-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Graph field-wise node merge (focus-set-invariant donation identity) + live depth chip** — Adding a second focus entity clobbered the first's node payloads via last-write-wins `Map.set` merge — e.g. add Kamala (FFPAC $498M donor), then add Trump (FFPAC opposition-scoped, NO donationTotal) and FFPAC visually lost its Kamala identity. Fix: field-wise merge — derive donationTotal/connectionCount in one post-merge pass over the edge set so they're invariant to fetch order; collapsed = prev && incoming. Also: the depth chip [1|2] in FocusTree was inert — `updateEntity(id,{depth})` changed state but fetchedIds skipped the already-fetched entity, so nothing refetched. Fix: a depth change evicts that entity from fetchedIds + its owned nodes/edges [[FIX-850]] and refetches it surgically. Post-G5 wave 2. <!--id:FIX-851-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Graph depth-2 connector invariant + edge-guard + client zero-edge drop + truncation badge** — Depth 2 on most officials scattered dozens of tiny 2-node islands. Fix (server): restore the connector invariant — an individual whose donation rows reach >=2 distinct recipients IN THE RESPONSE passes through as a real node (reuse individualMode==='connector' logic); only add a donor to skipEntityKeys when ALL its rows were aggregated (fixes the edge-guard dropping non-donation rows whose endpoint was bracketed). Fix (client): drop non-focus/non-user/non-group nodes with zero incident edges after merge; consume meta.depth2Truncated / partial as a canvas truncation badge (read by nothing today). Post-G5 wave 2 [[FIX-849]]. <!--id:FIX-852-->

- [x] 🟡 M — **Donation-side industry-tag fan-out: multi-tag donors double-counted across sectors on graph money surfaces** — Sweep rider from the FIX-873 session (which fixed the contract-RECIPIENT-side multi-industry-tag fan-out). The DONATION/donor side has the same class unfixed on 5 surfaces that JOIN entity_tags(industry) on the DONOR and aggregate money WITHOUT a single-tag-per-entity pick, so a donor carrying more than one industry tag has its dollars counted under EVERY tag (or emitted as N duplicate donor rows). Measured multi-tag financial_entities: 1058 local / 1654 prod; of those, 478 local are donation donors (from_id). Sites, all donation donor-side: (1) official_sector_dollars_mv (FIX-506) INNER JOIN entity_tags, GROUP BY (official, et.tag) counts a multi-tag donor under each tag AND drops untagged donors entirely (INNER JOIN); consumers get_group_sector_totals + chord_sector_vote_for_officials. (2) chord_industry_flows_mv (FIX-207/222, nightly) LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY (COALESCE(et.tag,untagged), party_chamber) double-counts multi-tag donors in the platform-wide industry-party chord. (3) chord_industry_flows_for_official(uuid) (FIX-854) GROUP BY COALESCE(et.tag,untagged): FIX-854 only collapsed SAME-tag display-metadata splits, a donor with genuinely DIFFERENT tags still fans out. (4) chord_top_pacs_for_official(uuid,int) GROUP BY fe.id + tag: a multi-tag PAC emitted as N duplicate rows each with full total, LIMIT can be consumed by dups. (5) get_official_donors(uuid) GROUP BY fe.id + tag: multi-tag donor emitted as N duplicate donor rows. Do NOT bundle one fix: each surface has its own display semantics (per-donor row list vs per-sector aggregate vs an INNER-JOIN MV that also drops untagged) and needs its own equality analysis + before/after delta, exactly as FIX-873 did for the contract side. The deterministic fix per site is the FIX-836/777/873 smallest-tag DISTINCT ON pick (or the refresh_group_donor_rollup _gdr_ind MIN() pick, already the SAFE pattern). Verified SAFE this sweep (already single-tag): refresh_group_donor_rollup (_gdr_ind MIN(display_label) per donor), sector_affinity_rebuild_officials (FIX-777/872 DISTINCT ON), and the FIX-704/518/836 donor-rollup machinery.
