- [x] 🟠 M — **Group route live donor fallback pages full entity_connections fan-out — budget-blown on whale cohorts; swap to a cohort-aggregation RPC** — Any official cohort that is NOT gb-materialized (`rollupGbId` null — ad-hoc/custom groups, state-narrowed gb groups per [[FIX-495]], legacy state/party groups, and any gb whose `group_donor_rollup` row is a miss) falls through [[FIX-500]]'s rollup-first read to the live path in `apps/civitics/app/api/graph/group/route.ts`. That path (1) pages EVERY `entity_connections` donation row for the members — including the individual-donor long tail — through `fetchPagedConnections` under `DONOR_FETCH_BUDGET_MS = 8000` with a `maxRows: 50000` ceiling, then (2) resolves every distinct donor's name/entity_type/sector via 100-id `financial_entities` chunks + `fetchIndustryTagsByEntityId`, and only then (3) discards individuals JS-side and takes top-N institutional. Individuals are ~87% of the rows fetched and are thrown away. Local floors (stale clone — prod is larger): senators average ~1,433 donation edges each, p50 79, p90 3,140, max 38,617 — so a random 4-senator cohort has roughly a 1-in-3 chance of containing a top-decile member, one whale alone means 30–50+ sequential pages inside the 8s budget, and stage 2 for thousands of distinct donors is dozens-to-hundreds of concurrent PostgREST chunk queries. `raceWithBudget` also abandons rather than aborts the losing fetch, so it keeps burning pool connections after the flagged response ships. Reproduced 2026-07-24 on `governingBody=senate&state=TX` (2 members, 34,285 edges, Ted Cruz 31,219): LOCAL `donorFetchError: true` / `donorFetchErrorCode: null` at 15.8s, PROD same flag at 8.97s; a repeat local run surfaced the stage-2 failure mode directly (`financial_entities chunk error: TypeError: fetch failed`, 20.7s). This is the [[FIX-497]] fail-open doing its job over a request-path live aggregation that should never have been on the request path. Fix: replace stages 1+2 of the official-branch live path with ONE server-side aggregation RPC over `entity_connections` — same source, same filters, so donorCount / totalDonatedUsd / the top-N list stay byte-identical to a successful live run; uses the existing `entity_connections_donation_to_official_idx` partial covering index. Same caller-swap pattern as [[FIX-774]], same request-path-materialization class the [[FIX-775]] audit closed elsewhere. NOT `official_donor_rollup_mv` ([[FIX-518]]/[[FIX-704]]/[[FIX-809]]/[[FIX-832]]), which was the first candidate: its `rank` is computed over ALL donors including individuals, so `rank <= 200 AND entity_type <> 'individual'` keeps only the institutional donors that outrank the individual long tail — measured on the TX cohort, 196 donors / $1.09M top-25 vs the live path's 1,126 / $16.9M (a 94% understatement, 9 of 25 donors overlapping; Ted Cruz alone has 174 individuals in his top-200, leaving 26 institutional slots). Independently, the MV is built from `financial_relationships` ($32.0M for Cruz) while the route reads `entity_connections` ($41.1M), a 28% source gap. Documented here so the MV is not proposed again for cohort donor display. <!--id:FIX-883-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **BUNDLE AS GROUP discards the row selection — bare-officials handoff aggregates the whole platform; add officialIds mode end-to-end** — The /search explorer's BUNDLE AS GROUP button (`ExplorerActionBar.handleBundleConfirm`) derives only a "dominant kind" from the checked rows and hands off `/graph?groupType=official&groupName=…` — **the selected row ids are discarded**. The dialog says "N items will be sent to the graph as a group", then sends none of them. GraphPage's handoff decode turns that into a bare `{entity_type:'official'}` filter; the group route's legacy no-gb path resolves up to 1,000 active officials (`.limit(1000)`) and calls `get_cohort_top_donors()` at whole-platform scale, which blows the statement timeout (57014) and surfaces as the [[FIX-497]] fail-open donor popup with a member count in the hundreds/thousands. This is the root cause of Craig's 2026-07-24 "4 random senators time out" sighting — NOT the filter-cohort perf class closed by [[FIX-883]]/[[FIX-884]]/[[FIX-885]]. ADD TO GRAPH (the `addEntityIds` path) is unaffected; the lossiness is specific to the bundle path, and predates the Browse redesign — [[FIX-751]] explicitly preserved "exact pre-W1 handoff semantics". Fix: `GroupFilter.officialIds?: string[]` serialized by `graphGroupParams`, decoded by the GraphPage handoff, and honored by the group route's official branch (validate/dedup/cap 50, skip cohort resolution, straight into `get_cohort_top_donors()` — the [[FIX-883]] RPC already takes `uuid[]`, nothing UI-side ever fed it ids). BUNDLE AS GROUP enabled only when every selected row is an official. Ids-groups are in-session only (BrowseState cannot express hand-picked ids, so no saved-view persistence). Client-only shift-click selection groups ([[FIX-826]]) are untouched. <!--id:FIX-886-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **Group route: refuse degenerate/oversized live cohorts (422) instead of aggregate-and-timeout** — Guard the /api/graph/group official branch's NON-materialized (live `get_cohort_top_donors()`) path against cohorts no legitimate UI affordance produces. Two refusals, both structured 422 so [[FIX-490]]'s client error path surfaces a visible notice rather than a blank bubble: (1) a legacy no-gb cohort with NO narrowing at all (no party, no state, no officialIds) — "all active officials" is never a legitimate group, and today it is reachable only via the [[FIX-886]] bug and hand-built URLs — returns `filter_too_broad`; (2) a resolved cohort larger than a measured `MAX_LIVE_COHORT` returns `cohort_too_large` with the memberCount in the body. The gb rollup-first path ([[FIX-500]]) is untouched — materialized cohorts read a single indexed top-N regardless of size, so the guard applies only where the request-path aggregation actually runs. Cap chosen from measured RPC latency across cohort sizes on prod (warm), with clear headroom above the largest legitimate live cohort (House-class ~436 must pass). Complements [[FIX-883]], which made the aggregation server-side but left it unbounded in cohort size. <!--id:FIX-887-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **tag-groups route silently truncates at the PostgREST 1000-row cap** — `/api/graph/tag-groups` aggregates proposal topic counts in JS over an unbounded `.select()`, on the stated assumption that 'the row volume is bounded (~1.4k topic rows total)'. That assumption expired: local now has 5,600 qualifying rows and prod ~7,500 after [[FIX-889]]. PostgREST caps a plain select at `max_rows=1000`, so the route sees ~1,000 arbitrary rows and reports counts that are wrong by roughly 6x — measured local sum of returned counts was 986 against 5,600 real rows. Every displayed tag-group count is therefore understated, and low-volume topics can fall below the `count >= 10` floor and vanish from the browse list entirely. Discovered while verifying [[FIX-889]]; pre-existing and independent of it. Fix is a server-side GROUP BY (an RPC returning one jsonb aggregate, per the standing `reference_postgrest_rpc_row_cap` rule that set-returning RPCs must not be `.range()`-paginated), not a bigger `.limit()`. <!--id:FIX-892-->

### DASHBOARD

- [x] 🟠 L — **Add sparklines to stat cards** — build `/api/stats/trends` returning last 30 days of daily counts per metric <!--id:FIX-090-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **Dashboard AlertBanner copy self-contradicts on prod** — Dashboard AlertBanner copy self-contradicts on prod: "System issue detected: Connections pipeline healthy · The team has been notified and is investigating" — alert condition or message interpolation is wrong; possibly related to the paused ec-rebuild ([[FIX-697]]/[[FIX-703]]). Spotted during Wave-1 prod verification. <!--id:FIX-725-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **connections_pipeline_healthy REBUILD_STALE_MS too tight for pg_cron Mon+Wed cadence** — getSelfTests in apps/civitics/app/api/claude/status/_lib/sections.ts used REBUILD_STALE_MS=4.5d, calibrated for the retired Sun+Wed GHA rebuild cadence (max gap ~3.5-4d). [[FIX-688]] moved the rebuild to pg_cron (rebuild-ec-full Mon 08:00 UTC, rebuild-ec-incremental Wed 08:00 UTC), so the max gap between successful runs is Wed→Mon = 5 days, plus Monday's full can run up to its 6h CALL budget before writing its completing row. On a healthy week the newest completed row reaches ~5.25d and trips the 4.5d threshold ~12h every week (recurring false alarm). Bumped REBUILD_STALE_MS to 6d and corrected the stale 'Sun+Wed GHA' comment + empty-state detail string to the pg_cron reality. Cross-ref [[FIX-725]]. <!--id:FIX-831-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Enrichment-backlog tile counts a status value that does not exist; abandoned processing claims are invisible** — The Data Health card's enrichment-backlog sub-line counted `enrichment_queue.status='in_progress'` — a value `public.enrichment_queue` cannot hold. Its vocabulary is `pending | processing | done | failed` (migration `20260420030000_enrichment_queue.sql`, FIX-064) plus `skipped_no_source_text` / `skipped_feature_retired` (FIX-895/896). `in_progress` belongs to `shadow.enrichment_queue` from the stage-1 schema (`20260421000006`) — a table that does not exist in the database at all (exactly one relation named `enrichment_queue` across every schema, in `public`; the `shadow` schema itself was retired at the 2026-04-22 cutover). The count therefore returned 0 from day one and the tile has always read 'queue idle'. A stale comment above `getPipelines()` claiming the table was 'from FIX-101 stage 1 schema' is the root cause and is corrected here. Consequence: 44 abandoned `processing` claims (all `task_type='tag'`, claimed 2026-04-29, orphaned by an interrupted drain wave) sat invisible for three months — invisible to `pending_tag`/`pending_summary` (not pending) and to `in_progress` (never existed). Fixed: `getPipelines()` now reports `processing` and `stale_processing` (claim older than `ENRICHMENT_STALE_CLAIM_MINUTES` = 60, a deliberately looser threshold than `data:drain:status`'s 10-minute reclaim default — the script answers 'what can I reclaim now', the dashboard answers 'does this look abandoned'). The threshold governs only the warn; `processing` is reported unconditionally. `backlogTotal`/`backlogTone` stay pending-driven. Note the persisted `status_snapshot` payload also carries this shape, so `/api/claude/status/core` serves the old key until the next 10-min cron write — self-healing, renders 'queue idle' in the interim. Not fixed here and deliberately out of scope: surfacing permanently-`failed` rows (148), and whether a scheduled reclaim sweep deserves a cron. <!--id:FIX-924-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Vercel billing math was wrong: Pro includes $20 of usage, so the dashboard showed $31.38 on a $0.00-overage month** — Craig-stated 2026-08-16: Vercel Pro is \$20/month AND THAT \$20 BUYS \$20 OF INCLUDED USAGE, so the bill is \$20 base + max(0, metered usage - \$20). The snapshot and the dashboard both treated the ENTIRE EffectiveCost sum as money owed. EffectiveCost is the LIST VALUE of all consumption PLUS the prorated Pro subscription line, so the headline was the gross list price of everything — and every dollar of it sat below the included credit. **Measured on prod 2026-08-16 (platform_usage_snapshot, fetched_at 03:13 UTC): the card read \$31.38/mo when the actual projected billable overage was \$0.00 with \$8.62 of the credit still unspent.** BEFORE: gross MTD \$15.1852, projected \$31.3828, displayed as the Vercel cost. AFTER: usage MTD \$5.5078 (gross minus the \$9.6774 Pro line), credit remaining \$14.49, projected usage \$11.38, projected billable overage \$0.00, projected total bill \$20.00. **This is a DETECTION defect, not a cosmetic one.** A headline that reads \$31 on a perfectly normal month cannot alarm — there is no band you can put on it that separates healthy from burning, which is part of why the 08-15 burn had nowhere to show up. **The Pro line must come out FIRST.** The FOCUS charge export carries the subscription as its own ServiceName (Pro), accruing \$20/31 = \$0.6452/day — verified against prod where day 15 read exactly \$9.6774. That line is the SUBSCRIPTION, not consumption, so it does not draw down the credit the subscription buys; counting it would peg the account at 100 pct of credit from the first of every month. Added plan_base_usd as a first-class field on VercelUsage rather than deriving it downstream from cost_breakdown, which is sliced to top-8 before persistence ([[FIX-1041]]). Matching is anchored /^(hobby|pro|enterprise)\$/i, not a substring — a substring test on pro swallows Fluid Provisioned Memory and silently inflates remaining credit by a real consumption line. **New pure module packages/db/src/vercel-billing.ts** (no clock, no network, no DB) with table-driven tests whose first row is the live prod reading, so the old interpretation cannot be reintroduced silently. **Two new platform_limits rows:** included_usage_usd (consumption vs the \$20 credit — finally a percentage bar that means something, warns at 80 pct) and billable_overage_usd (THE headline). monthly_spend_usd is KEPT unchanged as the gross list value because it is the leading indicator and the only figure that reconciles against the Vercel dashboard. The \$20 lives in platform_limits.included_limit and is READ BY the collector, so retuning the credit is an UPDATE and not a deploy. **CYCLE-BASIS CAVEAT, stated rather than hidden:** getVercelUsage queries charges from the first of the CALENDAR month and the Pro line prorates over 31, so the projection is calendar-month; the Vercel usage page separately describes an Aug 14 - Sep 14 cycle and nothing in the charges API discriminates between the two. daysInCycle is an argument, not a hard-coded 31, so correcting the basis is a one-line call-site change. **USER ITEM (open):** is there a hard page-me-at-\$X number for true overage? billable_overage_usd.included_limit is provisionally 20 (page when the bill doubles) with warning at 50 pct = \$10/mo; answering the question is an UPDATE. Cross-ref [[FIX-648]], [[FIX-1041]], [[FIX-1044]]. <!--id:FIX-1046-->

Every threshold change to date has been a migration — [[FIX-1044]] derived the 3000/hr origin-request limit, [[FIX-1046]] set the 20 USD credit, [[FIX-1050]] moved R2 to 24 GiB and the Vercel page to 10 USD — and each one needed a deploy to land a number that is, by design, meant to be retuned as the platform grows. DESIGN-GATED ON TWO THINGS, both of which must land first. (1) The UI rework — this belongs inside whatever the platform-costs card becomes, not bolted onto the current section. (2) An admin-auth story, which does not exist today: every civic surface is public-read by design and platform_limits itself is publicly readable, so the read side is already fine but a WRITE path needs a real authenticated-admin boundary. Not scheduled. <!--id:FIX-1051-->

(1) TRUE-COST TOTALS: the headline sums Vercel projected bill + non-Vercel per-metric overages + Anthropic actual, so it counts Vercel Pro 20 USD (which arrives inside projected_total_bill_usd) but SILENTLY EXCLUDES the Supabase Pro 25 USD subscription — there is no subscription concept in the payload at all, so a recurring charge not expressible as a metric overage is invisible. (2) PER-METRIC RATES: rows show a quantity and a bar and no price, so no row explains its own contribution to the bill. Each metric gains rate_usd_per_unit + implied_cost_usd + implied_cost_basis (usage vs overage, documented per metric). (3) BILLING-CYCLE ANCHORING: every provider is silently assumed to be on the calendar month. Vercel is not (Aug 14 to Sep 14, and its own API says so) and Upstash is not (13th-of-month anniversary). (4) PCT MISJOIN: supabase.db_size_bytes renders 29.6 GB / 8.0 GB with pct=56 — the label divides by included_limit, the bar divides by display_limit (the 53 GiB provisioned disk FIX-353 writes there for capacity context). Two denominators, one row, no way to tell which. pct becomes value over its-own-included-limit for every metric and the capacity reading survives additively as capacity_pct. It is the only affected row (the only one with display_limit set) and its honest pct is ~370 percent, so its 80/95 bands need re-basing or it is a permanent critical. See [[FIX-1090]] for the collector half. **cc-233 (2026-10-14): the Upstash reset is calendar, not this anchor.** The 10-13 07:51Z anniversary did not reset the allotment: total_monthly_requests read 499,686 at 06:01Z, 499,693 at 08:01Z and 499,774 at 10-15T02:01Z, and cc-220's ring read on 10-14 was still refused at 500,001 of 500,000. The only observed reset was 09-01T00:01:16Z (cc-229). The cycles.upstash code is [[FIX-1314]]. <!--id:FIX-1089-->

(b) UPSTASH is API-collected since FIX-1038 but cycle-blind: the allotment is per BILLING PERIOD, not per calendar month, and the anniversary is the 13th (creation_time 2026-06-13T07:51:33Z from the management API). Without the cycle a 99.8-percent reading gives no answer to 'when does this clear'. (c) RESEND has no usage endpoint that survives (GET /emails lists only ~84 retained rows, has_more=false at limit 100) — self-count at the sendEmail choke point in apps/civitics/src/lib/email.ts, which every one of the 12 send sites funnels through. Count the server geocode exactly, beacon the client map mount best-effort, expose one monthly self-counted lower-bound map_loads metric vs the 50k free tier; manual entry retires for Mapbox (the has_public_api=false machinery stays for a future provider that truly needs it). Mapbox has no usable usage API on the credentials we hold: the token is a pk. publishable token and analytics/v1 answers 403 'requires a token with analytics:read scope'. (e) GOOGLE CLOUD: inventory only. Zero references to google-cloud / googleapis / bigquery / firebase / vertex anywhere in apps, packages, scripts or workflows; the sole Google surface is SUPABASE_AUTH_EXTERNAL_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/SECRET, i.e. a Sign-in-with-Google OAuth client, which is free and is not a billable GCP service. - [x] 🟠 L — **Costs section rebuild: true-cost headline, named alerts strip, bullet meters with pace/projection/overage anatomy, uniform cards with details** — R4b presentation rebuild on top of the [[FIX-1089]]/[[FIX-1090]] data plane. The card headline was the only number the section exists to produce and it was assembled UI-side out of three unrelated fields; it now renders payload.total_monthly_usd with the itemized decomposition (subscriptions + billable usage + unspent-credit note) directly beneath, so the figure can be audited line by line against vendor invoices. Severity derivation is display-side only and deliberately NOT the band ladder: band state and billing state are different things — supabase.db_size_bytes bills 2.70/mo while its FIX-1089 cost bands (500/750) correctly call it healthy, so over is any metric with implied_cost_basis of overage or actual AND implied_cost_usd above zero, OR band-critical; watch is band-warning, Vercel credit at or above 90 pct used, elevated burn, or a payload-provided projection crossing its included limit before cycle end; steady carries burn/CF-loop/first-cent as sentences. Nothing here touches computeMetricStatus or the email-alert machinery. One meter anatomy everywhere (variant A): included allowance occupies the left three quarters with a dashed boundary mark, the right quarter is a hatched overage zone that over-limit fills enter on a COMPRESSED scale, and the true magnitude plus implied dollars is ALWAYS printed as text so colour and geometry never carry the number alone. Pace tick position comes from the cycles map only and is suppressed where pacing would lie: rolling providers (cloudflare_edge), payload-stated gauges (billing_cycle none/realtime) and Vercel rows whose quantities are projected on a calendar-month basis that is NOT the Aug 14 to Sep 14 billing window the cycle states (re-basing that projection is out of scope — it feeds tuned alert rows). Projection markers are rendered only where the payload provides one (metadata.is_projected) and are never re-derived client-side. Every provider gets the same full-width card: status dot, plan and cycle line with day N of M, right-aligned true dollars per provider derived from the same itemized lists as the headline (so the cards sum to it), a bill-decomposition line where non-zero, two to three headline meters and a collapsible details section holding the rest. - [x] 🟠 M — **Supabase disk denominator flaps across snapshot ticks: Disk row wobbles 58 to 87 percent; stabilize the Prometheus source and settle capacity_pct** — Prod evidence (2026-08-24 read of platform_usage_snapshot, 30-day retention): the /data provisioned-disk figure the Costs card divides by has exactly TWO values in history, 37,930,876,928 and 56,950,861,824. The step from the first to the second at 2026-08-19 08:56 UTC is a genuine Supabase disk grow (40 GB to 60 GB nominal; the 1.5x step is the auto-scale ratio). Since that step, 160 of 161 ticks carried the new value and exactly ONE did not: 2026-08-23 01:20:27 UTC reported the PRE-resize size, which put supabase.disk_used_bytes.included_limit at 37.93 GB and db_size_bytes.display_limit at the same, so the public Disk Utilization row read 87.26 percent instead of 58.12 and capacity_pct read 83.88 instead of 55.87. It stayed wrong for 81 minutes until the 02:41 tick overwrote it. Root shape: getSupabasePrometheusMetrics writes whatever a single scrape says straight into platform_limits, which is DURABLE config, so one divergent scrape poisons a public row until the next tick and poisons the persisted snapshot forever. Two defects behind it. (1) parsePrometheusText SUMS every row matching mountpoint /data, so if the endpoint ever exposed two /data filesystems the denominator would silently become their sum with nothing to say so; the live endpoint today has exactly one row (device /dev/nvme1n1) so the sum is currently a no-op, but it is an unguarded fabrication path. (2) there is no corroboration on a SHRINK: a provisioned disk grows on auto-scale and effectively never shrinks, yet a lone scrape reporting a smaller disk is applied immediately. Fix: require exactly one matching filesystem row (refuse 0 or 2+ rather than sum), and gate a shrink on two consecutive agreeing scrapes so a single divergent reading is a no-op. Also settle capacity_pct, which cc-83 left computed and rendered nowhere. <!--id:FIX-1104-->

- [x] 🔴 S — **status/core + /quality return 500 whenever the snapshot read times out — withDbTimeout's timeout sentinel is truthy, so every !snapshot guard takes the wrong branch** — LIVE ON PROD, observed 2026-08-29 06:20 UTC while verifying [[FIX-090]]: GET /api/claude/status/core returned 500 with an empty body, four times in 45 seconds. Pre-existing since fd233013 (2026-05-18, [[FIX-297]]); nothing in FIX-090 touched the failing block, which added only a daily_counts field to the response object. ROOT CAUSE: withDbTimeout resolves its timeout branch to the literal { data: null, error: Error } cast 'as unknown as T' (apps/civitics/src/lib/supabase-check.ts:61,77). That envelope is the correct shape for a PostgREST builder, but readStatusSnapshot is a PLAIN promise that resolves to a StatusSnapshotRow or null -- it has already unwrapped the envelope. So on timeout the caller does not get null, it gets a TRUTHY object with no fetched_at and no payload, while the type annotation says StatusSnapshotRow | null and hides it completely. The failure then cascades through three guards in a row, each of which reads correct: (1) fresh = Date.now() - new Date(undefined).getTime() < STALE evaluates NaN < n = false, so a perfectly good cache decision becomes 'stale' and the route falls through to live recompute; (2) the live recompute is capped at SNAPSHOT_FALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS = 5000 but genuinely costs 10.1-17.8s on prod (measured, status_snapshot.query_time_ms over the last five rows), so on this path it ALWAYS times out -- the fallback is not a safety net, it is a guaranteed miss; (3) the last-resort branch 'if (!snapshot) return 503' does not fire, because the sentinel is truthy, so the route assigns payload = snapshot.payload = undefined and dies on payload.version with TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined. A 503 that was deliberately written for exactly this case is unreachable. Observed log line proves the truthy branch: '[status/core] live-compute fallback timed out after 5000 ms { fetched_at: undefined, served_stale: true }'. THREE CALL SITES share the misuse -- core/route.ts:49, quality/route.ts:46, dashboard/page.tsx:123. The two API routes 500. dashboard/page.tsx does NOT, but only by luck: its whole body sits in a try/catch that returns null, so /dashboard degrades to a client-fetch render and still serves 200, which is why this has been invisible. TRIGGER is DB slowness, not traffic: the 2s snapshot read only times out when the box is under load, which is why it surfaced during the 06:00 UTC nightly window with refresh_derived_mvs and entity_connections_rebuild both running, the same window where the pooler was refusing connections outright with ECHECKOUTTIMEOUT. So this fires precisely when the dashboard is most needed -- during an incident. FIX SHAPE: make withDbTimeout's timeout value distinguishable rather than adding defensive checks at each call site. Either return a unique sentinel the caller must narrow, or add a withDbTimeoutValue variant for already-unwrapped promises that resolves to null on timeout. Then the existing !snapshot guards are correct as written. Also worth reconsidering: a 5s cap in front of a 10-17s operation is not a timeout, it is an unconditional failure -- either raise it above the measured cost or drop the live-recompute fallback and serve stale. Same class as project_withdbtimeout_any_infers_unknown but a different mechanism: there the generic inferred unknown, here the 'as unknown as T' cast makes a structurally wrong value type-compatible. Cross-ref [[FIX-297]], [[FIX-327]], [[FIX-1094]], [[FIX-090]]. <!--id:FIX-1120-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **Transparency stat cards render as blank skeletons on most prod ticks — getDatabase's votes exact count loses to the snapshot's own concurrency, and one partial count blanks all four cards** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-08-29 while verifying [[FIX-090]]: 6 of 7 retained status_snapshot ticks carry database.error = 'count failed for: votes' (one also failed proposals). Consequence is NOT a missing number, it is FOUR MISSING CARDS. getDatabase sets partial:true on the whole database object when ANY of its 11 counts fails; DashboardClient does 'const db = isPartial(database) ? null : database' and passes loading={!db} to every StatCard; StatCard returns its animate-pulse skeleton when loading. So a single failed count on one of eleven blanks Officials, Open Proposals, Votes and Donation Flow simultaneously. Confirmed by headless render against the live vercel.app origin, cache-disabled: 5 skeletons, 0 stat-card labels, 0 hero numbers, 0 sparklines. THE COUNT IS NOT SLOW AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT. Measured on prod the same minute: SELECT count(*) FROM votes = 261 ms via psql; the same count through PostgREST as the app issues it = 555 ms; and a faithful replay of getDatabase's entire 11-way fan-out from outside the lambda completed in 559 ms WALL CLOCK with all 11 returning 206 and correct values. Against an 8s statement_timeout on the authenticator role, that is a 14x margin. The failure only appears INSIDE computeStatusPayload, whose total is 8.9-17.8s (avg 11.4s over the retained ticks), because that function fans out ELEVEN SECTIONS in parallel and getDatabase's eleven counts are only a fraction of the concurrent PostgREST requests in flight. So this is self-inflicted contention on a Small instance, not query cost, which is why it is INTERMITTENT: a manually dispatched tick at 08:09:32 came back clean (votes 969302, database.error NULL) four minutes after the 08:05:18 tick failed. Same code, same data, different luck. NOTE THE INTERACTION WITH [[FIX-1095]]: switching votes/officials/proposals to count exact was correct (reltuples was 31 percent wrong) and the fix is NOT to revert it -- an exact count that costs 261 ms is affordable by any measure. The defect is that the payload computes eleven sections at once with no concurrency bound, and that a single count failure is escalated to a whole-section partial that a consumer then escalates again to a whole-ROW blackout. FIX SHAPE, three independent levers, any one of which helps: (a) bound the fan-out in computeStatusPayload (the counts do not need to race each other); (b) make getDatabase report per-count failure instead of poisoning the section, so a failed votes count blanks the Votes card and nothing else; (c) make StatCard's loading state per-metric rather than per-section in DashboardClient, so a card with a good number renders it. (b) is the smallest and most valuable -- it converts a four-card blackout into one honest missing figure. Also worth noting the retention interaction: status_snapshot prunes at 24h, so there is no history to tell how long this has been happening; it has been invisible since [[FIX-1095]] landed 2026-08-22 precisely because nothing retains the evidence. Cross-ref [[FIX-1095]], [[FIX-297]], [[FIX-1120]], [[FIX-090]], [[FIX-1077]]. <!--id:FIX-1121-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **daily_platform_counts row is labelled source=observed even when the tick only wrote some of its metrics** — Found immediately after [[FIX-090]] shipped, by the [[FIX-1121]] partial tick. recordDailyCounts correctly OMITS officials and votes from the upsert when the database section came back partial -- that guard works and is what preserved the good reconstructed values on prod 2026-08-29 08:05. But the upsert still sends source: 'observed' unconditionally, so the row ends up labelled observed while two of its four metrics are still the reconstructed backfill values. Verified on prod: the 08-29 row read source=observed with officials 37242 / votes 969302 carried over from the migration backfill, not from that tick. Nothing reads source today, so there is no user-visible wrong number -- but this is a PROVENANCE label on a feature whose entire design rationale is refusing to present reconstructed data as observed, so a label that lies is worse here than in most places. Fix is to send source only when the metrics that define it were actually observed this tick (i.e. gate it on the same dbOk the metric writes are gated on), letting the existing value stand otherwise. Consider also whether one row-level source can honestly describe a row whose four metrics have different provenances -- a per-metric provenance, or simply dropping the column in favour of inferring 'reconstructed' from the backfill's day range, may be more truthful than a single flag. Cross-ref [[FIX-090]], [[FIX-1121]]. <!--id:FIX-1122-->

The FIX-877 stranded-dir message says 're-run pnpm session:worktree:done <id>' — but that plain re-run FAILS: done()'s porcelain safety check runs 'git -C <dir> status --porcelain', which errors 'not a working tree' on the orphan, so cleanIgnoringArtifacts is false and it refuses without --force ('could not read git status / refusing to remove a dirty worktree'). The working recovery is --force (per the FIX-876 memo), which the message did NOT mention. Also, on that path the backoff loop wastes ~34s pointlessly retrying 'git worktree remove' against a permanent 'not a working tree' error. Fix: detect the de-registered-orphan case (path absent from 'git worktree list') and, for it, skip the git-worktree-remove retries and go straight to the containment-guarded fs.rm (no --force needed) — making the plain recovery re-run in FIX-877's message actually work. - [x] 🟠 M — **Shared chunked-by-ids fetch helper (fetchChunkedByIds); migrate three call sites** — `.in()` over an unbounded id list is the most-repeated bug in this codebase — four independent instances ([[FIX-509]], [[FIX-514]], [[FIX-774]], [[FIX-899]]). Mechanism is always the same and always silent: a large id list builds a request URL past the gateway's header limit, Kong 414s (`URI too long`) before PostgREST sees it, `withDbTimeout` returns `{data:null}`, and a `?? []` fallback turns the failure into an empty result. **The bound is URL LENGTH at roughly 200 ids, not the 1,000-row PostgREST cap.** [[FIX-899]] is the case that forced a structural fix: `app/officials/page.tsx` fetched tags with one `.in()` over ~1,000 officials (~40 KB URL) and every official card rendered zero tag pills, silently, for months — surfacing only because [[FIX-897]] added industry pills to that exact surface and they did not appear. Two facts set the shape: (a) a warning comment 15 lines ABOVE the bug already described this precise trap for a different fetch, and the fetch below it did it anyway — comments do not enforce; (b) the pattern had already been hand-written three times locally ([[FIX-732]] `ID_CHUNK` + local helper in `api/graph/connections/route.ts`, [[FIX-778]] in `api/graph/agency-staffing/route.ts`, [[FIX-899]] inline in `officials/page.tsx`) — not a knowledge problem. **Deliverable:** one shared `fetchChunkedByIds` in `apps/civitics/src/lib/paginate.ts`, beside `fetchAllRows`, so 'how do I read a lot of rows' and 'how do I read by a lot of ids' are found together. Contract: default chunk size 200 via an exported named constant (`ID_CHUNK_SIZE`); **returns a result OBJECT carrying rows AND failed-chunk info, never a bare array** — a helper that returns `T[]` and swallows a failed chunk reproduces the bug class one layer down; does NOT throw by default (some surfaces legitimately prefer partial data) but offers opt-in `strict` for callers where partial is worse than nothing; dedupes and drops empty/nullish ids before chunking; short-circuits an empty list to zero requests rather than issuing `.in("id", [])`; optional per-chunk timeout label so it composes with `withDbTimeout`. **Three migrations only** — the three sites above, where correct behaviour is already known and verified so migration is provably behaviour-preserving. The remaining id-list surface is a separate audit. <!--id:FIX-901-->

The result contract is unchanged for any input: rows in chunk order, `failed` in chunk-index order, `chunkCount` unaffected, and `strict` still issues EVERY chunk before throwing (a pool that cancelled the queue on first error would change failure semantics, not just pacing; `paginate.test.ts` pins it). KNOWN LIMIT, documented in the JSDoc rather than fixed: the cap is per CALL, so a route issuing N concurrent `fetchChunkedByIds` calls can have N × maxConcurrency in flight — `app/api/graph/connections/route.ts` does exactly that with seven concurrent calls. A shared module-level limiter was considered and left out of scope. Measured: all three existing call sites are at or under 6 chunks on their heaviest local inputs (officials index ≤ 1,000 ids = 5; agency-staffing 124 active federal agencies = 1; connections at depth 2 on the top-degree official = 5 raw-financial / 3 official / 3 proposal), so none of their timing changes. <!--id:FIX-926-->

- [x] 🟡 M — **No launcher-side runtime record for GHA-launched pipelines — reaped data_sync_log spans are read as runtimes and there is no second source to correct them** — **Found while correcting [[FIX-944]]'s runtimes during [[FIX-968]] (2026-08-06).** There is an asymmetry in how we can know when a pipeline actually stopped. For anything **pg_cron** launched, `cron.job_run_details` records `start_time` / `end_time` / `status` / `return_message` **from the launcher's side, independently of anything the job wrote about itself** — so a job that died without closing its own log row can still be timed exactly. For anything **GitHub-Actions** launched (`nightly.yml`, `rebuild-entity-connections.yml`, `usaspending-bulk.yml`, `fec-backfill.yml`, …) there is **no equivalent**: the only record is `data_sync_log`, which is *self-reported*. When the process is SIGTERM'd at the GHA cap, OOMs, or the runner is evicted, it never writes a terminal row, the row stays `status='running'`, and the only thing that ever touches it again is the reaper. **And the reaper stamps its own clock** — `packages/data/src/scripts/mark-killed.ts` writes `completed_at: now` (line ~146) — so the resulting `started_at`..`completed_at` span is bounded by **when the reaper ran**, not by when the work stopped. **This has already produced a materially wrong diagnosis.** [[FIX-944]]'s bullet reported its failing runs as 20h15m / 20h22m / 20h09m and concluded "the nightly's startup reaps the still-running rollup … the job can never win: it needs longer than the gap to the next nightly" — a causal story that shaped [[FIX-950]]'s framing too. `cron.job_run_details` (runids 105/116/123/129) shows those runs were **6h08m / 6h00m / 6h00m / 6h00m**, every one starting 09:00 and dying at ~15:00 on the `postgres` role's 6h `statement_timeout` — already dead ~14 hours before the nightly that supposedly reaped them. The nightly never killed that job. **That was correctable ONLY because `donor-rollup-refresh` happens to be a pg_cron job.** Had the same reap landed on a GHA-launched pipeline — which is where the reaper primarily operates, on `nightly_cron` / `fec_bulk` rows — there would have been **no second source and the wrong duration would be permanently uncorrectable**. Note `data_sync_log` already carries several `reaped` / `reaped_orphan` GHA rows in exactly this shape (e.g. `fec_bulk` on 08-02/08-03/08-05, `nightly_cron` 08-03), whose spans are being read as runtimes today. **The truth does exist externally** — the GHA API returns `run_started_at`, `updated_at` and `conclusion` per run (`gh api /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{id}`, plus per-job timings via `/jobs`) — it is simply never joined to `data_sync_log`, and cannot be joined after the fact because **no run identifier is recorded**: neither `packages/data/src/pipelines/sync-log.ts` nor `mark-killed.ts` reads `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT` or `GITHUB_WORKFLOW`. **Fix shape, cheapest first:** (1) record `GITHUB_RUN_ID` / `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT` / `GITHUB_WORKFLOW` into `data_sync_log.metadata` at `startSync()` — a few lines in `sync-log.ts`, no migration, and it makes every future row joinable to the authoritative external record forever; (2) stop overloading `completed_at` for reaped rows — either a distinct `reaped_at` column or a `metadata.reaped=true` marker plus leaving `completed_at` NULL, so a span can never again be mistaken for a runtime (note `check_rollup_freshness()` and the [[FIX-234]] canary both read these columns, so change them together); (3) optionally a `metadata.last_progress_at` heartbeat written per chunk/phase, which bounds the true stop time to one heartbeat interval even with no external source. **Rule worth encoding wherever these get read:** a `reaped_orphan` row's `started_at`..`completed_at` span is an upper bound on *reaper latency*, never a runtime — `cron.job_run_details` is authoritative for pg_cron work and the GHA API for workflow work. See `docs/audits/2026-08-06-fix968-cron-window-envelopes.md` §6b for the corrected FIX-944 run table and the full derivation. Cross-ref [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-950]], [[FIX-290]], [[FIX-462]], [[FIX-234]], [[FIX-969]]. <!--id:FIX-971-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **donor-rollup drain stops at exactly 600 recipients per window with 27–32% of its budget unspent, and its cursor timestamp reports the chunk's START not its end** — **Found auditing the first day of the [[FIX-968]] `0 9,12 * * *` schedule (prod runids 181/182, 2026-08-06).** Two defects, unrelated causes. **(1) The 600 ceiling.** Both windows cleared EXACTLY 600 recipients and stopped at 601. Not a `LIMIT`, not an array cap, not a dirty-set fetch that is never re-fetched — the fetch is uncapped and correctly built sets of 10,286 and 9,686. 600 is `3 × c_chunk_size`, produced by the [[FIX-944]] predictive budget guard `v_elapsed + (v_max_chunk × 1.25) > c_budget` doing exactly what it was designed to do at a quantum that no longer fits: runid 181 `11,770 + 1.25×4,247 = 17,079 > 16,200`; runid 182 `11,054 + 1.25×6,546 = 19,236 > 16,200`. It repeats at exactly 600 because it is arithmetic, not coincidence — for any roughly uniform per-chunk cost `c`, three chunks complete and the fourth is refused whenever `3,812 s < c < 4,985 s`, and prod sits at `c ≈ 3,900 s`. The cost is **quantization**: the guard can only stop BETWEEN chunks, so the least budget it can leave unspent is one reservation (`1.25 × slowest chunk`), which at a 65-min chunk is **27–32% of the window**. Those constants were correct when FIX-944 set them — the 07-31 sweep (runid 135) ran 42 chunks with a slowest chunk of 749 s, where the same reservation costs 936 s, under 6%. **(2) The phantom 1h49m tail.** runid 182's last cursor write is stamped 13:31:23 while the run ended 15:20:29, reading as 1h49m of stall after the final commit. It is **chunk 3 running**. Proof by exact equality: `15:20:29 − 13:31:23 = 6,546 s`, precisely the run's recorded `slowest_chunk_seconds`. The cursor UPDATE wrote `updated_at = NOW()`, and `NOW()` is `transaction_timestamp()`; in this procedure every chunk runs in its own transaction that BEGINS immediately after the previous chunk's COMMIT, so `NOW()` inside chunk N's cursor write returns the moment chunk N *started* — one whole chunk early. The cursor VALUE was never wrong; only its timestamp, by up to one chunk. That is a live observability defect, not cosmetics: `pipeline_state.updated_at` is the natural thing for an operator or a future stall detector to read, and during a slow chunk it reports a working sweep as idle for over an hour. It cost a full diagnostic pass. **Fix (migration `20260806230000_fix972_donor_rollup_chunk_quantum.sql`):** `c_chunk_size` 200 → 50 so the quantum is ~7% of the budget instead of ~24%; chunk size becomes overridable via a `civitics.donor_rollup_chunk_size` SESSION GUC mirroring the existing `civitics.donor_rollup_budget_seconds` contract (session-scoped so it can never strand a widened setting into the scheduled job, and clamped to [1,1000] because 0 would make the loop never advance while holding an advisory lock); `NOW()` → `clock_timestamp()` on both cursor-write paths; `chunk_size` + `recipients_done` added to run metadata so a future rate detector has something to read. Smaller chunks also shrink the blast radius of the outer 6h role-level `statement_timeout` backstop — a run cancelled mid-chunk discards that chunk's uncommitted work, which was up to 109 min and is now ~27 min. Body rebuilt from the CURRENT live prod definition (`pg_get_functiondef` md5 `b21f8f65452415e4dcd55d725691e6ef`, verified byte-identical to the FIX-944 migration text and to local) so the FIX-776/777/779/836/868 layering is preserved rather than reverted. **Deliberately NOT changed: `c_budget` stays 4h30m.** The 5,400 s between it and the 6h `statement_timeout` is real and unused, but spending it is a SCHEDULING decision, not a defect fix — prod runs **chain back-to-back** (runid 182 began 1 s after 181 ended; the 12:00 firing was deferred while 181 held the job, so the FIX-968 backstop does NOT log `status='skipped'` as its migration predicted, it runs a second full window), so a longer window pushes the second run deep into US active hours. Left for a human call. Cross-ref [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-951]], [[FIX-965]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-973]], [[FIX-589]]. <!--id:FIX-972-->
- [x] 🔴 L — **donor-rollup per-chunk cost regressed ~9× per FR row between 07-31 and 08-06 with FR vacuum-clean — this, not the chunk ceiling, sets the drain ETA** — **Found while diagnosing the [[FIX-972]] 600-recipient ceiling (2026-08-06). This is the finding that contradicts the premise that removing that ceiling would give 2–3× throughput.** Measured on prod: the **07-31** sweep (runid 135, `complete`) cleared **8,381 recipients in 42 chunks in 3h08m** = **1.35 s/recipient**; the **08-06** sweeps (runids 181+182, both `partial`) cleared **1,200 recipients in 6 chunks in 6h20m** = **19.0 s/recipient**. **Density is not the explanation** — counted as they actually were at the time, the 07-31 dirty set carried 3,127,537 rows over 7,402 recipients (**422 rows/recipient**) and today's carries **584**, a 1.38× difference against a 14× wall-clock difference. Normalizing for it still leaves **~9× per FR row (3.6 ms → 33.0 ms)**. The documented playbook for "this job went slow again" ([[FIX-943]], recorded in the header of `packages/data/src/scripts/donor-rollup-sweep.ts`) is `financial_relationships` dead tuples / visibility-map decay — **checked and clean**: FR is 0.72% dead, 94.1% all-visible, last `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` 2026-08-06 00:56. **So this is not FIX-943 recurring, and the existing playbook has no next step.** Leading hypothesis is **working set vs cache**: FR donation rows grew **+52% in six days** (4,253,944 → 6,457,535; 2,203,591 created since 07-31, from the 08-03/08-04 FEC bulk loads of ~1.1M rows each). The table is now 10.27M rows / 448,249 pages / ~3.5 GB with a 616 MB `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx`, against **256 MB `shared_buffers`** on the Pro Small ([[FIX-589]]). `donor_rollup_rebuild_recipients()` has six arms that each re-scan the same recipients' rows, so one 200-recipient chunk moves on the order of GBs of buffer traffic through a 256 MB cache — consistent with the FIX-968 audit finding the backend pinned on `IO/DataFileRead` for 64+ min. **Explicitly NOT yet proven:** an `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of arm 1 over 25 real remaining recipients returned in **47 ms** with `shared hit=11674 read=2` — but against a cache warmed by the preceding density query, so it measures only the warm path and does not settle the cold-cache question. Proving it needs per-arm cold-cache profiling, which cannot be done read-only on prod; local Docker (4.37M FR donation rows) can host it. **Why it matters:** at 19.0 s/recipient the 9,086 remaining recipients need ~48 h of pure compute. Daily throughput is `wall-clock spent × rate`, and prod runs chain (see [[FIX-972]]), so the box works continuously 09:00→15:20 and clears ~1,200/day — meaning **~1,200/day is close to what the current window genuinely allows, and the 600-per-window ceiling was costing ~33%, not 50–66%.** At the 07-31 rate the entire remaining set would clear in a single ~3.4 h run. So the cost regression, not the chunk quantum, is the lever worth the next unit of effort, and it is the strongest concrete evidence yet for the [[FIX-589]] instance-size conversation. Sequence: profile per-arm cost under a cold cache, attribute it, then choose between (a) more `shared_buffers` / a larger instance, (b) [[FIX-970]]'s dirty-set scoping (~30% of row work), (c) [[FIX-969]]'s delta-apply. **⚠ MEASUREMENT 2026-08-07, from the [[FIX-974]] bulk run — the regression is ACCESS PATTERN, not the box, so option (a) is NOT indicated by this evidence.** The same work in a `to_id`-RANGE, set-based regime ran on the SAME instance the SAME night at **0.060 s/recipient** (all 15,316 recipients in 926 s, one CALL) against the 19.0 s/recipient measured here — **~314×** — and the per-chunk `EXPLAIN` is an `Index Only Scan` at **0.118 ms/FR row vs the 33.0 ms/row above**. Two causes, both properties of the per-recipient regime rather than of the hardware: (1) `to_id = ANY(uuid[])` over scattered uuids is N independent index descents plus scattered heap access, where a range predicate on the same index is one dense walk; (2) `fr.to_type='official'` is not in `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx`, so arms 2–6 forced a heap visit per row — and that predicate turns out to be **exactly** `to_id IN (SELECT id FROM officials)` (measured: 0 exceptions in either direction across all 6,457,535 rows in the index scope), so resolving it off the index keeps the whole scan index-only. Cache warming was visible in-run (62.5 s/chunk over the first 10, **13.7 s/chunk** over the last 22), which is corroborating evidence for the working-set hypothesis in this bullet but *not* evidence that the box is undersized for this work. **This bullet stays OPEN**: FIX-974 routes around the regression without explaining why the per-recipient path went 3.6 ms → 33.0 ms per row in six days, and that path is still what the daily trickle uses. The per-arm cold-cache profiling asked for above is still unwritten. Cross-ref [[FIX-974]], [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-951]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-970]], [[FIX-589]], [[FIX-884]]. - [x] 🔴 M — **0 of 7 scheduled detectors measures a RATE — every one reads an AGE or a STATE, and FIX-972's per-run rate substrate is transported to the canary and dropped by the TypeScript destructure** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 6; SURVIVED adversarial verification.** Playbook **D4 signature A**: *a throughput regression that converges inside the freshness window is invisible by construction.* The arc paid for this once — the canary fired correctly for the stale rollup and could not see the same job's per-row cost regress **~9× in six days** ([[FIX-973]], still open) — and [[FIX-972]] responded by recording `chunk_size` and `recipients_done` per run **specifically so a rate detector would have something to read**. Nothing divides. **Why this is the audit's most structural finding:** every detector on the box answers *"is it stale?"*; none answers *"is it getting slower?"*. A job that doubles in cost but still lands inside its window is invisible until it crosses the 6 h ceiling — at which point it becomes a [[FIX-969]] blowout, and blowouts are report-only by design. So the platform has no way to see a regression coming, only to see it arrive. **This audit's own class-4 findings are that blind spot cashing out:** `entity-connection-stats-rebuild` at 86% of its ceiling and `contract_flow_rollups_rebuild` at 7.2× week-over-week were both found by hand here; nothing running would have surfaced either. **Fix shape:** (a) extend the `canary-check.ts` destructure and its `Freshness` type to read `last_metadata`, and compute `elapsed_seconds / rows_done` per run — the transport already carries it; (b) store a trailing baseline (median per-unit cost over the previous N runs) and **REPORT, not escalate**, when a run exceeds it by a factor, per the [[FIX-943]] cause-vs-consequence split; (c) the cheapest universal version needs no new writes at all — `data_sync_log` already carries `completed_at - started_at` and `rows_inserted + rows_updated` for 11 of 12 pipelines, so a generic rate panel is a view, not a migration. **But it must exclude the zero-span writers first**: 8 of 46 pipelines currently report a 0 ms duration (filed separately) and would divide to an infinite rate. - [x] 🟠 S — **8 of 46 pipelines report p50=p95=max=0 ms on the admin pipeline-health page — their data_sync_log rows stamp started_at AND completed_at with now(), bound at transaction entry** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`); the class-5 (lying timestamps) and class-8 (status-as-liveness) passes converged on it, and it SURVIVED adversarial verification.** Same `NOW()` root cause as [[FIX-972]] — `NOW()` is `transaction_timestamp()`, frozen at transaction start — surfacing somewhere FIX-972 never looked, which is the playbook **E5** lesson: after fixing one site, grep for the mechanism. **The defect.** Several rollup procedures close out with a single terminal row — `20260721010000_fix873_contract_flow_tag_dedup.sql:391`, `20260719000000_fix837_materialize_official_vote_stats.sql:243`, `20260715020000_fix778_materialize_agency_staffing_rollup.sql:162`: `INSERT INTO data_sync_log (pipeline, status, started_at, completed_at, …) VALUES ('…','complete', now(), now(), …)`. The whole procedure body runs in one transaction, so **both** `now()` calls return the *entry* timestamp: `completed_at` records when the run STARTED and the recorded duration is **exactly zero**. **Precision on the failure mode** (an earlier framing of this finding was refuted for overreaching): the row is not visible until `COMMIT`, so it does **not** advertise completion early to other readers, and per playbook **D2** a missing `running` row is not itself a liveness defect. The defect is the **timestamps**. **Measured on prod:** every retained row for `official_vote_stats_rebuild`, `agency_staffing_rollup_refresh` and `contract_flow_rollups_rebuild` has `completed_at - started_at = 0.000000`. Exact-alignment proof: `contract_flow_rollups_rebuild` runid 130 ran **14:00:02.448368 → 15:58:48.014711 = 7,125.6 s** per `cron.job_run_details`, while its `data_sync_log` row reads `started_at = completed_at = 14:00:02.448486` — **understating the finish by 1h58m**. Agency-staffing likewise: cron says 00:19:43.262714 / 00:09:06.698344 / 00:03:16.057629; `data_sync_log` says 00:00:00 / 00:00:00 / 00:00:00. **The consequence is rendered as fact.** `pipeline_runtime_stats_mv` (`20260510000002_pipeline_runtime_stats_mv.sql:31-38`) derives every duration percentile from `completed_at - started_at`, and `apps/civitics/app/admin/pipeline-health/page.tsx:85` renders it. Measured on prod: **8 of 46 pipelines report `p50_duration_ms = p95_duration_ms = max_duration_ms = 0`** — `canary_check` (32 runs), `official_vote_stats_rebuild` (17), **`treemap_individuals_global_refresh` (5)**, `agency_staffing_rollup_refresh` (4), `contract_flow_rollups_rebuild` (4), `sector_affinity_rollup_backfill` (4), `small_dollar_rollup_backfill` (1), `treemap_individuals_focused_backfill` (1). **`treemap_individuals_global_refresh` is one of [[FIX-969]]'s ceiling-blowing jobs — its 21,615.9 s run renders as 0 ms** on the only runtime surface the platform has. So the single runtime-rate view is structurally blind to a daily job and to two of the longest-running weekly ones, which is part of why [[FIX-973]]'s ~9× regression had to be reconstructed by hand. **Fix shape:** (a) `clock_timestamp()` for `completed_at` in every one of these terminal-row writers — playbook **E7**, `NOW()` is for transactional consistency, not observability; (b) better, write the row in two steps as `sync-log.ts` does (a row at entry, a terminal `UPDATE` at exit) so the span is real; (c) have `pipeline_runtime_stats_mv` exclude or flag zero-span rows so a future rate detector (see the rate-measure FIX) cannot silently read 0 as truth. The reaped-row hazard from [[FIX-971]] lands on the same two columns — fix them together. Cross-ref [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-971]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-973]], [[FIX-837]], [[FIX-838]], [[FIX-778]], [[FIX-873]]. <!--id:FIX-979-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Nothing watches the watchman — canary_check is in no detector's coverage, is not a pg_cron job, and produced zero rows on 2026-08-06, the day with the most incidents in the retained window** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 6; SURVIVED adversarial verification — every load-bearing fact re-derived, all refutation attempts failed.** Playbook **D4** (coverage is enumeration — the watchman is in no enumeration) plus **C3** (a guard must be able to fire in the case it exists for). **The exposure.** `canary_check` is a GHA workflow (`.github/workflows/sync-canary-check.yml`, `cron: 0 5 * * *`), so `check_cron_job_health()` structurally cannot see it — that function reads `cron.job_run_details`, and there is no pg_cron job for the canary. It is also absent from `ROLLUP_PIPELINES`, and no workflow asserts on another workflow. Coverage check by mechanism: `grep -rn "canary_check" --include=*.ts --include=*.sql apps packages supabase` returns **only the writer itself**. **Measured on prod:** `canary_check` rows in `data_sync_log` are present on **19 consecutive UTC days, 2026-07-18 → 08-05**, then **ZERO rows on 2026-08-06**, giving 45.3 h since last complete against a daily cadence. When the canary does not run, **all of them go dark simultaneously**, and the silence is indistinguishable from health. **Fix shape:** (a) make the meta-row write the thing that cannot fail quietly — non-zero process exit on insert failure, so GHA marks the run failed and the workflow's own failure surface catches it; (b) add a dead-man check that reads the canary's OWN freshness — cheapest as a pg_cron job (the one scheduler that can observe the GHA side), escalating when `max(started_at)` for `pipeline='canary_check'` exceeds ~30 h; (c) note this is the same class as [[FIX-971]]'s GHA-has-no-launcher-record gap and shares its fix substrate — recording `GITHUB_RUN_ID` at `startSync()` makes the canary's own runs joinable to the authoritative external record. - [x] 🟡 S — **Three operator-facing 'is anything in flight on prod?' probes read data_sync_log.status='running' as liveness — one of them gates a prod close-out** — **Found by the 2026-08-07 site-wide efficiency audit (`docs/audits/2026-08-07-efficiency-audit.md`), class 8 — status-as-liveness (population 60 sites); SURVIVED adversarial verification at 🟡 after its siblings were refuted.** Playbook **D2**: *a `running` row is not liveness — orphan rows outlive dead processes; liveness comes from `pg_stat_activity`, history from `cron.job_run_details` (pg_cron) or the GHA API (workflows).* [[FIX-971]] filed the *recording* half of this problem; this is the *reading* half, and it is the part that can make a decision. **Three probes decide something on a status column:** `scripts/verify-fix916-closeout.sql:33-35` — a **gate on a prod close-out**, 12 h window; `scripts/db-clone-prod.mjs:249-251` — 6 h window, gates a clone; and the prod-merge runbook step recorded at `docs/audits/2026-07-30-fix933-same-person-merge-local.md:202-203`. All three infer in-flight-ness from `status='running'`, which is **wrong in both directions**: a dead process leaves the row set (false positive), and a process that never wrote a start row is invisible (false negative). **The expensive failure mode is the refusal, not the false clear** — a guard that declines to run because a dead row says `running` is a self-inflicted outage, and one of these three gates a prod close-out. That is playbook **C3** territory (a guard must be able to fire — and must not fire spuriously — in the case it exists for). **Scoped honestly.** Verification measured the current orphan population and it is **not** alarming: `data_sync_log` spans 107.3 days, orphan arrival is **0.87/day**, and **resident orphans on prod right now: 0** — the single `status='running'` row at the time of measurement was a live cron run, not a corpse. [[FIX-944]] also stopped stamping `completed_at` on reaped rows, so the older long-lived-orphan numbers no longer describe the current regime. **So this is filed as a latent correctness-of-mechanism defect at 🟡, not as an active incident** — the probes are wrong about what they measure, and the cost lands the day an orphan and a close-out coincide. **Explicitly NOT part of this bullet (both refuted on verification, recorded so nobody re-files them):** `reap_stale_sync_log()` having no pg_cron schedule is *not* a defect — `mark-killed.ts` runs as an `if: always()` post-step in **every** GHA workflow (nightly ×4 phases, fec-backfill, rebuild-entity-connections, usaspending-bulk) and writes an authoritative `nightly_killed` row minutes after a kill (40 such rows on prod), covering exactly the three pipelines that produce most orphans. And `startSync()` swallowing its insert error is not a defect either, because D2 inverts it: a `running` row was never liveness, so its absence masks nothing. **Fix shape:** replace all three probes with the mechanism that cannot go stale — `pg_stat_activity` for "is a backend alive right now", `cron.job_run_details` for pg_cron history, the [[FIX-971]] `GITHUB_RUN_ID` join for GHA work once it lands. The cheap intermediate is an **advisory-lock probe**, which this repo already uses correctly in the chunked writers (`pg_try_advisory_lock`) and which dies with its session by construction. Cross-ref [[FIX-971]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-962]], [[FIX-924]], [[FIX-290]], [[FIX-462]]. <!--id:FIX-989-->

(2) It correlates to NO pg_cron job under either name-normalisation or run-interval containment, and has a single pg_cron-sourced row in the 90-day window, so no cadence can be derived from either the schedule or the observed gap. It is written by reconcile_financial_entity_totals() (jobid 14, monthly '0 12 1 * *') alongside financial_entity_totals_reconcile, which DOES correlate — so the likely cause is that its data_sync_log row is written outside jobid 14's run interval. Measured 812.5h since last complete; against jobid 14's real 730h cadence that is 1.1 cycles, i.e. FINE — which is exactly why FIX-977b made an underived cadence report-only instead of letting it escalate off a guessed 168h default. Fix shape: write a real completed_at, and either give it its own job or record the driving jobid in metadata so correlation is not inferred. Cross-ref [[FIX-977]], [[FIX-978]], [[FIX-971]]. <!--id:FIX-994-->

It is skipped entirely before chunk 1 and can only be evaluated BETWEEN chunks, so a run whose FIRST chunk exceeds the whole window never evaluates it even once. Run 195's chunk 1 was 50 recipients and ran past 21,600s against a slowest-ever chunk of 5,447s recorded three hours earlier. Underlying defect: the chunk is quantised by RECIPIENT COUNT while the real cost driver is per-recipient financial_relationships fan-out, which varies by orders of magnitude across the uuid-ordered dirty set, so a fixed 50-recipient quantum has unbounded cost. Second finding, which falsifies a stated FIX-968 premise: pg_cron QUEUES the 12:00 firing behind a still-running 09:00 one rather than letting it hit the advisory lock and log skipped -- measured on 08-06, 08-07 and 08-08, the second run starts within ~1s of the first ending, chaining two full budget windows into one continuous 9.5h block. Fix shape: chunk by estimated FR-row weight (official_donor_totals.donor_count is already maintained by this same procedure and costs 117 pages to read) instead of by count; arm the guard from chunk 1 with a durable cross-run slowest-chunk seed; cut c_budget from 4h30m to 2h so a firing cannot still be running when the next is due; yield between chunks. - [x] 🔴 M — **FEC bulk writers rewrite ~95% unchanged rows every Sunday — skip no-op upserts** — The weekly FEC file is a cumulative SUPERSET, so every Sunday run re-upserts the WHOLE cycle, but MEASURED on prod 2026-08-09 only 0.5-6.3% of the rows written are new (`created_at` histogram, cycle 2026 `financial_relationships`: 6,841-86,818 new rows per weekly run against 1,375,438 total; individual donor entities 15k-45k new against 3.42M). The other ~95% were byte-identical re-upserts that still cost a FULL write. WHY THAT IS EXPENSIVE: `financial_relationships` takes **exactly zero** HOT updates (`n_tup_upd` 4,911,666 / `n_tup_hot_upd` **0**), because the unpredicated `financial_relationships_updated_at` btree (159 MB) indexes a column the `set_updated_at()` BEFORE UPDATE trigger changes on EVERY update — so HOT is impossible by construction and every upsert rewrites all 16 indexes (4,855 MB) and leaves a dead tuple. `financial_entities` carries the SAME trigger but does NOT index `updated_at`, which is exactly why it gets 27.06% HOT and FR gets 0.00%. Fix: `BulkUpsertSpec.skipUnchangedRows` in `packages/data/src/lib/direct-pg-upsert.ts` emits `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET ... WHERE (any SET column IS DISTINCT FROM EXCLUDED)`, so an unchanged conflict row is left completely alone — no heap write, no index maintenance, no dead tuple, no WAL, no `updated_at` bump. The predicate always covers EXACTLY the SET list (never a caller-chosen subset: a SET column outside the predicate could change silently). Wired into all four fec-bulk writers; the donor writer additionally re-reads the ids that RETURNING no longer emits (an unchanged row returns no row) on the same direct-pg connection, which also closes a pre-existing gap where [[FIX-754]]'s mid-stage resume never got RETURNING rows for chunks committed by an earlier run. MEASURED before/after, local prod-clone, same table, same 4,000-row chunk, 4 alternating slices per variant, source rows pre-materialised so only the upsert is timed: `financial_relationships` 6,941 ms -> 1,289 ms per chunk (1.735 -> 0.322 ms/row, **5.39x**), `financial_entities` 1,377 ms -> 433 ms (0.344 -> 0.108 ms/row, **3.18x**), with `rows_written = 0` on every skip slice confirming the no-op. Gate impact: a from-zero cycle-2026 indiv run costs 348.9 min of writer work at the prod pg_stat_statements means (840,338 FE rows @ 11.246 ms + 1,375,438 FR rows @ 8.349 ms, both from 4,000-row chunk samples) against `fec-backfill.yml`'s 350-min cap — it does NOT fit. With this fix it is ~123 min (65% headroom), and even assuming the donor stage gets ZERO benefit it is ~200 min (43% headroom), so the FR half alone clears the 25%-headroom bar. Cross-ref [[FIX-995]], [[FIX-999]], [[FIX-943]]. <!--id:FIX-1008-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **fec_bulk donor writer overwrites the authoritative all-cycle total_donated_cents with a cycle-only value every run** — Surfaced by [[FIX-1008]]'s skip-unchanged measurement, and it directly caps that fix's payoff on the donor stage. `upsertIndividualDonorsBatch` writes `total_donated_cents` = the donor's aggregate FOR THE CYCLE BEING INGESTED. The post-cycle `rebuild_financial_entity_donation_totals()` ([[FIX-269]]) then overwrites it with the live SUM across ALL cycles — which is the authoritative value, and the reason that rebuild exists at all ('replaces the lossy per-cycle overwrite that left multi-cycle individuals with only the latest cycle's total'). So for every multi-cycle donor the pipeline writes a value it KNOWS is wrong, and repairs it minutes later. Two costs. (1) It is pure write thrash on the platform's hottest table. (2) It defeats [[FIX-1008]]'s predicate: the stored all-cycle value never equals the cycle-only value being written, so those donors are rewritten every single week no matter what. MEASURED on prod 2026-08-09 (sample of 2,576 individual donors with donation rows): **75.8% are single-cycle**, so ~24% of donors are permanently un-skippable for this reason alone — [[FIX-1008]]'s donor-stage skip rate is bounded at ~72% (0.758 x ~0.95 unchanged) instead of ~95%. The machinery to fix it already exists and is already correct: [[FIX-700]]'s `skipAggregateOverwrite` drops `total_donated_cents`/`total_received_cents` from the INSERT column list entirely, so an existing donor keeps their current aggregate and a new donor takes the `BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`; it is currently applied only to SCOPED runs. Direction: apply it to unscoped runs too and let the totals rebuild be the single writer of that column. Care needed on one point before doing it — confirm the rebuild covers every donor an unscoped run can introduce, including donors whose only rows are in a cycle the rebuild's predicate does not reach, otherwise a brand-new donor could sit at 0 until the next full rebuild. Cross-ref [[FIX-1008]], [[FIX-700]], [[FIX-269]]. <!--id:FIX-1009-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **FIX-999's below-cursor-count invariant does not converge — re-scope now that FIX-1008 makes the re-pass cheap** — Correction to the design sketched in [[FIX-999]], found while sizing it 2026-08-09. The proposed completeness guard was: store the count of rows at or below the content-key cursor, and on resume re-run that slice if the count differs. That guard is correct but, on this data, it is equivalent to no cursor at all. The sort key must be the conflict arbiter (`donor_fingerprint`, or `(from_id, to_id)`) to be stable across a republish, and those key spaces are effectively RANDOM with respect to newness — a donor who first appears this week gets a fingerprint uniformly distributed over the whole range. So a republished superset almost always adds rows BELOW the cursor, the below-count always differs, the slice is always re-run, and the re-run slice IS all the progress the cursor bought. Net saving on a mid-file cursor: zero. Nor can the hole be closed by probing the DB for which below-cursor keys already exist — that finds rows that are ABSENT but is blind to rows that are PRESENT WITH A CHANGED VALUE (a donor who gave again), so it would silently drop real updates. What actually closes it is [[FIX-1008]]: with `skipUnchangedRows`, re-running the below-cursor slice costs an arbiter probe plus a predicate evaluation and writes nothing, MEASURED at 5.39x cheaper on `financial_relationships` and 3.18x on `financial_entities`. That removes the need for the below-count bookkeeping, the existence probe, and the sweep ordering entirely — the correct resume becomes 'replay the whole file, let the DB skip the no-ops'. It also removes the ORIGINAL motivation: with [[FIX-1008]] a from-zero cycle-2026 indiv run fits one dispatch (~123 min of writer work, 65% headroom, vs 348.9 min before), so the cursor no longer has to survive a republish for the cycle to converge. Recommendation: leave [[FIX-999]] OPEN but re-scope it to 'confirm from a completed post-FIX-1008 dispatch whether a content-keyed cursor is still needed at all' rather than building the offset-to-key conversion on spec. Do not build the below-count guard as originally specified. Cross-ref [[FIX-999]], [[FIX-1008]], [[FIX-754]]. <!--id:FIX-1010-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **fec_bulk has no freshness watch at all — invisible to the FIX-977 registry while FIX-998's hold is on** — Carried over from the cc-prompt-49 investigation and re-confirmed 2026-08-09; filed rather than fixed because the clean version is a registry change, not a one-liner. `list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines(90)` returns 13 pipelines and NONE of them is `fec_bulk`: the census selects on `metadata->>'source' = 'pg_cron'` and fec_bulk's sync-log rows carry a NULL source (it runs from GHA, not pg_cron). So fec_bulk could stop ingesting for a month without any monitoring surface noticing. That is not hypothetical right now — [[FIX-998]] deliberately holds fec_bulk off the nightly until a completed in-budget run proves [[FIX-995]], and that hold is itself invisible: nothing distinguishes 'intentionally held' from 'silently broken'. `nightly_cron` reports the PHASE, not the pipeline, so the fec-phase row tells you the phase ran, not that fec_bulk ingested anything. The real freshness signal already exists and is cheap: `pipeline_state.fec_indiv_watermark` carries a per-cycle `last_modified`, and FEC republishes weekly, so 'watermark for the active cycle is more than ~10 days behind FEC's published Last-Modified' is a precise, low-false-positive staleness test. Two candidate shapes, deliberately not chosen here: (a) widen the registry census so a GHA-sourced pipeline can register with its own cadence expectation instead of being filtered out by the `pg_cron` source predicate — the right fix, but it touches the [[FIX-977]] registry contract and every consumer of it; (b) a standalone watermark-freshness check reporting through the existing daily canary, which is smaller but adds a second monitoring path for one pipeline. - [x] 🟠 S — **R2 cache freshness compares our upload time to FEC's publish time — a republish mid-run can pin stale bytes for a full ingest cycle** — `downloadWithR2Cache` in `packages/data/src/pipelines/fec-bulk/util.ts` decides cache freshness with `r2Fresh = r2Lm >= fecLm`, where `r2Lm` is the R2 OBJECT's own LastModified — i.e. when WE finished uploading — and `fecLm` is FEC's publish time. Those answer different questions, and the object timestamp answers the wrong one. The race: HEAD FEC at T0 and get the old Last-Modified; download the old bytes; FEC republishes at T1; our upload of the OLD bytes completes at T2 > T1. R2 now holds superseded content stamped NEWER than FEC's current file, so `r2Fresh` is true and every subsequent run is served the stale copy without ever re-reading FEC. NEAR-MISS MEASURED 2026-08-09 — the sequence happened, only the upload did not. `fec-backfill.yml` dispatch (GHA run 31322394244) HEADed indiv26.zip at 15:57:17Z and got `Sun, 02 Aug 2026 15:45:35 GMT` / etag `...-238`; FEC republished at **16:03:26 GMT** (live HEAD: `Last-Modified: Sun, 09 Aug 2026 16:03:26 GMT`, etag `"9167f97b6dfbd1c58e4f4f50997b8c2f-246"`, Content-Length **2,061,619,898**); the run's R2 uploads drained 16:54:40-16:55:32Z, comfortably after T1. It did not fire only because indiv26 took the CACHE branch that run (R2 `fec/2026/indiv26.zip` LastModified 2026-08-06T06:41:27Z, 1,995,728,131 bytes) and a cache hit returns `r2UploadPromise: null`, so nothing was re-uploaded. Had the sizing gone the other way — indiv26 fetched from FEC and uploaded at ~16:55 — the bucket would now hold the Aug 2 bytes stamped 16:55, newer than FEC's 16:03, and every run until the next publish would be served them. Four of the six cycle-2026 files DID re-upload with today's timestamps (cm26 15:55:54, weball26 15:55:53, cn26 15:55:54, ccl26 15:57:17), so the upload path is live and routinely lands inside the window. BLAST RADIUS IS ONE INGEST CYCLE, NOT PERMANENT — and that is the right way to size it. A cache HIT does not re-upload, so `r2Lm` stays frozen at T2 rather than ratcheting forward; FEC's next weekly publish (Sundays ~15:20 UTC) produces a Last-Modified later than T2 and freshness resolves itself with no intervention. So the cost is bounded at one full ingest cycle of silently-stale donor data — which is EXACTLY the outcome [[FIX-903]] exists to prevent (prod donor data a full week behind FEC, one real ingest per two weeks), arriving through the cache layer instead of the watermark. Same failure, different door, and unlike FIX-903 this one leaves no signal: the run logs `complete`, the row counts look plausible, and only the `fec_bulk_run_state` lm value betrays it. FIX SHAPE — compare like with like, and add size. Store FEC's OWN reported headers as R2 object metadata at upload time (`x-amz-meta-fec-last-modified`, `x-amz-meta-fec-content-length`, `x-amz-meta-fec-etag`) and make freshness `stored_fec_* == live_fec_*`, so the comparison is FEC-reported-then vs FEC-reported-now and the R2 object's own timestamp drops out of the decision entirely. Content-Length is the cheap belt-and-braces and should NOT be omitted as redundant: today's two files are 1,995,728,131 vs 2,061,619,898 bytes — **65,891,767 apart, 3.3%** — so a size check alone would have caught this instance, and it costs one integer compare. CAUTION on ETag: R2's object ETag is NOT comparable to FEC's, because multipart chunk sizes differ between our uploader and theirs — our cached indiv26 reads `"44e6967bdbad3e73b09964f1e7677b28-119"` against FEC's `-238`/`-246` for the same class of file. That is precisely why the stored value must be FEC's etag as a metadata string, never the object's own. Cross-ref [[FIX-903]], [[FIX-192]], [[FIX-1010]], [[FIX-995]]. <!--id:FIX-1014-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **fixes-sync.mjs carries a literal NUL byte, so every repo-wide grep treats the FIXES-workflow script as binary** — `scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` builds a cache key as ``${trunk}<U+0000>${sha}`` where the source was meant to carry the two-character escape `\0`. What is actually stored in the file at **byte offset 8362 is a literal U+0000 control character**. Node parses it fine — it is a legal character inside a template literal and the cache key behaves exactly as intended — so nothing fails and nothing has ever surfaced it at runtime. **The entire cost is in search.** ripgrep, `git grep` and the Claude Code Grep tool all sniff for NUL to classify a file as binary, so any repo-wide content search that would match this file returns a binary-file notice instead of the matching lines. Measured 2026-08-09: `grep -n 'closes-as' scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` returns `Binary file scripts/fixes-sync.mjs matches`, and the same query through the Grep tool returns `binary file matches (found \0 byte around offset 8362)`. Reading the file with `node -e` or the Read tool works normally, so it is not corrupt — it is simply invisible to the one access pattern people actually use on it. **Why this is worth more than its size suggests:** this is the script that owns the whole FIXES workflow — the `Fixes:` / `Closes:` / `Verified[FIX-NNN]:` trailer grammar, the closure vocabulary, the [[FIX-461]] trunk-ancestry guard, the done.log column format. It is the single most likely file in the repo to be grepped for 'how does trailer X actually work', and it is the single file in the repo that silently refuses to answer. Every future session of this workflow pays the toll: the real behaviour has to be recovered by reading the file whole or decoding it through node, and a session that greps, gets a binary-file notice and moves on may reasonably conclude the pattern is absent. Encountered exactly that way twice in the 2026-08-09 closure session. **Fix:** replace the literal control character with the escape sequence `\0`; or, cleaner and leaving no NUL in the file at all, use a separator that cannot collide with either operand — both are ref/sha-shaped, so `|` or `::` is unambiguous. One character either way. **Verify:** `node -e "console.log(require('fs').readFileSync('scripts/fixes-sync.mjs').indexOf(0))"` must print `-1`; then `grep -c 'closes-as' scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` must return a count rather than a binary-file notice; then `pnpm fixes:test` and `pnpm fixes:check` to prove the trunk-ancestry cache still behaves. Worth sweeping for the same typo elsewhere in the same breath — `grep -rlP '\x00' --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git .` over tracked text files. Found while auditing the trailer grammar during the FIX-1004/999/944/920 closure pass. Cross-ref [[FIX-1001]] (the four-digit regex widening, same file), [[FIX-314]], [[FIX-369]], [[FIX-461]]. <!--id:FIX-1015-->
