Five consecutive cancelled runs spanning exactly the degraded window, zero emails. That is the whole finding: this is **alerting on an existing signal, not new monitoring**. **What shipped:** a `request-path-probe` job added to `.github/workflows/platform-snapshot.yml` (Craig's call — no new scheduled workflow; GHA cron is unreliable at tight cadences). It runs independently of the snapshot job, curls three surfaces verified 200 + `X-Vercel-Cache: MISS` on 2026-08-12 so none can answer from the CDN while the DB is unreachable (`/`, `/officials`, `/api/officials/<id>/responsiveness`), retries 3 x 20s with `--max-time 25`, and **exits non-zero itself** rather than hanging into a timeout. **The API endpoint is `/responsiveness` and NOT `/summary` deliberately: `/summary` FAILS OPEN** — its own header documents that the `summary: null` variants (kill switch, spend cap, no data, **DB error**) return unstamped 200s, so it is blind to exactly the outage this job catches; `/responsiveness` returns 500 on a DB error (route.ts:36, :111). Both verified against prod. Probe verified end-to-end in both directions before commit: 3/3 200s exit 0, unreachable host exits 1 with the `::error::` annotation. **Known limit:** the two page routes are not proven to fail closed on a DB-down-but-Vercel-up partial outage; on the 08-11 failure mode (Cloudflare 522, origin unreachable) every endpoint fails, but a partial outage rests on `/responsiveness` alone. Three properties are load-bearing and must survive future edits: (1) `concurrency` was moved from workflow level onto the `trigger` job only — a workflow-level `cancel-in-progress` makes the whole RUN `cancelled` and re-launders the signal; (2) the probe carries no concurrency group at all; (3) its worst case (~3.5 min) sits far inside `timeout-minutes: 10`, so it can only ever conclude `success` or `failure`. **The residual gap, stated plainly:** GHA cron does not honour its own schedule. Configured `*/10`, the **observed** gaps on 2026-08-11..12 were 38, 50, 56, 63, 87, 107 and 153 minutes (playbook D2 applied to GHA — read observed starts, never cron expressions). So detection latency is about **one hour, not minutes** — a ~10x improvement on 14 hours at zero new cost, and **not** minutes-scale monitoring. True minutes-scale detection means an external uptime service (e.g. UptimeRobot's free 5-minute checks): zero repo code, entirely in that service's dashboard, Craig can set it up whenever he wants. **Also unresolved:** GitHub routes scheduled-workflow failure mail to the account that last committed the workflow file, currently `Civitics Platform <civitics.platform@gmail.com>` (96c2204c). - [x] 🟠 M — **14 of 15 procedures cannot close their own data_sync_log row on cancel — WHEN OTHERS does not match query_canceled** — **Found while fixing [[FIX-1021]]; the census is catalog-derived, not a hand-kept list.** PL/pgSQL's `EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` **matches every error type EXCEPT `query_canceled` and `assert_failure`**, and `statement_timeout` raises `query_canceled` (57014). So a procedure that opens a `data_sync_log` row with `status='running'`, COMMITs it, and relies on a trailing `UPDATE` to close it will have that `UPDATE` skipped entirely when the 6h axe (or any `pg_cancel_backend`, or a client disconnect) lands — the error blows through the handler and out of the procedure, leaving the row stranded `running` until the nightly reaper finds it. **This is not hypothetical and it is not one procedure.** It is exactly what happened to the 2026-08-11 07:00 `refresh_derived_mvs('weekly')` row, which sat `running` for **15 hours** until `reap_stale_sync_log` closed it at 08-12 04:08:28. **Census, prod 2026-08-13:** of the **15** procedures that write a `running` row AND use transaction control, **14 cannot close it on cancel** — `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk`, `rebuild_entity_connection_stats`, `reconcile_donation_edge_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_party_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_entity_connection_stats_orphans`, `reconcile_financial_entity_totals`, `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental`, `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental`, `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental`, `refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`, `run_entity_connections_rebuild`, `run_rule_taggers`. Only `refresh_derived_mvs` handles it, as of [[FIX-1021]]. Reproduce the census with `pg_get_functiondef(p.oid) LIKE '%WHEN query_canceled%'` over that set. **This is very likely the shared root cause of the stranded-`running` population** that [[FIX-990]] keeps re-discovering (two EC rows stranded from 08-10 alone), the stranded `treemap_individuals_global_refresh` row, and the recurring `fec_bulk` `reaped` rows — every one of those is a job that was cancelled or killed, not one that crashed. **Consequences beyond tidiness:** (1) a stranded `running` row makes the pipeline look alive to anything reading `data_sync_log`, which is what `list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines()` and `check_cron_job_health()` ([[FIX-968]], [[FIX-977]]) read for freshness — so a killed job masks itself as an in-flight one for up to the reaper's 60-minute stale window; (2) the reaper's own note is explicit that elapsed-since-`started_at` is an **upper bound, not a measurement**, so every reaped row permanently loses its true runtime; (3) advisory locks taken with `pg_try_advisory_lock` are released by session teardown so stampede guards still hold — that part is fine. **Fix shape, mirroring what [[FIX-1021]] shipped:** add `WHEN query_canceled THEN` **by name** to each per-unit/per-chunk handler, record the cancel, `EXIT` the loop rather than continuing (the box has just proven it cannot finish one unit), and let the existing trailing `UPDATE` close the row as `partial`. **Verified locally in FIX-1021 that this works:** the `statement_timeout` timer is disarmed once it has thrown, so the bookkeeping `UPDATE` after the catch does run — the repro closed the row with `canceled=true` and 4 units named as skipped. Note the handler CANNOT be an outer block wrapping the loop: PL/pgSQL forbids `COMMIT` inside a block that has an `EXCEPTION` clause, so it must go on the existing inner per-iteration block. Do these in priority order by blast radius — `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental` and `run_entity_connections_rebuild` are the two that actually get cancelled in practice. **⏳ PROGRESS 2026-08-13 (cc-prompt-60): 2 of 14 done — FIX STAYS OPEN.** Migration `20260813010000_fix1028_query_canceled_handlers.sql` fixed the two named above as highest blast radius: `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental()` and `run_entity_connections_rebuild()`. Both bodies were taken from prod `pg_get_functiondef()` and edited in place, so the migration cannot silently revert an intermediate definition. **Verified locally by repro, not by inspection:** with `SET statement_timeout='4s'` the EC procedure logged `[chunk] rebuild_entity_connections_donations — CANCELED`, the `CALL` returned normally instead of raising 57014, and its row closed itself `status=partial, canceled=true, elapsed_seconds=4`; with `'8s'` the donor procedure logged `chunk 2 CANCELED` / `PARTIAL (canceled) — 32 of 6995 recipients, resumable at chunk 3` and closed `stop_reason=canceled`. **Two things found while doing it that the bullet did not anticipate.** (1) The EC procedure's existing per-window handler carried the comment *'WHEN OTHERS catches a statement_timeout cancel too'* — the exact inversion of the trapping rule, now corrected in place; a future census should grep for that claim as well as for its absence. (2) **A cancelled `mode='full'` EC rebuild was leaving autovacuum STRANDED OFF on `entity_connections`**: the procedure COMMITs `autovacuum_enabled=false` before the chunk loop and re-enables it after, and the un-caught cancel jumped straight over the re-enable. That is precisely the [[FIX-884]] mechanism (2026-06-28 run cancelled at its cap → flag off ~4 weeks → 9.5M dead tuples, all-visible 0.9%, index-only scans degraded to per-row heap fetches); [[FIX-885]]'s startup reconcile heals it on the NEXT run, but the cancelling run now cleans up after itself. This makes the EXIT-and-fall-through shape load-bearing rather than merely tidy. (3) The donor procedure needed one extra invariant the generic idiom does not imply: its resume cursor must NOT advance past a CANCELLED chunk. A FAILED chunk may advance it (sweep_failures then blocks the watermark and the whole set is retried), but a cancel routes to the `partial` branch which does not set sweep_failures, so an advanced cursor there would permanently SKIP the recipients whose work had just rolled back — the cursor write is now gated on `v_canceled IS NULL`, and the repro confirms the cursor stopped at chunk 1's end while chunk 2 (recipients 33..239) was the cancelled one. **Remaining 12, unchanged:** `donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk`, `rebuild_entity_connection_stats`, `reconcile_donation_edge_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_party_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_donor_rollup_orphans`, `reconcile_entity_connection_stats_orphans`, `reconcile_financial_entity_totals`, `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental`, `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental`, `refresh_sector_affinity_from_tag_changes`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`, `run_rule_taggers`. Cross-ref [[FIX-1021]], [[FIX-990]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-885]], [[FIX-884]]. <!--id:FIX-1028-->

It did not reach a verdict: prod restarted underneath it. **Timeline, all UTC.** 01:05:09 fired `CALL public.refresh_derived_mvs('weekly')` exactly as cron 10 does — role `postgres`, db `postgres`, inherited `statement_timeout=6h`, budget GUC unset so the compiled-in 4200 s applied (pre-flight asserted all four). 01:05-01:10 units 1-2 (`chord_industry_flows_mv`, `chord_donor_type_party_flows_mv`) both logged `ok`. ~01:10 unit 3 `chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv` began and ran ~35 min, `wait_event_type='IO' / DataFileRead` for most of it. **01:45:27.788819 `pg_postmaster_start_time()` — the instance restarted**, killing the backend mid-unit. **Evidence it was this workload and not an unrelated platform event:** `cron.job_run_details` is EMPTY for the preceding 3 hours and `pg_stat_activity` showed exactly one non-idle backend (the firing) throughout, so nothing else was running to blame or to co-die. The chord MVs are tiny as OUTPUT (64-120 kB) — the cost is the aggregation over `financial_relationships` behind them, which is the [[FIX-443]] OOM shape on a cache-starved box. **THREE CONSEQUENCES, each independent.** **(1) The stranded-`running` row has a SECOND root cause that [[FIX-1028]] does not address, partially contradicting that bullet's 'very likely the shared root cause' framing.** A backend killed by a restart dies on FATAL, not `query_canceled` (57014). FIX-1021's by-name handler — and the two FIX-1028 shipped tonight — catch CANCELS only. Nothing in PL/pgSQL can catch its own backend being killed, so the reaper is the ONLY mechanism for this class and must not be treated as a backstop for it. This row sat `running` 48+ min before the reaper's 60-minute window. Any census of stranded rows should therefore partition by cause (cancelled vs killed) before attributing them to the WHEN-OTHERS defect. **(2) FIX-1021's budget is sized against a premise this falsifies.** The predictive guard evaluates BETWEEN units only (playbook C3 — a REFRESH cannot be interrupted from inside), so it is a guard on TOTAL runtime. Unit 3 alone consumed ~35 min of the 70-min weekly budget without returning. A single unit that can outlive the whole budget, or kill the box, sits UNDERNEATH the guard where it cannot act. Re-enabling jobid 10 on the strength of a between-unit budget is therefore not yet justified. **(3) The new per-MV instrumentation produced NOTHING, because it is only durable at the end.** `v_unit_times` accumulates in a local variable and is written solely by the terminal UPDATE, which a killed backend never reaches — so the run that most needed per-unit timings is exactly the run that recorded none. Same shape as the reaper's own 'elapsed is an upper bound, not a measurement' note. **Fix directions, in rough priority.** (a) Confirm the mechanism from the Supabase Analytics logs API around 01:45:27 (OOM kill vs platform restart) before anything else — this bullet asserts correlation and exclusion of other load, NOT a proven OOM. (b) If OOM: make the chord units bounded — the four chord MVs are the only weekly units and they all aggregate the same large table, so consider per-unit `work_mem`, forcing `max_parallel_workers_per_gather=0` for them, or materialising their input once instead of four independent scans. (c) Persist per-unit timings AS THEY HAPPEN (a row or an UPDATE per unit, committed at the existing per-unit COMMIT) so a killed run still leaves measurements — without this, every future incident is unfalsifiable the same way. (d) Only then re-run the supervised firing and re-decide jobid 10. **jobid 10 remains `active=false`; it was never enabled.** **🔬 LOG EVIDENCE 2026-08-13 (Management API / Analytics, same night): the mechanism is `chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv`, and it has now done this TWICE.** **(a) It WAS a crash, not a platform restart — established by controlled comparison against this project's own logs.** `postgres_logs` at this project's verbosity does not carry postmaster start/stop lines in general, so absence alone would prove nothing — except that the 2026-08-11 22:51 restart DOES log the full orderly sequence (`archive command failed with exit code 1` ×3 → `received fast shutdown request` → `aborting any active transactions` → `pg_cron scheduler shutting down` → `terminating connection due to administrator command` → `the database system is starting up` ×4 → `pg_cron scheduler started`). **None of those lines appear at 01:45:27 on 08-13.** All that appears is `the database system is not accepting connections` ×2 at 01:45:28. Two independent confirmations: `pg_stat_bgwriter.stats_reset = 2026-08-13 01:45:27.903088+00`, i.e. **114 ms after `pg_postmaster_start_time()`** — on PG 17.6 the cumulative stats file is persisted across a clean shutdown and discarded only when recovery runs, so a reset at startup means the prior shutdown was unclean; and **no shutdown checkpoint was logged**, though routine `checkpoint starting: time` lines are logged either side (01:40:03 and 01:50:28). No line names a dying process and there is no OOM message — the kernel OOM killer logs outside postgres, so OOM remains the leading hypothesis but is still NOT proven. **(b) The per-unit timings the terminal UPDATE lost are recoverable from `auto_explain`, and they indict one MV.** 08-13 firing: `chord_industry_flows_mv` **189,390.752 ms** (completed 01:08:19), `chord_donor_type_party_flows_mv` **143,557.390 ms** (completed 01:10:42), `chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv` **no completion line at all** — it began ~01:10:43 and the box died at 01:45:27, so it ran **≥34m44s against siblings of ~3 min**, a >10× outlier. Unit 1's 189 s also sits exactly in the 185-198 s band FIX-1021 measured on 08-12, so the box was behaving normally until unit 3. **(c) THE 08-11 LOG-DARK GAP AND THIS INCIDENT DO UNIFY — but on TRIGGER, not on signature; the bullet should not merge them naively.** Same window on 08-11: `cron job 10 starting` at 07:00:00.139, `chord_industry_flows_mv` **262,648.595 ms** (completed 07:04:23), `chord_donor_type_party_flows_mv` **220,533.129 ms** (completed 07:08:04), and **`chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv` again has no completion line.** What follows is the box dying by degrees rather than at once: `cron job 25 job startup timeout` at 07:30:12, `cron job 26 job startup timeout` at 08:15:49 (pg_cron could not launch a worker at all), then postgres stops logging at **08:29:07** and stays dark **14h22m** until an administrator's fast shutdown at 22:51:20. **So both of the last two `refresh_derived_mvs('weekly')` firings stalled on the SAME unit and took prod down — once as a 14-hour wedge ended by a manual restart, once as an outright crash.** The 08-11 gap is therefore no longer a mystery: it was this job. **The endings differ because the box failed differently, and that difference is not the interesting variable — the trigger is.** **Consequences for the fix directions above:** (i) direction (a) is now ANSWERED for the crash-vs-restart question and only the OOM-vs-other question remains open; (ii) direction (b) should be scoped to `chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv` FIRST rather than to all four chord MVs — its two siblings complete in ~3 min every time and are not implicated; (iii) a new direction: **jobid 10 has now failed catastrophically on 2 of its last 2 firings and must not be re-enabled until this one MV is understood**, and note that everything scheduled behind it on a Tuesday inherits the damage (see the FIX-1024 re-file — jobid 13's `job startup timeout` failures at 09:00 on 08-04 and 08-11 sit inside exactly this window). **Retention caveat:** the Analytics API returned nothing for 2026-08-04, so this census covers only ~7 days and cannot say when the regression began. **✅ MECHANISM NAMED AND FIXED 2026-08-13 (cc-prompt-61) — migration `20260813030000_fix1030_chord_donor_state_plan_fix_and_unit_watchdog.sql`; full writeup `docs/audits/2026-08-13-fix1030-chord-donor-state-plan-flip.md`.** **It is a PLAN FLIP, and fix direction (b) above was aimed at the wrong thing** — the four chord MVs do not share a problem, and per-unit `work_mem` / `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` would not have helped. Prod's plan for unit 3 is a `Nested Loop` whose inner side is `Memoize → Index Scan using financial_entities_pkey`, driven by ~950k outer rows; its siblings use `Parallel Hash Join`. It wins on cost by 19% (613,522 vs 756,100 with `enable_nestloop=off`), and that win is manufactured by three compounding defects: **(1) a 298.5× underestimate** of the `financial_entities` filter — `LENGTH(metadata->>'state')=2` is an expression no index or statistics object covers, so it gets the hardcoded `DEFAULT_EQ_SEL` 0.005; prod estimates **10,714** rows of 3,679,374 where the measured truth is **3,198,178 (87.13%)**; **(2) a 41× underestimate** of `n_distinct(financial_relationships.from_id)` — pg_stats says **42,267**, measured truth **1,745,921** distinct donors across 4,183,604 rows, which is what makes Memoize look ~99%-effective; **(3) `random_page_cost = 1.1`** (prod's Supabase default; local Docker and stock postgres are 4) — **isolated one-at-a-time on the clone, this is the SINGLE setting that flips the plan**, and with prod's GUCs replayed the clone reproduces prod's plan node-for-node (602,475 vs 607,984). **The TRIGGER is confirmed as candidate (a), [[FIX-1018]]'s `financial_relationships_donor_rollup_dirty_idx`, built ~03:00 UTC 08-11 — four hours before the first death.** Its predicate covers unit 3's WHERE almost exactly, so it handed the nested loop a cheaper outer path than it had ever had (bitmap startup 17,539 vs 41,217; 953,828 est rows vs 1,519,884), dropping the total below the hash join. Dropping the index in a rolled-back transaction on the clone restores the hash join. **The index is not at fault and is not touched** — it made a pre-existing misestimate reachable. Candidates (b) FIX-1013 vacuum, (c) 08-09 ingest cardinality and (d) definition drift are all excluded (prod's live MV definitions match the migration; siblings got faster after the vacuum). **Measured execution** (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the clone): `Memoize Hits: 2,328,993 Misses: 1,854,611 Evictions: 869,096 Memory Usage: 262,145 kB` — a **44.3% miss rate** against a model assuming ~99%, and **256 MB in ONE node**, because Memoize sizes at `work_mem × hash_mem_multiplier` (128MB×2) — i.e. a single plan node may allocate the entire size of prod's `shared_buffers`. **That is the OOM-consistent shape** answering direction (a)'s remaining question as far as it can be answered in-database; no server memory parameter is tuned. Join output estimated 4,722, actual 3,593,976 (761×). **Buffers: 7,752,465 → 514,004 (15.1×), and 7,418,444 → 179,993 (41.2×) on financial_entities alone — landing within 3% of healthy sibling unit 2's 498,015**, with 1.85M scattered pkey descents replaced by one sequential scan. **⚠ PREMISE CONTRADICTED — the clone cannot reproduce this outage by DURATION.** It completes the original in 23.5–37 s, not 35 minutes, because its OS page cache holds the whole 1,632 MB `financial_entities` heap, so prod's physical reads are RAM hits here. The clone reproduces the PLAN and the I/O DEMAND exactly and the WALL CLOCK never — which is why the evidence is buffer counts, not seconds. Standing caveat for future perf repro on this clone. **THE FIX, two parts.** **(i)** The FE filter and state extraction are hoisted into a CTE `AS MATERIALIZED` fence, so FE is scanned once and projected narrow (width 48 vs 163) before the join; with no index on a CTE there is no parameterised inner path, so the nested loop is not merely unattractive but **unavailable** — the fix deliberately does not depend on the planner estimating anything correctly. Output identical (`LENGTH(x)=2` subsumes the `IS NOT NULL` and `<> ''` quals): full symmetric-difference parity, **325 rows before and after, 0 either direction, identical SUM 2,197,387,010.00**. **(ii)** `enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget()` on a 2-minute pg_cron job (`derived-mvs-unit-watchdog`) cancels a unit outliving **900 s** (GUC `civitics.derived_mvs_unit_budget_seconds`; the procedure now publishes the in-flight unit + pid + start + budget, COMMITted before each unit). **The prompt's prescribed `SET LOCAL statement_timeout` is NOT implementable and this was re-verified, not assumed** — both `SET LOCAL` and plain `SET` report the new value while `pg_sleep(8)` completes under a nominal 2 s cap, because `statement_timeout` is armed once in `start_xact_command()` and a procedure's `SPI` COMMIT never re-arms it ([[FIX-703]]'s finding, still true on PG 17); `SET …; CALL …` from pg_cron fails with *invalid transaction termination*. **A cancel from outside the backend is the only mechanism that can interrupt a running unit**, and it lands in FIX-1021's existing `query_canceled` handler, so nothing about that path is new. **Local proof, both paths.** Post-fix weekly cadence **6/6 `complete`, 85 s**, with units 4-6 measured for the FIRST time (FIX-1021's instrumentation shipped 08-13 and the run that would have recorded them died): industry 26.5 s / donor_type 20.0 s / **donor_state 18.7 s (was unbounded, now 3rd fastest)** / subject 1.2 s / sector_dollars 3.2 s / spending_totals 15.7 s — so **no weekly unit comes within an order of magnitude of 900 s**, which is why that budget is chosen rather than guessed. Forced-timeout path at a 5 s budget: watchdog returned `{"action":"canceled","unit":"chord_industry_flows_mv","signaled":true,"unit_age_seconds":6.7}`, procedure logged `PARTIAL — 0/6 units ok (5 skipped)`, row closed `status='partial'` with the unit named in `error_message` and `watchdog_canceled_unit`, all 5 skipped units listed, **no stranded `running` row**, and the cancel-once guard stopped later polls from touching the bookkeeping. **STILL OPEN, deliberately not shipped:** statistics (1) and (2) remain wrong — the durable follow-up is `CREATE STATISTICS` on `(LENGTH(metadata->>'state'))` plus an `n_distinct` override on `from_id`, both excluded here because they need an `ANALYZE` to arm and both change plan choice prod-wide. The fence works regardless. **🚀 PROD APPLIED 2026-08-13 03:55:29-04:03:15 UTC — and the apply itself caused ~5.5 min of request-path timeouts. See [[FIX-1032]].** Gate was clean at 03:55 (0 non-idle backends, 0 running data_sync_log rows, last cron 03:30 succeeded in 13s, jobid 10 paused, daily cadence 2h away). But an MV definition cannot be replaced in place, so the migration does DROP + CREATE ... AS (which populates), and prod logged `duration: 442115.812 ms` for that CREATE plus `process 13991 still waiting for AccessShareLock on relation 127653 ... after 1000.090 ms`, dozens of 57014 `canceling statement due to statement timeout`, and 08006 `connection to client lost`, from 03:57:43 to 04:03:12 — stopping dead at the apply's end. Two compounding mechanisms: **(1) LOCK** — DROP+CREATE holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the MV name for the whole 442s rebuild, so readers block on AccessShareLock then die at the 8s service_role timeout; **(2) I/O** — the CREATE's seq scan of the 1,632MB financial_entities heap ran on a box up only 2h10m since the 01:45:27 crash, so the 256MB shared_buffers was cold and starved the request path generally, which is why the damage was site-wide rather than confined to /graph chord callers. **Self-resolved, no escalation:** no restart (pm_start unchanged at 01:45:27), 0 errors in the following 4 min, `/` 200 in 2.2s and `/graph` 200 in 0.57s at 04:07. **⚠ ESTIMATE MISS — corrects this session's own numbers.** The apply was predicted at "2-3 min, blocked on that MV's readers", extrapolating the clone's warm 18.7s by the ~7x steady-state factor; the real cold-box factor was **~24x** and the blast radius was site-wide. **So the migration header's "900s is ~3.4x the slowest healthy unit" is warm-cache only — the true cold-box headroom is ~2x** (442s measured). The budget still stands: 442s is worst-case cold, the weekly fires at 07:00 an hour after the 06:00 daily has warmed the same heaps, and a cold false-trip closes the row `partial` and skips the rest, which is the safe direction. The applied migration file is deliberately NOT edited (never modify an applied migration); the correction lives in the audit doc §7 and here. **Post-apply prod state verified:** MV 325 rows / SUM 2,197,387,010.00 (byte-identical to the clone's rebuild); `AS MATERIALIZED` fence present in the live definition; unique index, GRANTs and [[FIX-1003b]] autovacuum reloptions all survived the swap; prod's plan for the new definition is all hash joins, no Memoize; `enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget()` present, SECURITY INVOKER, EXECUTE only postgres/service_role; cron job 40 `derived-mvs-unit-watchdog` active `*/2 * * * *`, 4 runs, all succeeded, slowest **58ms**. - [x] 🟠 S — **Swapping a materialized view definition via DROP+CREATE holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the whole rebuild — 442s of prod request-path timeouts on 08-13** — Caused a real user-visible incident during the [[FIX-1030]] prod apply, 2026-08-13 03:57:43-04:03:12 UTC. A materialized view's definition cannot be replaced in place, so the FIX-1030 migration did DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW + CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS (which populates). Postgres logs: 'duration: 442115.812 ms plan: Query Text: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW public.chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv AS WITH donor_states AS MATERIALIZED (...)', alongside 'process 13991 still waiting for AccessShareLock on relation 127653 of database 5 after 1000.090 ms', dozens of 57014 'canceling statement due to statement timeout', and 08006 'connection to client lost'. TWO compounding mechanisms, and the second is the one that made it a whole-site event rather than a chord-page event. (1) LOCK: the DROP+CREATE pair holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the MV name for the ENTIRE 442s rebuild, so every reader of that MV blocks on AccessShareLock and then dies at the 8s service_role statement_timeout. (2) I/O: the CREATE's sequential scan of the 1.6GB financial_entities heap ran on a box that had been up only 2h10m since the 01:45:27 crash, so shared_buffers (256MB) was cold and the scan paid full physical-read cost — which starved the request path generally, not just the blocked readers. This is why the timeouts were not confined to /graph chord callers. ESTIMATE MISS WORTH RECORDING: the same statement measured 18.7s on the warm prod-scale clone. The session extrapolated a ~7x clone-to-prod factor from steady-state weekly unit timings and predicted 2-3 min; the real cold-box factor was ~24x. A warm-cache clone timing is NOT a safe basis for predicting a cold-prod DDL window. DURABLE FIX SHAPE: build the replacement out of line and make the exclusive window milliseconds instead of minutes. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW x_new AS <def> WITH NO DATA (instant, no lock on x); REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW x_new (populates, still no lock on x, so readers keep being served the old data throughout); then one short transaction that does DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW x and ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW x_new RENAME TO x. Remember the things a DROP discards and the swap must re-apply: the unique index required for REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY (rename it too), the GRANTs, the COMMENT, and any per-relation autovacuum reloptions ([[FIX-1003b]] sets these on all four chord MVs — FIX-1030 did re-apply them, but only because it was checked for deliberately). SECONDARY RULE: schedule MV-definition swaps against a WARM box. A box within a few hours of a restart has a cold 256MB shared_buffers against multi-GB heaps and will pay worst-case I/O for any full scan. Cross-ref [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1003b]], [[FIX-1021]], [[FIX-884]]. <!--id:FIX-1032-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **Two live planner statistics defects on financial_entities / financial_relationships — FIX-1030's fence protects ONE query, nothing protects the next** — Split out of [[FIX-1030]], where both were measured but deliberately not corrected. They are the loaded gun that FIX-1018's index merely pulled the trigger on, and they are still loaded. DEFECT 1 — expression selectivity. The predicate LENGTH(metadata->>'state') = 2 on financial_entities is an expression that no index and no statistics object covers, so the planner falls back to its hardcoded DEFAULT_EQ_SEL of 0.005: prod estimates 10,714 rows of 3,679,374 where the measured truth is 3,198,178, i.e. 87.13 percent. That is a 298.5x underestimate and it is what makes a nested loop's inner side look ~300x smaller than it is. DEFECT 2 — n_distinct. pg_stats reports n_distinct = 42,267 for financial_relationships.from_id (42,600 on the clone, so this is not a clone artifact); the measured distinct-donor count is 1,745,921 across the 4,183,604 qualifying donation rows alone. That is at least a 41x underestimate, and it is what makes Memoize look ~99 percent effective when its real miss rate is 44.3 percent with 869,096 evictions. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN FIX. Together, at prod's random_page_cost of 1.1, these two made a Memoize-backed nested loop price 19 percent BELOW the hash join, and that plan wedged prod for 14h22m on 2026-08-11 and crashed it on 2026-08-13. FIX-1030 fixed the symptom the only way that was safe in one session: a CTE AS MATERIALIZED optimiser fence on chord_donor_state_party_flows_mv, which makes THAT query structurally immune because a CTE has no index and therefore no parameterised inner path. The statistics themselves were left wrong. So any OTHER query joining financial_relationships to financial_entities, or filtering on a metadata expression, can still flip the same way — and the trigger does not have to be exotic: FIX-1018 flipped it by adding one perfectly reasonable partial index whose predicate happened to offer a cheaper outer path. The next such index is not predictable. FIX SHAPE, three steps. (1) CREATE STATISTICS on the expression, PG14+ expression statistics, for LENGTH(metadata->>'state') and probably also for the bare metadata->>'state' on financial_entities, since the two are separate expressions and stats on one do not help the other. (2) Correct n_distinct on financial_relationships.from_id with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN from_id SET (n_distinct = ...). Measure count(DISTINCT from_id) over the WHOLE table first, not just the donation subset, then express it as a NEGATIVE value, which postgres reads as a fraction of reltuples and therefore stays correct as the table grows; a positive absolute would go stale the same way the sampled one did. (3) ANALYZE both tables — neither change does anything until the stats are rebuilt. GATE BEFORE LANDING. This changes plan choice prod-wide for every consumer of these two tables, which is precisely why it was excluded from FIX-1030's bounded scope. Take before/after EXPLAIN diffs on the main FR/FE consumers and land only if none regresses: the six donor-rollup arms, run_entity_connections_rebuild, the treemap RPCs including the resumable individuals sweep, the get_*_page consolidating RPCs, get_cohort_top_donors, and the chord cohort paths. Note that making an estimate HONEST usually improves plans, but 'usually' is not a standard this particular code path has earned. OPERATIONAL NOTE. The ANALYZE itself is a full-scan-class cost against a 1,632MB and a 3,502MB heap, so schedule it per [[FIX-1032]]'s warm-box rule and off-peak, not within a few hours of a restart. Cross-ref [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1018]], [[FIX-1032]], [[FIX-884]], [[FIX-443]]. <!--id:FIX-1034-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **Unit watchdog cannot tell a long-running unit from a dead backend until the 900s budget elapses — add per-poll pid liveness** — Demonstrated live on prod 2026-08-13 during the first (aborted) [[FIX-1033]] supervised firing. enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget() ([[FIX-1030]]) checks whether the published backend_pid is still a live refresh_derived_mvs backend ONLY on the branch it reaches AFTER unit_age exceeds the budget. Every earlier poll short-circuits at 'within budget' using nothing but arithmetic on metadata.current_unit_started_at — a timestamp that is FROZEN once the backend dies, so it keeps growing forever and looks exactly like healthy long-running work. Observed: the backend was terminated at ~04:35:56 mid unit 2, and at 04:44 the watchdog still returned {action: none, reason: within budget, unit_age_seconds: 702.5} for a process that had been gone eleven minutes. It also fooled the operator — this session reported to Craig that unit 2 was 'running long at 486s then 638s, heading for the fence' when unit 2 had in fact only ever accrued ~149s of real work. WHAT IS NOT BROKEN, so nobody re-opens it: the post-budget guard itself is CORRECT and was verified — it refuses to cancel when the pid is absent or is not running this procedure, which is the safe direction and protects against pid reuse. Separately verified the same day that a pg_cron worker IS visible to that guard: application_name pg_cron, backend_type client backend, state active (NOT null), query CALL public.refresh_derived_mvs('weekly'), and the guard's full predicate evaluates TRUE against it — so the 900s fence is live for pg_cron-launched runs, which was an open worry and is now closed. THE GAP is purely detection latency for the dead-backend case: today such a run stays 'running' until unit_age crosses the budget (up to 900s of nothing), at which point the watchdog correctly declines to cancel, and the row then waits for reap_stale_sync_log's window (up to 60 min) before anything closes it. A stranded non-terminal row is not cosmetic — it is what poisoned connections_pipeline_healthy in [[FIX-833]], because health checks that order by completed_at see a NULL and sort it first. FIX SHAPE: hoist the pg_stat_activity liveness probe ABOVE the budget comparison so it runs on every poll. If the published pid is gone (or is no longer running this procedure) while the row is still 'running', do not cancel anything — there is nothing to cancel — but close the row immediately as 'reaped' with an error_message naming the last published unit and stating that started_at..close is NOT a runtime, mirroring reap_stale_sync_log's existing FIX-944 wording. That turns a 900s-plus-60-minute blind spot into a 2-minute one and makes the last-known unit durable at the moment of death, which is the same instrumentation gap [[FIX-1030]] consequence (3) was about. Keep the existing post-budget cancel path exactly as it is. Cross-ref [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1033]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-833]], [[FIX-1028]]. <!--id:FIX-1035-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **sync-canary-check has been red for 10 days and every failure is a TRUE POSITIVE — the gap is alert delivery, not the checker** — sync-canary-check has failed every morning since 2026-08-04 (last pass 08-03; 10 consecutive red runs through 08-13), which reads as a broken checker. It is not. **Every failure is a true positive, and the red X IS the alarm** — [[FIX-885]] made the DB-health findings exit non-zero precisely because an email alone is not escalation. Layer verdict (playbook E11): not the canary, not the checker logic, not the workflow env/secrets. Two things are actually wrong and neither is the canary. **(1) The conditions it reports are real, and they ROTATE — which is why a week of red looks stuck.** 08-04: vm_degraded on financial_entities at 47.6 pct all-visible. 08-05: donor_rollup_refresh stale 68.49h against a 48h window. 08-08: financial_entities again. 08-09 through 08-13: escalating rollups under the [[FIX-977]] derived registry, latest being entity_connections_rebuild at 356.65h against an escalate-past-210h bound. That last one is a live operational gap in its own right: prod data_sync_log shows entity_connections_rebuild status=reaped on 08-03 and 08-10 (both Monday, jobid 22) with NO row at all on the Wednesday firings (jobid 2) of 08-05 and 08-12, and last status=complete on 2026-07-29. entity_connection_stats_rebuild is reaped since 08-10, donor_party_rollup_refresh since 08-04. Those need their own FIX; they are not canary defects. **(2) A distinct checker-side failure on 08-06 that is NOT an escalation.** That run died with "canary-check failed: data_sync_log query failed: canceling statement due to statement timeout" and wrote no meta row — prod data_sync_log carries canary_check rows for 08-01 through 08-13 with 08-06 missing. This is the one run where the checker itself broke rather than reported. [[FIX-968]] built nightly_check_unavailable for this class but the failure here lands a layer above it. **The notification gap — why no alert reached Craig.** The runs wore status completed/failure, never cancelled, and metadata.alert_sent was true on every escalating run. sendAlert THROWS on a Resend error, so a true value means the Resend API ACCEPTED roughly ten sends to ADMIN_EMAIL. The gap is therefore downstream of the API accept: delivery, spam filing, a wrong ADMIN_EMAIL secret, or an unverified RESEND_FROM sender domain. None of that is checkable from the repo — it needs the Resend dashboard delivery log. Rule out at the same time: GitHub Actions scheduled-workflow failure notifications should have produced ten emails on their own and evidently did not. Feeds the [[FIX-1026]] / [[FIX-969]] residual-alerting story. **Observability defect surfaced while diagnosing (small, real, fix alongside).** The escalation verdict lives ONLY in the stdout JSON, never in the canary_check meta row: writeMetaRow runs BEFORE the failures array is computed, so escalating_rollups, alert_sent and escalated are all absent from data_sync_log.metadata. Diagnosing ten days of red therefore required pulling ten sets of GHA logs when one SQL query should have answered it. Persist the escalation reason and alert_sent into the meta row so the arc is greppable. **Not fixed in session, deliberately:** there is no S-class change available — the checker is behaving correctly, and the real work splits into an alert-delivery investigation needing external dashboards plus a separate rollup-not-completing FIX. Cross-ref [[FIX-234]], [[FIX-885]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-978]]. **RE-SCOPED 2026-08-17 (cc-prompt-63), on Craig's delivery evidence — the premise above is half wrong.** This bullet assumed the gap was alert DELIVERY. It is not: Resend delivered every one of the ten alerts, verified in Gmail. So there is no delivery investigation to run and no external-dashboard dependency, which removes the stated reason this was not S-class. **The actual failure is SALIENCE — ten identical daily emails that each say the same thing become invisible, and the eleventh, which mattered, read exactly like the ten that did not.** That is a notification-design problem, not an infrastructure one, and the fix is small and local. New fix shape, three parts: (1) **Severity tiers in the SUBJECT LINE**, so the tier is legible in a notification list without opening anything — today every alert shares one subject and the reader cannot triage without reading the body. (2) **Page on DELTA, not on STATE.** The current design re-alerts every morning for as long as the condition holds, which is what manufactured the ten identical mails; alert on the TRANSITION into a bad state, on a material worsening, and on recovery, and stay quiet while a known-bad state is merely persisting. A daily "still red, day 7" digest line is fine — a daily page is not. (3) **Split the duty between the two existing checkers by what they can actually prove:** [[FIX-1026]]'s probe owns the "site down" tier (request-path reachability, page-worthy immediately), and the canary owns the "data stale" tier (rollup freshness, digest-worthy and escalating only on delta). Conflating them is why a data-staleness signal and an outage signal arrive looking identical. The meta-row persistence item above (escalating_rollups / alert_sent / escalated absent from data_sync_log.metadata because writeMetaRow runs before the failures array is computed) SURVIVES this re-scope unchanged and is still the cheapest single improvement — it is what makes "did this alert fire, and why" a SQL query instead of ten GHA log pulls. Docs-correction style per the `5dbe3405` precedent: the original text is left standing above so the corrected premise is visible rather than silently rewritten. Cross-ref [[FIX-1026]], [[FIX-1052]]. <!--id:FIX-1036-->

- [x] 🔴 M — **Upstash free-tier command allotment is exhausted — the entire edge rate limiter is failing open, silently, and Upstash is the one vendor platform_usage_snapshot does not track** — **Found by the 2026-08-15 traffic/cost-spike triage (docs/audits/2026-08-15-traffic-cost-spike.md).** Observed verbatim in prod Vercel logs at 2026-08-16 00:28-01:26 UTC, on 92 of 100 sampled requests: '[ratelimit] Upstash error on bucket=entity_leaf — failing open (allow): Command failed: ERR max requests limit exceeded. Limit: 500000, Usage: 500002.' **Every crawl defense the codebase has is a no-op right now.** The FIX-637 entity_pages cap, the FIX-683 entity_leaf cap and the FIX-797 entity_prefetch bucket all route through checkRateLimit in apps/civitics/src/lib/ratelimit.ts, which catches the Upstash error and returns ALLOW. All 100 sampled requests returned HTTP 200; zero 429s. A crawler walking distinct entity UUIDs across /officials, /donors, /proposals and /jurisdictions was proceeding completely unthrottled at the time of measurement, every request a cold cache MISS and a full SSR render. **The fail-open is CORRECT and is not the defect** — it is load-bearing per the module header and it kept the site up. The defect is that it is **unobservable and un-alerted**: nothing anywhere pages when the secondary cost/volumetric layer switches itself off. **Root cause of the blindness.** packages/db/src/platform-snapshot.ts computes usage for anthropic, supabase, cloudflare (R2), github and vercel. **Upstash is absent from all of it** — there is no getUpstashUsage helper, no platform_limits rows, no metric, nothing. So a hard $0-ceiling cost control (design: free tier, auto-upgrade OFF, so exhaustion rate-limits the DATABASE rather than billing) can hit its cap and go fully open with zero signal on the Platform Costs card, zero warning status, and zero auto-trip evaluation. **Fix shape — cheapest durable option in the whole remediation list.** Add an Upstash block to the existing 10-minute snapshot: a getUpstashUsage() helper alongside the existing vendor helpers, platform_limits rows for the command allotment, and updateUsage writes so commands-used rides the SAME warning/critical machinery every other metric already uses. No new cron, no new workflow, no new alerting path. **Sizing note:** 'Usage: 500002' is only 2 over the cap because the counter freezes on crossing, so it carries NO information about WHEN exhaustion happened — the Upstash console is the only source for that, and it bounds the FIX-1040 ordering claim. **Secondary, separable:** reduce commands spent per request (skip the check on cache hits, or coarsen buckets) so the next allotment does not burn at the same rate. Software lever before compute lever — raising the Upstash tier is deliberately NOT proposed. Cross-ref [[FIX-570]] (the limiter this instruments), [[FIX-637]], [[FIX-683]], [[FIX-797]] (the three defenses currently disabled), [[FIX-281]] (the snapshot to extend), [[FIX-880]], [[FIX-1039]], [[FIX-1040]], [[FIX-1041]]. <!--id:FIX-1038-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **The rate limiter's fail-open path logs once per bucketed request, and nothing durably records a 429 or a fail-open anywhere — the app cannot answer 'was the limiter firing?' after the fact** — **Found by the 2026-08-15 traffic/cost-spike triage (docs/audits/2026-08-15-traffic-cost-spike.md).** Two coupled observability gaps on the edge limiter, both surfaced by the same incident. **(1) Per-request log line on the failure path.** apps/civitics/src/lib/ratelimit.ts:168 emits console.warn('[ratelimit] Upstash error on bucket=...') inside the catch, so once Upstash is exhausted EVERY bucketed request produces a Vercel observability event. Measured in prod logs 2026-08-16 00:28-01:26 UTC: 92 of 100 sampled requests carried the warn. **Size it honestly before fixing it:** at the observed ratio this is worth roughly $0.03-0.30/day — Observability Events is a $2.87/month projected line. This is a hygiene fix, NOT a cost fix, and it should not be sold as one. Its real value is that a per-request log line makes the failure mode expensive to leave running for weeks. Fix shape: sample or rate-limit the warn (once per bucket per N seconds per instance), or replace it with a counter. **THE TENSION IS LOAD-BEARING: silencing this log without adding the [[FIX-1038]] Upstash alarm makes the fail-open MORE invisible, which is the actual defect. Ship the alarm first or together — never this alone.** **(2) No durable record of 429s or fail-opens.** rateLimitResponse in apps/civitics/middleware.ts:144 returns the status and logs nothing. public.abuse_events — the [[FIX-880]] observe-only substrate built for exactly this — holds **0 rows** for the last 12 days on prod (verified: SELECT count(*) FROM abuse_events WHERE occurred_at >= now() - interval '12 days'), so either recordAbuseEvent is not wired to the limiter path or ABUSE_EVENT_PEPPER is still absent from Vercel env (a known pending item). The consequence: the ONLY way to answer 'was the limiter firing during the incident?' is Vercel logs, which retain about an hour and cap the CLI at 100 rows. This triage had to reconstruct the whole incident from billing counters because of it. **RateLimitResult already carries the right primitive** — the `limited` boolean exists specifically to distinguish a real 429 from a fail-open allow ('so callers can log/observe quota pressure without breaking', per the type's own comment) and NOTHING reads it. Wire it: count fail-opens and 429s per bucket, and land them somewhere queryable — abuse_events is the obvious home and already exists. **Explicitly NOT in scope: the fail-open semantics do not change.** It is load-bearing, it kept the site up during this incident, and it is correct. The projection arithmetic is unaffected and still correct, but the comment misleads anyone reasoning about resolution. **The resolution limitation is worth documenting where the readers are.** Because values are cumulative MTD and step ONCE PER DAY at ~06:00-07:00 UTC (midnight Pacific — Vercel's ChargePeriodStart days are Pacific days), consecutive 10-minute snapshots are byte-identical to 16 decimal places. **The 10-minute snapshot cadence buys ZERO additional resolution for any Vercel metric.** An incident can only ever be localised to a calendar day, never to an hour. The crawler here is **meta-webindexer/1.1** (ASN 32934, Facebook Inc.) and it walked "/graph?entity=UUID" anyway, having fetched /robots.txt 88 times in the same window. Two candidate causes and they need distinguishing before anything is changed: (a) the crawler ignores robots.txt, or (b) **it does not support the star mid-path wildcard** — wildcard support in robots.txt is a Google/Bing extension, NOT part of the original standard, so a conforming-but-basic parser reads "Disallow: /*?" as a literal path and matches nothing. A 3.2x GAP separates the busiest legitimate hour ever recorded from the quietest crawl hour, so anything in [2500, 7000] classifies both sets perfectly. Chose 3000 = max-legit x 1.35: zero false positives across all 147 legitimate hours, 2.4x below the crawl floor so it also catches a crawl at 40 pct of this one rate, and ~\$8.85/day if sustained (~27x a baseline day 0.33 of consumption). NB this reads the last THREE complete hours per tick, not one: GHA cadence measured over 200 runs / 6.8 days is p50 46 min, p75 60, p90 87, max 155 — a single-hour read would silently skip hours on 26 pct of runs. **D2 — burn-rate layer.** The 08-15 audit established the spike was 3.7x baseline by hand-writing a window function over the cumulative MTD series; nothing automated it. Fires only when BOTH conditions hold: delta >= \$1.00 absolute floor AND delta >= 3x the trailing-7-day median. Neither alone works — a pure multiple pages on every ordinary day once a quiet week drags the median down, a pure floor misses a burn starting from an elevated baseline. - [x] 🔴 M — **Closed-loop auto-mitigation: the cron raises the Cloudflare security level itself and reports what it did** — Craig explicit choice: on a sustained origin-volume spike the platform should ACT, then tell him — not ask him to act. On 2026-08-15 Under Attack mode cut origin-reaching traffic ~99 pct within one hour of enablement (21:00 UTC 7,313 x 200 / 0 x 403; 22:00 UTC 445 x 200 / 6,850 x 403), worth ~\$21/day. The mitigation works. What was missing was the detection and the hand on the switch, and both are mechanisable. New packages/db/src/cf-mitigation-loop.ts, run from the same Cloudflare reading [[FIX-1044]] collects so the decision and the number behind it can never disagree. **TRIGGER:** origin-reaching >= 3000/hr in >= 2 DISTINCT complete clock hours within a rolling 6h window. **ACTION:** PATCH security_level to under_attack. **REVERT:** automatic after 6h to the level it found, then re-trip on fresh evidence if the burn resumes (Under Attack mode is a dam, not a fix — it 403s every scripted client and challenges search crawlers, so leaving it up indefinitely has its own cost, and the revert is what makes the loop safe to leave armed). **SIX SAFETY RAILS, every one covered by tests that fail if the rail is removed.** (1) ESCALATE-ONLY: only ever raises, and only reverts an escalation IT made. If the zone is already at or above the target when the trigger fires it records NO TRIP AT ALL — claiming a level it did not set is exactly what would later make it auto-revert a human decision. (2) SUSTAINED MEANS MEASURED-SUSTAINED: the CF hourly bucket is already an hour of evidence, and the count is keyed on the BUCKET TIMESTAMP, never on tick count — at the measured p50 46-minute GHA cadence the cron re-reads the same bucket most ticks, so counting readings would let one bad hour trip it alone. Detection latency ~2-3h, ~\$1.80 of burn, accepted deliberately. (3) AUTO-REVERT WITH RE-TRIP. (4) DEBOUNCE: evidence is consumed on every transition and a fresh trip needs 2h since the last revert, so it cannot flap more than once per revert window. (5) FAIL-SAFE: any CF API error records, alerts, and takes no further action — and critically, a FAILED write records NO trip, because a phantom trip record would make the next run LOWER the zone security on the strength of a write that never landed. (6) KILL SWITCH: new cf_auto_mitigation switch plus CF_AUTO_MITIGATION_ENABLED env hard-kill disarms the WRITE while leaving detection, metrics and alerting fully live — disabling the loop can never make the platform blinder than before it shipped. Deliberately the ONLY kill switch with no auto_trip_threshold_pct: a cost metric must never be able to switch off the machinery that defends against cost. State lives in pipeline_state.cf_mitigation_loop, following the FIX-1040 precedent (durable signals are state TRANSITIONS, not per-request rows; abuse_events does not fit — it needs node:crypto and an admin client). Every transition emails via a new renderMitigationEmail template, debounced on the ACTION so a persistent condition reports once. **SHIPS ALERT-ONLY.** Measured 2026-08-16: the existing CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN does GET security_level fine (200, under_attack, modified 2026-08-15 22:03 UTC) but PATCH returns 403 code 9109, and GET /user/tokens/{id} is also refused so the scope cannot be read directly — it is inferred from the shape of the write failure. USER ITEM: mint a token with Zone Settings:Edit (keep Analytics:Read) and add CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN + optionally CLOUDFLARE_ZONE_ID to the Vercel env; the loop starts acting the moment it exists, no deploy. Documented in docs/CLOUDFLARE.md (how to tell an automatic change from a manual one) and docs/OPERATIONS.md (how to disable it). Cross-ref [[FIX-1039]], [[FIX-1040]], [[FIX-1044]]. <!--id:FIX-1045-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **The mitigation loop proves its own Cloudflare write scope instead of discovering it mid-incident** — Follow-up to [[FIX-1045]], found while confirming Craig token edit. **THE GAP:** the loop only ever learned whether its Cloudflare token could WRITE at the moment it first tried to — i.e. during a live burn. isScopeError() classifies a 9109 correctly and the loop degrades to alert-only and emails, so it fails SAFE, but the question "is this thing actually armed?" was unanswerable until the one moment the answer had to be right. A token minted without Zone Settings:Edit, later rolled, re-scoped to the wrong zone, or expired stayed invisible until the mitigation was already needed. That is the same class of silent failure that made 2026-08-15 cost what it did — a hard control switched off with no signal. **THE PROBE:** twice a day, issue a PATCH of security_level with THE VALUE THE ZONE ALREADY HAS. 200 proves Edit, 9109 proves Read-only. Cloudflare accepts it, changes nothing, and does NOT move modified_on — verified by hand across the permission change on 2026-08-16, pinned at 2026-08-15T22:03:19Z through no-op PATCHes on both sides of it. There is no safer write available; every other zone setting would be a real change. The caller contract is load-bearing and enforced by making currentLevel a REQUIRED argument rather than something the probe fetches itself: pass anything other than a value just read from that zone and the probe becomes a real mutation. **WHY TWICE A DAY AND NOT EVERY TICK:** an idempotent PATCH still writes a Cloudflare AUDIT LOG entry, and the audit log is one of the three documented ways to tell an automatic change from a manual one (docs/CLOUDFLARE.md). At the measured cron cadence, probing every tick would produce ~40 no-op entries/day and bury exactly the signal it exists to protect. Cached in pipeline_state.cf_mitigation_loop.scope_probe with a 12h interval. Staleness is harmless for CORRECTNESS — before a real trip the loop attempts the actual write regardless and that write is authoritative — so a stale cache can only make the REPORTED status lag, never cause a wrong action. A DISARMED loop never probes (a no-op write is still a write) and a THROWN probe keeps the prior verdict rather than inventing a pessimistic one that would suppress a real mitigation. **ALSO: the trip threshold is now env-overridable** via CF_TRIP_ORIGIN_REQ_THRESHOLD, mirroring LEADING_DB_CONN_THRESHOLD ([[FIX-642]]) and LEADING_FLUID_USD_THRESHOLD ([[FIX-648]]) which are overridable for exactly this reason: an alarm nobody has watched fire is an alarm nobody should trust, and before this the only way to exercise the write path end-to-end was to wait for a real crawl. Set it to 50 and the next two breached hours trip for real, email, hold 6h and auto-revert. A non-numeric or non-positive value is IGNORED rather than obeyed — an env typo must never be able to set the threshold to 0 and trip the loop on every quiet hour. The EFFECTIVE threshold rides in the snapshot payload and the card shows "threshold OVERRIDDEN to N/hr" in amber whenever it differs from the derived 3000, because a verify-run value left in place is its own incident. **Card wording now distinguishes four states** — armed+verified, ALERT-ONLY, armed (unverified, i.e. a pre-FIX-1047 snapshot or never probed), and disarmed — where before "armed" meant only that the kill switch was on. **PREMISE CORRECTED WHILE INVESTIGATING:** a vercel env pull comparison appeared to show Vercel holding a DIFFERENT Cloudflare token than the local files. That was wrong and the check was invalid — Vercel cannot read encrypted values back, and all 40+ sensitive vars returned an identical 11-character redaction placeholder. Never diff a Vercel secret against a local one this way; compare token IDs via /user/tokens/verify instead. Cross-ref [[FIX-1045]], [[FIX-1039]]. <!--id:FIX-1047-->

- [x] 🔴 L — **EC rebuild cannot finish inside 6h because the CONTRACTS arm's throughput collapsed 3.2x — growth alone does not explain it, and FIX-1034 did not help** — Fix-shape spec for the next rollup-lane prompt. Diagnosed 2026-08-17 (cc-prompt-63); no rework done in that session by design. THE THROUGHPUT TABLE is the whole diagnosis — edges_total and runtime are both in data_sync_log/cron.job_run_details for every run, so this is measured, not inferred: 07-15 695,640 edges in 1,077s = 646 edges/s; 07-20 1,349,007 in 2,252s = 599/s; 07-22 1,313,229 in 2,206s = 595/s; 07-29 3,184,880 in 5,350s = 595/s; 08-17 4,011,180 in 21,615s = 186 edges/s. Throughput held flat at 595-646 edges/s across a 4.6x growth in edge count, then COLLAPSED to 186/s — a 3.2x regression. GROWTH ALONE DOES NOT EXPLAIN THE FAILURE: at the old steady 595 edges/s, even 4.0M edges finishes in about 6,700s, comfortably inside the 6h ceiling. It is the rate regression that pushes it past the wall, not the size. THE COLLAPSE IS LOCALIZED AND NAMED: the 08-17 run's cancel_detail is 'rebuild_entity_connections_contracts: canceling statement due to statement timeout', so the contracts arm specifically is where the 6h is spent. chunk_failures is 0, so this is not error-retry churn — it is one arm running slow. FIX-1034 DID NOT HELP: it landed 08-14 and 08-17 was the first post-statistics Monday. Runtime 21,615s vs the pre-statistics 08-10 run's 22,380s — inside noise, both pinned at the ceiling. The FR/FE planner statistics corrected a different query family; the contracts arm needs its own EXPLAIN. THE STEP CHANGE IS DATED: 07-29 completed in 5,350s, 08-03 was already dead at the ceiling. Whatever changed sits in that window and should be the first thing looked for — a plan flip (cf. the FIX-1030 nested-loop/Memoize mechanism, same shape and the same random_page_cost=1.1 cost model), or bloat in a contracts-side table with no vacuum owner (cf. FIX-884's all-visible collapse, and note per FIX-943 that entity_connections gets a vacuum but the contracts SOURCE tables may not). THE COMPOUNDING DEFECT — it never banks progress. The 08-17 run wrote 4,011,180 edges and then closed status='partial' with no resume marker; contrast donor_rollup_refresh, which closes 'budget exhausted — resumable at recipien...' and picks up next firing (FIX-1002/1021). So every EC firing restarts from the top, burns 6h, and dies at the same place — it can never win no matter how many times it runs, which is why the rebuild has not completed since 2026-07-29 and why [[FIX-1053]]'s recipient_count_reconcile arm (called only from the tail of run_entity_connections_rebuild) has not run since. FIX SHAPE, in order: (1) EXPLAIN the contracts arm on prod and find the 3.2x — do this BEFORE any budget work, because if it is a plan flip the budget becomes unnecessary; (2) give the rebuild the FIX-1002/1021 treatment — an explicit time budget and a durable resume checkpoint per arm, so a firing that runs out of budget banks its edges and the next one continues; (3) only then consider splitting the arms into separate jobs. Do NOT simply raise the 6h statement_timeout: [[FIX-985]] set that ceiling deliberately, and a job that needs longer than the gap to its next firing is the failure mode [[FIX-971]] corrected the record on. Cross-ref [[FIX-985]], [[FIX-1002]], [[FIX-1021]], [[FIX-1034]], [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-884]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1053]]. **✅ RESOLVED 2026-08-18 (cc-prompt-66) — AND THE DIAGNOSIS ABOVE IS CORRECTED ON ITS CENTRAL POINT.** Step 1 was run before any budget work, as specified, and it refutes the contracts-arm attribution. MEASURED ON PROD (read-only, idle box, bounded at 300s, work_mem=256MB — exactly what the procedure sets) the contracts arm's aggregate is **128.5 seconds**, not hours: GroupAggregate (actual time=125131.882..128408.178 rows=189949 loops=1), Sort Method: external merge Disk: 359544kB, Bitmap Heap Scan on financial_relationships (actual time=768.903..95472.569 rows=3908956, Heap Blocks: exact=295464), Buffers: shared hit=9 read=301515 temp read=44943 written=44944, Execution Time: 128456.054 ms. cancel_detail names contracts because that is where the AXE FELL, not where the time went — an important general lesson about reading cancel messages as attribution. WHERE THE 6 HOURS ACTUALLY WENT, measured rather than inferred, from the per-arm clock the run leaves behind: each incremental arm stamps its watermark row with now(), which is that chunk transaction's start, so pipeline_state.entity_connections_donations updated_at=2026-08-17 08:00:00 is arm 1's start and entity_connections_votes updated_at=2026-08-17 11:17:04 is arm 2's start, i.e. arm 1's end; the cancel landed at 14:00:24. **The DONATIONS arm ran 11,824s — 3h17m, 55% of the budget** — and votes+cosponsors+appointments+oversight+holds+gifts+contracts shared the remaining 9,800s. WHY: donations is incremental on an updated_at watermark, and the FEC merge/re-split work ([[FIX-933]]/[[FIX-934]]/[[FIX-954]]/[[FIX-955]]) bulk-rewrote financial_relationships — by week of updated_at, 2026-07-27 touched 1,201,953 rows across 820,602 distinct donors and 2026-08-03 touched 2,721,613 rows across 1,358,662 donors — so the incremental arm degenerated into a near-full rebuild and wrote 4,011,180 edges against the 5,706,655 donation edges that exist, ~70% of the table, matching the ~71% of donors the dirty set covered. That IS inside the 07-29..08-03 window this bullet correctly dated; the bullet attributed it to the wrong arm. THE THROUGHPUT METRIC WAS STRUCTURALLY BLIND TO IT: the contracts arm's cost scales with its INPUT (3.9M FR rows) while its OUTPUT (189,949 edges) barely moves, so no edges-per-second reading can see contracts growth at all — and conversely the donations blow-up looked like a rate collapse because the edges were real but the work per edge was not. A SECOND, INDEPENDENT REGRESSION IS ALSO REAL BUT IS NOT THE 6h: contract+grant FR rows went 1,467,389 → 3,822,744 across the weeks of 2026-07-06 and 2026-07-13 (a USASpending ingest, EARLIER than the dated window), which pushed the contracts sort past work_mem into a 359MB external merge; and the group estimate is 2,327,285 against 189,949 actual, a 12.3x over-estimate off from_id n_distinct=-0.268211 ([[FIX-1034]]). ALSO CORRECTED: the arm functions' SET statement_timeout TO '30min' clause is DECORATIVE — statement_timeout is armed at CALL start and a nested function cannot re-arm it, which is why the run died at the 6h mark rather than 30 minutes into contracts. WHAT SHIPPED (step 2, which the spec rightly said ships regardless of step 1): migration 20260818000000 — a 5h wall-clock budget checked at ARM BOUNDARIES so the exit is orderly rather than axed mid-statement (1h under the 6h ceiling so the terminal bookkeeping and cursor write always land; the ceiling itself is NOT raised, per [[FIX-985]]), a durable per-arm resume checkpoint in pipeline_state.entity_connections_rebuild_cursor so a budget exit banks its arms and the next firing skips them, and per-arm elapsed seconds in metadata.arm_timings — that last being the observability gap that permitted the misattribution in the first place. The budget is overridable via pipeline_state.entity_connections_rebuild_budget so the repros exercise shipped code rather than a test variant. Reproduced locally against prod-clone data, both paths: budget exit banked arm 1 and closed partial with 'budget exhausted — resumable at arm rebuild_entity_connections_votes (1 of 11 arms banked)', the next firing logged 'resuming cycle ... 1 arm(s) already banked', SKIPPED donations and banked votes+cosponsors; and a forced 5s statement_timeout closed the row partial with canceled=true, elapsed_seconds=5, the cancelled arm correctly NOT banked. Step 3 (arm splitting) stays DEFERRED and is now much less obviously needed. Follow-ups filed: [[FIX-1058]] (the bgworker starvation this session's log pull named), [[FIX-1059]] (the retired-vs-broken detector gap that [[FIX-1053]] surfaced). <!--id:FIX-1056-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **The request-path probe is blind to the Cloudflare layer — it curls the Vercel origin, and cannot be repointed while Under Attack is on** — Found 2026-08-17 (cc-prompt-63) while adding the 526 note to docs/CLOUDFLARE.md. THE DEFECT: the [[FIX-1026]] request-path-probe job in .github/workflows/platform-snapshot.yml inherited the snapshot job's APP_URL default, which is the VERCEL ORIGIN (civitics-civitics.vercel.app). The probe exists to answer 'can a user load the site', but a user's request traverses Cloudflare then Vercel — so probing the origin tests only the second half and is structurally blind to every edge-layer failure. NOT THEORETICAL, TWICE OVER: on 2026-08-12 civitics.com served Cloudflare 526 for much of the day (expired ORIGIN certificate, renewals failing silently behind the proxy) while the vercel.app URL kept serving — platform-snapshot stayed GREEN through the whole outage. That is the same shape as the 2026-08-11 522 that FIX-1026 was built for; the job was pointed at the one host that cannot see it. THE OBVIOUS FIX IS BLOCKED, AND THAT IS THE REAL FINDING. Repointing at civitics.com today makes the job fail every hour forever, because the zone is still at security_level=under_attack and challenges non-browser clients. Measured against the live zone the same day: GET / -> 403, /officials -> 403, /api/officials/<id>/responsiveness -> 403, every one carrying 'Cf-Mitigated: challenge', and the 403 persists with a browser User-Agent. A permanently-red pager is a disabled pager, so this is strictly worse than the blind spot and was NOT shipped. THE UNDER ATTACK STATE IS ITSELF A CORRECTION: a planning note recorded Under Attack as turned off on 08-12, but the zone says otherwise and so does the platform's own loop — pipeline_state.cf_mitigation_loop.tripped is null, which by the CLOUDFLARE.md rule means the loop did not set the level, and the loop logged skip_already_escalated twice on 2026-08-16 ('3 breach hours, but the zone is already at security_level=under_attack and this loop did not set it'). So it is a human setting still in force, and docs/CLOUDFLARE.md has been corrected accordingly. SAME ROOT BLOCKS THE OTHER HALF OF THE MONITORING GAP: FIX-1026's header already notes that true minutes-scale detection needs an external uptime service, and Under Attack blocks those too — so the zone posture, not the repo, is the binding constraint on request-path monitoring. WHAT SHIPPED THIS SESSION: the probe env now reads a dedicated PROBE_URL secret first, falling back to CIVITICS_APP_URL then the origin default, so the eventual flip is a secret change with no code change; and the workflow carries the measured 403s plus the two conditions that unblock it. FIX SHAPE, pick one: (1) take the zone off under_attack (already the standing Pending item in CLOUDFLARE.md, and the real test of whether Common Exploit Paths holds alone), then set PROBE_URL to https://civitics.com; or (2) leave the posture and add a WAF skip rule admitting this probe specifically — a secret header is the cleanest key, since UA and IP are both weak. Prefer (1); it fixes the external-uptime gap in the same move. Whichever is chosen, verify with the three curls above BEFORE flipping the secret. ALSO CORRECTED while reading the live zone: Always Use HTTPS is On, not Off as the posture table said, and there are three custom WAF rules (Common Exploit Paths, the WAF - SSL ACME skip, Meta), not two. - [x] 🟠 M — **Monday/Wednesday starvation window is bgworker-slot exhaustion, not query contention — pg_cron may request 32 concurrent jobs from a 12-slot pool** — Found 2026-08-18 (cc-prompt-66) while hunting the Monday 09:xx-16:08 starvation window named in [[FIX-1052]]. THE MECHANISM IS NAMED, THE CONSUMER IS NOT. Pulled the Supabase Analytics postgres_logs for 2026-08-17 13:50-16:25 UTC. Through the entire 14:00-16:08 tail — that is, AFTER the EC rebuild was cancelled at 14:00:24 and with nothing at all in data_sync_log — the log carries three independent message classes that all mean "a process could not be started in time": (1) jobid 40 (derived-mvs-unit-watchdog, every 2 min) logs "cron job 40 starting" followed EXACTLY 10 seconds later by "cron job 40 job startup timeout", firing after firing for hours — 10s is pg_cron cron.task_start_timeout, so the bgworker never registered; (2) "autovacuum worker took too long to start; canceled" and "autovacuum worker started without a worker entry", which the autovacuum launcher emits when a requested worker does not register in time; (3) "could not accept SSL connection: EOF detected" and "Connection reset by peer" in a continuous drip, i.e. clients abandoning during the TLS handshake because the postmaster cannot complete accepts. THE DECISIVE NEGATIVE RESULT — IT IS NOT A HEAVY QUERY. auto_explain.log_min_duration is 10000 on prod, so EVERY statement over 10s in that window was logged. The only ones that appear are Supabase platform telemetry: SUM(pg_database_size(...)) at 10.4s and 17.6s, and the pg_stat_statements roll-ups at 12.7s, 13.5s, 13.9s and 16.5s. Not one pipeline query, not one user query. That is precisely why data_sync_log is silent across the tail and why FIX-1052 could not find a culprit in it: none of our work was running. The box was not busy executing — it could not START processes. THE STRUCTURAL OVER-SUBSCRIPTION, measured on prod the same night: max_worker_processes=12 (configuration file), cron.max_running_jobs=32 (default, and per the Supabase config note NOT overridable), max_parallel_workers=2, max_logical_replication_workers=4, max_connections=60, autovacuum_max_workers=3. pg_cron is permitted 32 concurrent job workers out of a 12-slot pool it shares with parallel query and logical replication, and nothing enforces the difference — the ceiling is discovered at runtime as "job startup timeout". Note this is the same mwp=12 that failed its first Monday. WHAT WAS SHIPPED, AND WHAT IT IS FOR: a self-limiting bgworker census sampler (migration 20260818002000) — an UNLOGGED bgworker_census table plus sample_bgworker_census(), scheduled every 2 minutes as jobname bgworker-census, deliberately on the SAME cadence as the jobid-40 watchdog whose startup timeout is the symptom, so a MISSING sample is itself data (this job could not get a worker either). It no-ops unless pipeline_state.bgworker_census.expires_at is in the future, armed for 48h from 2026-08-18, so it disarms itself even if the cron job outlives the investigation. NEXT READ: Wednesday 2026-08-19 08:00 UTC and its tail, then Thursday read the census to answer WHICH backends hold the slots. TEARDOWN, one line, do not leave this armed: SELECT cron.unschedule(bgworker-census); DROP TABLE public.bgworker_census; DELETE FROM pipeline_state WHERE key = bgworker_census; (quote the two literals). CANDIDATE FIXES once the consumer is known, none shipped tonight because guessing the remedy before the consumer is exactly the error [[FIX-1056]] corrected: raise max_worker_processes; thin the pg_cron job population in the window; or stagger the */2 watchdog off the boundary minutes. Cross-ref [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1056]], [[FIX-1055]], [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-968]]. <!--id:FIX-1058-->

Mechanism: the two workflows declare DIFFERENT GitHub Actions concurrency groups (nightly.yml group: nightly-sync, fec-backfill.yml group: fec-backfill), so each is serialized only against ITSELF. Nothing serializes them against each other even though both reach the same pipeline, the same financial_relationships / financial_entities write path, and — the sharp edge — the same single pipeline_state key fec_bulk_run_state. That key holds the FIX-754 per-stage resume cursor, so two live runs read and overwrite each others progress: immediately after the backfill finished all three stages (donor-entities 1944958/1944958, indiv-to-candidate 2165106/2165106, indiv-to-committee 1149355/1149355) the key was observed back at indiv-to-committee cursor=1060000 status=in-progress, i.e. the nightly had re-established state for the same cycle and was redoing work the backfill had completed. NOT DATA DAMAGE in this instance: the writes are ON CONFLICT upserts and FIX-1008 skip-overwrite means unchanged rows are skipped, so the cost was wasted IO on a box whose write throughput is the known bottleneck ([[FIX-961]]). But the resume cursor is not idempotent state — a crash during an overlap can strand a cursor that neither run owns, and the FIX-754 accounting silently under- or over-reports. Direction: give both workflows the SAME concurrency group (e.g. group: fec-pipeline) so GHA serializes them, and/or take a DB-level advisory lock around runFecBulkPipeline() so a second invocation refuses rather than interleaves (the pg_cron procedures already use a session advisory lock for exactly this — see the reference_pgcron_procedure_pattern precedent).
