- [x] 🟠 M — **Census result: the Mon/Wed starvation is NOT bgworker-slot exhaustion — pg_cron with use_background_workers=off never takes a worker slot at all** — The bgworker census [[FIX-1058]] armed on 2026-08-18 has been read (2026-08-20 01:5x UTC, 1,182 samples over 08-18 01:12 to 08-20 01:10, self-disarmed on schedule). IT REFUTES THE HYPOTHESIS IT WAS BUILT TO CONFIRM. THE MEASUREMENT. Through the 2026-08-19 saturation, non-client backends peaked at EIGHT against max_worker_processes=12, and every single backend_type present was a singleton: archiver, autovacuum launcher, background writer, checkpointer, logical replication launcher, pg_cron launcher, pg_net worker, walwriter, plus an occasional autovacuum worker (max_concurrent 1 for each of the nine). There was no pool of workers competing for slots at any sampled moment. Client backends peaked at 25 against max_connections=60, so connections were not exhausted either. THE STRUCTURAL POINT THAT SETTLES IT INDEPENDENTLY OF THE CENSUS: cron.use_background_workers is OFF on prod. With that setting pg_cron does NOT request a background worker per job — it opens a libpq CLIENT CONNECTION and sends the command as one simple query, which is the same fact [[FIX-1063]] relies on for its invalid-transaction-termination finding. So FIX-1058's central arithmetic (pg_cron may request 32 concurrent job workers from a 12-slot pool) cannot be the mechanism: pg_cron never asks that pool for a job worker. cron.max_running_jobs=32 bounds concurrent libpq connections, not bgworkers, and 32 against max_connections=60 is not over-subscribed. WHAT job startup timeout ACTUALLY MEANS HERE: failure to ESTABLISH A CONNECTION within pg_cron's task-start window, not failure to acquire a worker slot. That relocates the bottleneck to the postmaster's ability to fork and complete a handshake, which is exactly what FIX-1058's own log evidence showed and mis-filed as corroboration — could not accept SSL connection EOF detected and Connection reset by peer are clients dying IN THE HANDSHAKE, the signature of a postmaster that cannot accept, not of a worker pool that is full. THE CENSUS CORROBORATES A BOX-WIDE STALL BY ITS OWN ABSENCE, which is what it was designed to do: sampling every 2 minutes it should land 15 samples per half hour, and it landed 15/15 through 08:30, then 8, 4, 10, 8, 9, 2 as the morning degraded, then ZERO samples in BOTH the 12:00 and 12:30 buckets, then 1/15 at 13:00, 14:00 and 14:30. The 12:00-13:00 blackout is precisely the window in which 91 of 91 cron firings died. The sampler could not get a connection either. POSITIVE ATTRIBUTION IS STILL INHERITED, NOT PROVEN HERE: the I/O-starvation reading (roughly 265 GB of physical reads against a 256 MB shared_buffers, confirmed here as shared_buffers=32768 8kB pages) comes from the 08-19 triage, not from this census. The census establishes the NEGATIVES (not slots, not connections) and the box-wide stall; it does not by itself prove which resource saturated. Do not record I/O starvation as census-proven. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE CANDIDATE FIXES in FIX-1058: raising max_worker_processes further is a non-remedy for cron startup timeouts and should be dropped from the list; thinning the job population and staggering the every-2-minute watchdogs off boundary minutes remain live but now target connection-accept pressure rather than slot contention. TEARDOWN performed with this bullet per FIX-1058's own instruction. **MEASURED EVIDENCE FOR THE CONNECTION-ACCEPT MECHANISM — AND ITS BOUND (appended 2026-08-24, cc-prompt-76; append-only, nothing above is rewritten).** Three prod windows, all counted from `cron.job_run_details`, isolate the variable this bullet relocated the problem to. **(1) One long statement — 2026-08-19 12:00–13:30 UTC, the unwindowed single-statement EC donations arm: 136 firings, 5 succeeded, 131 failed, all 131 `job startup timeout` — 96.3 percent dead.** **(2) Windowed writes on an otherwise IDLE box — 2026-08-21, drain 2: 1,457 firings across the full 24h, 0 failures, 0 startup timeouts** (the 144/0/0 figure quoted from that session's 2h15m slice holds for the entire day, not just the slice). **(3) Windowed writes with CONCURRENT load — 2026-08-24 08:00–13:16 UTC, jobid 22's first scheduled firing under [[FIX-1069]]: 327 firings, 128 succeeded, 199 failed, all 199 `job startup timeout` — 60.9 percent dead.** Window (2) is the first direct evidence for this bullet's mechanism: short committed transactions do leave the postmaster able to accept connections, where one long statement does not. **Window (3) is the bound on that finding, and the bullet must be read carrying both halves — windowing alone does NOT keep the box accepting connections when other writers share it.** THE CORRECTED STATEMENT: what tracks the failure rate is **the duration of the longest single uninterrupted statement**, not the number of statements and not the total write volume. Drain 2's windows were all short and cost 0 percent; 08-24's donations window 5 ran 3h49m as one statement (see [[FIX-1101]]) and its hours cost 42–49 failures each; 08-19's single statement ran ~6h and cost 96 percent. On 08-24 the starvation is visible from 08:00 — the EC job's own start, not from 11:00 when it was noticed — and the per-hour failed counts rise with it (08:00 34, 09:00 23, 10:00 35, 11:00 42, 12:00 49 of 61) then fall to 0 by 14:00, 45 minutes after the job was cancelled. The self-amplification is explicit and measured: jobid 44, the watchdog holding the [[FIX-1071]] 18,000 s budget row, lost 24 of its 30 firings in the 12:00 hour and therefore cancelled the offending run 976 s late. **So this bullet's §9.2-style claim that windowed writes do not starve the box is TRUE ONLY ON AN IDLE BOX** — it is a property of the measurement conditions, not of windowing. Windowing made the writer bounded and resumable, which is what FIX-1069 claimed and delivered; it did not make the box available. Cross-ref [[FIX-1058]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1022]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-1071]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-969]]. <!--id:FIX-1072-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **A pg_cron job startup timeout is a SILENT SKIP — the firing is lost with no retry, no alert, and no gap in any log a human reads** — FILE-ONLY (design options below; do NOT build from this bullet without picking one first). Surfaced by the 2026-08-19 saturation triage. When pg_cron cannot start a job it records status=failed with return_message job startup timeout in cron.job_run_details and MOVES ON. There is no retry and no backoff: the firing is simply gone, and the next occurrence is one full cadence away. For a daily job that is 24h of skipped work; for the weekly arms it is a week. THE SCALE IS NOT MARGINAL. On 2026-08-19 between 12:00 and 13:29 UTC, 91 of 91 firings across all jobs died this way. Lifetime, the class has killed hundreds of firings (see [[FIX-1022]] for 29 as of 08-11, [[FIX-1052]] for 191 over 08-10..08-17). WHY IT IS INVISIBLE RATHER THAN MERELY BAD: a job that never STARTS writes nothing to data_sync_log, so the pipeline-health surfaces that operators and the canary actually read cannot see it — a skipped firing and a job that was never scheduled look identical from data_sync_log. [[FIX-968]]'s check_cron_job_health() does read cron.job_run_details, but it deliberately treats this class as REPORT-ONLY, because escalating on it would fire the canary most weeks and train the alert to be ignored (the FIX-943 cause-vs-consequence rule). That reasoning was right for a noisy symptom and is now hiding a real one. TWO DESIGN OPTIONS, deliberately NOT chosen here. (A) RE-FIRE ONCE. A small watchdog (the [[FIX-1063]] jobid-44 pattern) scans for a startup-timeout row whose job has not since succeeded and re-invokes the command once, with a lockout so a persistently-starved job cannot spin. Pro: recovers the lost work the same day, which is the actual harm. Con: it re-fires INTO the same starved window that killed the first attempt, so it must carry a delay and a give-up count, and any job that is not idempotent must be excluded by name — that exclusion list is the real design work, not the watchdog. (B) ALERT TIER. Leave the firing lost but make the LOSS loud: give the canary a distinct condition for consecutive-startup-timeouts-on-one-job and for a burst across many jobs, separate from the existing report-only line, so the noise concern is handled by tiering rather than by silence. Pro: no new execution paths, no idempotency risk. Con: recovers nothing; a human still has to re-run it. RECOMMENDATION IF FORCED: (B) first because it is safe and immediately informative, then (A) narrowly scoped to the jobs whose procedures are already resumable and idempotent — which after [[FIX-1069]] includes the EC rebuild. PREREQUISITE: [[FIX-1072]] relocated the mechanism from bgworker-slot exhaustion to connection-accept pressure, so any re-fire design should assume the constraint is the postmaster accepting connections, not a worker pool draining. Cross-ref [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-1022]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-1058]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1072]]. <!--id:FIX-1073-->

That assertion is FALSE for two of the seven jobs it budgets. FIX SHAPE: add WHEN query_canceled handlers to both procedures on the FIX-1028 pattern (by name, FIRST, before WHEN OTHERS), closing the row partial with the elapsed span and the cancel detail. - [x] 🔴 S — **The supervised EC drain is the one window driver FIX-1101's watchdog cannot see — and --until cannot interrupt a window already running** — MEASURED on prod during the FIX-1101 acceptance drain, 2026-08-25 23:59 to 2026-08-26 01:58 UTC. The drain banked 12 of 16 windows cleanly at a mean of 343s (sigma 16s) and 1,794,291 edges, then window 13 ran 1,902s and took the box into connection starvation: jobids 40 and 44 failed on job startup timeout at 01:52, 01:54, 01:56 and 01:58, recovering only at 01:58:07. THREE DISTINCT DEFECTS, all in the operator path rather than the scheduled path. ONE, scripts/drain-ec-donations.mjs does not publish pipeline_state.entity_connections_window_inflight, so enforce_ec_window_budget() (FIX-1101) is structurally blind to it. The 30-minute per-window bound shipped the same night would have cancelled window 13 at 1,800s; instead it ran unbounded. The scheduled driver publishes and is bounded; the hand-driven one that runs for two hours in a quiet window is not, which is exactly backwards. TWO, --until is checked only BETWEEN windows (the loop tests the deadline before starting window i). Window 13 started at about 01:26, legally ahead of the 01:45 stop, and then overran it by 13 minutes. The flag is documented as a hard stop and is not one; it is a hard START gate. THREE, and this is the operationally nastiest: KILLING THE CLIENT DOES NOT STOP THE QUERY. The node process and its psql child were killed at 01:53 and pg_stat_activity still showed pid 162913 running rebuild_ec_donations_incr_window at 1,902s two minutes later, waiting on IO DataFileRead. PostgreSQL does not notice a departed client mid-statement (client_connection_check_interval defaults to 0), so the window kept consuming I/O until a manual pg_cancel_backend(162913) at 01:58:08. Any runbook step that says stop the drain by killing it is wrong. FOURTH THING, a near-miss worth recording: killing the drain also skipped its FIX-943 vacuum tail, leaving entity_connections at 418,198 dead tuples after a 1.79M-edge bulk rewrite. A single drain consumes about two thirds of provisioned IOPS on an otherwise idle box, so a degraded window tips it over the cap. See [[FIX-1107]] and docs/audits/2026-08-20-fix1069-ec-incremental-windowing.md section 13. Cross-ref [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-943]], [[FIX-1035]], [[FIX-1063]]. <!--id:FIX-1110-->
- [x] 🟠 L — **EC rebuild becomes a paced background crawl — one bounded unit per firing, spend under refill** — **Structural answer to [[FIX-1107]]/[[FIX-969]]'s "no scheduled writer knows the I/O budget exists": the EC rebuild becomes a background crawl — ONE bounded unit per firing, paced so spend is under refill.** Craig locked the scheduling philosophy on 2026-08-27 after three measured I/O-budget exhaustions in three days (08-24 EC window 5; 08-25 jobid 13; 08-26 the FIX-1101 acceptance drain): derived-layer staleness of a few days is acceptable, the box's daily Disk IO burst budget is the constraint, and bulk work becomes a slow constant background crawl that yields to users. SHIPPED (migration 20260827000000): (1) `p_max_units int DEFAULT NULL` on the EXISTING `run_entity_connections_rebuild()` — NULL is byte-for-byte the prior behaviour, N runs at most N PENDING units (one donations window, or one non-donations arm — exactly what [[FIX-1056]]/[[FIX-1069]] already made bankable) and exits 'partial' with `unit_capped=true` and a resumable cursor. NOT a fork: one body, one truth. (2) A unit-duration ring of the last 50 in `pipeline_state.ec_crawl.recent_units` plus a 2x-rolling-median backoff (2 h) — the throttle sensor. Duration is the sensor because the burst balance is readable from no catalog, and because the throttle announces itself in duration: prod 08-25 jobid 13 went ~3 s -> ~8 s -> >1,680 s per chunk across the 11:15 throttle inflection. Median not mean, per unit CLASS, with a 5-sample cold-start guard. (3) Blackout windows (UTC, wrap-around supported) — mechanism ships, policy is data, default empty. (4) `ec-crawl` pg_cron job at `*/15` with a [[FIX-1071]] outside budget row at 1,800 s, created INACTIVE for a Craig-gated Phase 4. THE PACING ARITHMETIC, from FIX-1101's clean 08-26 receipt (jobid 2, 2,654 s, arm_timings donations_incr_windows 1385 / _external 878 / _contracts 307 / eight arms 0-26 s each): a donations window is ~346 s at ~2,500 IOPS against a 1,000 IOPS baseline, which is ~540 s of burst refill, which is why 12-13 back-to-back windows exhaust the pool and match the measured 75-minute 08-25 burst. Pacing is per-FIRING not per-cycle, so the ceiling does not depend on cycle composition: 96 firings/day x 346 s = 33,216 writer-s = 51,817 refill-s = 60 percent of the day's refill, with 40 percent headroom, and no cycle shape can exceed it. ONE KNOB THE ARITHMETIC ADDED, not in the original design: `min_cycle_interval_minutes` (default 360). The ten non-donations arms are UNCONDITIONAL full rebuilds and rerun every cycle; because already-banked windows skip WITHOUT consuming a firing, a small-dirty-set cycle completes in ~13 firings ~3.3 h, which would spin those arms 6-7x/day against once-a-week today. Not a budget problem (8 of 10 cost <=26 s) but `_external` 878 s + `_contracts` 307 s is ~2 h/day of recomputing unchanged edges. HAZARD FOUND AND FIXED IN THE MIGRATION, worth recording: adding a parameter creates a SECOND procedure, it does not replace the old one, and `CALL run_entity_connections_rebuild('incremental')` then fails with `procedure ... is not unique` — a HARD ERROR that would have silently stopped the EC arm entirely. Measured on local before writing. The migration DROPs `(text)` before creating `(text,int)`; any future parameter add must do the same. PROVEN ON LOCAL against a 25,932-donor / 214,031-edge dirty set: (i) EQUIVALENCE — 26 firings of `p_max_units := 1` produced 214,031 edges and one `p_max_units := NULL` run produced 214,031 edges, symmetric difference 0 in BOTH directions over every column with evidence_ids sorted, and identical closed cycle (staging truncated, all 16 window watermarks at target, cursor cleared); (ii) BACKOFF — a 7 s unit against a seeded 1 s median over 5 samples set backoff_until, the next firing gate-skipped with a distinct `skipped` data_sync_log row, expiry resumed; (iii) BLACKOUT — a window covering now skipped (including the midnight wrap case 23:13-01:13), one not covering now ran; (iv) INTERLOCK — `fec_bulk_run_state` present deferred, cleared ran; (vi) the [[FIX-1063]] outside bound CANCEL BRANCH, never before exercised anywhere, fired on a forced overrun (ec-crawl cancelled at 16 s against a 10 s budget, signaled=t, `cron_job_budget_action` row written) while the FIX-1101 inside bound correctly declined on the same firing (16 s < 1,800 s) — the two bounds layering exactly as designed; (vii) CYCLE COOLDOWN — a closed cycle 3 min old under a 360-min minimum skipped, an OPEN cycle (cursor present) correctly ignored the cooldown and ran. Phase 4 (Craig-gated, quiet window): activate ec-crawl, pause jobid 2 `rebuild-ec-incremental` BY NAME, confirm jobid 22 stays paused; both stay defined for their cron.job_run_details history and the un-pause condition is "never, unless the crawl is retired". Ledger and the crawl's own daily consumption: docs/audits/2026-08-27-io-budget-burst-ledger.md. Cross-ref [[FIX-1107]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1069]], [[FIX-1056]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1071]], [[FIX-1110]], [[FIX-1030]], [[FIX-1035]], [[FIX-1028]]. **cc-189 (2026-10-04):** the logging asymmetry is kept for FIX-1124's two new gate reasons. `peer_running` and `peer_due` land in `pipeline_state.<crawl>.skips` through the callers' generic `v_gate->>'reason'` key and write NO `data_sync_log` row, exactly like `blackout` and `cycle_cooldown`; neither caller was edited (proven on the clone, ec and fe). <!--id:FIX-1111-->
- [x] 🔴 M — **Watermark-ratchet census: three budget-cancellable cron procedures bank chunks but not progress** — **Census: three budget-cancellable cron procedures write their progress watermark ONLY at end-of-run, so a watchdog cancel discards every chunk they committed and the job can never converge.** MECHANISM, established by [[FIX-1107]]'s attribution of the 08-25 stall: `QUERY_CANCELED` (57014) is NOT matched by `EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` — PL/pgSQL's OTHERS matches every error except query_canceled and assert_failure — so a cancel from `enforce_cron_job_budgets()` ([[FIX-1063]]) or the unit watchdog propagates straight out of the procedure, skipping the terminal watermark write. The work the per-chunk COMMITs already banked is real and durable; the watermark that would let the next run SKIP it is not. So the next firing redoes everything from the old watermark, hits the same budget, and is cancelled again. This is not a slow job — it is an UNCONVERGEABLE one. INSTRUMENT: pg_proc.prosrc on prod (bodies verified byte-identical to local by md5), classifying each procedure by (a) does it carry a `cron_job_budget` row or fall under `enforce_derived_mvs_unit_budget()`, (b) is the watermark write inside the chunk loop or after it; plus cron.job_run_details across the full retained window for whether a cancel has ALREADY happened. AT RISK — (a) AND (b) both true, zero `WHEN query_canceled` handlers in all three: (1) `refresh_financial_entity_totals_incremental` (jobid 13, budget 7,200 s), watermark key `financial_entity_totals_watermark`, written after all three chunk loops at ~84 percent through the body while the loops commit at 60/71/80 percent — **2 budget cancels already, most recently 2026-08-25 10:00 runid 15453 at 8,047.8 s**, which is the confirmed case this census generalises; (2) `refresh_donor_party_rollup_incremental` (jobid 17, budget 1,800 s), key `donor_party_rollup_watermark`, written at ~87 percent after loops committing at 72 and 84 percent — 0 budget cancels but **1 statement_timeout cancel already**, and a timeout cancel is the same 57014 through the same unguarded OTHERS; (3) `run_rule_taggers` (jobid 12, budget 7,200 s), key `size_tags:donation_watermark` — DIFFERENT SHAPE and a partial exception: the signature write and the rebuild share one transaction and roll back together, so there is no watermark ratchet, but the unguarded OTHERS still lets a cancel skip the terminal data_sync_log update and strand the row 'running' ([[FIX-1028]]'s class) — **1 budget cancel already, 2026-08-25 16:00 at 7,325.8 s**, plus 3 statement_timeout cancels. NOT AT RISK, and worth recording so the pattern is legible: `refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental` (jobid 24) writes its watermark INSIDE the chunk loop and carries a query_canceled handler (5 timeout cancels survived, [[FIX-1002]]/[[FIX-1003]]); `refresh_treemap_individuals_global` (jobid 26) updates a per-chunk cursor inside the loop (1 budget cancel survived); `run_entity_connections_rebuild` (jobids 2/22/ec-crawl) carries per-window watermarks and three query_canceled handlers ([[FIX-1069]]/[[FIX-1028]], and [[FIX-1111]] preserves this); `refresh_agency_staffing_rollup` (jobid 25) has no watermark at all so there is nothing to ratchet; `refresh_contract_flow_rollups` (jobid 28) has ZERO COMMITs — the whole procedure is one transaction, so a cancel is atomic and mis-records nothing, but it is also unresumable, which is a different and currently-unexercised risk at a 10,800 s budget on a job measured at 1,053 s. THE RULE THIS ESTABLISHES: **a procedure that can be cancelled from outside must either write its watermark in the same transaction as the chunk that earned it, or catch `query_canceled` BY NAME and write the watermark before re-raising. A per-chunk COMMIT without a per-chunk watermark is not resumability — it is work that will be done again.** Filed as a census only; nothing is fixed here except what [[FIX-1111]] already covers for the EC arm. Fix order should follow the evidence: jobid 13 first (2 cancels, currently PAUSED for exactly this reason), then jobid 17, then jobid 12's stranded-row leg. Cross-ref [[FIX-1107]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1028]], [[FIX-969]], [[FIX-1031]], [[FIX-1111]]. <!--id:FIX-1112-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **anon can EXECUTE refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental() on prod; no sweep exists for re-widened grants** — **`refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental()` is EXECUTE-able by `anon` on prod — an unauthenticated /rest/v1/rpc/ request is one connection away from starting the 4-hour donor rollup.** MEASURED on prod 2026-08-27 while auditing grants after [[FIX-1111]] recreated a sibling procedure: `pg_proc.proacl` carries `anon=X/postgres | authenticated=X/postgres`. This is Supabase's default-grant behaviour on newly created routines (project_rpc_execute_grant_hardening), not something anyone chose. SCOPE OF THE AUDIT: of six cron-only procedures sampled, four are already correctly revoked (`enforce_cron_job_budgets`, `refresh_treemap_individuals_global`, `rebuild_official_vote_stats`, and FIX-1111's own `ec_crawl_gate`/`ec_crawl_record_unit`), and `run_entity_connections_rebuild` was revoked by FIX-1111 (migration 20260827000200) because FIX-1111's own DROP+CREATE is what re-applied the default to it. **This one is the remaining outlier and was NOT touched, because it is not FIX-1111's object to change.** WHY IT MATTERS: jobid 24 `donor-rollup-refresh` carries a 14,400 s [[FIX-1063]] budget and has been measured at 7,171.9 s and 7,186.6 s in a single day; [[FIX-1107]] establishes that the box's whole daily I/O burst pool is 30-75 minutes, so an attacker-triggered or accident-triggered firing is materially expensive, not merely untidy. It is also idempotent and advisory-locked, so the blast radius is I/O and connections rather than data corruption. WHY IT IS PROBABLY SAFE TO FIX: no PostgREST caller exists. Every reference in the tree is a pg_cron command, a dashboard display string (`apps/civitics/app/dashboard/DashboardClient.tsx` retryCmd), or a `packages/data` script using a direct `pg.Client` that connects as `postgres` — verified by grep 2026-08-27. FIX SHAPE: a one-line migration, `REVOKE ALL ON PROCEDURE public.refresh_official_donor_rollup_incremental() FROM PUBLIC, anon, authenticated;` plus `NOTIFY pgrst`, mirroring 20260827000200 exactly. BROADER FOLLOW-UP worth doing at the same time: this was a six-procedure spot check, not a sweep. The real work is enumerating EVERY `public` routine whose `proacl` grants anon/authenticated EXECUTE, classifying each as route-called or cron-only, and revoking the cron-only set — and adding that check to the daily canary so a future CREATE OR REPLACE cannot silently re-widen one, which is exactly the trap FIX-1111 fell into and caught. Cross-ref [[FIX-1111]], [[FIX-1101]], [[FIX-1107]], [[FIX-1063]], [[FIX-1002]], [[FIX-1003]]. <!--id:FIX-1113-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Ship get_ec_crawl_health() — the lag metric the tier-vs-ingest decision reads from** — FIX-1111 made the EC rebuild a paced crawl, which converts an availability problem into a LATENCY one: the crawl cannot starve the box, but it can fall arbitrarily far behind ingest and nothing measures that. This ships the instrument. get_ec_crawl_health() returns ONE jsonb aggregate (PostgREST caps set-returning RPCs at 1000 rows) carrying: EC scalar watermark age in days, dirty-set rows/donors, trailing-7d firing census split into units-run vs skipped vs backoff vs failed, cumulative per-reason skip counters, units-per-cycle for the last 5 closed cycles, last cycle closed at, the open cycle, and the live ec_crawl config. Wired into the persisted status-snapshot payload as section ec_crawl_health — NOTE the payload cutover lag: the dashboard reads the PERSISTED snapshot, so the tile appears only after platform-snapshot (every 10 min) picks it up, not at deploy. THE DECISION RULE IT SERVES, recorded verbatim: lag greater than 7 days for two consecutive weeks WITH backoffs on more than about 25 percent of firings means a compute-tier conversation; lag greater than 7 days with backoffs rare and units-per-cycle growing means an INGEST conversation (delta aggregation, write amplification, replay pacing). The two-consecutive-weeks half cannot be evaluated from one snapshot, so the RPC exposes lag_days and backoff_rate_7d and emits a signal of ok / lag_high_backoff_high / lag_high_backoff_low; the two-week persistence is the human read across two snapshots, deliberately not faked in SQL. Cross-ref [[FIX-1111]] (the crawl), [[FIX-1107]] (the I/O budget that forced it), [[FIX-1110]] (the supervised drain that shares its path). <!--id:FIX-1114-->
- [x] 🔴 M — **Rebuild entity_connection_stats as a bounded unit — the current procedure OOMs a 2GB box and takes the postmaster with it** — jobid 16 entity-connection-stats-rebuild is PAUSED as of 2026-08-28 (see [[FIX-1103]] for the correlation that justified it). This bullet is the replacement shape. WHY THE CURRENT ONE CANNOT STAY: rebuild_entity_connection_stats() does SET work_mem = 256MB and then CREATE TEMP TABLE ecs_stage AS SELECT ... FROM (SELECT from_id FROM entity_connections UNION ALL SELECT to_id FROM entity_connections) GROUP BY id — an unbounded HashAggregate over TWICE the entity_connections row count, producing about 2.66M groups, on a box with 2GB RAM and 256MB shared_buffers. The apply half is already disciplined (16 uuid-range windows, DELETE+INSERT, COMMIT per window, FIX-703) but the STAGE BUILD is one unbounded statement and it is the half that kills the box. Evidence: 2026-08-10 died at 21610s on statement timeout INSIDE the CREATE TEMP TABLE; the two firings after that both ended in a postmaster restart. REQUIRED SHAPE: make the stage build bounded the way the crawl bounds its units. Either (a) build the stage per uuid-range window so each statement aggregates 1/16th of the keyspace and commits, trading FIX-734's single-scan property for survivability, or (b) keep the single scan but drive it from a watermark so only entities whose edges CHANGED are re-aggregated, which is the same delta shape entity_connections_rebuild already uses. Option (b) is preferred and is a genuine crawl-class unit: it would slot into run_entity_connections_rebuild as one more arm and inherit the pacing, the budget bound, the sensor and the cycle cooldown for free, which also deletes the separate cron job. Whatever ships must lower work_mem to something the box can actually hold and must be measured against prod cardinality before it is scheduled. NOTE the staleness this leaves: entity_connection_stats_mv last rebuilt successfully 2026-08-05, so connection counts are already weeks stale and drifting further while the crawl writes edges continuously — the replacement is not optional maintenance. Cross-ref [[FIX-1103]], [[FIX-1052]], [[FIX-985]], [[FIX-734]], [[FIX-703]], [[FIX-1111]]. <!--id:FIX-1115-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **The EC crawl recomputes unchanged arms every cycle — _external and _contracts rebuild byte-identical row counts for ~1,250 s/cycle** — MEASURED on prod from the FIX-1111 crawl ring, 2026-08-27. The ten non-donations arms in run_entity_connections_rebuild are UNCONDITIONAL full rebuilds: each one DELETEs its connection_type and reinserts from source, every cycle, whether or not the source changed. The ring proves the waste is exact, not approximate — rebuild_entity_connections_external ran twice for 1,148,418 rows total (2 x 574,209, byte-identical) at a median 899.1 s, and rebuild_entity_connections_contracts ran three times for 569,847 rows total (3 x 189,949, byte-identical) at a median 344.6 s. That is ~1,244 s of writer per cycle spent recomputing edges that did not change, against a measured whole-cycle cost of roughly 1,830 s. On a box whose scarce resource is the daily disk burst budget (FIX-1107) this is the single largest remaining source of pure waste in the crawl. FIX SHAPE: a cheap per-arm source-change gate. For each non-donations arm, a fingerprint over that arm's OWN source scope — count plus max timestamp, chosen per arm because the sources differ (votes.updated_at, career_history.updated_at, agencies.updated_at, evidence_cards.updated_at, external_relationships.ingested_at, proposal_cosponsors.created_at which has no updated_at at all, and financial_relationships scoped by the arm's own relationship_type so the four FR-sourced arms do not all fire on any FR write). Skip the arm when the fingerprint is unchanged since its last successful build, banking it for the cycle so the cycle can still close, and record a skipped-unchanged mark so the lag metric can tell idle from gated. THE GATE MUST FAIL OPEN — a fingerprint probe that errors or times out means RUN the arm, never skip it. A gate that silently freezes an arm is the FIX-885 stranded-flag class and would be strictly worse than the waste it replaces. Measured probe costs on the local clone: external_relationships 586 ms, agencies 7 ms, evidence_cards 4 ms, financial_relationships scoped to contract 15,975 ms — all pennies next to the arms they skip. Cross-ref FIX-1111, FIX-1107, FIX-969, FIX-885, FIX-1115. <!--id:FIX-1117-->
- [x] 🟡 S — **The FIX-1117 contracts gate needs a partial index on financial_relationships(updated_at) WHERE relationship_type IN (contract,grant) — the probe costs 98s without one** — MEASURED ON PROD 2026-08-28, immediately after FIX-1117 landed. Nine of the ten per-arm source fingerprints are pennies exactly as designed — oversight 46 ms, gifts/holds/lobbying/cosponsors/appointments/investigation 20-35 ms each, the entity_connections stats fingerprint 1,440 ms, external_relationships 3,365 ms, votes 4,154 ms. One is not: rebuild_entity_connections_contracts measured 111,575 ms on its first prod call and 98,204 ms on a warm second call, so it is NOT a cold-cache artifact. Its scope is financial_relationships WHERE relationship_type IN ('contract','grant') = 3,908,956 rows inside a 12 GB table, and the plan is a Parallel Bitmap Heap Scan driven by financial_relationships_type: the bitmap index scan is cheap, the 3.9M heap fetches are not. Dropping max(updated_at) does not help — count(*) alone measured 98,692 ms with the identical plan, because no existing index can serve it index-only (financial_relationships_derivation leads with relationship_type but does not carry updated_at, and FR's visibility map is too degraded for an index-only scan to be chosen anyway; cf FIX-1034 and the FR dead-tuple work). CONSEQUENCE AND WHAT SHIPPED INSTEAD: 98 s to avoid a 344.6 s arm is still a net win, but it is a poor ratio and it spends the exact resource — prod's daily disk burst budget, FIX-1107 — that the whole FIX-1111 line of work exists to protect, on every cycle, up to four times a day. So FIX-1117 shipped a disabled_arms escape in pipeline_state.ec_arm_source_fingerprints, and rebuild_entity_connections_contracts is in it: a disabled arm returns a NULL fingerprint, which is the gate's fail-open value, so that arm simply runs every cycle exactly as it did before FIX-1117. Nothing is broken; one arm is un-gated. THE FIX: build CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY financial_relationships_contract_grant_updated_at ON public.financial_relationships (updated_at) WHERE relationship_type IN ('contract','grant') — roughly 3.9M entries, on the order of 90 MB — which makes max(updated_at) an O(1) backward index scan and count(*) an index-only scan over 90 MB instead of 3.9M heap fetches. CONCURRENTLY because a plain CREATE INDEX takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on a 12 GB table, and it cannot run inside a migration transaction, so this wants a supervised quiet window rather than a db:push:prod. Then remove rebuild_entity_connections_contracts from disabled_arms with a single UPDATE — no migration needed, which is why the escape is data rather than code — and re-measure. Expected saving once enabled: 344.6 s of writer per no-change cycle, which is the second largest arm after _external. Cross-ref FIX-1117, FIX-1111, FIX-1107, FIX-1034, FIX-943. <!--id:FIX-1118-->

- [x] 🟠 S — **platform-snapshot GHA cron fires every ~3 hours, not every 10 minutes** — Surfaced while verifying [[FIX-1121]] on prod 2026-08-29. The workflow header for .github/workflows/platform-snapshot.yml documents a 10-minute cadence with expected GHA drift of 5-15 min, and every downstream comment (status routes, dashboard SSR, SNAPSHOT_STALE_MS tuning) reasons from that number. That is EIGHT scheduled firings in 51 hours - a mean interval of about 6.4 hours and a shortest gap of 3.2 hours, against an advertised 10 minutes. GitHub drops scheduled workflow runs under platform load and offers no delivery guarantee; this is not drift, it is wholesale skipping. Consequences: (1) status_snapshot is routinely 3+ hours stale, which is inside SNAPSHOT_STALE_MS (4h) only by luck - one more skipped window and every dashboard read crosses into stale; (2) the FIX-1121 investigation had only 10 retained ticks over 51 hours to reason from, which is why the retention interaction looked worse than it is; (3) any per-10-min assumption in cost or freshness math is wrong by a factor of ~38. - [x] 🔴 M — **Nothing detects a wedged front door — the REST/pooler layer fails independently of the DB and only a project restart clears it** — The Supabase front door (REST + pooler) can wedge on its own and STAY wedged long after the database underneath is healthy, and no instrument in this repo notices. Reported shape: on 2026-08-31 it stayed wedged about 11 hours after the DB had recovered, and only a Supabase project restart cleared it. Measured corroboration pulled 2026-09-01 from the Logs API (analytics/endpoints/logs.all over edge_logs): the 08-31 22:00 UTC hour is 17 requests and 17 of them are Cloudflare-class 52x, i.e. 100 percent front-door failure, and the 23:00 hour is 1000 requests with 49 x 52x plus 61 total 5xx — while the Postgres side shows nothing that would explain it. The 52x family (520/521/522/525) is the tell: those are edge-to-origin failures, NOT application errors, so every DB-side instrument we own is blind to them by construction. Note the asymmetry that makes this dangerous: Cloudflare in front of the WEBSITE showed ZERO 5xx across the same 24h (verified via scripts/cf-analytics.mjs --by edgeResponseStatus: 403/200/400/301/307/404/204/401/499/302 and no 5xx at all), so a wedged data-plane front door does not necessarily surface as a red website. THE FIX: a detector for sustained front-door 5xx — poll the Logs API edge_logs 5xx rate on a schedule, and when it stays above a threshold for N consecutive intervals, send email on the EXISTING alerting rails (the same ones the canary uses, see FLAGS/EMAIL_ALERTS_ENABLED) rather than inventing a new channel. Pair it with a runbook line naming the only known remediation (project restart) so the on-call path is one step, not a diagnosis. Explicitly IN SCOPE: the detector must not depend on a Postgres connection succeeding, because the failure mode being detected is precisely one where the front door in front of Postgres is the broken component. Cross-ref [[FIX-1125]] for the sibling lesson that a guard starved by the condition it exists to end is not a guard. **cc-206 (2026-10-07):** the remediation is automated by [[FIX-1285]] — the watchdog decides a project restart itself after 30 min of DOWN (report mode until armed). **cc-207 (2026-10-07):** the probe arm pages every tick (isDownEdge true) and the Logs arm hourly, which is why the 10-06 subjects (all the Logs arm's) showed the keyless probe was answered through the wedge — see [[FIX-1286]]. <!--id:FIX-1130-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines derives cadence from the FIRING schedule, so both crawl arms read permanently stale to the canary** — Measured on prod 2026-09-02 01:35 UTC while re-taking the [[FIX-990]]/[[FIX-992]]/[[FIX-993]] freshness readings. list_scheduled_rollup_pipelines() (FIX-977) derives each pipeline's cadence_hours from its cron schedule, and canary-check.ts fetchRollupRegistry() feeds that straight into report_after_hours / escalate_after_hours. That mapping is correct for a job that does its whole unit of work in one firing. It is WRONG for the two bounded crawl arms, which park status=partial on EVERY firing by design and only write status=complete when a full cycle closes. Consequence, both measured: entity_connections_rebuild is keyed off jobname ec-crawl (jobid 45, schedule */15) so its derived cadence is 0.25h, giving report_after 0.4h and escalate_after 0.6h — against a real last_complete_at of 2026-08-31 19:20:45, i.e. 30.2h, so it escalates on every canary run and can never not escalate. get_ec_crawl_health() reports signal=ok, backoff_rate_7d 0.0217, and cycles_last5 ALL closed with spans of 240-1005 minutes, so the pipeline is healthy and converging while the registry calls it 121 cadence cycles behind. financial_entity_totals_refresh is the same shape (jobnames fe-crawl + financial-entity-totals-incremental, derived cadence 37h, 599.0h since complete) and is additionally a long linear replay whose watermark is deliberately weeks behind. This is not cosmetic: it is a permanent false escalation on the daily canary in exactly the detector FIX-977 built to stop pipelines going unwatched, and per the FIX-968 precedent a detector that always fires is a detector nobody reads. It also makes the registry unusable as the instrument for future EC freshness re-takes — the 84h Mon+Wed figure FIX-990 was judged against no longer exists anywhere in the registry, because jobids 2 and 22 are both inactive. Fix shape: give the registry a per-pipeline cycle-cadence override, or teach it that a pipeline whose recent rows are status=partial with sweep_in_progress should be judged on cycle closes rather than firings — the get_ec_crawl_health() cycles_last5 span is the honest denominator for the EC arm. - [x] 🟠 S — **rebuild_entity_connections_votes carries the FIX-983 watermark defect on votes.updated_at — same mechanism, different table, still unfixed** — CONFIRMED on live prod pg_proc 2026-09-03 while enumerating the FIX-983 census by mechanism. FIX-983 shipped the head-lag horizon for every financial_relationships.updated_at watermark (13 clamp sites, helper public.fr_watermark_horizon()). It deliberately did NOT touch the votes twin, which is byte-for-byte the same defect one table over. THE EVIDENCE. public.votes carries trigger votes_updated_at BEFORE UPDATE ... EXECUTE FUNCTION set_updated_at(), whose whole body is NEW.updated_at = NOW(); RETURN NEW; — NOW() is transaction_timestamp(), the moment the writing transaction BEGAN. rebuild_entity_connections_votes() then reads pipeline_state key entity_connections_votes -> last_indexed_at, builds its dirty set at line 28 as WHERE v.updated_at > v_last_indexed_at with NO upper bound, captures SELECT MAX(v.updated_at) at line 32, and writes COALESCE(v_new_max_updated_at, NOW()) as the new watermark at lines 41 and 95. rebuild_entity_connections_votes_full() writes a bare NOW() at line 49. So a vote-writing transaction that starts before the watermark read and commits after it stamps rows BELOW the new watermark that were invisible at read time, and no later run ever sees them: permanent, silent row loss in the vote-derivation arm of entity_connections. THE FIX IS ALREADY BUILT AND IS THREE LINES PER SITE. Apply the same invariant FIX-983 applied: (a) v_new_max_updated_at := LEAST(COALESCE(v_new_max_updated_at, v_horizon), v_horizon) where v_horizon := public.fr_watermark_horizon(); (b) bound the dirty set with AND v.updated_at <= v_new_max_updated_at; (c) add the caught-up branch so a clamped target at or below the watermark returns without moving the watermark BACKWARDS; and in _votes_full() replace the bare NOW() watermark write with the horizon. The helper is generic — it reads a clock and a GUC, nothing FR-specific — so it needs no votes-specific twin, though a rename to watermark_horizon() would read better once a second table uses it. WHY IT WAS SPLIT OUT rather than folded into FIX-983: the FIX-983 bundle was scoped to the financial_relationships population and its proofs were built against FR fixtures; landing a votes change on the same commit would have shipped an unproven edit next to three proven ones. EXPOSURE. Smaller than the FR case but the same class: the vote writer is the congress-votes ingest, which UPDATEs existing rows on re-fetch (that is what arms the BEFORE UPDATE trigger at all), and the arm runs inside run_entity_connections_rebuild. Size it before fixing by measuring the vote writer's transaction duration the way FIX-983 sized the FR writer (631 calls, mean 4.1 s, max 19.5 s from pg_stat_statements). Cross-ref [[FIX-983]], [[FIX-1074]], [[FIX-972]], [[FIX-747]]. <!--id:FIX-1139-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **The FIX-983 caught-up branch logged status=skipped, which does not reset the freshness clock — jobid 24 would have paged on a healthy rollup at the next firing** — SELF-INFLICTED BY [[FIX-983]], caught in the same session, one hop after the prod landing, before it fired. FIX-983's invariant (c) says a routine whose horizon-clamped target has not cleared its watermark must no-op cleanly rather than write the watermark BACKWARDS. In the two rollup PROCEDUREs that keep a data_sync_log row that was implemented as an early RETURN logging status = skipped. THE DEFECT. public.check_rollup_freshness() measures staleness as hours since the last data_sync_log row for the pipeline with status = complete, and canary-check.ts escalates off that; a skipped row does not reset the clock. So a stretch of legitimately caught-up firings would have driven donor_rollup_refresh past its freshness ceiling and paged with the rollup perfectly healthy — the exact FIX-968 shape (a frozen signal making a healthy system look broken) that the playbook's E1 entry exists to prevent. IT WAS REACHABLE ON THE VERY NEXT FIRING, measured on prod 2026-09-03 01:45 UTC, not argued from theory: pipeline_state.donor_rollup_watermark.last_indexed_at = 2026-09-01 07:28:45.938461 and MAX(fr.updated_at) over donation/ie_support/ie_oppose = 2026-09-01 07:28:45.938461 — EQUAL, because financial_relationships has taken no write in over 24h. LEAST(max, horizon) is therefore at or below the watermark, so jobid 24 donor-rollup-refresh would have taken the skip branch at 09:00 UTC that morning and at 12:00, and every firing until FR moves; last_complete was 2026-09-02 12:00 so the 48h ceiling would have tripped 2026-09-04. THE FIX IS TO DELETE THE BRANCH, NOT RELABEL IT. The early RETURN was only ever protecting against a backwards watermark write, and a floor does that in one line with no new control flow and no new status vocabulary: v_new_max := GREATEST(v_new_max, v_watermark). With the target floored at the watermark the dirty predicate (> v_watermark AND <= v_new_max) is empty BY CONSTRUCTION, the loop is a no-op, and the terminal write rewrites the SAME watermark — so the run reports complete, because it IS complete: everything readable has been read. GREATEST ignores NULLs so the bootstrap path (v_watermark IS NULL) is untouched. This is the same construction FIX-983 already used for donor_rollup_rebuild_bulk and [[FIX-987]] used for refresh_agency_staffing_rollup, both of which log complete on an empty dirty set and were never affected — the inconsistency was the tell. NOT CHANGED: refresh_donor_party_rollup_mv() and refresh_official_donor_rollup_mv() keep their RAISE NOTICE plus RETURN, because they write NO data_sync_log row at all and so cannot move a freshness clock in either direction. THE GENERAL LESSON, worth a playbook line: a new early-return path in a scheduled routine is a change to its OBSERVABILITY contract, not just its control flow. Before adding one, check what the freshness/canary layer counts — here it counts exactly one status value. Cross-ref [[FIX-983]], [[FIX-987]], [[FIX-968]], [[FIX-944]], [[FIX-1011]], [[FIX-1135]]. <!--id:FIX-1140-->

The 09-02 value sits at 202.5s, INSIDE the pre-incident normal band of 204-287s, between the 490.7 and the 1017.4 — so this is not a trend line, it is a bimodal distribution with a 5x spread on identical work. Two watchdog-visible failures in five days (08-29 hang, 09-03 cancel) plus one 08-31 kill. What that rules in and out: entity_connections growth (10,526,598 rows, roughly +0.6 percent/day) cannot produce a 5x swing in 24 hours and then halve again, so the driver is contention or plan instability, not volume. Candidates to separate, in order of cheapness — (a) the eight to_tsvector INSERT stages versus the FIX-1123 windowed _conn stage are NOT separately timed, so the 1017.4s is unattributable today; instrument per-stage seconds into metadata first, exactly as refresh_derived_mvs already does per unit. (b) 06:00 UTC is the worst hour on the box for startup timeouts (12.0 percent all-week, 21.5 percent on Tuesdays) and jobid 9 fires INTO that, so co-tenancy is a live hypothesis — cross-ref [[FIX-1124]]. (c) financial_entities and entity_connections index-only scans degrade with visibility-map decay and this unit reads both; check pg_stat_user_tables.last_vacuum against the slow days before blaming the query. EXPLICIT NON-ACTION: do not raise the 900s unit budget to make the slow days fit. The budget is doing its job — it converted a 21638s box-killer into a 1017s cancel with four units skipped and the search index intact. Confirmed intact on prod 2026-09-04: entity_search_index holds 364,129 rows, so the 09-03 cancel did NOT strand a TRUNCATE (the function TRUNCATEs then INSERTs in one unit transaction, and the cancel rolled both back together). Note the weekly jobid 10 no longer shares this stack — cc-105 moved it to Tue 00:47 UTC — so this is now purely a jobid 9 problem. Cross-ref [[FIX-1123]] [[FIX-1125]] [[FIX-1128]] [[FIX-1030]] [[FIX-1073]]. APPEND 2026-09-07: CLOSED as superseded by [[FIX-1152]], which answers all three of this bullet's candidates. (c) VM decay is CONFIRMED and is the driver: the search unit reads 236.0s on Mon 09-07 and 1017.4s on Thu 09-03 at the SAME 28h offset from an ec-vacuum-analyze run, so the variance tracks entity_connections write volume (the 09-01 3.65M-row FEC catch-up) rather than elapsed time or row growth — exactly the bimodal shape this bullet described, now with a mechanism. FIX-1152 ships the durable fix: both vacuum owners go daily at 04:30 / 04:50 UTC ahead of the 06:00 daily, and the daily records the visibility map it ran against. (b) co-tenancy is ruled out as the EXPLANATION — the Sunday 09-06 nightly started 06:54:07 against the daily's 06:00:00-06:05:30, a 48-minute gap with no overlap, and that day read 234.8s; hour 06 does measure 9.2% startup timeouts on the 14-day histogram, but that is a scheduling concern now carried by [[FIX-1163]] and [[FIX-1124]], not an account of the 5x swing. (a) per-stage instrumentation is NOT implementable as written, so it is superseded rather than deferred: rebuild_entity_search_index runs as ONE statement inside the unit's own transaction, so any per-stage timing row it wrote would roll back with the watchdog cancel — precisely the runs the instrumentation exists to explain. FIX-1152's metadata.vm_before supplies the attribution instead, and writes it on the RUNNING row so it survives a cancel. The EXPLICIT NON-ACTION stands and was honoured: the 900s unit budget is unchanged. <!--id:FIX-1144-->

- [x] 🟡 S — **A newly scheduled daily pg_cron job escalates the canary until its first firing** — check_cron_job_health()'s missing_daily arm selects active jobs whose schedule is daily (fields 3-5 all star) with NOT EXISTS any cron.job_run_details row inside the lookback window, and canary-check.ts ESCALATES on every entry. That predicate cannot distinguish never fired because it is starved - the real failure it exists to catch - from never fired because it was created twenty minutes ago. Observed 2026-09-04: scheduling platform-counts-daily (FIX-1146) at 53 3 * * * put it straight into the escalation list on the very next canary run, and it can only clear itself at 03:53 UTC. Harmless once, but it means every future daily job ships with a guaranteed page attached, which is exactly the cry-wolf training FIX-977's report-vs-escalate split exists to prevent. Fix: exclude a job whose earliest possible firing has not yet arrived. cron.job carries no created_at, so the cheap proxy is to require at least one full cadence period to have elapsed since the job first became observable - e.g. skip a job with zero run_details rows AND no row in cron.job_run_details for any jobid greater than its own (it is the newest job), or record a first_seen_at alongside the cron_job_budget row and gate on that. Prefer the explicit ledger over the jobid heuristic. <!--id:FIX-1150-->

- [x] 🟡 S — **55 role-ineligible officials carry an H/S/P fec_id with zero fec_bulk money — outside FIX-1153's money-keyed population, so the wrong id survives the remediation** — Surfaced by the FIX-1153 dry run on the 2026-09-07 clone. FIX-1153's population is deliberately MONEY-keyed — role can hold no FEC office AND holds fec_bulk-sourced financial_relationships rows — because the id-keyed predicate misses the 18 Federal Judges who hold 333,582 dollars with no stored id at all. The cost of that choice is the mirror case: an official whose role can hold no FEC office, carrying an H/S/P fec_id, holding NO fec_bulk money, is not in the population and so never reaches the retire step. Measured on the clone: 55 such officials, 2 of them ACTIVE. The FIX-1153 reconciliation surfaces them as the set difference against the FIX-937 manifests — 2 of 4 active rows and 53 of 115 inactive rows are not returned by the predicate, and every one checked was a zero-money id-carrier (Vanessa Fuentes H4TX33038, Dan Strauss S2MO00486, Lynne Howe H2NY14102, Bridget Molina H0FL27034). HOW EXPOSED IS THIS TODAY: contained, not closed. The fec-bulk matcher's byFecId pass 2 enforces the role/prefix rule (roleMayHoldFecOffice, FIX-1025), so a Council Member carrying an H-prefix id cannot bind money through the stored-id path, and FIX-937's write-side guard excludes the same rows from the NAME pool — the 2026-09-06 nightly logged 13,192 of 32,942 officials excluded. So both binding routes refuse them. What remains is a correctness-of-record problem rather than a live money problem: 55 officials rows assert an FEC candidate identity their role forbids, which is exactly the claim FIX-1153 retires for the money-holding half, and any future reader that trusts source_ids fec_id without re-checking the role inherits the bug. FIX SHAPE: one UPDATE in the same shape as FIX-1153 step 3 — rename fec_id to misattributed_fec_id where the role is not federally electable — run over the id-keyed population rather than the money-keyed one. It needs no delete, no rollup tail and no vacuum, so it is a much smaller operation than FIX-1153 and can ride any later prod window. Decide whether it lands as a step in the FIX-1153 script behind a flag, or as its own one-shot. Cross-ref [[FIX-1153]], [[FIX-1154]], [[FIX-937]], [[FIX-1025]], [[FIX-935]]. APPEND 2026-09-08 (CLOSED BY SET 1): all 55 zero-money id-carriers were folded into the set-1 manifest as the id-retire-only half of its 139 and applied on prod at 01:48 UTC. They carried no FR rows by definition, so the remediation for them was the id retirement alone, and the keyed check afterwards shows 0 of the 139 still carrying an fec_id. Manifest derived on the clone and committed as docs/audits/2026-09-07-fix1164-zero-money-id-carriers.tsv (55 officials, 2 active -- the predicate reproduced this bullet's filed numbers exactly). See [[FIX-1153]] for the full receipt. <!--id:FIX-1164-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **Daily canary has no alarm for 'a FEC drop is pending and nobody collected it'** — FIX-1163 made the FEC drop probe durable: the enrichment-light phase now writes pipeline_state.fec_drop_probe with cycle, pending, remote_last_modified, watermark_last_modified, probed_at and phase, every nightly, independent of whether fec-phase ran. Nothing READS that key yet, so the evidence exists but no one is watching it. Ask: teach the daily canary (the FIX-1011 registry/canary pipeline_state readers) to escalate when fec_drop_probe.pending is true AND the newest data_sync_log row for pipeline='fec_bulk' with status='complete' is older than fec_drop_probe.probed_at by more than 2 days. That is the condition FIX-1156 was really about — not 'did the nightly fail' but 'is there money sitting at FEC that nothing has collected'. Two days is deliberate: FEC publishes indiv{yy}.zip Sundays around 15:20 UTC, the Sunday nightly probes last week's file, so a one-day lag is normal and a two-day lag means the collector missed its window. Fail-closed detail the alarm must respect: a probe whose HEAD failed records pending=false with remote_last_modified NULL, so 'pending=false' alone is not proof of health — a run of NULL remote_last_modified is its own (quieter) signal that the probe cannot see FEC at all. Cross-ref FIX-1011, FIX-1156, FIX-1163, FIX-903. <!--id:FIX-1166-->

Prod evidence: the POST persists (rows land in user_custom_groups owned by the user, is_public=false) but the client's post-save reload GET returns 200 with an empty/anon list — that request authenticates as ANON while the mount GET authes fine. The only difference is timing: the reload GET fires immediately after the POST, and the POST's middleware rotates the session cookie writing it to the RESPONSE only (not the forwarded request; see apps/civitics/middleware.ts setAll) so the chained GET races a rotated-out token. FIX-782's catch only guards GET REJECTION; a GET that succeeds with {groups:[]} still runs setItems([]) and wipes. The /graph path has no optimistic insert so it depends wholly on that racing GET. Fix: stop re-fetching the whole list after our own write — the bus broadcasts the confirmed POST row object (upsert) / deleted id (remove) and each rail applies the delta, immune to the cookie race. Keep the single mount fetch (authes fine) + FIX-782 non-destructive catch. Also add graph-path optimistic insert via the broadcast. FOLLOW-UP: the middleware cookie-rotation pattern (response-only setAll) is a latent auth race for any POST-then-GET flow — investigate separately. References [[FIX-782]] [[FIX-770]]. <!--id:FIX-784-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **Per-user authed API endpoints are CDN-cached by the next.config catch-all (stale-after-write + cross-user leak)** — THE real cause of the saved-views 'revert on refresh' (FIX-782/784 chased client-side theories; the server was always fine). next.config.mjs headers() has a catch-all that stamps CDN-Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600 on everything except a short denylist (api/auth, api/admin, auth, profile, dashboard). /api/graph/custom-groups (and other per-user authed GET routes) are NOT excluded, so the Vercel/Cloudflare edge caches a user's saved-views list for 300s, and the cache key does NOT vary by Cookie. Result: a save/delete persists in the DB (POST returns 201) but a refresh serves the stale edge-cached list → the view 'reverts'. SECURITY: because the cache doesn't vary by user, one user's saved views (and other per-user responses) can be served to another. Confirmed by the live response headers on prod (cf-cache-status DYNAMIC, cdn-cache-control s-maxage=300). Fix: denylist the clearly per-user authed API routes (graph/custom-groups, graph/me, graph/my-representatives, notifications, follows, api/profile, constituent-status, officials/claim-status, representatives) from the cdnHot catch-all and pin them CDN no-store. FOLLOW-UP: audit the ambiguous public-or-private authed GET routes (comments, positions, statements, initiatives, investigations, questions) individually. References [[FIX-784]] [[FIX-782]]. <!--id:FIX-786-->

Fix: add to the userScopedApi CDN no-store denylist. api/positions uses an EXACT source (not /:path*) and a not-followed-by-slash exclusion so its PUBLIC /api/positions/rollup aggregate stays cached. Verified via response headers. References [[FIX-786]]. <!--id:FIX-787-->
- [x] 🔴 S — **CDN cache hotfix: per-user pages cross-user cached + comments read-your-own-writes broken** — Prod, authed (2026-07-11 captures): the cdnHot(300,600) catch-all in next.config.mjs headers() stamps CDN-Cache-Control on every route not in the [[FIX-786]]/[[FIX-787]] denylist — which only ever listed API routes. - [x] 🔴 M — **Harden the rebuild against GHA cancel/timeout — orphaned backends + stranded autovacuum** — Surfaced 2026-06-15 running mode=full ad-hoc: when GHA cancels a run (manual OR the 4h timeout-minutes cap — same path), it kills the node client but Postgres keeps executing the in-flight query as an ORPHANED backend that hammers prod until the session statement_timeout (observed run-1 finalize() orphaned 1h10m + run-2 prepare() DELETE orphaned 16m, together I/O-saturating Pro Small → request-path 503s / 57014 on the live site). Two compounding bugs: (1) GHA's SIGKILL skips the script's `finally`, so FIX-590's `autovacuum_enabled=false` is left stranded → the table never gets autovacuumed. (2) the donations prepare()→windows split is NON-atomic: if a run is cancelled after prepare()'s DELETE-all commits but before the windows finish, donation edges are left empty/partial (the old monolith DELETE+INSERT was one transaction → a cancel rolled back to the prior good data). Fix landed (script-only, rebuild-entity-connections.ts): tag the connection `application_name='entity_connections_rebuild'`; a SIGTERM/SIGINT handler opens a fresh connection, `pg_cancel_backend(myPid)` + re-enables autovacuum (GHA sends SIGTERM before SIGKILL, so this catches the timeout case); and a STARTUP RECONCILE that, before doing anything, cancels+terminates any orphaned backend carrying our application_name (workflow concurrency is cancel-in-progress:false so it's always a prior orphan, never a peer) and unconditionally re-enables autovacuum — self-healing after any dirty exit. Incident recovery (2026-06-15): cancelled both orphans via pg_cancel_backend (run-2 prepare DELETE rolled back → 4.48M donation edges preserved, no data loss), manually re-enabled autovacuum, refreshed group_donor_rollup. RESIDUAL (low-risk now, follow-up): the non-atomic empty/partial-donations-on-cancel (bug 2) is only fully closed by making each window an atomic DELETE+INSERT for its from_id range (needs a `(connection_type, from_id)` index on entity_connections for an efficient ranged DELETE) instead of the upfront prepare() DELETE-all; exposure is small now that donations finish in ~1h vs the 4h budget. OPERATIONAL: the full rebuild saturates Pro Small I/O for its whole duration — run ONLY at low traffic (the 08:00 UTC=midnight PT schedule exists for this); do not trigger ad-hoc during active hours. Cross-ref [[FIX-590]] [[FIX-588]] [[FIX-589]] (compute is the durable relief). <!--id:FIX-591-->

Fix = the materialization pattern (packages/db/CLAUDE.md): a small content_bearing_official_ids table (or MV) refreshed on the nightly tail (after entity_connections + the MV refreshes, like refresh_jurisdiction_page_cache / the donor rollup), then rewrite get_sitemap_official_ids' body to read it (O(1), same signature) and re-add the sitemap call. Content officials are currently still discoverable via internal links (jurisdiction rosters + institution pages, both in the sitemap) and empty officials are deindexed by FIX-683 item-3 noindex, so this is sitemap-completeness, not a correctness gap. - [x] 🟠 M — **Port entity_connections rebuild into a pg_cron SQL procedure** — Move rebuild_entity_connections out of the timeout-prone GHA runner and into the database via pg_cron. New procedure public.run_entity_connections_rebuild(p_mode text) reuses the existing per-chunk SQL functions unchanged (votes/donations windowed trio/cosponsors/etc.), guarded by a SESSION-scoped advisory lock, with data_sync_log observability (running→complete/failed/skipped) keyed to pipeline entity_connections_rebuild and the donations window-loop ported faithfully from packages/data/src/scripts/rebuild-entity-connections.ts. Governed by the chunk functions' statement_timeout instead of a GHA wall-clock budget so no external runner can SIGTERM it mid-rebuild. PR1 of the cron-resilience program. Pairs with [[FIX-589]]. <!--id:FIX-687-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **FEC financial_entity totals rebuilds are full-table UPDATEs that saturate the Pro Small — make them targeted/chunked** — The FEC bulk pipeline finishes with three full-table UPDATEs on financial_entities (rebuild_financial_entity_donation_totals / _ie_totals / _received_totals). Each builds a temp table by scanning the ENTIRE financial_relationships donation set (~2M+ rows) then rewrites the whole ~540k-row financial_entities table. On the cache-starved Pro Small (256MB shared_buffers) donation_totals alone ran ~80 min holding a RowExclusiveLock + saturating disk I/O, which timed out unrelated request-path RPCs (e.g. get_quality_counts) → live-site degradation. Surfaced live during the [[FIX-701]] D/B re-capture; had to abort the rebuilds mid-run and instead hand-run a TARGETED, index-scoped UPDATE (correlated subquery over financial_relationships_donor_rollup_idx) for only the ~1,827 affected recipient entities — sub-second, zero I/O storm. Durable fix options (FIX-704-style): (a) scope each rebuild to only the entity ids touched by the current run (pass the affected from_id/to_id set), or (b) move to pg_cron chunked/incremental like entity_connections. Also covers the donor-side gap: a SCOPED run skips donor total_donated_cents overwrite, so after [[FIX-701]] ~232k individual donors' totals understate their D/B slice until a (targeted) donation-totals rebuild runs. Related: [[FIX-717]] / [[FIX-718]] (large MVs → incremental). <!--id:FIX-726-->
- [x] 🟡 M — **Restore CDN caching on statements/questions by splitting per-viewer my_vote out of the cached payload** — Follow-up to [[FIX-787]]. api/statements and api/questions are hot entity-page reads but were pinned CDN no-store (FIX-787) to stop the my_vote cross-user cache leak. On the cache-starved prod Small this pushes those reads to the DB on every hit, including the majority anon traffic that has no my_vote. Restore edge caching by splitting the response: cache the public list (no per-viewer fields) at the CDN, and fetch the viewer's my_vote via a separate small uncached/no-store request (or a client-side merge). Then the hot public payload is cacheable again while per-viewer state stays private. References [[FIX-787]] [[FIX-786]]. <!--id:FIX-788-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **Elections pipeline: change-detection + set-based writes (drop ~27k per-row UPDATEs/run)** — runElectionsPipeline rewrote all five election-status columns for every active official (~27k) every run via per-row PostgREST UPDATE, ungated — a nightly enrichment-light write sink that collapsed under IO pressure (2026-07-12 incident, light SIGTERM'd at elections). Fix: fetch current values, only write rows whose values actually changed (usually ~0), and write the changed set via a chunked direct-pg UPDATE…FROM (withDirectClient) rather than N single-row round-trips. Value-computation logic (calendar.ts) unchanged. <!--id:FIX-819-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **enrichment_queue: VACUUM + task_type-leading claim index** — Nightly enrichment-tail staging (enqueue_enrichment) hung ~69 min on 2026-07-12; prod pg_stat_statements showed enrichment_queue disk-bound (~12.7% cache hit, ~5-8s ops at the 8s timeout) on a ~150k-row, churn-bloated table. Fix: (A) VACUUM (ANALYZE) to reclaim claim/submit dead-tuple bloat (out-of-band, can't be in a migration), optional per-table autovacuum scale-factor tightening; (B) add (task_type, priority DESC, entity_updated_at DESC) WHERE status='pending' so claim_enrichment_batch seeks one task's pending rows instead of scanning+filtering the whole pending partition (drain throughput on the 140k backlog). <!--id:FIX-820-->
- [x] 🟢 S — **Align enrichment_queue pending indexes to entity_updated_at DESC NULLS LAST** — claim_enrichment_batch's ORDER BY … entity_updated_at DESC NULLS LAST keeps a residual (harmless, NOT NULL) Incremental Sort because idx_enrichment_queue_pending_by_task (FIX-820) + idx_enrichment_queue_pending declare entity_updated_at DESC = NULLS FIRST; Postgres won't fold the null-orderings even on a NOT NULL col. Realign both index DDLs to DESC NULLS LAST to drop the sort node. <!--id:FIX-822-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **ai-tagger: server-side anti-join for untagged entities (drop the load-all + in-mem filter)** — runProposalAiTagger/runOfficialAiTagger/backlog-seeder onlyNew path loads the whole proposals/officials table + the full AI-topic-tagged id set into Node then filters in memory — two full scans on the cold Micro to feed a maxCostCents-capped run. Replace with a server-side NOT EXISTS anti-join (ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT n) via withDirectClient, using idx_entity_tags_entity; behavior-preserving (topic tags are entity-derived, onlyNew=untagged). Leaves onlyNew=false full-retag unchanged. <!--id:FIX-823-->

### OFFICIALS

- [x] 🟡 S — **Congress pipeline doesn't flip is_active when a member leaves office** — Surfaced during [[FIX-403]] prod verification 2026-05-27. The Congress.gov officials pipeline (packages/data/src/pipelines/congress/officials.ts) only ingests CURRENT members (the members API returns currentMember=true rows). When a sitting member leaves office (loses re-election, resigns, dies) and Congress.gov flips them to currentMember=false, our pipeline simply stops seeing them in the feed — it does NOT flip the existing officials row's is_active to false. Result: former members retain is_active=true indefinitely until manually corrected. Confirmed via prod query during FIX-403 smoke: zero is_active=false officials carry primary_source='congress_gov' (all inactive officials trace to other sources like FEC). Action: (a) decide the detection mechanism — either (i) fetch the currentMember=false delta from the Congress.gov members API and flip is_active on matched bioguide_ids, or (ii) a reconciliation pass that compares the set of bioguide_ids in the current feed against existing is_active=true congress officials and flips any that fell out of the feed (with a guard against false-positives from a partial/failed API fetch — only flip when the full member list fetched successfully). Option (ii) is more robust to API shape changes. (b) Consider whether former members should also get tier/term-end treatment — cross-ref [[FIX-249]] ('former' tier on officials, term-end tracking) which is the broader home for this. This FIX is the congress-specific detection half; FIX-249 is the schema/display half. Pre-existing behavior, not introduced by FIX-403 — just confirmed during its verification. Cross-ref [[FIX-249]] (former-tier schema), [[FIX-248]] (candidate→elected promotion, the inverse transition this pipeline already handles). <!--id:FIX-409-->
- [x] 🟠 S — **/officials/[id] 404s on some municipal officials despite valid rows (likely .single() PGRST116, not a filter)** — Surfaced during [[FIX-399]] prod verification 2026-05-27: /officials/[id] returns Next.js not-found for some municipal (Legistar) officials whose rows DO exist and have primary_source populated — e.g. Jennifer Samuels (Legistar Seattle, id 9504546c…). NOTE: the FIX-399 report hypothesized "the loader filters municipal officials out" — that is INCORRECT. getCachedOfficial (apps/civitics/app/officials/_lib/get-official.ts) has NO municipal/jurisdiction filter; the query is .from('officials').select(...embeds...).eq('id', id).single(). The likely real cause is .single() throwing PGRST116 because >1 officials row matches the id-adjacent identity — Legistar officials are prone to cross-body / casing duplicates (cf. [[FIX-375]] casing-dupe residue), and .single() errors (returns {data:null, error:PGRST116}) on >1 rows, NOT on the id .eq (which is unique). Investigate first: (a) is there genuinely a duplicate officials row for the affected people? (a single id .eq can only match one row by PK — so if .single() fails it implies the EMBED join (jurisdictions!jurisdiction_id or governing_bodies!governing_body_id) is fanning out to multiple rows, OR the row genuinely 404s for a different reason like an RLS/embed mismatch). (b) Reproduce with the exact failing id and capture the PostgREST error (the loader currently swallows it — only checks `if (!data) return null`, ignoring `error`). Surface the error first. (c) Fix per root cause: if embed fan-out, constrain the embed or switch to a two-step fetch; if genuine 404 for another reason, address that. Also: regardless of root cause, the loader should LOG the PostgREST error instead of silently returning not-found (mirrors the [[FIX-394]] "throw on .error so silent-zero surfaces" lesson). User-facing impact: valid municipal official pages 404, AND the /officials route currently surfaces zero local-category SourceBadges as a result. Cross-ref [[FIX-399]] (surfacing case), [[FIX-375]] (casing-dupe residue hypothesis), [[FIX-394]] (swallowed-PostgREST-error pattern). <!--id:FIX-412-->
- [x] 🟠 M — **governing_body membership pollution — audit + tier-scope institution rosters** — The `/institutions/[id]` GoverningBodyView computes its roster, party balance, and 'Active members' stat from `officials.governing_body_id` + `is_active` only, so legislature pages over-count members massively. Local: US Senate gb shows ~1,430 'active' (100 `tier='elected'` + 1,330 `tier='candidate'`); US House ~6,042 (436 elected + 5,606 candidates); Office of the President ~2,341 (2 elected + 2,339 candidates). FEC candidate ingest (cn{yy}.zip, FIX-246) parks every candidate on the body it runs for with `tier='candidate'`, so `tier` cleanly labels the pollution. **Hypothesis (verify on prod):** ingest is correct; bug is consumer-side — institution queries never filter `tier`. Fix scopes display surfaces to current members = `is_active = true AND tier = 'elected'` via a shared predicate (≥2 consumers: this + future [[FIX-468]] graph group-expansion). - [x] 🟠 S — **OpenStates bill ingestion passes `""` instead of `null` for empty dates → silent insert failures** — During the [[FIX-445]] backfill, the openstates pipeline logged `proposal insert 0-18: invalid input syntax for type date: ""` (AZ, repeatable) and the prod run reported 37 failed bill inserts. Some bills come back from the OpenStates `/bills` API with an empty-string `first_action_date`/`latest_action_date`; `openstates/index.ts` forwards `bill.first_action_date ?? null` / `bill.latest_action_date ?? null`, but `??` only catches `null`/`undefined` — an empty string `""` passes through and Postgres rejects it as an invalid `date`, failing the whole chunked insert (so good rows in the chunk are lost too). Fix: coerce empty-string dates to `null` before building `StateBillInput` (e.g. `bill.first_action_date?.trim() || null`). Same guard likely warranted anywhere else raw API date strings are forwarded. <!--id:FIX-449-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **Single opacity-resolver pipeline for hover/highlight/type-toggle + edge hover dollar labels** — G3. Four channels fight over dimming in visualizations/ForceGraph.tsx: hover sets attr('opacity'), the connection-style effect sets attr('stroke-opacity') + style('display'), SharedConnectionsBar highlight sets style('opacity') (inline style silently wins over attrs). Hover handlers are bound inside the [nodes,edges]-dep effect and close over a STALE edgeOpacityFn/connections — toggling a connection type doesn't rebuild them, so mouseleave restores last-load opacities. Rework: (a) one resolveNodeOpacity/resolveEdgeOpacity pair, ctx = {connection settings, hover target, shared-connections highlight, disabled types}; (b) applied through ONE channel — inline style('opacity') everywhere, style('display') for fully-disabled types computed in the same pass; (c) handlers read settings through a ref so no stale closures; (d) SharedConnectionsBar highlight + clear go through the same resolver. Spec: hover dims non-neighbors to 0.12; leaving hover restores CURRENT settings; toggle a type off/on then hover behaves identically to fresh load; pinned shared highlight survives hover and clears fully. Same commit: edge hover labels gain amounts — 'Type — $47.2M · 1,234 txs' via amountUsd + [[FIX-802]] txCount (tx segment omitted when txCount absent); vote edges keep type + date when occurredAt present. <!--id:FIX-807-->

Two causes: (1) default d3 cooling (alphaDecay 0.0228, alphaMin 0.001) takes ~5s+ per reheat; (2) the type-cluster effect restarts the sim at alpha 0.3 on every focusEntities identity change — GraphPage passes a fresh .filter() array every render, so unrelated re-renders reheat the layout. Fix: faster cooling (alphaDecay/alphaMin/velocityDecay) so layout settles within a few seconds of load or drag and still reheats on drag/expand; memoize focusEntities in GraphPage; guard the disabled type-cluster branch so it only restarts when tearing down an actually-mounted force. No other physics behavior change; Physics sliders keep working. <!--id:FIX-815-->

### INFRASTRUCTURE & PERFORMANCE

- [x] 🟢 S — **Tighten enrichment_queue.entity_type CHECK + update stale schema comment** — Surfaced during [[FIX-381]] investigation gate. The [supabase/migrations/20260420030000_enrichment_queue.sql:11](../supabase/migrations/20260420030000_enrichment_queue.sql#L11) comment says `entity_type TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'proposal' | 'official'` but the queue legitimately holds four entity_type values in prod: `proposal` (137,479), `official` (8,362), `financial_entity` (2,580), `agency` (25). Writers exist for all four: `seed-backlog.ts` seeds FE industry-tag rows at line 487; the agency monthly enrichment pass adds agency rows; drain-apply.ts handles `tagCategory = queueRow.entity_type === 'financial_entity' ? 'industry' : 'topic'` at line 152. The data shape is correct; the comment is stale and there's no CHECK constraint to lock the discriminator going forward. Action: (1) add CHECK constraint `entity_type IN ('proposal','official','financial_entity','agency')`, (2) refresh the schema comment to enumerate all four. Also reconsider whether `entity_id` should migrate from TEXT to UUID — all current writers pass UUID-shaped strings, but TEXT widens the surface in a way that no consumer needs. Defer the TEXT→UUID change to a separate FIX if scope grows. Cross-ref [[FIX-381]] (extended FK-rewrite template surface, parent), audit doc `docs/audits/2026-05-25-fe-fk-surface-audit-prod.md`. <!--id:FIX-391-->
- [x] 🟢 S — **Drift check for source_priority duplication (SQL function vs TS const)** — [[FIX-398]] deploy report (2026-05-26) flagged a maintenance hazard: source_priority is duplicated between the SQL function (supabase/migrations/<FIX-397-ts>_primary_source_materialization.sql) and a hand-inlined TS const in apps/civitics/app/api/attribution/[type]/[id]/route.ts. Required because PostgREST can't apply SQL functions inside .select() so the API route needs the priority logic client-side to sort/annotate xsr rows. If the priority list churns (new source added; existing source reranked) both sides must stay in sync or the API's is_primary flag will diverge from the materialized primary_source column. Today's mitigation: hand-sync + cross-reference comment. Options for a durable fix: (a) move source_priority to a shared TS module (packages/db/src/source-priority.ts) and expose it to SQL via a tiny RPC that the SQL trigger can CALL; awkward because plpgsql calling out for a constant is wasteful per-row. (b) hand-publish the priority list from a single shared TS file generated alongside db:types via a small codegen step; both SQL function and TS const are written from the same source. (c) extend pnpm db:types to emit a constant alongside the database types based on a marker in the migration. (d) accept the duplication, add a CI check that diffs the two and fails if they drift. Recommend (d) as cheapest — a small jest/vitest test that parses the SQL function's CASE branches and asserts they match the TS const. CI catches drift immediately; no codegen complexity. Cross-ref [[FIX-397]] (where the SQL function lives), [[FIX-398]] (where the TS const lives). <!--id:FIX-407-->

- [x] 🟠 M — **fixes:sync can record off-trunk commits as shipped (git log --all scans unmerged branches)** — Root cause of the 2026-05-31 silent-zero-sweep-tail incident: `scanCommits()` in `scripts/fixes-sync.mjs` uses `git log --all`, which scans **every ref including unmerged PR branches**.
